[[16:5|though hand should be joined to hand, he is not innocent|Etiamsi manus ad manum fuerit, non erit innocens]]. This was written and explained above[[Prov 11:21||]].

paras.t: Initium viæ bonæ, id est exordium bonæ conversationis, est facere justitiam, prout justitia est virtus communis, id est a peccatis recedere, et eadem confiteri. Nam, ut asserit Augustinus, Initium bonorum, confessio est malorum. Accepta est autem apud Deum ipsa justitia magis, quam immolare hostias, id est sacrificia legis, quæ (ut dictum est) non erant accepta in se, sed solum ex fide, caritate et devotione offerentium, et in quantum Christi passionem, immolationem atque mysteria figurabant. Unde et ipsa exterior immolatio non erat in se Deo accepta, sed ex interiore virtute. Attamen iste versus in Hebræo non habetur.
paras.en: [[16:5|The beginning of a good way|Initium viæ bonæ]], that is, the start of a good life, [[16:5|is to do justice|est facere justitiam]], taking justice as the general virtue [that is, justice as the sum of all righteousness, not the particular virtue that gives each his due]: that is, to withdraw from sins and to confess them. For, as Augustine says, the beginning of good works is the confession of evil ones. [[16:5|and this is more acceptable with God, than to offer sacrifices|Accepta est autem apud Deum ipsa justitia magis, quam immolare hostias]] [Denis's text reads "and justice itself is more acceptable"], that is, the sacrifices of the Law, which (as has been said[[Prov 15:8||]]) were not acceptable in themselves, but only by reason of the faith, charity and devotion of those who offered them, and in so far as they prefigured the passion, the sacrifice and the mysteries of Christ. Hence the outward sacrifice itself was not acceptable to God in itself, but by reason of the inward virtue. However, this verse is not found in the Hebrew.

paras.t: Misericordia et veritate redimitur iniquitas; in timore autem Domini declinatur a malo. Hoc est quod præcedenti fertur capitulo. Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata, per timorem autem Domini declinat omnis a malo : quod præcedenti articulo satis reor expositum.
paras.en: [[16:6|By mercy and truth iniquity is redeemed; and by the fear of the Lord men depart from evil|Misericordia et veritate redimitur iniquitas; in timore autem Domini declinatur a malo]]. This is what is said in the preceding chapter: [[Prov 15:27|By mercy and faith sins are purged away: and by the fear of the Lord every one declineth from evil|Per misericordiam et fidem purgantur peccata, per timorem autem Domini declinat omnis a malo]]: which I think was explained sufficiently in the preceding article.

paras.t: Quum placuerint Domino viæ, id est interiores exterioresque actus, hominis, inimicos quoque ejus convertet ad pacem, id est, corda adversariorum talis hominis Deus inclinabit ad habendum pacem cum hujusmodi homine : quod frequenter sic fit, quamvis non semper; imo multi invidi, ambitiosi, perversi, tanto plus contra justos insaniunt, quanto viderint eos exsistere magis exemplares, bonos, famosos. Tyranni quoque usque ad mortem persecuti sunt martyres sanctos. Aliqui vero mali, non sunt ita perversi, sed indolis bonæ, et cito inclinantur ad bonum : quemadmodum Nabuchodonosor, Darius et Cyrus, auditis seu visis mirabilibus Dei in Daniele, magnificaverunt Deum ipsius. Hinc ait Glossa : Tanta est sanctitas divinæ Religionis, ut eam plerumque etiam illi qui foris sunt, venerentur, et cum his habeant pacem, quos Deo perfecte servire considerant, quamvis Religione discordent, ut in Daniele et pueris tribus. Sæpe etiam persecutores non solum ad pacem cum prædicatoribus, sed et ad veritatem fidei sunt conversi.
paras.en: [[16:7|When the ways of man shall please the Lord|Quum placuerint Domino viæ]] (the *ways*, that is, his inward and outward acts), [[16:7|he will convert even his enemies to peace|inimicos quoque ejus convertet ad pacem]], that is, God will incline the hearts of such a man's adversaries to be at peace with him. This often happens so, though not always; indeed many who are envious, ambitious and perverse rage the more against the just, the more they see them to be exemplary, good and renowned. Tyrants too persecuted the holy martyrs even to death. But some evil men are not so perverse, but are of a good disposition and are quickly inclined to good: as Nabuchodonosor, Darius and Cyrus, when they had heard or seen the wonders of God in Daniel, magnified his God. Hence the Gloss says: So great is the holiness of the divine religion that for the most part even those who are outside it revere it, and are at peace with those whom they see serving God perfectly, though they differ from them in religion, as with Daniel and the three children. Often too persecutors have been converted not only to peace with the preachers, but to the truth of the faith.

paras.t: Melius est parum cum justitia, quam multi fructus cum iniquitate. Hoc patet ex elucidatione ejus quod scriptum est præcedenti capitulo, Melius est parum cum timore Domini, quam thesauri magni, etc.
paras.en: [[16:8|Better is a little with justice, than great revenues with iniquity|Melius est parum cum justitia, quam multi fructus cum iniquitate]]. This is plain from the explanation of what is written in the preceding chapter: [[Prov 15:16|Better is a little with the fear of the Lord, than great treasures|Melius est parum cum timore Domini, quam thesauri magni]], etc.

paras.t: Cor, id est ratio, hominis disponet viam suam, id est, intra se deliberabit ac proponet quid agere debeat, quid vitare; sed Domini est dirigere gressus ejus; id est, ad exsequendum idonee quod ratio disposuit in se, indiget homo directione et ope gratiæ Dei. Propter quod oravit Propheta : Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum. Et Jeremias ait : Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus : nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos. Apostolus quoque : Non volentis, inquit, neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei.
paras.en: [[16:9|The heart|Cor]], that is, the reason, [[16:9|of man disposeth his way|hominis disponet viam suam]], that is, will deliberate within itself and resolve what it ought to do and what to avoid; [[16:9|but the Lord must direct his steps|sed Domini est dirigere gressus ejus]]: that is, to carry out fittingly what the reason has disposed within itself, man needs the direction and help of God's grace. Wherefore the Prophet prayed: [[Ps 118:133|Direct my steps according to thy word|Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum]]. And Jeremias says: [[Jer 10:23|I know, O Lord, that the way of a man is not his: neither is it in a man to walk, and to direct his steps|Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus : nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos]]. The Apostle too: [[Rom 9:16|not of him that willeth|Non volentis]], he says, [[Rom 9:16|nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy|neque currentis, sed miserentis est Dei]].

paras.t: Divinatio in labiis regis. Divinatio accipi solet in malo, pro usurpata prænuntiatione contingentium futurorum. Unde dicuntur divini, quidam superstitiosi ac magi. Hic vero in bono accipitur, pro commemoratione futurorum secundum Scripturas, ut scilicet rex et quilibet judex penset, et aliis recolat ac proponat futurum Dei judicium, gaudia quoque justorum, et impiorum supplicia, quatenus nec ipse audeat judicare injuste, et alii timeant aliquid contra justitiam attentare. Quemadmodum Josaphat rex legitur suis dixisse judicibus : Videte quid faciatis : non enim hominum exercetis judicium, sed Domini; et quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit. Hinc subditur : In judicio non errabit os ejus, utpote regis sic facientis. Quidam per divinationem intelligunt lectionem divinam, quoniam jussum fuit ut rex Israelitici populi, statim ut sedisset in solio regni, describeret sibi Deuteronomium legis in volumine, et legeret illud omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, sicque secundum legem judicando non deviaret. Glossa per regem intelligit Christum : de quo fertur in Psalmo, Deus, judicium tuum regi da; qui solus videtur in judicio nunquam errare; in cujus ore est divinatio, quia non solum dirigit verba et facta suorum fidelium, sed et divinis gentilium interdum ostendit quid interrogantibus debeant respondere, ut primo Regum de divinis Philistæorum habetur, qui aptissime responderunt qualiter arca Dei esset remittenda.
paras.en: [[16:10|Divination is in the lips of the king|Divinatio in labiis regis]]. *Divinatio* is usually taken in a bad sense, for a usurped foretelling of contingent future events: hence certain superstitious men and magicians are called *divini* [that is, diviners]. But here it is taken in a good sense, for calling to mind the things to come according to the Scriptures: namely, that the king, and any judge, should ponder and recall and set before others the future judgment of God, the joys too of the just and the torments of the wicked, so that neither he himself should dare to judge unjustly, nor others to attempt anything against justice. So we read that King Josaphat said to his judges: [[2 Par 19:6|Take heed what you do: for you exercise not the judgment of man, but of the Lord: and whatsoever you judge, it shall redound to you|Videte quid faciatis : non enim hominum exercetis judicium, sed Domini; et quodcumque judicaveritis, in vos redundabit]]. Hence it is added: [[16:10|his mouth shall not err in judgment|In judicio non errabit os ejus]], namely, of the king who does so. Some understand by *divinatio* the reading of divine things, since it was commanded that the king of the people of Israel, as soon as he had sat on the throne of the kingdom, should copy out for himself the Deuteronomy of the law in a volume and read it all the days of his life, and so, judging according to the law, should not go astray. The Gloss understands by the king Christ, of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:2|Give to the king thy judgment, O God|Deus, judicium tuum regi da]]; who alone seems never to err in judgment; in whose mouth is *divinatio*, because he not only directs the words and deeds of his faithful, but sometimes even shows the diviners of the gentiles what they ought to answer those who question them, as we have in the first book of Kings of the diviners of the Philistines, who answered most fittingly how the ark of God should be sent back[[1 Kings 6:3||]] [the margin gives 1 Kings vi, 3–9].

paras.t: Pondus et statera judicia Domini sunt, id est, Deo sunt placita pondera justa, et justæ stateræ, ac mensurationes seu ponderationes quæ fiunt cum eis. Vel, Pondus et statera judicia Dei, quoniam Deus in sua sapientia ordinavit universa facere in numero, pondere et mensura. Et opera ejus, omnes lapides sæculi, id est omnes electi, qui tanquam lapides vivi, ponuntur nunc in ædificio militantis Ecclesiæ per fidem et caritatem, deinde in structura Ecclesiæ triumphantis per beatificam fruitionem. Isti sunt opera Dei, quia per supernaturalia dona pietatis ac gratiæ ejus, perducuntur ad ista, non viribus suis. De quibus in prima sua ait epistola gloriosissimus apostolici agminis princeps : Et vos tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini. Verumtamen quidam ait in Hebræo haberi, Lapides sacculi, et ex scriptorum vitio propter similitudinem dictionum, pro Sacculi, positum Sæculi. Antiquitus namque ponderationes fiebant per lapides in sacculo collocatos, sicut nunc fiunt per metalla : sicque lapides tales erant opera Deo placentia, in quantum per eos fiebat justitia seu ponderatio justa.
paras.en: [[16:11|Weight and balance are judgments of the Lord|Pondus et statera judicia Domini sunt]], that is, just weights and just balances are pleasing to God, and the measurings or weighings that are made with them. Or: Weight and balance are the judgments of God, because God in his wisdom ordained to make all things in number, weight and measure[[Wis 11:21||]]. [[16:11|and his work all the weights of the bag|Et opera ejus, omnes lapides sæculi]] [Denis's text reads *lapides sæculi*, "the stones of the world", where the Douay-Rheims, following *sacculi*, has "the weights of the bag"; see the end of this paragraph], that is, all the elect, who as living stones are now set in the building of the Church militant by faith and charity, and afterwards in the structure of the Church triumphant by the beatific enjoyment [of God]. These are the works of God, because they are brought to these things by the supernatural gifts of his love and grace, not by their own strength. Of them the most glorious prince of the apostolic band says in his first epistle: [[1 Pet 2:5|Be you also as living stones built up|Et vos tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini]]. But someone says that the Hebrew has *stones of the bag* (*sacculi*), and that through a fault of the copyists, because of the likeness of the words, *sæculi* ("of the world") was put for *sacculi* ("of the bag"). For in old times weighings were done with stones kept in a bag, as they are now done with metal weights; and so such stones were works pleasing to God in so far as justice, or just weighing, was done by them.

paras.t: Abominabiles regi qui agunt impie. Constat quod summo Regi (de quo ait Apostolus, Regi autem sæculorum immortali, invisibili) abominabiles sunt iniqui, ut tales; similiter unicuique regi justo, qui dignus est rex vocari : rex quippe iniquus voluntatem, non rationem, sequens, verius est tyrannus quam rex. Spiritualiter vero reges censentur, omnes qui sapientia et virtute regunt se ipsos, aut etiam sibi commissos : qui utique impios detestantur. Quoniam justitia firmatur solium : id est, thronus regis, et ejus auctoritas seu præsidentia, per justitiam roboratur, authenticatur, et perseverat in posteris. Sedes enim ducum superborum destruxit Deus, ut in Ecclesiastico fertur; atque, ut asserit Augustinus, Si tollatur justitia, quid sunt regna nisi latrocinia magna?
paras.en: [[16:12|They that act wickedly are abominable to the king|Abominabiles regi qui agunt impie]]. It is certain that the wicked, as such, are abominable to the supreme King (of whom the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 1:17|Now to the king of ages, immortal, invisible|Regi autem sæculorum immortali, invisibili]]); and likewise to every just king who is worthy to be called a king: for a wicked king, following his will and not reason, is more truly a tyrant than a king. Spiritually, however, all are reckoned kings who rule themselves, or also those committed to them, by wisdom and virtue; and these certainly detest the wicked. [[16:12|for the throne is established by justice|Quoniam justitia firmatur solium]]: that is, the throne of the king, and his authority or rule, is strengthened, made lawful, and lasts on in his descendants through justice. For [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes|Sedes enim ducum superborum destruxit Deus]], as is said in Ecclesiasticus; and, as Augustine says: If justice be taken away, what are kingdoms but great robberies?

paras.t: Voluntas regum, de quibus nunc dictum est, sunt labia justa : id est, qui vera et justa loquuntur, testantur et agunt, justis regibus placent. Qui recta, id est vera, justa, salubria, loquitur ex affectu, dirigetur a Spiritu Sancto in viam salutis æternæ, et per verba ac opera talia ad beatitudinem recto itinere perducetur. Contra quod ait Propheta : Vir linguosus non dirigetur in terra. Impiorum autem persona non dirigitur ita, sed eorum iniquitas dirigi dicitur, sicut in Daniele de sceleratissimo Antiocho est prædictum : Dolus in manu ejus dirigetur.
paras.en: [[16:13|the delight of kings|Voluntas regum]], of the kings just spoken of, are [[16:13|Just lips|sunt labia justa]]: that is, those who speak, bear witness to and do what is true and just are pleasing to just kings. [[16:13|he that speaketh right things|Qui recta]] (that is, things true, just and wholesome) from the heart *shall be directed* [Denis reads *dirigetur*, "shall be directed", where the Vulgate has *diligetur*, "shall be loved"] by the Holy Ghost into the way of eternal salvation, and by such words and works shall be led by a straight road to beatitude. Against which the Prophet says: [[Ps 139:12|A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth|Vir linguosus non dirigetur in terra]] [the Latin *non dirigetur* is literally "shall not be directed"]. But the person of the wicked is not directed so; rather their wickedness is said to be directed, as was foretold in Daniel of the most wicked Antiochus: [[Dan 8:25|craft shall be successful in his hand|Dolus in manu ejus dirigetur]] [literally, "craft shall be directed in his hand"].

paras.t: Indignatio regis est nuntius mortis, id est insinuatio interfectionis mox futuræ ei, contra quem rex indignatur : quod intelligendum est de indignatione prædominante, vel etiam justa, ex alicujus gravi excessu concepta a rege. Reges etenim taliter indignantes, proni sunt dictare sententiam mortis in eum cui indignantur. Et vir sapiens placabit eum, id est regem iratum, pie excusando reum pro posse, aut intercedendo pro eo.
paras.en: [[16:14|The wrath of a king|Indignatio regis]] is [[16:14|as messengers of death|nuntius mortis]] [Denis reads *nuntius*, "a messenger"], that is, a sign of the slaying soon to come upon him against whom the king is angered: which is to be understood of an anger that prevails, or that is even just, conceived by the king for some grave offence. For kings angered in this way are quick to pronounce sentence of death on him with whom they are angry. [[16:14|and the wise man will pacify it|Et vir sapiens placabit eum]] [Denis reads *eum*, "him"], that is, the angry king, by kindly excusing the guilty man as far as he can, or by interceding for him.

paras.t: In hilaritate vultus regis, vita : id est, subditorum seu reorum conservatio in vita, speratur ex hoc quod rex hilarem vultum eis ostendit; et clementia ejus quasi imber serotinus : id est, multum suavis et fructuosa est subditis clementia regis seu principis sui, sicut pluvia vespertina terræ nascentibus.
paras.en: [[16:15|In the cheerfulness of the king's countenance is life|In hilaritate vultus regis, vita]]: that is, the preservation in life of his subjects, or of the accused, is hoped for from the king's showing them a cheerful countenance; [[16:15|and his clemency is like the latter rain|et clementia ejus quasi imber serotinus]]: that is, the clemency of their king or prince is very sweet and fruitful to his subjects, as the evening rain to the things that spring from the earth [the Latin *serotinus* means both "late" and "of the evening"].

paras.t: Verum ista de Christo præsertim accipi queunt, quia in adspectu sui jucundissimi vultus, vita gloriæ æternalis consistit. Propter quod orat Psalmista : Ostende faciem tuam, et salvi erimus. Moyses quoque : Si inveni, inquit, gratiam in conspectu tuo, ostende mihi faciem tuam. De quo princeps Apostolorum fatetur, quia in ipsum desiderant angeli prospicere. Cujus clementia est quasi imber serotinus. Circa quod ait Glossa : Serotinus imber usque nunc in Judæa maturis solet fructibus provenire, ubi Dominus matutinam pluviam et serotinam promittit, per Prophetam dicendo : Dabo vobis pluviam matutinam et serotinam terræ. Spiritualiter autem, pluvia matutina est quando prima gratiæ seu doctrinæ semina credendi in Christum suscipimus; serotina vero, quando jam maturis seu perfectis virtutum fructibus, in horreo Dei recondimur. Et bene clementia Christi regis nostri, imbri serotino comparatur : quia quod fructum vitæ bene agentes percipimus, non facit libertas nostri arbitrii, sed irrigatio doni superni.
paras.en: But these words can be taken above all of Christ, because the life of eternal glory consists in the sight of his most joyful countenance. Wherefore the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 79:4|shew us thy face, and we shall be saved|Ostende faciem tuam, et salvi erimus]][[Ps 79:8||]][[Ps 79:20||]]. Moses too: [[Ex 33:13|If therefore I have found favour|Si inveni]], he says, [[Ex 33:13|in thy sight, shew me thy face|gratiam in conspectu tuo, ostende mihi faciem tuam]]. Of him the prince of the Apostles confesses that he is the one [[1 Pet 1:12|on whom the angels desire to look|in ipsum desiderant angeli prospicere]]. And [[16:15|his clemency is like the latter rain|clementia est quasi imber serotinus]]. On which the Gloss says: The latter rain is wont even now in Judæa to come upon the ripened crops, where the Lord promises the morning and the evening rain, saying by the Prophet: I will give you [[Joel 2:23|the early and the latter rain|pluviam matutinam et serotinam]] for the land [the margin gives "cf. Joel ii, 23"; the wording is closer to Deut 11:14]. Spiritually, the morning rain is when we receive the first seeds of grace or of the teaching that leads us to believe in Christ; the evening rain, when, with the fruits of the virtues now ripe or perfect, we are laid up in God's barn. And the clemency of Christ our king is well compared to the latter rain: because that we who do well receive the fruit of life is not the work of the freedom of our will, but of the watering of the gift from above.

paras.t: Posside sapientiam, quia auro melior est; et acquire prudentiam, quia pretiosior est argento. Istud præhabitum est, et satis expositum. Denique sapientia per violentiam non aufertur, antiquitate non corrumpitur; absconsione inordinata minuitur, communicatione caritativa multiplicatur : sapientia nihil ardentius diligitur, nil dulcius possidetur; atque, ut Tullius loquitur, rei publicæ commoda multa proveniunt, si moderatrix omnium rerum præsto sit sapientia. Hinc ad eos qui ipsam adepti sunt, laus, honor et dignitas confluunt. In sapientia excolenda, honestas vitæ est sita : et in ejus negligentia, turpitudo est maxima. Verum ad istam sapientiam non sufficit scire divina, sed exigitur conversatio virtuosa et impassionata. Propter quod dixit apostolus Jacobus : Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos? Ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ.
paras.en: [[16:16|Get wisdom, because it is better than gold: and purchase prudence, for it is more precious than silver|Posside sapientiam, quia auro melior est; et acquire prudentiam, quia pretiosior est argento]]. This was had before and sufficiently explained[[Prov 3:14||]][[Prov 8:10||]][[Prov 8:19||]]. Further, wisdom is not taken away by violence nor corrupted by age; it is lessened by being wrongly hidden and multiplied by being charitably shared: nothing is loved more ardently than wisdom, nothing possessed more sweetly; and, as Tully says, many benefits come to the commonwealth if wisdom, the governor of all things, is at hand. Hence praise, honour and dignity flow together to those who have gained it. In the cultivation of wisdom lies the honour of life, and in neglect of it the greatest shame. But for this wisdom it is not enough to know divine things: a virtuous life, free of the passions, is required. Wherefore the apostle James said: [[Jas 3:13|Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge, among you? Let him shew, by a good contestation, his work in the meekness of wisdom|Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos? Ostendat ex bona conversatione operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ]]

paras.t: Semita justorum, id est lex divina seu observantia præceptorum in quibus ambulant justi, declinat mala, id est, vitat peccata, et supplicia eis infligenda. Custos animæ suæ servat viam suam.
paras.en: [[16:17|The path of the just|Semita justorum]], that is, the divine law, or the keeping of the commandments, in which the just walk, [[16:17|departeth from evils|declinat mala]], that is, avoids sins and the punishments to be inflicted for them. [[16:17|he that keepeth his soul keepeth his way|Custos animæ suæ servat viam suam]].

paras.t: Contritionem præcedit superbia : quia superbiendo merentur homines destrui ac damnari; et ante ruinam exultatur spiritus, id est, se ipsum extollit, seque extollendo dejici promeretur, quemadmodum in Isaia habetur : Dies Domini super omnem superbum et excelsum, et super omnem arrogantem; et humiliabitur. Ideo per Abdiam loquitur Dominus : Si exaltatus fueris ut aquila, et si inter sidera posueris nidum tuum, inde detraham te. Unde de Nabuchodonosor potentissimo rege scriptum est : Quando elevatum est cor ejus, et spiritus illius obfirmatus est ad superbiam, depositus est de solio regni sui, et a filiis hominum ejectus est.
paras.en: [[16:18|Pride goeth before destruction|Contritionem præcedit superbia]]: because by being proud men deserve to be destroyed and damned; [[16:18|and the spirit is lifted up before a fall|et ante ruinam exultatur spiritus]], that is, it exalts itself, and by exalting itself deserves to be cast down, as we have in Isaias: [[Is 2:12|the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud and highminded, and upon every one that is arrogant, and he shall be humbled|Dies Domini super omnem superbum et excelsum, et super omnem arrogantem; et humiliabitur]]. Therefore the Lord says by Abdias: [[Abd 1:4|Though thou be exalted as an eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars: thence will I bring thee down|Si exaltatus fueris ut aquila, et si inter sidera posueris nidum tuum, inde detraham te]]. Hence it is written of Nabuchodonosor, the most mighty king: [[Dan 5:20|when his heart was lifted up, and his spirit hardened unto pride, he was put down from the throne of his kingdom|Quando elevatum est cor ejus, et spiritus illius obfirmatus est ad superbiam, depositus est de solio regni sui]], [[Dan 5:21|And he was driven out from the sons of men|et a filiis hominum ejectus est]].

paras.t: Melius est humiliari cum mitibus, quam dividere spolia cum superbis. Nam primum horum est virtuosum, secundum damnabile. Hinc ait Apostolus : Fide Moyses grandis effectus, negavit se filium filiæ Pharaonis, magis eligens affligi cum populo Dei, quam temporalis peccati habere jucunditatem, majores divitias æstimans thesauro Ægyptiorum, improperium Christi. Et Psalmista : Elegi, inquit, abjectus esse in domo Dei mei, magis quam habitare in tabernaculis peccatorum.
paras.en: [[16:19|It is better to be humbled with the meek, than to divide spoils with the proud|Melius est humiliari cum mitibus, quam dividere spolia cum superbis]]. For the first of these is virtuous, the second damnable. Hence the Apostle says: [[Heb 11:24|By faith Moses, when he was grown up, denied himself to be the son of Pharao's daughter|Fide Moyses grandis effectus, negavit se filium filiæ Pharaonis]], [[Heb 11:25|Rather choosing to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the pleasure of sin for a time|magis eligens affligi cum populo Dei, quam temporalis peccati habere jucunditatem]], [[Heb 11:26|Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians|majores divitias æstimans thesauro Ægyptiorum, improperium Christi]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 83:11|I have chosen|Elegi]], he says, [[Ps 83:11|to be an abject in the house of my God, rather than to dwell in the tabernacles of sinners|abjectus esse in domo Dei mei, magis quam habitare in tabernaculis peccatorum]].

paras.t: Eruditus in verbo, id est, qui alios instruit sapienter, eruditeque loquitur, reperiet bona gloriæ pro mercede, et profectum gratiæ in hac vita; et qui sperat in Domino spe formata, quæ ex gratia meritisque procedit, beatus est jam per inchoationem ac meritum. Ideo loquitur Isaias : Deus judicii Dominus; beati omnes qui exspectant eum.
paras.en: [[16:20|The learned in word|Eruditus in verbo]], that is, he who instructs others wisely and speaks learnedly, [[16:20|shall find good things|reperiet bona]] of glory as his reward, and progress in grace in this life; [[16:20|and he that trusteth in the Lord|et qui sperat in Domino]] with formed hope [that is, hope quickened by charity], which proceeds from grace and merits, [[16:20|is blessed|beatus est]] even now, by beginning and by merit. Therefore Isaias says: [[Is 30:18|the Lord is the God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him|Deus judicii Dominus; beati omnes qui exspectant eum]].

paras.t: Qui sapiens corde est, appellabitur prudens, quamvis in solitudine degens, nullique præsidens, non instruat alios. Sapientia autem et prudentia sunt connexæ, et frequenter unum pro alio sumitur. Et qui dulcis eloquio, majora reperiet : id est, qui non solum sapiens in corde est, sed alios quoque facunde et efficaciter docet, fidem contra perfidos protegit, et viam justitiæ toto defendit conatu, majora reperiet, id est præmia ampliora, ceteris paribus, quam is qui sapiens mente est, nec aliis prædicat : nam doctoribus et prædicatoribus datur aureola. Verumtamen magnitudo præmii essentialis correspondet perfectioni caritatis, in qua qui perfectior est in via, major et gloriosior erit in patria. Denique, Qui dulcis est eloquio, majora reperiet : quia facundi in verbis et sententiosi, sunt communiter valde accepti hominibus, et reputantur, magnaque commoda consequuntur. Dulcis autem eloquio nuncupatur, qui habet non solum bonam expressivam, sed bonam etiam impressivam; nec solum promptus est ad verborum prolationem rhetoricam, sed et verba sapientialia profert. Sapientes etenim auditores majorem sentiunt delectationem in sensu, quam in sono sermonis.
paras.en: [[16:21|The wise in heart shall be called prudent|Qui sapiens corde est, appellabitur prudens]], even though, living in solitude and set over no one, he does not instruct others. For wisdom and prudence are bound together, and one is often taken for the other. [[16:21|and he that is sweet in words, shall attain to greater things|Et qui dulcis eloquio, majora reperiet]]: that is, he who is not only wise in heart, but also teaches others eloquently and effectively, protects the faith against unbelievers, and defends the way of justice with all his striving, shall find greater things, that is, ampler rewards, other things being equal, than he who is wise in mind and does not preach to others: for to doctors and preachers is given the aureole [that is, the special crown added in heaven to the essential reward of virgins, martyrs and doctors]. Yet the greatness of the essential reward [that is, of the vision and enjoyment of God itself] answers to the perfection of charity, in which he who is more perfect on the way will be greater and more glorious in the homeland. Again, [[16:21|he that is sweet in words, shall attain to greater things|Qui dulcis est eloquio, majora reperiet]]: because those who are eloquent in words and full of sayings are commonly well received by men and highly esteemed, and gain great advantages. And he is called sweet in speech who has not only a good power of expressing but also a good power of impressing; and who is not only ready in the rhetorical delivery of words, but also utters words of wisdom. For wise hearers feel more delight in the sense than in the sound of a discourse.

paras.t: Fons vitæ, eruditio possidentis : id est, doctrina et informatio ejus qui sapientiam possidet, disponit audientium corda ad vitam gratiæ, adeptionemque gloriæ, revocando eos a vitiis, et ad pœnitentiam seu profectum virtutum alliciendo. Doctrina stultorum, fatuitas. Hoc præhabitum est.
paras.en: [[16:22|Knowledge is a fountain of life to him that possesseth it|Fons vitæ, eruditio possidentis]] [the Latin reads "the learning of him that possesseth it is a fountain of life"]: that is, the teaching and instruction of him who possesses wisdom disposes the hearts of the hearers to the life of grace and the gaining of glory, by calling them back from vices and drawing them to penance or to progress in the virtues. [[16:22|the instruction of fools is foolishness|Doctrina stultorum, fatuitas]]. This was had before[[Prov 1:7||]].

paras.t: Cor sapientis erudiet os ejus : id est, sapiens per sapientiam sui intellectus, diriget os suum ad loquendum salubria, loco et tempore opportuno, recta intentione, et cum discretionis moderatione; et labiis illius addet gratiam, id est acceptabilitatem in loquendo, seu fructum locutionis, ita quod verba ejus audientur libenter, et fructificabunt. Hinc dixit Propheta : Dixi : Custodiam vias meas, id est cogitationes et affectiones, ut non delinquam in lingua mea, id est, ne ex irrefrenata cogitatione aut inordinata affectione ad loquendum prorumpam.
paras.en: [[16:23|The heart of the wise shall instruct his mouth|Cor sapientis erudiet os ejus]]: that is, the wise man, by the wisdom of his understanding, will direct his mouth to speak wholesome things, at a fitting place and time, with a right intention, and with the moderation of discretion; [[16:23|and shall add grace to his lips|et labiis illius addet gratiam]], that is, acceptableness in speaking, or fruit of speech, so that his words will be heard gladly and will bear fruit. Hence the Prophet said: [[Ps 38:2|I said: I will take heed to my ways|Dixi : Custodiam vias meas]], that is, my thoughts and affections, [[Ps 38:2|that I sin not with my tongue|ut non delinquam in lingua mea]], that is, lest I break out into speech from unbridled thought or disordered affection.

paras.t: Favus mellis sunt verba composita, id est ordinate, facunde, sapienter prolata : quoniam audientium aures ac mentes delectant, quemadmodum favus mellis gustum. Ideo Seneca testatur : Comes facundus in via pro vehiculo est. Spiritualiter autem, verba Scripturæ dulcissima sunt, prout canit Psalmographus : Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua! super mel ori meo. Verumtamen, quamvis eloquentia sit donum naturæ non parvum, non tamen est importune optandum aut nimis appretiandum, nec contristari quis debet quoniam caret illa, quum sit multis occasio multiplicis culpæ et perditionis æternæ. Ipse quoque defectus loquelæ, est multis occasio vitandi diversa vitiorum pericula, et humiliandi se ipsos. Idcirco in libro de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus, quod pulchritudo et eloquentia magis frequenter dantur reprobis, quam electis, ne electi ea nimis appretientur.
paras.en: [[16:24|Well ordered words are as a honeycomb|Favus mellis sunt verba composita]], that is, words uttered in order, eloquently and wisely: for they delight the ears and minds of the hearers, as the honeycomb delights the taste. Hence Seneca says: An eloquent companion on the road serves as a carriage. Spiritually, the words of Scripture are most sweet, as the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 118:103|How sweet are thy words to my palate! more than honey to my mouth|Quam dulcia faucibus meis eloquia tua! super mel ori meo]]. Yet, although eloquence is no small gift of nature, it is not to be desired importunately nor prized too highly, nor ought anyone to be saddened because he lacks it, since for many it is the occasion of manifold fault and of eternal perdition. And the very want of speech is for many an occasion of avoiding various dangers of vice and of humbling themselves. Therefore Augustine says in the book of the City of God that beauty and eloquence are given more often to the reprobate than to the elect, lest the elect should prize them too highly.

paras.t: Dulcedo animæ est sanitas ossium : id est, bona et jucunda dispositio cordis redundat in corpus, et sanitatem ejus conservat vel auget; similiter sanitas ossium, id est bona corporis habitudo, redundat in animam, et eam oblectat. Possunt quoque per ossa virtutes intelligi : quarum sanitas, id est immunitas a læsione peccati, sinceritas seu perfectio, jucunda est animæ, quoniam virtus ex sua natura delectabilis est.
paras.en: [[16:24|sweet to the soul, and health to the bones|Dulcedo animæ est sanitas ossium]] [the Latin reads "the sweetness of the soul is the health of the bones"]: that is, a good and joyful disposition of the heart overflows into the body and preserves or increases its health; likewise the health of the bones, that is, the good condition of the body, overflows into the soul and delights it. By the bones the virtues may also be understood: their health, that is, their freedom from the hurt of sin, their soundness or perfection, is pleasant to the soul, since virtue is by its nature delightful.

paras.t: Est via quæ videtur homini recta, et novissima ejus deducunt ad mortem. Hoc quartodecimo capitulo expositum est.
paras.en: [[16:25|There is a way that seemeth to a man right: and the ends thereof lead to death|Est via quæ videtur homini recta, et novissima ejus deducunt ad mortem]]. This was explained in the fourteenth chapter[[Prov 14:12||]].

paras.t: Anima laborantis laborat sibi, id est, anima exercentis opera corporalia aut spiritualia bona, facit ea ad suum profectum aut commodum, et pro necessariis corpori aut animæ. Ideo monet Apostolus : Labora sicut bonus miles Christi; et rursus, Labor vester non erit inanis in Domino; itemque, Unusquisque accipiet secundum suum laborem. Quia compulit eum ad laborandum, os suum, id est sermo quo se adstrinxit ad bene agendum in fonte Baptismi, in susceptione ordinis sacri, aut in professione monastica, vel in foro confessionis, sive in actu prædicationis : quia quod alios docet, facere obligatur. Os quoque corporale quo comedit homo, compellit eum ad laborandum pro sustentaculo vitæ. Similiter primus homo de paradiso expulsus, laboravit sibi pro necessariis vitæ (sicut dictum est ei, In sudore vultus tui vescaris pane tuo) : quia compulit eum os suum, id est peccatum quod commisit ore proprio, manducando de pomo prohibito : propter quod fuit expulsus, laboribusque addictus.
paras.en: [[16:26|The soul of him that laboureth, laboureth for himself|Anima laborantis laborat sibi]], that is, the soul of one who performs good works, bodily or spiritual, does them for its own progress or advantage, and for what is needful to the body or the soul. Therefore the Apostle admonishes: [[2 Tim 2:3|Labour as a good soldier of Christ|Labora sicut bonus miles Christi]]; and again: [[1 Cor 15:58|your labour is not in vain in the Lord|Labor vester non erit inanis in Domino]]; and likewise: [[1 Cor 3:8|every man shall receive his own reward, according to his own labour|Unusquisque accipiet secundum suum laborem]]. [[16:26|because his mouth hath obliged him to it|Quia compulit eum ad laborandum, os suum]] [the Latin reads "because his mouth compelled him to labour"], that is, the word by which he bound himself to do well at the font of Baptism, in receiving holy orders, or in monastic profession, or in the court of confession, or in the act of preaching: for what he teaches others he is bound to do. The bodily mouth too, with which a man eats, compels him to labour for the support of life. Likewise the first man, cast out of paradise, laboured for himself for the necessities of life (as was said to him: [[Gen 3:19|In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread|In sudore vultus tui vescaris pane tuo]]): because his mouth compelled him, that is, the sin which he committed with his own mouth, eating of the forbidden fruit; for which he was cast out and given over to labours.

paras.t: Vir impius fodit malum, id est, exquirit ac excogitat qualiter prava sua desideria ad effectum perducat, sicut ait Jeremias propheta : Ut inique agerent, laboraverunt; et Psalmista, Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso. De talibus ait Scriptura : Quasi de industria recesserunt a Deo; et alibi, Sapientes sunt ut faciant malum. Vel, Impius fodit malum, id est, dolose præparat proximo suo damnum, laqueum sive periculum, sicut ait Salvator per Prophetam : Foderunt foveam animæ meæ. Hoc modo hæretici ac alii deceptores fodiunt malum, dum ex Scripturis quasdam extrahunt auctoritates, ad comprobandum suos errores, quibus alios student illaqueare. Et in labiis ejus ignis ardescit, id est locutio male fervens, flamma iræ, impatientiæ, falsique dogmatis, spirituales divitias consumentis.
paras.en: [[16:27|The wicked man diggeth evil|Vir impius fodit malum]], that is, he seeks out and devises how he may bring his wicked desires to effect, as Jeremias the prophet says: [[Jer 9:5|they have laboured to commit iniquity|Ut inique agerent, laboraverunt]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 35:2|The unjust hath said within himself, that he would sin|Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso]]. Of such the Scripture says: [[Job 34:27|Who as it were on purpose have revolted from him|Quasi de industria recesserunt a Deo]]; and elsewhere: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil|Sapientes sunt ut faciant malum]]. Or: [[16:27|The wicked man diggeth evil|Impius fodit malum]], that is, he craftily prepares harm, a snare or a danger for his neighbour, as the Saviour says by the Prophet: [[Jer 18:20|they have digged a pit for my soul|Foderunt foveam animæ meæ]]. In this way heretics and other deceivers dig evil, when they draw certain texts out of the Scriptures to prove their errors, with which they strive to ensnare others. [[16:27|and in his lips is a burning fire|Et in labiis ejus ignis ardescit]], that is, speech that burns wickedly, the flame of anger, of impatience and of false doctrine, which consumes spiritual riches.

paras.t: Homo perversus suscitat lites, id est per verba injuriosa, aut opera violenta, per quæ inter se et alium, vel inter alios contentiones et bella procurat; et verbosus separat principes, seminando inter eos discordias, seu unum contra alium instigando.
paras.en: [[16:28|A perverse man stirreth up quarrels|Homo perversus suscitat lites]], that is, by insulting words or violent deeds, by which he brings about strife and wars between himself and another, or between others; [[16:28|and one full of words separateth princes|et verbosus separat principes]], by sowing discord among them, or stirring up one against another.

paras.t: Vir iniquus lactat, id est, blandiendo fallit, amicum suum, id est proximum a quo amatur, vel quem ipse simulat se amare; et ducit eum per viam non bonam, id est, ad vitia et incommoda trahit eum : juxta illud Psalmi, Loquuntur pacem cum proximo suo, mala autem in cordibus eorum.
paras.en: [[16:29|An unjust man allureth|Vir iniquus lactat]], that is, deceives by flattering [the Latin *lactat* is literally "gives milk to", "suckles", and so "coaxes"], [[16:29|his friend|amicum suum]], that is, the neighbour by whom he is loved, or whom he pretends to love; [[16:29|and leadeth him into a way that is not good|et ducit eum per viam non bonam]], that is, draws him into vices and harm: according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 27:3|Who speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts|Loquuntur pacem cum proximo suo, mala autem in cordibus eorum]] [the margin gives Ps. xxxvii, 3; the words are Ps 27:3].

paras.t: Qui attonitis oculis, id est oculis corporalibus cum signo superbiæ elevatis, aut quasi quodam pavore concussis, cogitat prava, quæ alteri cupit inferre aut facere. Unde dicitur ad Job : Quid te elevat cor tuum, et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos? Mordens labia sua, ex phantasia proterva, atque imaginatione intensa, qua cupit implere quod cogitat : juxta illud, Dentibus suis fremet, et tabescet; perficit malum, id est, ad effectum citius quo potest, suum vitiosum affectum perducit.
paras.en: [[16:30|He that with fixed eyes|Qui attonitis oculis]] [the Latin *attonitis* is "astonished", "thunderstruck"], that is, with his bodily eyes raised as a sign of pride, or as though struck by some fear, [[16:30|deviseth wicked things|cogitat prava]], which he desires to bring upon another or to do to him. Hence it is said to Job: [[Job 15:12|Why doth thy heart elevate thee, and why dost thou stare with thy eyes, as if they were thinking great things?|Quid te elevat cor tuum, et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos?]]? [[16:30|biting his lips|Mordens labia sua]], from wanton fancy and intense imagining, by which he longs to carry out what he devises: according to the words: [[Ps 111:10|he shall gnash with his teeth and pine away|Dentibus suis fremet, et tabescet]]; [[16:30|bringeth evil to pass|perficit malum]], that is, he brings his sinful desire to effect as quickly as he can.

paras.t: Corona dignitatis est senectus, quæ in viis justitiæ reperitur : id est, senium sanctum in virtutibus exercitatum, seu cordis maturitas, est dignitas valde præclara coronationeque digna. Unde scriptum est : Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis.
paras.en: [[16:31|Old age is a crown of dignity, when it is found in the ways of justice|Corona dignitatis est senectus, quæ in viis justitiæ reperitur]]: that is, a holy old age, practised in the virtues, or ripeness of heart, is a very glorious dignity and worthy of a crown. Hence it is written: [[Lev 19:32|Rise up before the hoary head, and honour the person of the aged man|Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis]].

paras.t: Melior est patiens viro forti, corporali robore, non virtutum vigore. Patientia enim est præclara et utilissima virtus, et necessaria valde : quæ passionem tristitiæ moderatur ac frenat, et naturalibus ac corporalibus donis longe præstantior est. De qua asserit Dominus : In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras. Et qui dominatur animo suo, id est animositati propriæ ac ceteris motibus passionum, per virtutes morales, melior et fortior est expugnatore urbium. Incomparabiliter enim virtuosius est, per gratiam et virtutes superare se ipsum, et vitia exstirpare, passionesque reformare, quam armis et viribus corporalibus destruere urbes.
paras.en: [[16:32|The patient man is better than the valiant|Melior est patiens viro forti]], valiant in bodily strength, not in the vigour of the virtues. For patience is a glorious and most useful virtue, and very necessary: it moderates and bridles the passion of sadness, and is far more excellent than the gifts of nature and of the body. Of it the Lord says: [[Luke 21:19|In your patience you shall possess your souls|In patientia vestra possidebitis animas vestras]]. [[16:32|and he that ruleth his spirit|Et qui dominatur animo suo]], that is, his own animosity [the Latin *animositas*, from *animus*, "spirit", means hot temper, vehemence] and the other movements of the passions, by the moral virtues, is better and stronger [[16:32|than he that taketh cities|expugnatore urbium]]. For it is incomparably more virtuous to overcome oneself by grace and the virtues, to root out vices and reform the passions, than to destroy cities by arms and bodily strength.

paras.t: Sortes mittuntur in sinum, id est, in abscondito reconduntur; sed a Domino temperantur : id est, divina providentia eas disponit, atque ex justi ac sapientissimi Dei voluntate ordinationeque provenit quis quid accipiat, quæ sors illi aut illi proveniat, et quod talis aut talis sors cadat super illum aut illum. Universa namque et singula, sub divinæ providentiæ ordinatione comprehenduntur, quemadmodum asserit Christus : Nonne quinque passeres veneunt dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo? Sed et capilli capitis vestri omnes numerati sunt. Quod Matthæus sic expressit : Nonne duo passeres asse veneunt, et unus ex illis non cadet super terram sine Patre vestro? Possent autem hic multa introduci de sortibus, utpote quid sit sors, et de speciebus ipsius, qualiter etiam liceat sortibus uti, et qualiter non. De quibus hoc loco pertranseo, quoniam alibi inde scripsi, præsertim super Jonam. Et Thomas in secunda secundæ de his tractat diffuse : cujus determinationem hic sequitur Lyra.
paras.en: [[16:33|Lots are cast into the lap|Sortes mittuntur in sinum]], that is, they are laid up in a hidden place; [[16:33|but they are disposed of by the Lord|sed a Domino temperantur]]: that is, divine providence disposes them, and it comes from the will and ordinance of the just and all-wise God who receives what, which lot falls to this man or that, and that such or such a lot falls on this man or that. For all things together and each singly are included under the ordinance of divine providence, as Christ says: [[Luke 12:6|Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?|Nonne quinque passeres veneunt dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo?]]? [[Luke 12:7|the very hairs of your head are all numbered|Sed et capilli capitis vestri omnes numerati sunt]]. Which Matthew expressed thus: [[Matt 10:29|Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and not one of them shall fall on the ground without your Father|Nonne duo passeres asse veneunt, et unus ex illis non cadet super terram sine Patre vestro?]]? Much could be brought in here about lots: what a lot is, and its kinds, and how it is lawful to use lots and how not. These I pass over here, since I have written of them elsewhere, especially on Jonas[[Jon 1:7||]]. And Thomas treats of them at length in the Second of the Second Part, whose determination Lyra follows here.

paras.t: Postremo, quod dictum est, Melior est patiens viro forti, et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium : cordibus nostris indelebiliter inscribamus, et patientiam tanquam sponsam carissimam jugiter amplectamur, vincamus nos ipsos, et omnem animositatem, impetuositatem, impatientiam detestemur ac fugiamus, quum ad Hebræos dicat Apostolus : Patientia vobis necessaria est, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, reportetis promissionem; et alibi, Cum patientia supportate invicem in caritate. Nempe, ut ait Gregorius, In hoc mens justi ab injusta discernitur, quod mens justi laudem Omnipotentis inter adversa confitetur, quod rebus adversis non frangitur, quod casu gloriæ exterioris non labitur. Qui iterum ait : Non est perfecte bonus, nisi qui et inter malos est bonus; nec bonus dici meretur, qui malos tolerare detestatur. Hinc et Seneca in suis ait Proverbiis : Feras quod lædit, ut prosit tibi quod fers; fer difficilia, ut prospera et facilia bene feras. Velox doloris remedium est patientia. Quid autem sit patientia, Tullius docet : Patientia (inquiens) est, honestatis aut utilitatis causa, rerum arduarum ac difficilium voluntaria ac diuturna perpessio.
paras.en: Lastly, let us write indelibly on our hearts what was said: [[16:32|The patient man is better than the valiant: and he that ruleth his spirit, than he that taketh cities|Melior est patiens viro forti, et qui dominatur animo suo, expugnatore urbium]]. Let us embrace patience continually as a most dear bride, let us conquer ourselves, and let us detest and flee all animosity, impetuousness and impatience, since the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:36|patience is necessary for you: that, doing the will of God, you may receive the promise|Patientia vobis necessaria est, ut voluntatem Dei facientes, reportetis promissionem]]; and elsewhere: [[Eph 4:2|with patience, supporting one another in charity|Cum patientia supportate invicem in caritate]]. For, as Gregory says, the mind of the just is distinguished from the unjust in this: that the mind of the just confesses the praise of the Almighty amid adversities, that it is not broken by adverse things, that it does not fall by the loss of outward glory. And again he says: He is not perfectly good who is not good among the wicked too; nor does he deserve to be called good who refuses to bear with the wicked. Hence Seneca too says in his Proverbs: Bear what hurts, that what thou bearest may profit thee; bear hard things, that thou mayest bear prosperous and easy things well. Patience is a swift remedy for grief. And what patience is, Tully teaches: Patience, he says, is the voluntary and long-continued enduring of arduous and difficult things for the sake of what is honourable or useful.

17.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI SEPTIMIDECIMI : MELIOR EST BUCCELLA SICCA CUM GAUDIO.
17.title_en: Declaration of the seventeenth chapter: Better is a dry morsel with joy.

paras.t: Melior est buccella sicca cum gaudio spirituali, quod habet vir sobrius in refectione frugali, moderata et abstinentiali, quam domus plena victimis, id est delicatissimis epulis, quæ ex oblationibus cesserunt in usum et esum offerentium: meliora namque in lege jubebantur offerri; cum jurgio. Modicum enim temporale cum adjuncto bono virtutis, incomparabiliter melius est quacumque re temporali magna et pretiosa. Atque, ut ait Chrysostomus, simplicior victus et mensa mediocris, plurimum jucunditatis habet et sinceritatis, ac sobrii hominis mensam ornant panis et aqua; econtrario divitum mensæ exsecrabiles sunt et horridæ, et contaminationis corporum animarumque plenæ. Ex his insinuatur quam enorme peccatum sit jurgium, et quam abominabiles exsistant epulationes in quibus lis et jurgium admiscentur.
paras.en: [[17:1|Better is a dry morsel with joy|Melior est buccella sicca cum gaudio]], that is, with the spiritual joy which a sober man has in a frugal, moderate and abstinent meal, [[17:1|than a house full of victims|quam domus plena victimis]], that is, of the most delicate dishes, which out of the offerings went to the use and eating of those who offered them: for the better parts were commanded in the law to be offered[[Lev 3:3||]] [the margin gives Lev. iii, 3, 4, 9, 10, 14–17]; [[17:1|with strife|cum jurgio]]. For a little of temporal things, with the good of virtue joined to it, is incomparably better than any temporal thing however great and precious. And, as Chrysostom says, plainer fare and a modest table hold a great deal of pleasantness and sincerity, and bread and water adorn the table of a sober man; whereas the tables of the rich are accursed and frightful, and full of the defilement of bodies and souls. From this it is hinted how enormous a sin strife is, and how abominable are the feasts in which quarrelling and strife are mixed.

paras.t: Servus sapiens dominabitur filiis stultis. Nam, ut primo Politicorum ait Philosophus, Hi qui ratione intellectuque vigent, naturaliter sunt domini et rectores aliorum. Sæpe quoque parentes committunt suis ministris prudentibus dirigere sobolem suam adhuc imprudentem. Sapientes etiam servi, per suam sapientiam frequenter prosperantur et sublimantur; filii autem stulti econtrario per regimen malum depauperantur ac deprimuntur. Et inter fratres hereditatem dividet, quum fuerit dominans eis: quia tunc fratribus seu filiis stultis discordantibus de modo dividendi bona paterna, eligunt eum in judicem hujus rei, vel ipse concordat ac dirigit eos. Vel sensus est, quod filiis stultis patrimonia sua vendentibus, ipse partem illorum acquirit et emit, sicque dividit inter eos, id est, partem hereditatis ipsorum sortitur.
paras.en: [[17:2|A wise servant shall rule over foolish sons|Servus sapiens dominabitur filiis stultis]]. For, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the Politics, those who are strong in reason and understanding are by nature the masters and rulers of others. Parents too often entrust to their prudent servants the guidance of their offspring while it is still imprudent. Wise servants, moreover, often prosper and are raised up through their wisdom; foolish sons, on the contrary, are impoverished and brought low through bad management. [[17:2|And shall divide the inheritance among the brethren|Et inter fratres hereditatem dividet]], when he has come to be master over them: because then, when the brothers, or foolish sons, disagree about the way of dividing their father's goods, they choose him as judge of the matter, or he himself brings them to agreement and directs them. Or the sense is that, when the foolish sons sell their patrimony, he acquires and buys their share, and so divides among them, that is, he obtains a part of their inheritance.

paras.t: Sicut igne probatur argentum, et aurum camino, ita corda probat Dominus: id est, sicut per ignem examinatur ac depuratur argentum et aurum, sic Dominus judex universorum, per adversa justos suos probat, tentat, examinatque electos et justos, an vere sint justi, non ut sibi hoc innotescat, sed pro majori eorum mercede et saluberrima exercitatione, atque ut virtutes eorum aliis in exemplum ponantur. Non enim coronatur, nisi qui legitime certaverit. Hinc scriptum est: Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos. Patientia igitur in adversis, signum est veræ virtuositatis: quia dum homo ficte bonus, in camino adversitatis statuitur, mox instar malæ ollæ per impatientiam crepat, et per verba ac signa impatientiæ exsilit. Unde scriptum est: Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis. Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Perfacile est vestem contemptam portare, capite inclinato incedere, velum super oculos demittere; sed vere virtuosum ac humilem patientia monstrat. Concordatque cum his, quod Seneca in suis dicit Proverbiis: Ignis aurum probat, miseria (id est adversitas) magna fortes viros.
paras.en: [[17:3|As silver is tried by fire, and gold in the furnace: so the Lord trieth the hearts|Sicut igne probatur argentum, et aurum camino, ita corda probat Dominus]][[Ps 7:10||]]: that is, as silver and gold are tested and refined by fire, so the Lord, the judge of all, proves his just ones by adversities; he tries and examines the elect and the just, whether they are truly just: not that this may become known to him, but for their greater reward and most wholesome exercise, and that their virtues may be set before others as an example. For [[2 Tim 2:5|is not crowned, except he strive lawfully|Non enim coronatur, nisi qui legitime certaverit]]. Hence it is written: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit illos]] [the margin gives only "Sap. iii"; the words are Wis 3:6]. Patience in adversity, then, is the sign of true virtue: because when a man who is good only in pretence is set in the furnace of adversity, he presently cracks through impatience like a bad pot, and bursts out in words and signs of impatience. Whence it is written: [[Ecclus 27:6|The furnace trieth the potter's vessels, and the trial of affliction just men|Vasa figuli probat fornax, et homines justos tentatio tribulationis]]. Hence Augustine says: It is very easy to wear a despised garment, to walk with head bowed, to let a veil down over the eyes; but it is patience that shows the truly virtuous and humble man. And with this agrees what Seneca says in his Proverbs: Fire proves gold, great misery (that is, adversity) brave men.

paras.t: Malus obedit linguæ iniquæ, id est ei qui jubet illicita et iniqua, et quæ scit talia esse: quod malum est. In licitis etenim et honestis tantum est obediendum. Sed impii servi ac subditi citius obtemperant superiori suo in vitiis, quam in actibus virtuosis. Et fallax obtemperat labiis mendacibus. Sic judex iniquus audientiam præbet testibus falsis ac fraudulentis, [et] ut suam excuset et coloret nequitiam, fingit se propter aliorum dicta sic agere, quum tamen sciat eos false locutos.
paras.en: [[17:4|The evil man obeyeth an unjust tongue|Malus obedit linguæ iniquæ]], that is, him who commands what is unlawful and wicked, and things he knows to be such: which is evil. For obedience is due only in what is lawful and honest. But wicked servants and subjects obey their superior more quickly in vices than in virtuous acts. [[17:4|And the deceitful hearkeneth to lying lips|Et fallax obtemperat labiis mendacibus]]. So a wicked judge gives a hearing to false and fraudulent witnesses, and, to excuse and colour his own wickedness, pretends that he acts so on account of what others have said, though he knows that they have spoken falsely.

paras.t: Qui despicit pauperem, exprobrat factori ejus. Hoc supra expositum est. Et qui in ruina lætatur alterius, non erit impunitus. Nunquam licet gloriari de proximorum ruina in culpam, hoc est de transgressione eorum, quia hoc contrariaretur caritati Dei, qui peccato inhonoratur, caritatique proximi, qui peccando spiritualiter moritur. Sed de ruina pœnæ, id est justa punitione alterius, lætari ex zelo justitiæ, et in quantum expediens est saluti, non est illicitum; gaudere vero de adversitate et pœna proximi, in quantum est adversitas quædam et pœna, non in quantum est medicina, et utile quid pro pace communi et conservatione justitiæ, manifeste illicitum est. Similiter lætari de quacumque ruina alterius ex ira seu odio, similive radice perversa, certum est esse iniquum. Talis ergo non erit impunitus, quia aut punietur a judice Deo, aut per contritionem et pœnitentialem satisfactionem puniet semetipsum, aut alio modo debitam feret pœnam. Hinc sanctus Job ait: Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui oderat me, et exsultavi quod invenisset eum malum. Et Michæas propheta ait: Ne læteris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi. Itaque labentibus et peccantibus condoleamus ex corde, et oremus pro eis, dicentes: Ille hodie, et ego cras.
paras.en: [[17:5|He that despiseth the poor, reproacheth his maker|Qui despicit pauperem, exprobrat factori ejus]]. This has been expounded above[[Prov 14:31||]]. [[17:5|And he that rejoiceth at another man's ruin, shall not be unpunished|Et qui in ruina lætatur alterius, non erit impunitus]]. It is never lawful to glory in our neighbours' ruin into fault, that is, in their transgression, because this would be contrary to the love of God, who is dishonoured by sin, and to the love of our neighbour, who by sinning dies spiritually. But to rejoice at the ruin of punishment, that is, at the just punishment of another, out of zeal for justice, and in so far as it is expedient for salvation, is not unlawful; whereas to rejoice at the adversity and punishment of one's neighbour in so far as it is a certain adversity and punishment, not in so far as it is a medicine and something useful for the common peace and the preservation of justice, is plainly unlawful. Likewise, to rejoice at any ruin of another out of anger or hatred, or a like perverse root, is certainly wicked. Such a one, then, shall not be unpunished: because either he will be punished by God the judge, or he will punish himself by contrition and penitential satisfaction, or he will bear the punishment due in some other way. Hence holy Job says: [[Job 31:29|If I have been glad at the downfall of him that hated me, and have rejoiced that evil had found him|Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui oderat me, et exsultavi quod invenisset eum malum]]. And Micheas the prophet says: [[Mich 7:8|Rejoice not, thou my enemy, over me, because I am fallen|Ne læteris, inimica mea, super me, quia cecidi]]. Let us therefore grieve from the heart with those who fall and sin, and pray for them, saying: He today, and I tomorrow.

paras.t: Corona senum, filii filiorum: id est, bona posteritas est dignitas et exsultatio progenitorum suorum, præsertim justorum. Sic Apostoli facti sunt corona Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum, ex quibus duxerunt originem. Similiter spirituales filii, utputa imitatores fideles prælatorum et institutorum suorum religiosorum ac devotorum, sunt corona ipsorum, quoniam patres tales sunt principes meritorum ac præmiorum suorum sequacium. Propter quod in prima ad Thessalonicenses epistola scribit Apostolus: Quæ est enim spes nostra, aut gaudium, aut corona gloriæ? Nonne vos? Et gloria filiorum, patres eorum: quia hoc gloriosum et jucundum est filiis, quod de virtuosis et prudentibus parentibus nati sunt. Similiter fidelibus gloriosum est, quod spirituales patres eorum sancti Apostoli, cæterique apostolici viri et prælati, tales ac tanti fuerunt. Unde Corinthiis scribit Apostolus: Vos estis gloria nostra, sicut et nos vestra. Verumtamen in hac re frequenter error contingit, quoniam multi superbi et vani magis gloriantur de suorum parentum nobilitate carnali, quam spirituali. Rursus, quidam de patrum suorum sanctitate et sagacitate se jactant, quum tamen eorum virtutes imitari non studeant. Talibus enim ait sacratissimus Joannes Baptista: Ne cœperitis dicere. Patrem habemus Abraham; Christus quoque: Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite.
paras.en: [[17:6|Children's children are the crown of old men|Corona senum, filii filiorum]]: that is, a good posterity is the honour and exultation of its forebears, especially of the just. So the Apostles became the crown of the Patriarchs and Prophets, from whom they took their origin. Likewise spiritual sons, for instance the faithful imitators of their prelates and of their religious and devout founders, are their crown, since such fathers are princes [the margin gives the variant *participes*, "sharers"] of the merits and rewards of their followers. For which reason the Apostle writes in the first epistle to the Thessalonians: [[1 Thess 2:19|For what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Are not you|Quæ est enim spes nostra, aut gaudium, aut corona gloriæ? Nonne vos]]? [[17:6|And the glory of children are their fathers|Et gloria filiorum, patres eorum]]: because it is glorious and pleasant to children that they were born of virtuous and prudent parents. Likewise it is glorious to the faithful that their spiritual fathers, the holy Apostles and the other apostolic men and prelates, were such and so great. Whence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: You are our glory, as we also are yours[[2 Cor 1:14||]] [Denis's wording is closer to 1 Thess 2:20, "you are our glory"; 2 Cor 1:14 reads "we are your glory: as you also are ours"]. Yet in this matter error often occurs, since many proud and vain men glory more in the carnal nobility of their parents than in the spiritual. Again, some boast of the holiness and wisdom of their fathers, though they do not strive to imitate their virtues. For to such the most holy John the Baptist says: [[Luke 3:8|do not begin to say, We have Abraham for our father|Ne cœperitis dicere. Patrem habemus Abraham]]; and Christ also: [[John 8:39|If you be the children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham|Si filii Abrahæ estis, opera Abrahæ facite]].

paras.t: Non decent stultum verba composita: quia non vivit secundum Scripturam, nec dignus est alios edocere, nec aptus ut ei committatur negotium arduum, ad cujus expeditionem exiguntur aut conferunt verba sapientia ordinate prolata. Nec principem, labium mentiens. Princeps namque et judex et omnis qui præest, debet esse quasi viva lex et animata justitia, director et regula quædam subditorum suorum, ut eos ab erroribus et vitiis revocet, et ad vera justaque dirigat. Ideo maxime indecens est eum esse mendosum sive injustum.
paras.en: [[17:7|Eloquent words do not become a fool|Non decent stultum verba composita]] [*verba composita*, literally "well-ordered words"]: because he does not live according to Scripture, nor is he worthy to teach others, nor fit to be entrusted with a difficult business, for the dispatch of which wise words spoken in good order are required or are of help. [[17:7|Nor lying lips a prince|Nec principem, labium mentiens]]. For a prince and a judge, and everyone who is in authority, ought to be as it were a living law and justice given a soul, a director and a kind of rule for his subjects, to call them back from errors and vices and direct them to what is true and just. Therefore it is most unbecoming for him to be false or unjust.

paras.t: Gemma gratissima, exspectatio præstolantis: id est, ipsa spes copiosæ mercedis ac futuræ consolationis, exhilarat exspectantem ac laborantem, tanquam pretiosissimus lapis. Unde ait Apostolus: Spe gaudentes; et Salvator: Gaudete in illa hora et exsultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis. Propterea ait Hieronymus: Spes præmii minuit vim flagelli. Iterum, Exspectatio præstolantis, id est bonum a præstolante exspectatum, tanquam gratissima gemma ipsum lætificat; et maxime beatitudo cœlestis et ejus exspectatio consolantur viatores hujus exsilii: quæ beatitudo per pretiosam margaritam designatur. Hinc et Apostolus ait: Gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum Dei. Quocumque se vertit, id est, quidquid talis præstolans egerit, prudenter intelligit, id est, vigilanter considerat bonum illud quod finaliter præstolatur, et taliter operatur sicut necessarium est ad obtinendum hoc bonum speratum.
paras.en: [[17:8|The expectation of him that expecteth is a most acceptable jewel|Gemma gratissima, exspectatio præstolantis]]: that is, the very hope of a plentiful reward and of consolation to come gladdens him who waits and labours, like a most precious stone. Whence the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:12|Rejoicing in hope|Spe gaudentes]]; and the Saviour: [[Matt 5:12|Be glad|Gaudete]] in that hour [[Matt 5:12|and rejoice for your reward is very great in heaven|et exsultate, quoniam merces vestra copiosa est in cœlis]]. Therefore Jerome says: The hope of reward lessens the force of the scourge. Again, [[17:8|The expectation of him that expecteth|Exspectatio præstolantis]], that is, the good awaited by him who waits, gladdens him like a most acceptable jewel; and above all the heavenly beatitude and the expectation of it console the wayfarers of this exile: which beatitude is signified by the precious pearl[[Matt 13:46||]]. Hence the Apostle too says: We [[Rom 5:2|glory in the hope of the glory of the sons of God|Gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum Dei]]. [[17:8|Whithersoever he turneth himself|Quocumque se vertit]], that is, whatever such a one who waits may do, [[17:8|he understandeth wisely|prudenter intelligit]], that is, he watchfully considers that good which he awaits at the end, and works in such a way as is necessary for obtaining this hoped-for good.

paras.t: Qui celat delictum, id est, qui culpam proximi sui non manifestat aliis inordinate, nec eum diffamat neque irridet, sed potius, sicut docet Salvator, corripit illum caritative inter se et illum solum; quærit amicitias, id est, per hoc procurat sibi amicitiam illius, et est amator caritatis ac pacis. Verumtamen, si crimen alterius vergeret in dispendium boni communis, vel de illius emendatione spes nulla aut pauca haberetur, aliter esset agendum. Providendum est autem famæ proximi, quantum salvis justitia et ordine caritatis, convenienter fieri potest.
paras.en: [[17:9|He that concealeth a transgression|Qui celat delictum]], that is, he who does not disclose his neighbour's fault to others without due order, nor defames him nor mocks him, but rather, as the Saviour teaches, rebukes him charitably between himself and him alone[[Matt 18:15||]]; [[17:9|seeketh friendships|quærit amicitias]], that is, by this he wins that man's friendship for himself, and is a lover of charity and peace. Yet if the other's crime tended to the loss of the common good, or there were no hope, or little, of his amendment, one would have to act otherwise. But one's neighbour's good name must be cared for as far as can fittingly be done, saving justice and the order of charity.

paras.t: Qui altero sermone repetit, id est, ea quæ audivit, aliter quam audivit, resumit, verba mutando aut aliqua adjiciendo, seu quæ bona intentione prolata sunt, interpretando perverse; separat fœderatos, id est, discordiam seminat inter amicos fœdere pacis conjunctos, qui credunt tali repetitioni: sicque unus eorum credit alium de se male locutum, propterea concitatur adversus illum. Istud frequenter contingit a dolosis pravissimisque hominibus, qui sunt cooperatores, satellites et instrumenta diaboli ad faciendum turbationem, discordiam, litem, inimicitiam inter fideles. Summe ergo vitandum est vitium istud, atque opposito modo agendum est, ut scilicet male prolata et discordiæ provocativa taceantur, et bene prolata resumantur: nisi forsan ad advisandum proximum de imminenti periculo, oporteret aliquid tangi de male prolatis: quod tamen tunc cum magna cautela fieri debet.
paras.en: [[17:9|He that repeateth it again|Qui altero sermone repetit]] [literally "he that repeateth in other words"], that is, he who takes up again what he has heard otherwise than he heard it, changing the words or adding something, or perversely interpreting what was said with a good intention; [[17:9|separateth friends|separat fœderatos]], that is, sows discord among friends joined in a covenant of peace, who believe such a report: and so one of them believes the other has spoken ill of him, and for that reason is stirred up against him. This is often done by deceitful and most depraved men, who are the fellow-workers, henchmen and instruments of the devil for making disturbance, discord, strife and enmity among the faithful. This vice, then, is to be shunned above all, and the opposite done: namely, that what was ill said and provokes discord be kept quiet, and what was well said be repeated; unless perhaps, to warn one's neighbour of an imminent danger, something of what was ill said had to be touched on: which, however, must then be done with great caution.

paras.t: Quidam legunt: Qui alto sermone repetit, id est, clamorose culpam alterius sine rationabili causa pandit; separat fœderatos, id est, fœdus pacis inter se et alium violat, quia illum per hoc offendit.
paras.en: Some read: He that repeateth it with a loud voice [*alto sermone* for *altero sermone*], that is, who noisily lays open another's fault without reasonable cause; [[17:9|separateth friends|separat fœderatos]], that is, he breaks the covenant of peace between himself and the other, because by this he offends him.

paras.t: Plus proficit correctio, id est verbalis et caritativa correptio seu disciplinæ inflictio, apud prudentem, id est in eo qui correptionem sumit gratanter, exhibendo se docilem, dirigibilem, gratum, quod pertinet ad prudentem; quam centum plagæ apud stultum, id est durum, indirigibilem, impatientem, superbum, qui ex medicinali castigatione fit pejor. De tali prudente ait Hieronymus: Quid necesse est bis pungere non recalcitrantem, et per se satis erubescentem confundere amplius? cui sua ratio est magistra; cui propria conscientia, virga; cui ingenita verecundia, lex disciplinæ.
paras.en: [[17:10|A reproof availeth more|Plus proficit correctio]], that is, a spoken and charitable rebuke, or the infliction of discipline, [[17:10|with a wise man|apud prudentem]], that is, in him who receives rebuke gratefully, showing himself teachable, ready to be directed, and thankful, which belongs to the prudent man; [[17:10|than a hundred stripes with a fool|quam centum plagæ apud stultum]], that is, with the hard, the undirectable, the impatient, the proud man, who becomes worse from medicinal chastisement. Of such a prudent man Jerome says: What need is there to goad twice one who does not kick back, and to confound further one who of himself blushes enough? one whose own reason is his mistress, his own conscience his rod, his inborn modesty his law of discipline.

paras.t: Semper jurgia quærit malus, id est homo inquietus, passionatus, præsertim qui in irascibili abundat. Cholerici autem et melancholici, nisi virtute et gratia reprimantur, ad jurgia proni sunt. Angelus autem crudelis mittetur contra eum. Per angelum crudelem, quidam intelligunt judicis servum, qui mittitur ad talem capiendum et puniendum. Sed quum pœnæ vitæ præsentis sint medicinales, et pia intentione infligendæ, non videtur quod nuntius judicis sæcularis vocetur crudelis. Idcirco per angelum crudelem aptius designatur spiritus malignus, qui tempore mortis mittitur ad trahendum talem ad Dei judicium et ad pœnas, vel etiam permittitur talem iniquum ad majora quotidie crimina in præsenti vita inducere, aut quibusdam tormentis afficere, quemadmodum de Ægyptiis fertur in Psalmo: Misit in eos iram indignationis suæ, immissiones per angelos malos. Sicque in regula sua allegat hæc verba S. Basilius, qui et verba statim præhabita, scilicet, Jurgia quærit malus, juxta antiquam translationem allegat sic: Contradictionem suscitat omnis malus: quod de inobedientibus exponit.
paras.en: [[17:11|An evil man always seeketh quarrels|Semper jurgia quærit malus]], that is, a restless, passionate man, especially one in whom the irascible part [that is, the power of the soul that resists and fights, the seat of anger] abounds. Choleric and melancholic men, unless they are held back by virtue and grace, are prone to quarrels. [[17:11|But a cruel angel shall be sent against him|Angelus autem crudelis mittetur contra eum]]. By the cruel angel some understand the judge's officer, who is sent to seize and punish such a man. But since the punishments of the present life are medicinal, and to be inflicted with a loving intention, it does not seem that the messenger of a secular judge should be called cruel. Therefore the cruel angel more fittingly signifies the evil spirit, who at the time of death is sent to drag such a man to God's judgment and to punishment, or else is permitted to lead such a wicked man into greater crimes day by day in the present life, or to afflict him with certain torments, as is said of the Egyptians in the Psalm: [[Ps 77:49|And he sent upon them the wrath of his indignation|Misit in eos iram indignationis suæ]], [[Ps 77:49|which he sent by evil angels|immissiones per angelos malos]]. And so St. Basil cites these words in his Rule; he also cites the words just before, namely An evil man [[17:11|seeketh quarrels|Jurgia quærit malus]], according to the old translation, thus: Every evil man stirs up contradiction: which he expounds of the disobedient.

paras.t: Expedit magis, id est, minus periculosum est, ursæ occurrere raptis fetibus, id est, quæ perdidit catulos suos: propter quod valde sævit, et primum sibi occurrentem solet invadere, suspicans catulos suos per illum sibi subtractos; quam fatuo confidenti sibi in stultitia sua, id est superbo præsumptuosoque homini in sua perversitate speranti, qui non solum corpus, sed et animam quærit occidere. Nam, ut in Politicis ait Philosophus, homo vitiosus, lege atque justitia destitutus, est pessimum animal, et millies pejor brutis.
paras.en: [[17:12|It is better|Expedit magis]], that is, it is less dangerous, [[17:12|to meet a bear robbed of her whelps|ursæ occurrere raptis fetibus]], that is, one that has lost her cubs: for which reason she rages fiercely, and is wont to attack the first one who meets her, suspecting that her cubs were taken from her by him; [[17:12|than a fool trusting in his own folly|quam fatuo confidenti sibi in stultitia sua]], that is, than a proud and presumptuous man putting his hope in his own perversity, who seeks to kill not only the body but the soul as well. For, as the Philosopher says in the Politics, a vicious man, bereft of law and justice, is the worst of animals, and a thousand times worse than the brutes.

paras.t: Spiritualiter autem, per ursam designatur gentilitas: cui occurrere levius fuit catholicis viris, qui catulos gentilitatis rapuerunt, convertendo eos ad Christum, quam stulto confidenti in sua stultitia, id est hæreticis in suis argumentis vanis ac frivolis stulte præsumentibus.
paras.en: Spiritually, the bear signifies the heathen world: to meet it was easier for catholic men, who carried off the cubs of the heathen by converting them to Christ, than to meet a fool trusting in his own folly, that is, heretics foolishly presuming on their vain and frivolous arguments.

paras.t: Qui reddit mala pro bonis: sicut populus Judæorum Christo, qui per Prophetam effatur: Numquid redditur malum pro bono? Non recedet malum de domo ejus, id est de corde ipsius, vel de sobole atque familia sua, ipsum in malis sequente. Istud namque, ingratitudo est maxima, ad quam sequuntur et alia crimina multa. Sicque talis ingratus impletur malis culpæ ac pœnæ. Verum, ut Seneca in libro de Beneficiis tangit, Primus gradus ingratitudinis est, beneficium non recognoscere, neque recolere, sed potius oblivisci aut dissimulare; secundus gradus est, bona pro bonis non exhibere; tertius, mala pro bonis rependere. Ingratitudo itaque est enorme peccatum, quo meretur homo amittere quod accepit.
paras.en: [[17:13|He that rendereth evil for good|Qui reddit mala pro bonis]]: as the Jewish people did to Christ, who speaks through the Prophet: [[Jer 18:20|Shall evil be rendered for good|Numquid redditur malum pro bono]]? [the margin gives Jer. xvii, 20; the words are Jer 18:20] [[17:13|evil shall not depart from his house|Non recedet malum de domo ejus]], that is, from his heart, or from his offspring and household that follow him in evil.
