For this is the greatest ingratitude, upon which many other crimes follow too. And so such an ingrate is filled with the evils of fault and of punishment. Indeed, as Seneca touches on in his book On Benefits, the first degree of ingratitude is not to acknowledge a benefit nor to call it to mind, but rather to forget it or pretend not to know it; the second degree is not to show good for good; the third, to pay back evil for good. Ingratitude, then, is an enormous sin, by which a man deserves to lose what he has received.

paras.t: Qui dimittit aquam, caput est jurgiorum. Hoc quidam exponunt sic: Qui omittit bibere aquam, et potat vina, origo est contentionum et litium, quæ ex vini potatione sæpe sequuntur. Videtur autem sic potius exponendum: Qui aquam facit ex fluvio deservienti communitati aut personæ alieni, decurrere, causa est jurgiorum, quæ ex tali damno communitati vel personæ illato sequuntur. Circa hoc dicit Lyra, in Hebræo haberi: Qui aperit aquam, principium est jurgiorum. id est, qui aperturam facit in alveo fluminis, per quam exeat et decurrat, principium est jurgiorum: quoniam sicut apertura illa primo est parva, et paulatim augetur; sic jurgium in principio modicum, paulatim fit grande. Sed juxta expositionem magis jam approbatam. Dimittere, sumitur hic satis apte pro Aperire: ex quo etiam constat, quod prima quorundam expositio, primo inducta, non consonat Hebraicæ veritati.
paras.en: [[17:14|The beginning of quarrels is as when one letteth out water|Qui dimittit aquam, caput est jurgiorum]] [literally "he that letteth out water is the head of quarrels"]. Some expound this thus: he who leaves off drinking water and drinks wine is the origin of contentions and lawsuits, which often follow from wine-drinking. But it seems it should rather be expounded thus: he who makes water run off from a stream that serves a community, or another person, is the cause of the quarrels that follow from such damage done to the community or the person. On this Lyra says that the Hebrew has: He that openeth water is the beginning of quarrels; that is, he who makes an opening in the bed of a river, through which the water may go out and run off, is the beginning of quarrels: since just as that opening is small at first and grows little by little, so a quarrel, small in the beginning, little by little becomes great. But according to the exposition now more approved, *let out* is taken here, fittingly enough, for *open*: from which it is also clear that the first exposition of some, given first above, does not agree with the Hebrew truth.

paras.t: Porro Glossa per aquam intelligit fluxam et irrefrenatam locutionem, ex qua lites nascuntur: sicque, aquam dimittere, est linguam in fluxum verborum reprehensibilium relaxare. Qui ergo dimittit aquam, caput est jurgiorum: quia qui linguam non frenat, concordiam dissipat proximorum. Contra quod scriptum est: Qui imponit stulto silentium, iras mitigat. Econverso lingua in bonam accipitur partem, quum dicitur: Aqua profunda, verba ex ore viri.
paras.en: The Gloss, further, understands by water loose and unbridled speech, from which quarrels are born: and so to let out water is to loosen the tongue into a flood of blameworthy words. [[17:14|The beginning of quarrels is as when one letteth out water|Qui ergo dimittit aquam, caput est jurgiorum]], then: because he who does not bridle his tongue scatters the concord of his neighbours. Against which it is written: [[Prov 26:10|he that putteth a fool to silence, appeaseth anger|Qui imponit stulto silentium, iras mitigat]]. Conversely the tongue [that is, water as a figure of speech] is taken in a good sense when it is said: [[Prov 18:4|Words from the mouth of a man are as deep water|Aqua profunda, verba ex ore viri]].

paras.t: Et antequam patiatur contumeliam a proximo talis contentiosus, judicium deserit: id est, rectum rationis judicium atque discretionem relinquit primo, irrationabiliter aliis injuriando: de quo judicio scriptum est, Numquid qui non amat judicium, sanari potest? Deserit quoque judicium disceptationis, quia in foro contentioso coram judice refugit apparere ac respondere, conscius sibi de suo excessu in proximum: per quod ostenditur reus. Ideo Seneca in suis scribit Proverbiis: Fatetur facinus is qui judicium fugit; et rursus, Legem nocens veretur, fortunam innocens.
paras.en: [[17:14|And before he suffereth reproach|Et antequam patiatur contumeliam]] from his neighbour, such a contentious man [[17:14|forsaketh judgment|judicium deserit]]: that is, he first abandons the right judgment and discretion of reason, by unreasonably wronging others: of which judgment it is written: [[Job 34:17|Can he be healed that loveth not judgment|Numquid qui non amat judicium, sanari potest]]? He also forsakes the judgment of a hearing, because he shrinks from appearing and answering before the judge in a contested court, being conscious of his own excess against his neighbour: by which he is shown to be guilty. Therefore Seneca writes in his Proverbs: He who flees judgment confesses the crime; and again: The guilty man fears the law, the innocent fears fortune.

paras.t: Et qui justificat impium, id est, eum quem probabiliter scit esse reum, asserit esse justum; et qui condemnat justum, abominabilis est uterque apud Deum. Tales fuerunt Judaei petentes sibi Barabbam, tanquam Christo innocentiorem, dimitti, et Christum occidi. De talibus loquitur Deus in Ezechiele: Interfecerunt animas quæ non moriuntur, et vivificabant animas quæ non vivunt, mentientes propter pugillum hordei et fragmen panis. Tales sunt injusti prælati, in quibus regnat personarum acceptio, et prædicatores blandi, qui propter commoda sua veritatem relinquunt. Circa hæc posset grandis inquisitio fieri: quid agendum sit judici in foro judicii, dum innocens coram eo convincitur testibus et reus probatur, quem judex scit justum et innocentem. De qua quæstione super Exodum plenius scripsi, idcirco jam transeo.
paras.en: [[17:15|He that justifieth the wicked|Et qui justificat impium]], that is, who asserts that a man is just whom he knows, on good grounds, to be guilty; [[17:15|and he that condemneth the just|et qui condemnat justum]], [[17:15|both are abominable before God|abominabilis est uterque apud Deum]]. Such were the Jews, who asked that Barabbas be released to them, as more innocent than Christ, and that Christ be put to death[[Matt 27:21||]][[Matt 27:23||]]. Of such God speaks in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 13:19|to kill souls which should not die|Interfecerunt animas quæ non moriuntur]], [[Ezech 13:19|and to save souls alive which should not live|et vivificabant animas quæ non vivunt]], [[Ezech 13:19|telling lies|mentientes]] [[Ezech 13:19|for a handful of barley, and a piece of bread|propter pugillum hordei et fragmen panis]] [Denis gives the verse in his own order and wording: "they have slain souls … and made souls alive"]. Such are unjust prelates, in whom respect of persons reigns, and flattering preachers, who abandon the truth for their own advantage. On these things a great inquiry could be made: what a judge must do in court when an innocent man is convicted before him by witnesses and proved guilty, whom the judge knows to be just and innocent. I have written more fully of this question on Exodus[[Ex 23:7||]], and therefore pass over it now.

paras.t: Quid prodest habere divitias stulto, quum sapientiam emere non possit? quasi dicat: Homini vitioso magis obest quam prosit opulentia terrenorum, quum ea non utatur ad spiritualia charismata obtinenda: qua si bene uteretur, posset per opera misericordiæ, dona gratiæ sapientiamque acquirere. Nec istud ideo dictum est, quasi liceat spiritualia bona per temporalia comparare; sed metaphorice loquitur, sicut in Evangelio Dominus: Quare, inquiens, non dedisti pecuniam meam numulariis, et ego veniens accepissem utique quod meum est, cum usura? Itaque exteriores divitiæ sine interiori opulentia obsunt, et ingratum multisque peccatis obnoxium efficiunt hominem. Conformiter nihil prodest Judæis, et hæreticis, ac impiis Christianis, habere divitias Scripturarum, ingenium, sapientiam acquisitam copiamque verborum, quum Christum, qui est virtus et sapientia Dei Patris, non habeant. Hinc Cyrillus in suis testatur Proverbiis: Avaritia habet oculum, sed non visum; nam bonum diligit, et summum bonum (propter quod cetera suo modo appetibilia sunt) non agnoscit. Si igitur finem amabilium, verum et summum bonum, quæris, fuge aurum, sperne divitias, flammam exstingue cupiditatis. Non enim ditant, sed depauperant, dum animum vitiositate captivant. Quære virtutem, et summum bonum quod quæris, intus habes: thesaurus etenim summæ bonitatis, non nisi in amatoribus suis consistit.
paras.en: [[17:16|What doth it avail a fool to have riches, seeing he cannot buy wisdom|Quid prodest habere divitias stulto, quum sapientiam emere non possit]]? As if to say: wealth in earthly things harms a vicious man more than it profits him, since he does not use it to obtain spiritual gifts: if he used it well, he could acquire the gifts of grace and wisdom through works of mercy. Nor is this said as though it were lawful to buy spiritual goods with temporal ones; but he speaks metaphorically, as does the Lord in the Gospel: [[Luke 19:23|why|Quare]], saith he, [[Luke 19:23|didst thou not give my money|non dedisti pecuniam meam]] [[Matt 25:27|to the bankers: and at my coming I should have received my own with usury|numulariis, et ego veniens accepissem utique quod meum est, cum usura]]? So outward riches without inward wealth do harm, and make a man ungrateful and liable to many sins. In the same way it profits nothing to Jews, heretics and wicked Christians to have the riches of the Scriptures, talent, acquired wisdom and abundance of words, since they do not have Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God the Father[[1 Cor 1:24||]]. Hence Cyril testifies in his Proverbs: Avarice has an eye, but no sight; for it loves good, and does not know the highest good (for whose sake the other things are, in their own way, desirable). If then you seek the end of all lovable things, the true and highest good, flee gold, spurn riches, put out the flame of covetousness. For they do not enrich but impoverish, while they hold the mind captive by vice. Seek virtue, and you have within you the highest good that you seek: for the treasure of the highest goodness is found only in those who love it.

paras.t: Qui altam facit domum suam, id est, se ipsum aut suam cognationem superbe extollit, quærit ruinam, id est sui ipsius dejectionem: quia qui se exaltat, humiliabitur; et qui evitat discere ea quæ necessaria sunt ad salutem, vel ad victum habendum, incidit in mala, id est diversa et magna peccata atque pericula: quia, ut ait Apostolus, qui ignorat, ignorabitur. Imo, secundum Ambrosium, ignorantia talium est peccatum gravissimum, id est maxime periculosum. Qui enim ignorat quid vitare, quid facere teneatur, in omne malum præcipitatur. Attamen versus iste in Hebræo non continetur.
paras.en: [[17:16|He that maketh his house high|Qui altam facit domum suam]], that is, proudly exalts himself or his kindred, [[17:16|seeketh a downfall|quærit ruinam]], that is, his own casting down: because he [[Luke 14:11|that exalteth himself shall be humbled|qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]][[Luke 18:14||]]; [[17:16|and he that refuseth to learn|et qui evitat discere]] the things that are necessary for salvation, or for getting a living, [[17:16|shall fall into evils|incidit in mala]], that is, into various and great sins and dangers: because, as the Apostle says, if any man [[1 Cor 14:38|know not, he shall not be known|qui ignorat, ignorabitur]]. Indeed, according to Ambrose, ignorance of such things is a most grievous sin, that is, most dangerous. For he who does not know what he is bound to avoid and what to do is cast headlong into every evil. This verse, however, is not contained in the Hebrew.

paras.t: Omni tempore diligit Deum et proximum, qui amicus est, id est verus amator Dei et proximorum: non quod omni tempore actualiter diligat, sed omni tempore opportuno. Nec sic intelligendum est, quod habens caritatem, non possit eam amittere, aut amissam recuperare, recuperatamque denuo perdere, ut quidam finxerunt hæretici, allegantes illud Apostoli, Caritas nunquam excidit; sed ideo dicitur verus amator semper amare, quia ad veram et spiritualem spectat dilectionem, ut quantum in ea est, nusquam deficiat, quamvis ex libertate, mutabilitate et infirmitate sui subjecti, possit deficere et amitti. Juxta quem modum apud juristas, justitia definitur esse constans atque perpetua voluntas exhibendi unicuique quod ei debetur. Vel dicitur amicus omni diligere tempore, quia non solum tempore prosperitatis, sed et tempore amat adversitatis, in quo maxime innotescit an sit verus amator. Propter quod subditur: et frater in angustiis comprobatur, id est, in adversitatibus et indigentiis patet an quis fraternaliter diligat proximum suum: quia si tunc deserat eum, non est sincerus ejus amator. Ideo in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Si possides amicum, in tentatione posside eum, et ne facile credas ei te ipsum; est enim amicus secundum tempus suum, et non permanebit in die tribulationis. Sic quoque tempore persecutionis et adversitatis ostenditur, quis vere ac stabiliter diligat Deum. Unde de quibusdam ait Salvator, quod radices non habent, quia ad tempus credunt, et tempore tentationis, facta scilicet persecutione propter verbum Dei, recedunt. Præinductis autem de caritatis inviolatione, concordat quod Cassiodorus ait: Qui vere amicus est, omni tempore diligit: tormentum non separat, labor non lassat, thesaurus non superat, alienus amor non occupat. Hinc ait et Seneca: Amicos secundæ (id est prosperæ) res optime parant, adversæ certissime probant.
paras.en: [[17:17|He that is a friend|qui amicus est]] [[17:17|loveth at all times|Omni tempore diligit]] God and his neighbour [Denis's text adds *Deum et proximum*], that is, the true lover of God and of his neighbours: not that he loves in act at every moment, but at every fitting time. Nor is it to be understood that one who has charity cannot lose it, or recover it once lost, and lose it again once recovered, as certain heretics have imagined, alleging that saying of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 13:8|Charity never falleth away|Caritas nunquam excidit]]; but the true lover is said to love always because this belongs to true and spiritual love, that as far as lies in it, it should never fail, although through the freedom, changeableness and weakness of its subject it can fail and be lost. In the same manner, among the jurists, justice is defined as the constant and perpetual will to render to each what is due to him. Or a friend is said to love at all times because he loves not only in time of prosperity but also in time of adversity, in which it is chiefly made known whether he is a true lover. For which reason it is added: [[17:17|and a brother is proved in distress|et frater in angustiis comprobatur]], that is, in adversities and needs it is plain whether someone loves his neighbour as a brother: because if he deserts him then, he is not his sincere lover. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:7|If thou wouldst get a friend, try him before thou takest him, and do not credit him easily|Si possides amicum, in tentatione posside eum, et ne facile credas ei te ipsum]] [Denis's text reads "If thou hast a friend, possess him in temptation, and do not easily trust thyself to him"]; [[Ecclus 6:8|For there is a friend for his own occasion, and he will not abide in the day of thy trouble|est enim amicus secundum tempus suum, et non permanebit in die tribulationis]]. So too, in time of persecution and adversity it is shown who loves God truly and steadfastly. Whence the Saviour says of some that they [[Luke 8:13|have no roots|radices non habent]], because [[Luke 8:13|they believe for a while|ad tempus credunt]], and in the time of temptation, that is, when [[Matt 13:21|persecution because of the word|persecutione propter verbum Dei]] has arisen, they [[Luke 8:13|fall away|recedunt]]. With what has been said above of the inviolability of charity agrees what Cassiodorus says: He who is truly a friend loves at all times: torment does not part him, toil does not weary him, treasure does not overcome him, another's love does not take his place. Hence Seneca too says: Favourable (that is, prosperous) circumstances best make friends, adverse ones most surely prove them.

paras.t: Homo stultus plaudet manibus, id est, mente gaudet, et signa lætitiæ foris ostendit, quum spoponderit pro amico, id est proximo suo, quasi exsultans se tantæ esse reputationis, quod creditur ei pro alio, et æstimans se magnum quid perpetrasse, non advertens quanto periculo se ipsum subjecit spondendo pro alio, nec sollicitus de satisfactione, prout dictum est super illud, Fili mi, si spoponderis pro amico tuo.
paras.en: [[17:18|A foolish man will clap hands|Homo stultus plaudet manibus]], that is, he rejoices in mind and shows signs of gladness outwardly, [[17:18|when he is surety for his friend|quum spoponderit pro amico]], that is, for his neighbour, as if exulting that he is of such repute that he is trusted for another, and thinking he has done some great thing, not noticing to how great a danger he has subjected himself by going surety for another, nor careful about making payment, as was said on the words: [[Prov 6:1|My son, if thou be surety for thy friend|Fili mi, si spoponderis pro amico tuo]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter autem loquendo, multi jam sunt prorsus stultissimi, qui quum curam acceperint animarum, plaudunt manibus, non pensantes quod adstrinxerint se ad reddendum rationem Judici summo pro animabus eorum, quorum sibi curam assumpserunt; nec pro illorum salute agentes quidquid tenentur, sed sola temporalia commoda, propriumque honorem adspicientes ac intendentes.
paras.en: Speaking spiritually, there are many today who are utterly foolish, who, when they have received the care of souls, clap their hands, not weighing that they have bound themselves to render an account to the supreme Judge for the souls of those whose care they have taken upon themselves[[Heb 13:17||]]; nor doing all they are bound to do for their salvation, but looking to and aiming at temporal advantages alone and their own honour.

paras.t: Qui meditatur discordias, id est, intra se excogitat qualiter inter alios possit discordias seminare, diligit rixas: quæ ex discordiis oriuntur. Ideo, sicut pacifici sunt beati, et filii Dei vocantur; sic talis turbator est miser, filiusque diaboli merito nuncupatur. Et qui exaltat os suum, animose seu jactanter loquendo, vel se ipsum laudando, aut verba injuriosa contra alios proferendo; quærit ruinam, id est propriam improbitatem, perversitatem, et mala pœnalia ad suam iniquitatem sequentia: quæ dicitur quærere, quoniam quærit ea quibus illa annexa sunt, sicut qui furatur, quærit suspendi: et talia, secundum Philosophum, quæruntur præter intentionem et indirecte.
paras.en: [[17:19|He that studieth discords|Qui meditatur discordias]], that is, who thinks out within himself how he may sow discords among others, [[17:19|loveth quarrels|diligit rixas]], which arise from discords. Therefore, as the peacemakers are blessed and are called the children of God[[Matt 5:9||]], so such a troublemaker is wretched, and is rightly called a son of the devil. [[17:19|And he that exalteth|Et qui exaltat]] his mouth [Denis's text reads *os suum*, "his mouth", where the Vulgate has *ostium*, "door"], by speaking boldly or boastfully, or by praising himself, or by uttering injurious words against others, [[17:19|seeketh ruin|quærit ruinam]], that is, his own wickedness, perversity, and the penal evils that follow upon his iniquity: which he is said to seek, since he seeks the things to which they are joined, as he who steals seeks to be hanged: and such things, according to the Philosopher, are sought beside one's intention and indirectly.

paras.t: Qui perversi cordis est, utpote a Deo aversus, et in malitia habituatus, non invenit bonum, id est pacem, gratiam, aut salutem. Imo in se ipso divisus est, et ratio sensualitati suæ subjicitur: contra quod synderesis murmurat, et conscientia habet remorsum. Idcirco, teste Philosopho, homo vitiosus, nec ad se ipsum neque ad alterum amicitiam habet veram. Et qui vertit linguam, loquendo secundum favorem et affectionem, non secundum rationem et veritatem; sicut qui blanditur in facie, et retro pungit; incidit in malum peccati atque supplicii, et frequenter incurrit diffamiam, dum linguæ suæ duplicitas innotescit.
paras.en: [[17:20|He that is of a perverse heart|Qui perversi cordis est]], being turned away from God and settled in malice, [[17:20|shall not find good|non invenit bonum]], that is, peace, grace or salvation. Rather, he is divided within himself, and his reason is subjected to his sensuality: against which synderesis [that is, the natural habit of the first principles of moral action, the spark of conscience] murmurs, and conscience feels remorse. Therefore, as the Philosopher witnesses, a vicious man has no true friendship either towards himself or towards another. [[17:20|And he that perverteth his tongue|Et qui vertit linguam]], speaking according to favour and affection, not according to reason and truth, like him who flatters to one's face and stings behind one's back, [[17:20|shall fall into evil|incidit in malum]] of sin and of punishment, and often incurs ill fame, when the doubleness of his tongue becomes known.

paras.t: Natus est stultus in ignominia sua: id est, ad suam nativitatem consequitur despectio sua, quia ob suam iniquitatem et fatuitatem juste contemnitur, in quantum talis, non in quantum homo. Sed nec pater in fatuo lætabitur: quia de insipientia et perversitate iniqui aut stolidi filii contristatur, si bonus sit pater. Similiter pater spiritualis de inobediente subdito mœret.
paras.en: [[17:21|A fool is born to his own disgrace|Natus est stultus in ignominia sua]]: that is, his being despised follows upon his birth, because on account of his wickedness and folly he is justly despised, in so far as he is such, not in so far as he is a man. [[17:21|And even his father shall not rejoice in a fool|Sed nec pater in fatuo lætabitur]]: because he is saddened by the folly and perversity of a wicked or stupid son, if he is a good father. Likewise a spiritual father mourns over a disobedient subject.

paras.t: Animus gaudens ætatem floridam facit: quia interior lætitia redundat in corpus, facitque hominem cum jucunditate tempus suum expendere, atque ad floridam pertingere senectutem, nisi aliunde occurrat abbreviatio vitæ. Hinc in Ecclesiastico legitur: Jucunditas cordis, hæc est vita hominis. Similiter qui gloriatur in Domino, Sanctique Spiritus consolatione assidue recreatur, vitam suam cum floribus actuum virtuosorum deducit, interiorque refloritio mentis in Deo relucet in corpore suo et apparatu externo. Unde in libro Judith dicitur: Erat populus jucundus secundum faciem sanctorum. Et Lucas ait, quod Ecclesia per totam Judæam et Galilæam et Samariam habebat pacem, et ædificabatur ambulans in timore Domini, et consolatione Spiritus Sancti replebatur. Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa. Inordinata namque et sæcularis tristitia, quæ est passio vitiosa de damno temporali seu adversitate, est valde pœnalis, corrosivaque cordis, complexionem distemperans et vitam abbrevians. Ideo ait Apostolus: Tristitia sæculi mortem operatur. Et in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Tristitiam non des animæ tuæ; multos enim occidit tristitia, et non est utilitas in ea. Quæ autem secundum Deum tristitia est, utpote ordinata, ex consideratione proprii vel alieni peccati, vel alia rationabili causa descendens, vitam gratiæ in salutem stabilem operatur. De qua in Ecclesiaste asseritur: Cor sapientium ubi tristitia.
paras.en: [[17:22|A joyful mind maketh age flourishing|Animus gaudens ætatem floridam facit]]: because inward gladness overflows into the body, and makes a man spend his time with pleasure, and reach a flourishing old age, unless a shortening of life comes from some other cause. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:23|The joyfulness of the heart, is the life of a man|Jucunditas cordis, hæc est vita hominis]]. Likewise he who glories in the Lord and is continually refreshed by the consolation of the Holy Spirit leads his life with the flowers of virtuous deeds, and the inward reflowering of the mind in God shines out again in his body and outward bearing. Whence it is said in the book of Judith: [[Jdt 16:24|And the people were joyful in the sight of the sanctuary|Erat populus jucundus secundum faciem sanctorum]]. And Luke says that [[Acts 9:31|the church had peace throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria: and was edified, walking in the fear of the Lord: and was filled with the consolation of the Holy Ghost|Ecclesia per totam Judæam et Galilæam et Samariam habebat pacem, et ædificabatur ambulans in timore Domini, et consolatione Spiritus Sancti replebatur]]. [[17:22|A sorrowful spirit drieth up the bones|Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa]]. For disordered and worldly sorrow, which is a vicious passion about temporal loss or adversity, is very painful and eats away the heart, upsetting the temperament [that is, the balance of the bodily humours] and shortening life. Therefore the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 7:10|the sorrow of the world worketh death|Tristitia sæculi mortem operatur]]. And it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 30:22|Give not up thy soul to sadness|Tristitiam non des animæ tuæ]]; [[Ecclus 30:25|For sadness hath killed many, and there is no profit in it|multos enim occidit tristitia, et non est utilitas in ea]]. But [[2 Cor 7:10|the sorrow that is according to God|Quæ autem secundum Deum tristitia est]], being ordered, and coming from the consideration of one's own sin or another's, or from some other reasonable cause, works the life of grace [[2 Cor 7:10|steadfast unto salvation|in salutem stabilem]]. Of this it is asserted in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:5|The heart of the wise is where there is mourning|Cor sapientium ubi tristitia]].

paras.t: Munera de sinu impius accipit, id est, judex injustus occulte accipit dona, ut pervertat semitas judicii, id est processum et ordinem juris, per quos ad justum pervenitur judicium: quod quam vitiosum sit et vitandum, dictum est supra.
paras.en: [[17:23|The wicked man taketh gifts out of the bosom|Munera de sinu impius accipit]], that is, an unjust judge secretly accepts gifts, [[17:23|that he may pervert the paths of judgment|ut pervertat semitas judicii]], that is, the process and order of law, by which a just judgment is reached: how vicious this is and how much to be avoided has been said above.

paras.t: In facie prudentis lucet sapientia: id est, interior sapientia mentis resplendet in vultu, per morum compositionem, oculorum custodiam, maturitatemque vultus: in quo tanquam in fronte pudoris, et exteriorum sensuum loco, præsertim resultat ac representatur dispositio cordis. Ideo in Ecclesiastico dicitur: Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus. Hinc Seneca: Formosa, inquit, facies, occulta commendatio est. Unde de multis legitur Sanctis, quod interioris sanctitatis ac gratiæ affluentia, in eorum vultibus mirabiliter fulsit: quod maxime fuit in Christo. Nihilo minus quidam hypocritæ et versuti frequenter prætendunt maturitatem ac sapientiæ signa in facie, quum intus pleni sint simulatione ac vanitate. De quibus monet Salvator: Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis, qui veniunt ad vos in vestimentis ovium, intrinsecus autem sunt lupi rapaces. Sunt ergo et alia certiora signa sapientiæ, scilicet conversatio virtuosa. Nec enim dicendus est sapiens, in quo a notitia dissonat vita. Oculi stultorum in finibus terræ: quia undique evagantur, et ad suæ vanitatis objecta insipientissime diriguntur; et quanta est instabilitas cordis in apprehendendo, imaginando et appetendo, tanta est evagatio oculorum ac ceterorum incustodia sensuum. Ideo sancti Patres testati sunt, quod incustoditus visus, incustoditæ mentis sit nuntius. Porro in divino Officio præcipue reprimendi sunt oculi; nec ibi, imo nec alibi incaute aut morose est intuendum, quod male accendere potest affectum.
paras.en: [[17:24|Wisdom shineth in the face of the wise|In facie prudentis lucet sapientia]]: that is, the inward wisdom of the mind shines out in the countenance, through composure of manners, custody of the eyes and gravity of look: in which, as in the seat of modesty and the place of the outward senses, the disposition of the heart is especially reflected and represented. Therefore it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:26|A man is known by his look, and a wise man, when thou meetest him, is known by his countenance|Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus]]. Hence Seneca says: A beautiful face is a silent recommendation. Whence we read of many Saints that the abundance of inward holiness and grace shone wonderfully in their faces: which was so above all in Christ. Nevertheless some hypocrites and crafty men often put on a show of gravity and signs of wisdom in their faces, while within they are full of pretence and vanity. Of whom the Saviour warns: [[Matt 7:15|Beware of false prophets, who come to you in the clothing of sheep, but inwardly they are ravening wolves|Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis, qui veniunt ad vos in vestimentis ovium, intrinsecus autem sunt lupi rapaces]]. There are therefore other, surer signs of wisdom, namely a virtuous way of life. For he is not to be called wise in whom life is out of tune with knowledge. [[17:24|The eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth|Oculi stultorum in finibus terræ]]: because they wander everywhere, and are most foolishly directed to the objects of their vanity; and as great as is the instability of the heart in apprehending, imagining and desiring, so great is the wandering of the eyes and the want of custody of the other senses. Therefore the holy Fathers have testified that unguarded sight is the messenger of an unguarded mind. Moreover, the eyes are to be restrained above all in the divine Office; neither there, nor indeed anywhere else, should one look heedlessly or lingeringly at what can wrongly kindle the affections.

paras.t: Ira patris, filius stultus, et dolor matris quæ genuit eum: id est, de pravitate, indisciplinatione et stultitia filii insipientis, irascitur pater, tam spiritualis quam carnalis; et de eadem causa mater pia tristatur, tam mater carnalis quam mater Ecclesia.
paras.en: [[17:25|A foolish son is the anger of the father: and the sorrow of the mother that bore him|Ira patris, filius stultus, et dolor matris quæ genuit eum]]: that is, at the depravity, indiscipline and folly of an unwise son the father is angry, spiritual as well as carnal; and for the same cause the loving mother is sad, the carnal mother as well as Mother Church.

paras.t: Non est bonum, damnum inferre justo, id est persecutionem, mortem, detractionem, rapinam aut furtum: imo hoc pessimum est, et pejus quam si inferantur injusto; nec percutere principem percussione corporali aut spirituali: de qua ait Apostolus, Peccantes in fratres, et percutientes conscientiam eorum infirmam, in Christum peccatis; qui recta judicat. Imo nec princeps injustus a subditis est percutiendus. Unde Paulus in Actibus allegat id legis: Principi populi tui non maledices. Moyses quoque: Diis, inquit, id est judicibus, non detrahes.
paras.en: [[17:26|It is no good thing to do hurt to the just|Non est bonum, damnum inferre justo]], that is, persecution, death, detraction, robbery or theft: indeed this is the worst, and worse than if they are inflicted on the unjust; [[17:26|nor to strike the prince|nec percutere principem]] with a bodily or a spiritual blow: of which the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 8:12|sin thus against the brethren and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ|Peccantes in fratres, et percutientes conscientiam eorum infirmam, in Christum peccatis]] [[17:26|who judgeth right|qui recta judicat]]. Indeed not even an unjust prince is to be struck by his subjects. Whence Paul in the Acts cites this from the law: [[Acts 23:5|Thou shalt not speak evil of the prince of thy people|Principi populi tui non maledices]][[Ex 22:28||]]. Moses also: [[Ex 22:28|Thou shalt not speak ill of|non detrahes]] [[Ex 22:28|the gods|Diis]], he says, that is, the judges.

paras.t: Qui moderatur sermones suos, loquendo utilia atque salubria, loco et tempore opportuno, ac mensurate, non excedendo notabiliter, magis aut minus quam decet loquendo: doctus et prudens est. Doctus est enim a Spiritu Sancto, etiamsi litteraturam ignoret: estque discretus et magnæ perfectionis, quia si quis in verbo non offendit, hic perfectus est vir. Hinc in Proverbiis suis Seneca scripsit: Imago animi est sermo. Qualis vir, talis et oratio (id est locutio) ejus; itemque, Tene semper vocis et silentii temperamentum. Et pretiosi spiritus vir eruditus.
paras.en: [[17:27|He that setteth bounds to his words|Qui moderatur sermones suos]], speaking useful and wholesome things, at a fitting place and time, and in measure, not going notably too far by speaking more or less than is fitting, [[17:27|is knowing and wise|doctus et prudens est]]. For he is taught by the Holy Spirit, even if he does not know letters; and he is discreet and of great perfection, because [[Jas 3:2|If any man offend not in word, the same is a perfect man|si quis in verbo non offendit, hic perfectus est vir]]. Hence Seneca wrote in his Proverbs: Speech is the image of the mind. As the man is, so is his speech (that is, his talk); and again: Always keep a due measure of speech and of silence. [[17:27|and the man of understanding is of a precious spirit|Et pretiosi spiritus vir eruditus]].

paras.t: Stultus quoque si tacuerit inter homines colloquentes, sapiens reputabitur, id est, quantum ad hoc, aliquid sapientiæ videtur prætendere et habere, ac signum sapientiæ possidere, quod sic tacet. Stultus enim, ut alibi legitur, verba multiplicat. Ignorantes quoque stultitiam ejus, putabunt quod sapiens sit, eo quod taceat, adscribentes taciturnitatem ipsius maturitati et timori sapientiali.
paras.en: [[17:28|Even a fool, if he will hold his peace|Stultus quoque si tacuerit]] among men in conversation, [[17:28|shall be counted wise|sapiens reputabitur]], that is, in this respect he seems to show and to have something of wisdom, and to possess a sign of wisdom, in that he is silent. For, as we read elsewhere, [[Eccles 10:14|A fool multiplieth words|Stultus enim, ut alibi legitur, verba multiplicat]] [the margin gives only "v. 14"; the words are Eccles 10:14]. Those too who do not know his folly will think he is wise because he is silent, ascribing his silence to gravity and to the fear that belongs to wisdom.

paras.t: Et si compresserit labia sua, reprimendo ea a prolatione conceptæ locutionis, ne erumpat in stolida, superflua aut impertinentia verba: quæ compressio multis difficilis est, juxta illud, Conceptum sermonem tenere quis poterit? Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur: Sagitta infixa femori canis, sic verbum in corde stulti. reputabitur. Intelligens. Hinc apud Job dicitur: Utinam taceretis, ut putaretis esse sapientes. Et Seneca contestatur: Taciturnitas stulto homini pro sapientia est. Et Cyrillus in suis ait Proverbiis: Avarus sis verbi, et audi libenter. Hoc est quod Jacobus ait apostolus: Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus vero ad loquendum. Hoc mali et garruli non observant. Nam, ut ait Gregorius, Pravi sicut in sensu sunt leves, ita in locutione præcipites: quia quod levis mens concipit, levior lingua protinus prodit.
paras.en: [[17:28|And if he close his lips|Et si compresserit labia sua]], holding them back from uttering the speech he has conceived, lest he burst out into stupid, superfluous or irrelevant words: which holding back is hard for many, according to the saying: [[Job 4:2|who can withhold the words he hath conceived|Conceptum sermonem tenere quis poterit]]? Whence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:12|As an arrow that sticketh in a man's thigh: so is a word in the heart of a fool|Sagitta infixa femori canis, sic verbum in corde stulti]] [Denis's text reads "the thigh of a dog", *canis* for *carnis*]. He shall be counted [[17:28|a man of understanding|Intelligens]] [the lemma's last words stand here in the printed text, "reputabitur. Intelligens"]. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 13:5|I wish you would hold your peace, that you might be thought to be wise men|Utinam taceretis, ut putaretis esse sapientes]]. And Seneca bears witness: Silence stands a foolish man in place of wisdom. And Cyril says in his Proverbs: Be a miser of words, and listen gladly. This is what the apostle James says: [[Jas 1:19|let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak|Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus vero ad loquendum]]. This the wicked and the talkative do not observe. For, as Gregory says, the depraved, as they are light in mind, so are they headlong in speech: because what a light mind conceives, a lighter tongue at once brings forth.

18.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI OCTAVIDECIMI : OCCASIONES QUÆRIT, QUI VULT RECEDERE AB AMICO.
18.title_en: Explanation of the eighteenth chapter: He that hath a mind to depart from a friend, seeketh occasions.

paras.t: Occasiones quærit, qui vult recedere ab amico spirituali recessu : id est, qui cupit amicum relinquere, et amicitiam ejus sine justa ratione dimittere, excogitat calumnias contra amicum, et allegat non causam pro causa. Omni tempore erit execrabilis, qui hoc agit, nisi vere pœniteat, quoniam amicitiam falsat ac violat : quod tanto pejus est quam falsare pecuniam, quanto amicitia melior est quam pecunia, sicut octavo Ethicorum ait Philosophus. Istud tamen intelligendum est de vera amicitia, quæ in bono honesto fundatur : quæ, ut Tullius ait in libro de Amicitia, sola est amicitia vera ac virtuosa. Quæ autem fundatur in bono delectabili, qualis solet esse amicitia juvenum qui voluptatem sequuntur, vel in bono utili, qualis est amicitia senum qui utilitatem sectantur; sæpe utiliter frangitur, prout de hac materia octavo Ethicorum plenius pertractatur. Sit ergo amicitia nostra constans. Verum inter homines passionatos et iracundos, non potest esse amicitia stabilis, quia faciliter offendunt ac offenduntur, prout in secundo Collationum volumine plenarie Cassianus disserit. Sed, ut tangit Hieronymus, Vera est illa amicitia, et Christi glutino copulata, quam non utilitas rei familiaris, non corporum præsentia aut voluptas, non subdola et palpans adulatio, non conformitas vanitatum, sed timor Dei, similitudo affectuum ad virtutes ac divinarum studia Scripturarum conciliant.
paras.en: [[18:1|He that hath a mind to depart from a friend, seeketh occasions|Occasiones quærit, qui vult recedere ab amico]] by a withdrawal of the spirit [that is, in heart and affection, not in place]: that is, he who desires to leave a friend, and to give up his friendship without just reason, thinks up false charges against the friend, and alleges as a cause what is no cause. [[18:1|he shall ever be subject to reproach|Omni tempore erit execrabilis]] [Denis's text has *execrabilis*, "accursed"; the margin gives the reading *exprobrabilis*, "subject to reproach", which is the Vulgate's] who does this, unless he truly repents, because he falsifies and violates friendship: which is as much worse than falsifying money as friendship is better than money, as the Philosopher says in the eighth book of the *Ethics*. This, however, is to be understood of true friendship, which is founded on the honest good [that is, the good of virtue, loved for its own sake]: which, as Tully says in his book *On Friendship*, is alone true and virtuous friendship. But friendship that is founded on the pleasant good, such as the friendship of young men who follow pleasure usually is, or on the useful good, such as is the friendship of old men who pursue advantage, is often broken with profit, as is treated more fully of this matter in the eighth book of the *Ethics*. Let our friendship, then, be constant. But among men who are ruled by their passions and given to anger there cannot be stable friendship, because they easily give offence and take offence, as Cassian discusses at full length in the second volume of the *Conferences*. But, as Jerome touches on it, that is true friendship, and bound with the glue of Christ, which is brought about not by advantage in household affairs, not by bodily presence or pleasure, not by crafty and fawning flattery, not by likeness in vanities, but by the fear of God, likeness of affections towards the virtues, and the study of the divine Scriptures.

paras.t: Non recipit stultus verba prudentiæ : id est, exhortationibus et doctrinis sapientialibus atque salubribus non acquiescit, nec eas libenter audit, quia non sapiunt sibi, quum per habitus vitiosos ad contraria inclinetur. Ideo talibus dixit Salvator : Sermo meus non capit in vobis. Et in Ecclesiastico legitur : Cor stulti quasi vas confractum, et omnem sapientiam non retinebit. Nisi ea dixeris quæ versantur in corde ejus : id est, nulla locutio ei placebit, nisi quæ suis inanibus cogitationibus et pravis affectibus consonat. Verumtamen per prævenientem Dei gratiam, interdum contingit vanos impiosque per prudentem sermonem converti. Aliqui quoque, quamvis adhuc vitiosi, tamen libenter audiunt aliquid boni, et compunguntur ad horam. De quibus asserit Dominus : Cum gaudio suscipiunt verbum; et radices non habent, quia ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt.
paras.en: [[18:2|A fool receiveth not the words of prudence|Non recipit stultus verba prudentiæ]]: that is, he does not assent to wise and wholesome exhortations and teachings, nor listen to them gladly, because they have no savour for him [*non sapiunt sibi*: they do not taste good to him, with a play on *sapientia*, wisdom], since through vicious habits he is inclined to the contrary. Therefore the Saviour said to such men: [[John 8:37|my word hath no place in you|Sermo meus non capit in vobis]]. And in Ecclesiasticus we read: [[Ecclus 21:17|The heart of a fool is like a broken vessel, and no wisdom at all shall it hold|Cor stulti quasi vas confractum, et omnem sapientiam non retinebit]]. [[18:2|unless thou say those things which are in his heart|Nisi ea dixeris quæ versantur in corde ejus]]: that is, no speech will please him except what accords with his empty thoughts and wicked affections. Nevertheless, through the prevenient grace of God [that is, the grace that goes before and moves the will before any merit], it sometimes happens that vain and wicked men are converted by a prudent word. Some too, although still given to vice, nevertheless gladly hear something good, and are pricked to compunction for an hour. Of these the Lord declares: they [[Luke 8:13|receive the word with joy|Cum gaudio suscipiunt verbum]]; [[Luke 8:13|and these have no roots: for they believe for a while and in time of temptation they fall away|et radices non habent, quia ad tempus credunt, et in tempore tentationis recedunt]].

paras.t: Impius quum in profundum venerit peccatorum, id est, vitiorum voragine fuerit mersus, et prava consuetudine induratus; contemnit verba salubria, correptionem et correctionem : sicut in Genesi patet de Sodomitis, qui pie correpti a Lot, dixerunt : Habitare venisti, non leges dare; te ipsum ergo magis affligemus. Ideo orat Propheta : Neque absorbeat me profundum, neque urgeat super me puteus os suum. Hinc loquitur Augustinus : Peccata quamvis enormia et horrenda, quum in consuetudinem venerint, aut parva aut nulla esse videntur, in tantum ut non solum non occultanda, verum etiam prædicanda jactandaque videantur. Attamen de talibus non est penitus desperandum, quia ab omnipotenti animarum medico possunt curari, ut patuit in Manasse. Sed sequitur eum ignominia et opprobrium : quia in præsenti vita frequenter contemnitur talis, et opprobrium æternæ damnationis non evadit. De quo in Daniele legitur : Evigilabunt alii in vitam æternam, alii in opprobrium, ut videant semper.
paras.en: [[18:3|The wicked man, when he is come into the depths of sins|Impius quum in profundum venerit peccatorum]], that is, when he has been plunged into the whirlpool of vices and hardened by evil habit, [[18:3|contemneth|contemnit]] wholesome words, rebuke and correction: as is plain in Genesis of the Sodomites, who, when Lot dutifully rebuked them[[Gen 19:7||]], said: Thou camest to dwell here, not to give laws; [[Gen 19:9|therefore we will afflict thee more|te ipsum ergo magis affligemus]] [Denis gives the first words loosely; the margin gives Gen. xix, 7-9]. Therefore the Prophet prays: [[Ps 68:16|nor the deep water swallow me up: and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me|Neque absorbeat me profundum, neque urgeat super me puteus os suum]]. Hence Augustine says: Sins, however enormous and horrible, once they have become habitual, seem either small or nothing, so much so that they seem not only not to be hidden, but even to be proclaimed and boasted of. Yet of such men we must not utterly despair, because they can be cured by the almighty Physician of souls, as was seen in Manasses[[2 Par 33:12||]]. [[18:3|but ignominy and reproach follow him|Sed sequitur eum ignominia et opprobrium]]: because in the present life such a man is often despised, and he does not escape the reproach of eternal damnation. Of which we read in Daniel: [[Dan 12:2|shall awake: some unto life everlasting, and others unto reproach, to see it always|Evigilabunt alii in vitam æternam, alii in opprobrium, ut videant semper]].

paras.t: Aqua profunda, verba ex ore viri : id est, verba sapientialia a viro illuminato et perfecto prolata, assimilantur aquæ profundæ ad cujus fundum non est facile pervenire : sic verba hujusmodi non possunt a simplicibus et pusillis plenarie comprehendi. Propter quod dixit Apostolus : Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Eliu quoque inquit : Viri sapientes, audite verba mea, et viri eruditi, auscultate me. Et torrens redundans, fons sapientiæ. Hoc de Christo potissime verificatur, qui est fons sapientiæ universæ, et opulentissimo atque plenissimo comparatur torrenti. Unde in Psalmo cantatur : Torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos; itemque, Fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei. Propterea protestatur Dominus per Isaiam : Ecce ego declinabo in eos ut flumen pacis, et ut torrens inundans gloriæ gentium. Potest etiam de quocumque viro sapiente exponi, in cujus mente, fons sapientiæ est ipsum habituale sapientiæ donum, et copiosa doctrina : ex quo dono atque doctrina, tanquam ex fonte, procedunt rivuli documentorum sapientialium verborum, quemadmodum ex torrente prodeunt aquæ fluenta. Hinc Veritas ait : Aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam. Tales fontes fuerunt præsertim gloriosi Apostoli. De quibus in Psalmo : In ecclesiis benedicite Deo Domino de fontibus Israel. De quibus cecinit et Isaias : Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris.
paras.en: [[18:4|Words from the mouth of a man are as deep water|Aqua profunda, verba ex ore viri]]: that is, words of wisdom uttered by an enlightened and perfect man are likened to deep water, whose bottom it is not easy to reach: so words of this kind cannot be fully grasped by the simple and the little ones. For this reason the Apostle said: [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect|Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos]]. Eliu too says: [[Job 34:2|Hear ye, wise men, my words, and ye learned, hearken to me|Viri sapientes, audite verba mea, et viri eruditi, auscultate me]]. [[18:4|and the fountain of wisdom is an overflowing stream|Et torrens redundans, fons sapientiæ]]. This is verified above all of Christ, who is the fountain of all wisdom, and is compared to a most abundant and most full torrent. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 35:9|thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure|Torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos]]; and again, [[Ps 45:5|The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful|Fluminis impetus lætificat civitatem Dei]]. Therefore the Lord declares by Isaias: [[Is 66:12|Behold I will bring upon her as it were a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent the glory of the Gentiles|Ecce ego declinabo in eos ut flumen pacis, et ut torrens inundans gloriæ gentium]] [Denis has *upon them* where the Vulgate has *upon her*]. It can also be expounded of any wise man, in whose mind the fountain of wisdom is the habitual gift of wisdom itself, and abundant learning: from which gift and learning, as from a fountain, proceed the rivulets of wise teachings and words, just as streams of water flow out of a torrent. Hence the Truth says: [[John 4:14|the water that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting|Aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam]]. Such fountains were above all the glorious Apostles. Of whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 67:27|In the churches bless ye God the Lord, from the fountains of Israel|In ecclesiis benedicite Deo Domino de fontibus Israel]]. Of whom Isaias too sang: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]].

paras.t: Accipere personam impii in judicio, non est bonum : imo pessimum est, et contra divina præcepta, ac valde mortale peccatum, et partis alterius damnificativum. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Usquequo judicatis iniquitatem, et facies peccatorum sumitis? Hinc Dominus jussit : Juste judicabis, nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis. Ideo dicit Ambrosius : Inter omnia peccata præsidentium maximum est, quod non causas, sed personas considerant. Denique, sicut in secunda secundæ, quæstione 63, Thomas inducit, personarum acceptio opponitur justitiæ distributivæ, quæ tribuit diversis personis secundum earum dignitatem ac merita. Ideo acceptio personarum committitur, dum alicui aliquid datur vel adjudicatur, non propter ipsius dignitatem aut meritum, seu rationabilem causam, sed propter ipsius personam, et ob id propter quod illud ei non debetur. Itaque qui in judicio accipit personam, tenetur ad restitutionem ei cui injuste infert damnum. Ut declines a veritate judicii.
paras.en: [[18:5|It is not good to accept the person of the wicked|Accipere personam impii in judicio, non est bonum]] in judgment [*in judicio*: Denis's addition to the lemma]: nay, it is very bad, and against the divine precepts, and a grievously mortal sin, and does harm to the other party. For this reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 81:2|How long will you judge unjustly: and accept the persons of the wicked?|Usquequo judicatis iniquitatem, et facies peccatorum sumitis?]] Hence the Lord commanded: [[Lev 19:15|judge thy neighbour according to justice|Juste judicabis]], [[Lev 19:15|Respect not the person of the poor: nor honour the countenance of the mighty|nec consideres personam pauperis, neque honores vultum potentis]]. Therefore Ambrose says: Among all the sins of those who preside, the greatest is that they consider not the causes but the persons. Lastly, as Thomas brings out in the *Secunda secundæ*, question 63, respect of persons is opposed to distributive justice [that is, the justice that gives to each according to his worth], which allots to different persons according to their dignity and merits. Therefore respect of persons is committed when something is given or adjudged to someone, not on account of his dignity or merit, or some reasonable cause, but on account of his person, and so on account of that by which it is not owed to him. And so he who respects the person in judgment is bound to make restitution to him whom he unjustly harms. [[18:5|to decline from the truth of judgment|Ut declines a veritate judicii]].

paras.t: Labia stulti miscent se rixis aliorum, quos magis concordare deberent, exemplo Moysis, qui litigantibus dixit : Viri, fratres estis : ut quid nocetis alterutrum? Et os ejus, scilicet stulti, jurgia provocat per verba et facta injuriosa et improba.
paras.en: [[18:6|The lips of a fool intermeddle with strife|Labia stulti miscent se rixis]] of others, whom they ought rather to bring to agreement, after the example of Moses, who said to those at strife: [[Acts 7:26|Men, ye are brethren. Why hurt you one another?|Viri, fratres estis : ut quid nocetis alterutrum?]] [[18:6|and his mouth|Et os ejus]], namely the fool's, [[18:6|provoketh quarrels|jurgia provocat]] by injurious and wicked words and deeds.

paras.t: Os stulti, contritio ejus : id est, per abusum oris sui, videlicet per verba detractoria, pungitiva, mendosa, contentiosa, aut alio modo criminaliter vitiosa, occidit spiritualiter animam suam, juxta illud : Os quod mentitur, occidit animam. Imo quandoque corporalem incurrit interitum. Et labia ipsius, id est verba illicita per labia ejus prolata, sunt ruina animæ ejus : per quæ tandem corruit in infernum.
paras.en: [[18:7|The mouth of a fool is his destruction|Os stulti, contritio ejus]]: that is, by the abuse of his mouth, namely by words that detract, sting, lie, quarrel, or are in some other way grievously sinful, he kills his soul spiritually, according to that saying: [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os quod mentitur, occidit animam]]. Nay, sometimes he brings on himself bodily death as well. [[18:7|and his lips|Et labia ipsius]], that is, the unlawful words uttered by his lips, [[18:7|are the ruin of his soul|sunt ruina animæ ejus]]: by which at last he falls headlong into hell.

paras.t: Verba bilinguis, quasi simplicia : id est, bilinguis, qui aliter loquitur in absentia, aliterque in præsentia ejus de quo loquitur, ita colorat, ornat, et linit verba sua, quasi nihil dolositatis ac duplicitatis in eis exsistat : et ipsa perveniunt usque ad interiora ventris, id est, magna et intima damna infligunt, et viscera animæ lædunt.
paras.en: [[18:8|The words of the double tongued are as if they were harmless|Verba bilinguis, quasi simplicia]]: that is, the double-tongued man, who speaks one way in the absence and another in the presence of him of whom he speaks, so colours, adorns and smooths over his words as though there were no guile or doubleness in them: [[18:8|and they reach even to the inner parts of the bowels|et ipsa perveniunt usque ad interiora ventris]], that is, they inflict great and inward harm, and wound the bowels of the soul.

paras.t: Pigrum dejicit timor, id est, inordinatus, mundanus, carnalis timor revocat pigrum ab opere bono : a quo faciliter retrahi se permittit, sicut et infra habetur : Dicit piger, Leo est in via. Anima autem effeminatorum, id est mollium atque debilium, ad femineam mollitiem collapsorum, esurient, id est, bonis spiritualibus, et interdum etiam temporalibus indigebunt, sicut præhabitum est : Manus remissa operata est egestatem.
paras.en: [[18:8|Fear casteth down the slothful|Pigrum dejicit timor]], that is, inordinate, worldly, carnal fear calls the slothful man back from good work, from which he easily lets himself be drawn away, as is also found below: [[Prov 26:13|The slothful man saith: There is a lion in the way|Dicit piger, Leo est in via]]. [[18:8|and the souls of the effeminate|Anima autem effeminatorum]], that is, of the soft and weak, who have sunk into womanish softness, [[18:8|shall be hungry|esurient]], that is, shall be in want of spiritual goods, and sometimes of temporal ones too, as was said before: [[Prov 10:4|The slothful hand hath wrought poverty|Manus remissa operata est egestatem]].

paras.t: Qui mollis et dissolutus est in opere suo, id est remissus et negligens in exsecutione operis sui, frater est sua opera dissipantis, id est destruentis, non prosequentis : quia in peccato sunt similes, qui tepide servit Deo, et qui opus Dei postponit; estque utrisque timendum quod loquitur Jeremias, Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter aut fraudulenter. Istis, quum sint præhabita, non immoror.
paras.en: [[18:9|He that is loose and slack in his work|Qui mollis et dissolutus est in opere suo]], that is, slack and negligent in carrying out his work, [[18:9|is the brother of him that wasteth his own works|frater est sua opera dissipantis]], that is, of him who destroys them and does not carry them through: because he who serves God lukewarmly and he who puts off the work of God are alike in sin; and both have to fear what Jeremias says: [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord deceitfully|Maledictus qui facit opus Dei negligenter aut fraudulenter]] [Denis reads *negligently or deceitfully*]. On these things, since they have been treated before, I do not dwell.

paras.t: Turris fortissima, nomen Domini : id est, Deus sperantes in se, et confugientes ad se, tuetur et conservat, sicut turris inexpugnabilis protegit existentes in ea, imo ineffabiliter plus. Ideo ait Job : Libera me, et pone me juxta te; et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me. Unde nunc subditur : Ad ipsum currit justus, id est, festinanter ac fervide confugit semper ad Deum; et exaltabitur : quia per hoc suis prævalet inimicis, Omnipotentem jugiter invocando. Ideo orat vir sanctus : Esto mihi in Deum protectorem, et in locum munitum, ut salvum me facias. Et rursus gratias agens psallit : Deduxisti me, quia factus es spes mea, turris fortitudinis a facie inimici. Unde Bernardus : Si mihi præmia promittantur, per te, o Domine, me ea obtinere sperabo. Si insurgant adversum me prælia, si sæviat, si terreat malignus, si caro adversus spiritum concupiscat, in te ego sperabo, et dicam : Mihi adhærere Deo bonum est, ponere in Domino Deo spem meam. Hinc scriptum est : Domine, fortitudo mea, et refugium meum, et robur meum in die tribulationis.
paras.en: [[18:10|The name of the Lord is a strong tower|Turris fortissima, nomen Domini]]: that is, God guards and preserves those who hope in Him and flee to Him for refuge, as an impregnable tower protects those who are in it; nay, unspeakably more. Therefore Job says: [[Job 17:3|Deliver me|Libera me]], [[Job 17:3|and set me beside thee, and let any man's hand fight against me|et pone me juxta te; et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me]]. Hence it is now added: [[18:10|the just runneth to it|Ad ipsum currit justus]], that is, he always flees in haste and fervour to God; [[18:10|and shall be exalted|et exaltabitur]]: because by this he prevails over his enemies, calling continually on the Almighty. Therefore the holy man prays: [[Ps 70:3|Be thou unto me a God, a protector, and a place of strength: that thou mayst make me safe|Esto mihi in Deum protectorem, et in locum munitum, ut salvum me facias]]. And again, giving thanks, he sings: [[Ps 60:3|Thou hast conducted me|Deduxisti me]], [[Ps 60:4|For thou hast been my hope; a tower of strength against the face of the enemy|quia factus es spes mea, turris fortitudinis a facie inimici]]. Hence Bernard: If rewards are promised me, I shall hope to obtain them through Thee, O Lord. If battles rise up against me[[Ps 26:3||]], if he rage, if the evil one terrify me, if the flesh lust against the spirit[[Gal 5:17||]], in Thee will I hope, and I shall say: [[Ps 72:28|it is good for me to adhere to my God, to put my hope in the Lord God|Mihi adhærere Deo bonum est, ponere in Domino Deo spem meam]]. Hence it is written: [[Jer 16:19|O Lord, my might, and my strength, and my refuge in the day of tribulation|Domine, fortitudo mea, et refugium meum, et robur meum in die tribulationis]] [Denis's order is *my might, and my refuge, and my strength*].

paras.t: Substantia divitis, urbs roboris ejus, et quasi murus validus circumdans eum. Hoc supra scriptum est atque expositum.
paras.en: [[18:11|The substance of the rich man is the city of his strength, and as a strong wall compassing him about|Substantia divitis, urbs roboris ejus, et quasi murus validus circumdans eum]]. This was written above[[Prov 10:15||]] and expounded.

paras.t: Antequam conteratur, exaltatur cor hominis, id est, per superbiam intumescit antequam per debitam pœnam dejiciatur et condemnetur : culpa enim pœnam præcedit. Propter quod loquitur Judex : Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Et antequam glorificetur a Deo in patria, humiliatur, id est, oportet ut primo in via humiliet se, juxta illud : Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur.
paras.en: [[18:12|Before destruction, the heart of a man is exalted|Antequam conteratur, exaltatur cor hominis]], that is, it swells with pride before it is cast down and condemned by due punishment: for guilt goes before punishment. For this reason the Judge says: [[Luke 14:11|that exalteth himself shall be humbled|Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]] [the margin gives Luke xiv, 11 and xviii, 14]. [[18:12|and before he be glorified|Et antequam glorificetur]] by God in our fatherland [that is, in heaven], [[18:12|it is humbled|humiliatur]], that is, he must first humble himself on the way [that is, in this life], according to that saying: [[Luke 14:11|he that humbleth himself shall be exalted|Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur]].

paras.t: Qui prius respondet quam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat, et confusione dignum. Est enim indiscretus et præceps ad loquendum, et antequam sciat mentem quærentis, incipit ad quæstionem ipsius respondere. Similiter qui tanquam doctor et magister præsumit respondere discipulis et informationem quærentibus, antequam didicit ea de quibus interrogatur, ab ore doctorum seu libris, vel ex illuminatione superna, aut ex consideratione idonea, præsumptuosus esse censetur. Simili modo, qui facta et causas aliorum vult judicare, antequam plene fuerit informatus de motivis utriusque partis, stulte se habet, quum sanctus Job fateatur : Causam quam ignorabam, diligentissime investigabam. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Patienter audi, et diu considera quid loquendum, quidve respondendum sit; et adhuc tacens, provide ne quid dixisse pœniteat. Sapiens ut fructuose loquatur, multa prius considerat : quid, cui, quo loco et tempore, qua intentione, et qualiter dicat. Seneca quoque : In hoc, inquit, incumbe, ut libentius audias quam loquaris; auribus frequentius quam lingua utere; quidquid dicturus es aliis, primo die tibi.
paras.en: [[18:13|He that answereth before he heareth, sheweth himself to be a fool, and worthy of confusion|Qui prius respondet quam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat, et confusione dignum]]. For he is indiscreet and headlong in speaking, and before he knows the mind of the questioner he begins to answer his question. Likewise he who, as a doctor and master, presumes to answer disciples and those who seek instruction before he has learned the things he is asked about, from the mouth of doctors or from books, or by enlightenment from above, or by fitting reflection, is judged presumptuous. In the same way, he who wishes to judge the deeds and causes of others before he has been fully informed of the reasons of both parties behaves foolishly, since holy Job confesses: [[Job 29:16|the cause which I knew not, I searched out most diligently|Causam quam ignorabam, diligentissime investigabam]]. Hence Jerome says: Listen patiently, and consider long what is to be said or answered; and while still silent, take care that you may not repent of having said anything. The wise man, that he may speak fruitfully, first considers many things: what he is to say, to whom, in what place and at what time, with what intention, and in what manner. Seneca too: Give yourself to this, he says, that you listen more gladly than you speak; use your ears more often than your tongue; whatever you are going to say to others, say it first to yourself.

paras.t: Spiritus viri, id est virtus et gratia cordis boni viri, sustentat imbecillitatem suam, id est, naturæ infirmitatem confortat, et corporis debilitatem coadjuvat, ita ut illud quod est homini difficile, et quasi impossibile per naturam, fiat ei possibile, imo facile et jucundum per caritatem et gratiam, sicut ait Apostolus : Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat; et rursus, Spiritus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram. Ideo admonet Christus : Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos. Qui etiam de se ipso testatus est : Spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma. Hinc videmus quod aliqui debiles corpore, multo fortiores ac ferventiores existunt in exercitiis virtuosis, tam corporalibus quam spiritualibus, quam corpore validi ac robusti. Unde et Gregorius ait : Vires quas imperitia denegat, caritas subministrat.
paras.en: [[18:14|The spirit of a man|Spiritus viri]], that is, the virtue and grace of the heart of a good man, [[18:14|upholdeth his infirmity|sustentat imbecillitatem suam]], that is, strengthens the weakness of nature and helps the feebleness of the body, so that what is hard for a man, and as it were impossible by nature, becomes possible for him, nay, easy and delightful, through charity and grace, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]]; and again, [[Rom 8:26|the Spirit also helpeth our infirmity|Spiritus adjuvat infirmitatem nostram]]. Therefore Christ admonishes: [[Matt 11:28|Come to me all you that labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you|Venite ad me, omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos]]. Who also testified of Himself: [[Matt 26:41|The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak|Spiritus quidem promptus est, caro autem infirma]] [Denis takes the words as said of Christ's own human nature]. Hence we see that some who are weak in body are far stronger and more fervent in the exercises of virtue, bodily as well as spiritual, than those who are strong and robust in body. Hence Gregory too says: The strength that lack of skill denies, charity supplies.

paras.t: Spiritum vero ad irascendum facilem, quis poterit sustinere? quasi dicat : Difficile est ferre hominem iracundum, nisi valde benignum, mitibus, reformatis. Iratus namque, verbis, apparatu et factis molestus est aliis. Atque, ut Climacus loquitur, Sicut unus canis seu lupus sæpe inquietat totum gregem, sic unus homo iracundus, turbator ac turbulentus, totam communitatem frequenter perturbat. Valde ergo vitanda est ira, et consuetudo irascendi est periculosissima, præsertim quum ira ex suo genere sit peccatum mortale, et inter septem capitalia vitia numeretur. Ideo ait Gregorius : Per iram justitia vera relinquitur, gratia vitæ socialis amittitur, mansuetudo aufertur, et lux veritatis repellitur. Hinc ait Scriptura : Virum stultum interficit iracundia; et alibi : Sit omnis homo tardus ad iram; ira enim viri, justitiam Dei non operatur. Unde, ut habetur in Genesi, quum Joseph remitteret fratres suos, commisit eisdem : Ne irascamini in via. Christus quoque specialiter jussit et docuit : Discite, inquiens, a me, quia mitis sum, id est, iram per mansuetudinem exemplo mei vitetis. Istud præsertim pensandum est habitantibus in congregatione, imo et cunctis commorantibus simul, præsertim cholericis, et pravo usu infectis, ne impetu iræ suæ lædant, perturbent, contristent, aut perimant alios. Hinc in suis Proverbiis Seneca loquitur : Iracundiam qui vincit, hostem superat maximum; et rursus, Nihil minus quam irasci punientem decet, quum eo magis ad emendationem pœna proficiat, si judicio lata est.
paras.en: [[18:14|but a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum vero ad irascendum facilem, quis poterit sustinere?]] As if to say: it is hard to bear an angry man, unless one is very kind, meek and reformed. For the angry man is a burden to others by his words, his bearing and his deeds. And, as Climacus says, as one dog or wolf often disturbs the whole flock, so one angry man, a troubler and turbulent, often throws a whole community into disorder. Anger, then, is greatly to be avoided, and the habit of growing angry is most dangerous, especially since anger is of its kind a mortal sin [that is, in its nature, though it may be venial through smallness of the matter or want of full consent], and is numbered among the seven capital vices. Therefore Gregory says: Through anger true justice is abandoned, the grace of social life is lost, meekness is taken away, and the light of truth is driven off. Hence Scripture says: [[Job 5:2|Anger indeed killeth the foolish|Virum stultum interficit iracundia]]; and elsewhere: [[Jas 1:19|let every man be|Sit omnis homo]] [[Jas 1:19|slow to anger|tardus ad iram]]; [[Jas 1:20|For the anger of man worketh not the justice of God|ira enim viri, justitiam Dei non operatur]]. Hence, as is found in Genesis, when Joseph sent his brethren back, he charged them: [[Gen 45:24|Be not angry in the way|Ne irascamini in via]]. Christ too specially commanded and taught it: [[Matt 11:29|learn|Discite]], He says, [[Matt 11:29|of me, because I am meek|a me, quia mitis sum]], that is, avoid anger by meekness after My example. This is especially to be weighed by those who live in a community, nay, by all who dwell together, and above all by the choleric and those infected by bad habit, lest by the onrush of their anger they hurt, disturb, sadden or destroy others. Hence Seneca says in his *Proverbs*: He who conquers anger overcomes the greatest enemy; and again: Nothing becomes one who punishes less than anger, since punishment profits the more for amendment if it is inflicted with judgment.

paras.t: Cor prudentis possidebit scientiam, præsertim eorum quæ sunt necessaria ad salutem, et quæ scire tenetur; scientiam quoque, quæ est unum de septem donis : et quidquid utiliter didicit, diligenter custodiet. Et auris sapientium quærit doctrinam : id est, sapientes proficere in sapientia optant, sicut jam sæpe expositum est.
paras.en: [[18:15|A wise heart shall acquire knowledge|Cor prudentis possidebit scientiam]] [Denis reads *the heart of the prudent*], especially of the things that are necessary for salvation, and that it is bound to know; and also the knowledge that is one of the seven gifts[[Is 11:2||]]: and whatever it has usefully learned it will diligently keep. [[18:15|and the ear of the wise seeketh instruction|Et auris sapientium quærit doctrinam]]: that is, the wise desire to advance in wisdom, as has already often been expounded.

paras.t: Donum hominis dilatat viam ejus : id est, munera gratiæ, caritas et aliæ virtutes infusæ, homini desuper datæ, faciunt eum in adimpletionibus præceptorum late et copiose incedere atque proficere. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri, quum dilatasti cor meum. Apostolus quoque : Cor, inquit, nostrum dilatatum est. Et ante principes spatium ei facit, id est, dat ei aditum ad Dei electos, ad principes regni cœlestis, et ad justos prælatos : quibus assimilatur et placet, juxta illud, Suscitat de pulvere egenum, ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat. Præterea, quidam exponunt istud superficialiter ita : Donum hominis dilatat viam ejus, quia dum homo dat munera aliqua portariis ac ministris regum ac præsidentium, datur ei liber introitus, sicque acquirit accessum ad principem.
paras.en: [[18:16|A man's gift enlargeth his way|Donum hominis dilatat viam ejus]]: that is, the gifts of grace, charity and the other infused virtues, given to man from above, make him walk and advance broadly and abundantly in fulfilling the commandments. For this reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:32|I have run the way of thy commandments, when thou didst enlarge my heart|Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri, quum dilatasti cor meum]]. The Apostle too: [[2 Cor 6:11|our heart|Cor]], he says, [[2 Cor 6:11|is enlarged|nostrum dilatatum est]]. [[18:16|and maketh him room before princes|Et ante principes spatium ei facit]], that is, it gives him access to the elect of God, to the princes of the heavenly kingdom, and to just prelates, whom he comes to resemble and please, according to that saying: [[1 Kings 2:8|He raiseth up the needy from the dust|Suscitat de pulvere egenum]], [[1 Kings 2:8|that he may sit with princes, and hold the throne of glory|ut sedeat cum principibus, et solium gloriæ teneat]]. Besides, some expound this on the surface, thus: [[18:16|A man's gift enlargeth his way|Donum hominis dilatat viam ejus]], because when a man gives some presents to the doorkeepers and servants of kings and governors, free entrance is given him, and so he gains access to the prince.

paras.t: Justus prior est accusator sui, id est, quotidie se ipsum considerat, et quotidianas culpas ac cetera sua peccata intra se assidue reprehendit, accusatque coram Deo, et punit ea in semetipso. Caritas etenim incipit a suo subjecto, et qui se ipsum non purgat, indignus est alios castigare. Ideo justus tanquam vere humilis ac discretus, etiam dum ad alterius correptionem aut correctionem procedit, propriam in primis fragilitatem, defectuositatem et culpam pensat, reprehendit ac diluit : sicque corripit proximum aut subditum suum humiliter et modeste, compatienter et caritative. Nihilo minus in subditorum correptione debet se strenue gerere, nec immoderate se ipsum dejicere. Propter quod ait Isidorus : Bonus prælatus est, qui in humilitate servat disciplinam, et per disciplinam non incurrit superbiam. Verum istud multi non servant, qui in alios tam invective moventur, quasi sine peccato ipsimet essent : et aliena magis quam propria intuentur ponderantque peccata. Sicut et Seneca fassus est, dicens : Severissime adversum peccantes nos ingerimus, et ipsi eadem committimus. Denique, Cassiano testante, in hoc apparet an quis ex corde et vera humilitate se ipsum in primis accuset, si ea quæ ipse in se reprehendit, ab aliis quoque reprehendi et accusari, sibique objici æquanimiter patiatur. Venit amicus ejus, et investigabit eum. Per amicum potest intelligi Christus : qui loquitur, Vos autem dixi amicos. Qui rursus fatetur : Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis quæ ego præcipio vobis. Iste amicus per gratiæ incrementum et visitationem ac consolationem internam, venit in cor justi se primo humiliter accusantis, et illud considerat, approbat atque remunerat. Rursum, per amicum potest intelligi angelus custos hominis justi : quem angelus assidue visitat, consolatur ac discutit, intusque monet, inquirit et docet. Potest item per amicum intelligi proximus justi amator, qui venit ad justum se accusantem, ad consolandum et investigandum quomodo se res habeat.
paras.en: [[18:17|The just is first accuser of himself|Justus prior est accusator sui]], that is, he considers himself daily, and constantly reproves within himself his daily faults and his other sins, and accuses them before God, and punishes them in himself. For charity begins with its own subject, and he who does not purge himself is unworthy to chastise others. Therefore the just man, as one truly humble and discreet, even when he proceeds to the rebuke or correction of another, first weighs, reproves and washes away his own frailty, defectiveness and guilt: and so he rebukes his neighbour or his subject humbly and modestly, with compassion and charity. Nevertheless, in rebuking subjects he ought to bear himself vigorously, and not abase himself beyond measure. For this reason Isidore says: He is a good prelate who in humility keeps discipline, and through discipline does not fall into pride. But many do not observe this, who are moved against others so invectively as though they themselves were without sin: and they look at and weigh others' sins more than their own. As Seneca too confessed, saying: We bear down most severely on those who sin, and we ourselves commit the same things. Lastly, as Cassian testifies, it appears whether a man first accuses himself from the heart and with true humility by this: whether he bears with equanimity that the things he reproves in himself should be reproved and accused by others too, and laid to his charge. [[18:17|his friend cometh, and shall search him|Venit amicus ejus, et investigabit eum]]. By the friend Christ can be understood, who says: [[John 15:15|But I have called you friends|Vos autem dixi amicos]]. Who again declares: [[John 15:14|You are my friends, if you do the things that I command you|Vos amici mei estis, si feceritis quæ ego præcipio vobis]]. This friend, by the increase of grace and by inward visitation and consolation, comes into the heart of the just man who has first humbly accused himself, and considers it, approves it, and rewards it. Again, by the friend can be understood the guardian angel of the just man: whom the angel constantly visits, consoles and examines, and inwardly admonishes, questions and teaches. By the friend can likewise be understood a neighbour who loves the just man, who comes to the just man as he accuses himself, to console him and to search out how things stand with him.

paras.t: Contradictiones comprimit sors : quia dum homines sunt discordes circa alicujus rei divisionem, reducuntur ad pacem per sortium usum : et inter potentes quoque taliter dissentientes dijudicat sors, quid quilibet debeat obtinere.
paras.en: [[18:18|The lot suppresseth contentions|Contradictiones comprimit sors]]: because when men are at odds over the division of something, they are brought back to peace by the use of lots: and [[18:18|even between the mighty|inter potentes quoque]] who disagree in this way the lot [[18:18|determineth|dijudicat]] what each one should obtain.

paras.t: Frater qui adjuvatur a fratre, id est proximi se invicem caritative juvantes consilio et effectu, sunt quasi civitas firma : in qua cives se invicem juvant ac tuentur contra hostes. De hoc in Ecclesiaste scriptum est : Væ soli, quia si ceciderit, non habet sublevantem. Hinc congregatio devotorum, et conventus vere religiosorum, habent firmitatem præcipuam : in quibus sunt tot adjutores, quot habitatores. Hinc Christus misit discipulos suos combinatos ad prædicandum. Et Psalmista fatetur : Ecce quam bonum, et quam jucundum, habitare fratres in unum! Aristoteles quoque effatur : Duo simul venientes, intelligere et agere sunt potentiores. Et judicia, id est discretiones eorum ex mutua collatione prolatæ, vel sententiæ quas enuntiant, firma sunt quasi vectes urbium : qui vectes muniunt portas. Conformiter, frater, id est plebs gentilis, adjuta a fratre, id est a populo Judæorum, primum in Christum credente, puta Apostolis et eorum cooperatoribus primis, est quasi urbs munita, dum utrumque populus ille in Ecclesia per caritatem unitur.
paras.en: [[18:19|A brother that is helped by his brother|Frater qui adjuvatur a fratre]], that is, neighbours who help one another in charity by counsel and in deed, are [[18:19|like a strong city|quasi civitas firma]], in which the citizens help one another and defend one another against enemies. Of this it is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 4:10|woe to him that is alone, for when he falleth, he hath none to lift him up|Væ soli, quia si ceciderit, non habet sublevantem]]. Hence a congregation of devout men and a convent of true religious have a special firmness: in them there are as many helpers as dwellers. Hence Christ sent His disciples two by two to preach[[Luke 10:1||]]. And the Psalmist declares: [[Ps 132:1|Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity|Ecce quam bonum, et quam jucundum, habitare fratres in unum!]]! Aristotle too says: Two coming together are more able to understand and to act. [[18:19|and judgments|Et judicia]], that is, their discernments, put forward after conferring together, or the sentences they pronounce, are firm, [[18:19|like the bars of cities|quasi vectes urbium]], which bars make the gates fast.
