In like manner, the brother, that is, the Gentile people, helped by the brother, that is, by the people of the Jews who first believed in Christ (the Apostles, for instance, and their first fellow workers), is like a fortified city, while both peoples are united by charity in the Church.

paras.t: De fructu oris viri replebitur venter ejus. Hoc est quod dictum est supra, De fructu oris sui unusquisque replebitur bonis. Itaque vir bene loquendo, et alios sapienter docendo, Deum quoque ore laudando atque orando, meretur et consequitur sufficientiam spiritualium, corporaliumque bonorum, sicut ait Salvator : Primum quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, et hæc omnia adjicientur vobis. Et genimina, id est fructus et germina, labiorum ipsius, videlicet documenta, orationes, laudesque Dei, ac cetera verba bona, saturabunt eum, id est, necessaria abundanter procurabunt, quemadmodum in Evangelio Dominus prædicatoribus suis loquitur : In eadem domo manete, edentes et bibentes quæ apud illos sunt; dignus est enim operarius mercede sua. Ideo dixit Apostolus : Si nos vobis spiritualia seminavimus, magnum est si carnalia vestra metamus ? quasi dicat, Magnum non est.
paras.en: [[18:20|Of the fruit of a man's mouth shall his belly be satisfied|De fructu oris viri replebitur venter ejus]]. This is what was said above: [[Prov 12:14|By the fruit of his own mouth shall a man be filled with good things|De fructu oris sui unusquisque replebitur bonis]]. And so a man, by speaking well and teaching others wisely, and by praising God with his mouth and praying, merits and obtains a sufficiency of spiritual and bodily goods, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 6:33|Seek ye therefore first the kingdom of God, and his justice, and all these things shall be added unto you|Primum quærite regnum Dei et justitiam ejus, et hæc omnia adjicientur vobis]]. [[18:20|and the offspring|Et genimina]], that is, the fruits and shoots, [[18:20|of his lips|labiorum ipsius]], namely his teachings, prayers and praises of God, and his other good words, [[18:20|shall fill him|saturabunt eum]], that is, will procure him what he needs in abundance, as in the Gospel the Lord says to His preachers: [[Luke 10:7|in the same house, remain, eating and drinking such things as they have: for the labourer is worthy of his hire|In eadem domo manete, edentes et bibentes quæ apud illos sunt; dignus est enim operarius mercede sua]]. Therefore the Apostle said: [[1 Cor 9:11|If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?|Si nos vobis spiritualia seminavimus, magnum est si carnalia vestra metamus]]]] As if to say: It is no great matter.

paras.t: Mors et vita in manibus linguæ. Hoc est quod in Evangelio asserit Christus : Ex verbis tuis justificaberis, et ex verbis tuis condemnaberis. Itaque mors culpæ seu mortale peccatum, est in manibus, id est usibus seu actibus, linguæ, hoc est in verbis vitiosis prohibitis ; et vita gratiæ, ac meritum vitæ beatæ, consistit in bonis usibus linguæ, hoc est in orationibus et laudibus Dei, in prædicationibus et doctrinis, in protestatione fidei tempore persecutionis. Qui diligunt eam, comedent fructus ejus : id est, si linguam suam spiritualiter ament, et bene gubernent, recipient præmia gloriosa; sin autem, sortientur tormenta. Hinc sancti Patres inter observantias religiosas, præcipue instituerunt linguæ custodiam, id est observantiam sacri silentii : de quo loquitur Isaias, In silentio et spe erit fortitudo vestra.
paras.en: [[18:21|Death and life are in the power of the tongue|Mors et vita in manibus linguæ]] [literally *in the hands of the tongue*; Denis reads *manibus*, hands, for the Vulgate's *manu*, hand]. This is what Christ declares in the Gospel: [[Matt 12:37|by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned|Ex verbis tuis justificaberis, et ex verbis tuis condemnaberis]]. And so the death of guilt, or mortal sin, is in the hands, that is, in the uses or acts, of the tongue, that is, in vicious and forbidden words; and the life of grace, and the merit of the blessed life, consists in good uses of the tongue, that is, in prayers and praises of God, in preaching and teaching, in confessing the faith in time of persecution. [[18:21|they that love it, shall eat the fruits thereof|Qui diligunt eam, comedent fructus ejus]]: that is, if they love their tongue spiritually and govern it well, they will receive glorious rewards; but if not, they will have torments for their lot. Hence the holy Fathers, among the religious observances, especially established the guarding of the tongue, that is, the observance of sacred silence: of which Isaias speaks: [[Is 30:15|in silence and in hope shall your strength be|In silentio et spe erit fortitudo vestra]].

paras.t: Qui invenit, id est, acquirit legitime, mulierem bonam, invenit bonum : quia magnum Dei donum est hoc, sicut econverso uxor mala est onus gravissimum. Unde in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Gratia super gratiam mulier sancta ac pudorata et tacita. Et hauriet jucunditatem a Domino : quia delectabile est tali convivere mulieri, juxta illud : Mulieris bonæ beatus vir; numerus enim annorum vitæ illius, duplex. Et rursus : Mulier fortis oblectat virum suum. Spiritualiter, per mulierem bonam designatur Ecclesia, seu caro rationi subjecta, seu divina Scriptura.
paras.en: [[18:22|He that hath found|Qui invenit]], that is, lawfully acquires, [[18:22|a good wife, hath found a good thing|mulierem bonam, invenit bonum]]: because this is a great gift of God, as on the contrary a bad wife is a most grievous burden. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 26:19|A holy and shamefaced woman is grace upon grace|Gratia super gratiam mulier sancta ac pudorata]], and [[Ecclus 26:18|silent|tacita]]. [[18:22|and shall receive a pleasure from the Lord|Et hauriet jucunditatem a Domino]]: because it is delightful to live with such a wife, according to that saying: [[Ecclus 26:1|Happy is the husband of a good wife: for the number of his years is double|Mulieris bonæ beatus vir; numerus enim annorum vitæ illius, duplex]]. And again: [[Ecclus 26:2|A virtuous woman rejoiceth her husband|Mulier fortis oblectat virum suum]]. Spiritually, by the good wife is signified the Church, or the flesh subject to reason, or the divine Scripture.

paras.t: Qui expellit mulierem bonam, expellit bonum, et pessime atque stultissime agit. Pars ista hujus versiculi, non est in Hebræo, sicut nec particula sequens. Qui autem tenet adulteram non volentem se emendare, etsi ipsemet vir non sit adulter, stultus est et insipiens, agens contra Scripturam. Et quia incertus esset de prole, videretur quoque favere crimini talis adulteræ. Hinc et Christus in Evangelio dicit virum ab uxore non separandum, nisi ob fornicationem.
paras.en: [[18:22|He that driveth away a good wife, driveth away a good thing|Qui expellit mulierem bonam, expellit bonum]], and he acts most wickedly and most foolishly. This part of the verse is not in the Hebrew, nor is the clause that follows. [[18:22|but he that keepeth an adulteress|Qui autem tenet adulteram]] who will not amend herself, even if the husband himself is not an adulterer, [[18:22|is foolish and wicked|stultus est et insipiens]] [Denis reads *insipiens*, "unwise", for the Vulgate's *impius*, "wicked"], acting against Scripture[[Ex 20:14||]]. And because he would be uncertain of his offspring, he would also seem to favour the crime of such an adulteress. Hence Christ too says in the Gospel that a husband is not to be separated from his wife except for fornication[[Matt 5:32||]][[Matt 19:9||]].

paras.t: Cum obsecrationibus loquetur pauper, petendo eleemosynam aliudve subsidium. Similiter qui pauper est spiritu, et omnis fidelis, cum obsecratione loquitur Patri cœlesti, dicendo : Pater noster qui es in cœlis, etc. Et dives effabitur rigide, id est aspere, præsertim ad impotentiores, quia divites solent esse superbi. Quocontra in Ecclesiastico legitur : Congregationi pauperum te affabilem facito. Similiter qui se divitem reputat in charismatibus gratiæ, loquitur rigide, se jactando et alios aspernando, quemadmodum Pharisæus Publicanum, dicendo : Non sum sicut ceteri hominum, velut etiam hic publicanus.
paras.en: [[18:23|The poor will speak with supplications|Cum obsecrationibus loquetur pauper]], in asking for alms or some other help. Likewise he who is poor in spirit, and every one of the faithful, speaks with supplication to the heavenly Father, saying: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster qui es in cœlis]], etc. [[18:23|and the rich will speak roughly|Et dives effabitur rigide]], that is, harshly, especially to those less powerful, because the rich are usually proud. Against which we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 4:7|Make thyself affable to the congregation of the poor|Congregationi pauperum te affabilem facito]]. Likewise he who reckons himself rich in the gifts of grace speaks roughly, boasting of himself and spurning others, as the Pharisee did the Publican, saying: [[Luke 18:11|I am not as the rest of men|Non sum sicut ceteri hominum]], [[Luke 18:11|as also is this publican|velut etiam hic publicanus]].

paras.t: Vir amicabilis ad societatem, id est aptus ad habendum consortium familiare cum alio, et jucundus ad communionem convictus, quales sunt homines mansueti, læti, fideles, liberales, constantes; magis amicus erit socio sibi familiari, quam frater carnalis seu consanguineus, non ita amicabilis ad societatem suo fratri aut propinquo. Similitudo enim affectuum, mutua delectatio atque unanimis communicatio actuum, maxime gignunt, fovent, accendunt amicitiam talem. Similiter conformitas in naturalibus : quod excellentissime patuit in præclarissimis illis viris Amelio et Amico, quorum miri ac nobilissimi actus leguntur. Denique in naturalibus multum consimiles, solent ad societatem esse amicabiliores. Ideo juxta diversitatem complexionum, diversis diversi conveniunt. Ad veram autem amicitiam et societatem honestam (Tullio contestante) id pertinet, ut unus ab alio nil turpe aut indecens roget, nec alter propter alterum tale quid faciat. Spiritualiter, vir amicabilis ad societatem, id est quicumque gentilis conversus, in Ecclesia pacifice vivens, magis amicus et carus est Christo, atque Apostolis ex Judæorum progenie natis, quam frater, id est infidelis Judæus ex eadem stirpe progenitus.
paras.en: [[18:24|A man amiable in society|Vir amicabilis ad societatem]] [Denis reads *amicabilis*, "friendly", for the Vulgate's *amabilis*], that is, apt for having familiar companionship with another, and pleasant in the fellowship of common life, such as are men who are gentle, cheerful, faithful, generous, constant, [[18:24|shall be more friendly|magis amicus erit]] to a companion familiar to him [[18:24|than a brother|quam frater]] in the flesh or a kinsman who is not so amiable in society towards his brother or relative. For likeness of affections, mutual delight and a unanimous sharing of actions above all beget, foster and kindle such friendship. Likewise likeness in natural qualities: which was shown most excellently in those most renowned men Amelius and Amicus, whose wonderful and most noble deeds are read [that is, in the medieval legend of the two friends Amis and Amiles]. Lastly, those who are much alike in natural qualities are usually more friendly in companionship. Therefore, according to the diversity of temperaments [*complexiones*: the bodily constitutions of medieval medicine], different men suit different men. But to true friendship and honest companionship it belongs (as Tully testifies) that one ask nothing shameful or unseemly of the other, and that neither do any such thing for the other's sake. Spiritually, [[18:24|A man amiable in society|vir amicabilis ad societatem]], that is, any converted Gentile living peaceably in the Church, is more a friend to and dearer to Christ, and to the Apostles born of the stock of the Jews, [[18:24|than a brother|quam frater]], that is, an unbelieving Jew born of the same stock.

19.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI NONIDECIMI : MELIOR EST PAUPER QUI AMBULAT, ETC.
19.title_en: Declaration of the nineteenth chapter: Better is the poor man that walketh, etc.

paras.t: Melior est pauper in temporalibus, qui ambulat in simplicitate sua columbina, sine dolo, simulatione et singularitate serviens Deo, quam dives in temporalibus, torquens labia sua, id est ex elatione seu aliorum contemptu, deflectens et contrahens ea. Juxta quod scriptum est : Numquid elegi contorquere quasi circulum caput suum, et saccum et cinerem sternere? Spiritualiter, melior est pauper, id est idiota et modice eruditus, ambulans in simplicitate, id est vivens secundum ea quæ novit esse agenda ac evitanda, quam dives, id est ingeniosus et plurimum eruditus, torquens labia sua, id est ad proferendum vana, præsumptuosa sive hæretica, ea detorquens. Et insipiens. Talis etenim dono sapientiæ caret, et est mortalis peccati stultitia involutus.
paras.en: [[19:1|Better is the poor man|Melior est pauper]] in temporal things, [[19:1|that walketh in his simplicity|qui ambulat in simplicitate sua]], the simplicity of the dove, serving God without guile, pretence or singularity, [[19:1|than a rich man|quam dives]] in temporal things [[19:1|that is perverse in his lips|torquens labia sua]] [the Latin has "twisting his lips", hence Denis's gloss], that is, bending and drawing them in from pride or contempt of others. According to what is written: Have I chosen [[Is 58:5|to wind his head about like a circle, and to spread sackcloth and ashes?|contorquere quasi circulum caput suum, et saccum et cinerem sternere?]]? Spiritually, better is the poor man, that is, the unlettered man of little learning, walking in simplicity, that is, living according to what he knows must be done and avoided, than the rich man, that is, the man of great wit and much learning, who twists his lips, that is, twists them to utter vain, presumptuous or heretical things. [[19:1|And unwise|Et insipiens]]: for such a man lacks the gift of wisdom and is wrapped in the folly of mortal sin.

paras.t: Ubi non est scientia animæ, id est vera et spiritualis scientia, quæ est donum, vel notitia præceptorum, et eorum quæ necessaria sunt ad salutem; non est bonum, id est aliquid meritorium; nec potest quis vivere virtuose, nisi sciat ad quæ teneatur : imo nec potest appetere bonum, nisi aliquo modo cognitum, quum objectum voluntatis sit bonum intellectum, id est intellectualiter apprehensum seu notum. Ideo asserit Augustinus : Ignota amari non queunt. Et qui festinus est, pedibus offendit : id est, inordinate fervens in suis affectibus, agit præcipitanter, et immoderate se habet in factis, quia affectio talis rationem excæcat. Ideo hortatur Apostolus : Omnia decenter et secundum ordinem fiant in vobis. Unde et Seneca in suis Proverbiis : Nihil rationis est, ubi semel affectus adductus est. Cyrillus quoque primo Proverbiorum suorum libro : In omnibus, inquit, ordinata gravitate procede. An ignoras quod perditio derivetur a pede cito? Mortalia namque cuncta sunt plena periculis. Unde ubique oportet cum gravitate procedere, ut possis dato pede uno, ubi porrigendus sit alter salubriter providere. Verumtamen ad virtutum spectat perfectionem, agiliter et ferventer, expedite atque velociter ea quæ bona sunt prosequi, sicut et infra habetur : Vidisti hominem velocem in opere suo? Coram regibus stabit. Aristoteles quoque in Ethicis ait : Oportet morose consiliari, et consiliata velociter prosequi. Sed hæc de ordinata et sapientiali velocitate sunt intelligenda.
paras.en: [[19:2|Where there is no knowledge of the soul|Ubi non est scientia animæ]], that is, true and spiritual knowledge, which is a gift, or the knowledge of the commandments and of the things necessary for salvation, [[19:2|there is no good|non est bonum]], that is, nothing meritorious. Nor can anyone live virtuously unless he knows what he is bound to; indeed, he cannot even desire a good unless it is in some way known, since the object of the will is the good understood, that is, apprehended or known by the intellect. Therefore Augustine declares: Things unknown cannot be loved. [[19:2|And he that is hasty|Et qui festinus est]], [[19:2|with his feet shall stumble|pedibus offendit]]: that is, he who is inordinately heated in his affections acts headlong and behaves without measure in his deeds, because such an affection blinds the reason. Therefore the Apostle exhorts: Let [[1 Cor 14:40|all things be done decently and according to order|Omnia decenter et secundum ordinem fiant in vobis]] among you. Hence Seneca too in his Proverbs: There is nothing of reason where once the affection has been drawn in. Cyril also, in the first book of his Proverbs: In all things, he says, proceed with ordered gravity. Knowest thou not that ruin comes from a hasty foot? For all mortal things are full of dangers. Hence everywhere one must proceed with gravity, so that, having set down one foot, thou mayest safely see where the other is to be put forward. Yet it belongs to the perfection of the virtues to pursue what is good nimbly and fervently, readily and swiftly, as is also said below: [[Prov 22:29|Hast thou seen a man swift in his work? he shall stand before kings|Vidisti hominem velocem in opere suo? Coram regibus stabit]]. Aristotle too says in the Ethics: One must take counsel slowly, and carry out swiftly what has been counselled. But these things are to be understood of an ordered and wise swiftness.

paras.t: Stultitia hominis supplantat gressus ejus : id est, insipientia cordis, inordinata, vitiosa et stolida opera parit : quæ a dæmonibus supplantantur, et a proximis contemnuntur; et contra Deum fervet animo suo : id est, insipiens et iniquus impietatem suam in Deum retorquet, aut in blasphemiæ verba prorumpit, juxta illud in Psalmo : Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala. Unde in Job scriptum est : Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus? Talem putavit Eliu esse sanctum Job, loquens de eo ad Deum : Pater mi, ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis, qui addidit super peccata sua blasphemiam. Circa hoc ait Glossa : Stulti quum viam deseruerint veritatis, non se errasse fatentur, sed in Conditorem referunt culpam suam, quasi ipse occasionem peccandi tribuerit, eo quod hominem fecerit fragilem, vel tentari permiserit a versuto. Hinc Adam post peccatum increpatus a Domino, excusavit se, dicens : Mulier, quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi. [Et mulier : Serpens, inquit, decepit me.] Ambo culpam suam retulerunt in Creatorem : ille, quod mulierem sociam dederat ; illa, quod serpentem in paradiso posuerat. Is quoque contra Deum fervet animo suo, qui divina præcepta per inertiam suam contemnens, ipsum Dominum quasi importabilia hominibus onera imponentem, reprehendit.
paras.en: [[19:3|The folly of a man supplanteth his steps|Stultitia hominis supplantat gressus ejus]]: that is, the unwisdom of the heart brings forth disordered, vicious and stupid works, which are tripped up by the demons and despised by one's neighbours; [[19:3|and he fretteth in his mind against God|et contra Deum fervet animo suo]] [the Latin *fervet* is literally "boils"]: that is, the unwise and wicked man turns his impiety back upon God, or breaks out into words of blasphemy, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 20:12|For they have intended evils against thee|Quoniam declinaverunt in te mala]]. Hence it is written in Job: [[Job 15:13|Why doth thy spirit swell against God|Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus]]? Such Eliu thought holy Job to be, speaking of him to God: [[Job 34:36|My father|Pater mi]], [[Job 34:36|cease not from the man of iniquity|ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis]], who [[Job 34:37|addeth blasphemy upon his sins|addidit super peccata sua blasphemiam]]. On this the Gloss says: Fools, when they have left the way of truth, do not confess that they have erred, but lay their fault on the Creator, as though he had given them the occasion of sinning, because he made man frail or allowed him to be tempted by the crafty one. Hence Adam, rebuked by the Lord after his sin, excused himself, saying: [[Gen 3:12|The woman, whom thou gavest me to be my companion, gave me of the tree, and I did eat|Mulier, quam dedisti mihi sociam, dedit mihi de ligno, et comedi]]. (And the woman: [[Gen 3:13|The serpent|Serpens]], she said, [[Gen 3:13|deceived me|decepit me]].) Both laid their fault on the Creator: he, because he had given him the woman as companion; she, because he had put the serpent in paradise. He too frets in his mind against God who, despising the divine commandments through his own sloth, finds fault with the Lord himself as though he laid on men burdens that cannot be borne.

paras.t: Divitiæ addunt amicos plurimos : id est, multi diligunt divites propter eorum divitias, et ut commoda aliqua consequantur ab eis; a paupere autem et hi quos habuit, separantur : id est, multi desinunt diligere inopes, eo quod inopes sint : sicque de eorum amicitia erubescunt, sive non curant, quia nil utilitatis adipiscuntur ab eis. Similiter eorum qui spiritualiter divites sunt, id est sapientes, virtuosi et sancti, sunt multi amici, videlicet Deus, et omnes cives superni ac plures homines boni; a paupere autem, id est a philosophis, atque hæreticis, et perversis hominibus, in quibus nihil est sapientiæ salutaris, et hi quos habuit amicos, avertuntur, non per odium, sed per dissimilitudinem vitæ aut fidei.
paras.en: [[19:4|Riches make many friends|Divitiæ addunt amicos plurimos]]: that is, many love the rich for their riches, and in order to get some advantages from them; [[19:4|but from the poor man, even they whom he had, depart|a paupere autem et hi quos habuit, separantur]]: that is, many cease to love the needy because they are needy, and so they are ashamed of their friendship, or do not care for it, because they gain nothing useful from them. Likewise those who are rich spiritually, that is, the wise, the virtuous and the holy, have many friends, namely God and all the citizens on high and many good men; but from the poor man, that is, from the philosophers and heretics and perverse men, in whom there is nothing of saving wisdom, even the friends he had turn away, not through hatred, but through unlikeness of life or of faith.

paras.t: Testis falsus non erit impunitus. Non enim potest divinum evadere judicium, quamvis interdum evadat humanum. Et qui mendacia loquitur perniciosa, non effugiet judicium Dei. Cui ait Psalmista : Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium. De quo Eleazarus ille senex asseruit : Etsi in præsenti tempore suppliciis hominum eripiar, sed manum Omnipotentis neque vivens neque defunctus effugiam.
paras.en: [[19:5|A false witness shall not be unpunished|Testis falsus non erit impunitus]]: for he cannot escape the divine judgment, though at times he escapes the human. [[19:5|And he that speaketh lies|Et qui mendacia loquitur]] that do harm [[19:5|shall not escape|non effugiet]] the judgment of God. To whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 5:7|thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie|Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium]]. Of which that old man Eleazar declared: [[2 Mach 6:26|though, for the present time, I should be delivered from the punishments of men, yet should I not escape the hand of the Almighty neither alive nor dead|Etsi in præsenti tempore suppliciis hominum eripiar, sed manum Omnipotentis neque vivens neque defunctus effugiam]].

paras.t: Multi colunt, id est honorant, personam divitis : quod de divite corporaliter, seu spiritualiter, sicut jam patuit, accipi potest; et amici sunt dona tribuentis. Sicque diligunt eum propter beneficia sua : quod non est malum in se; tamen colere divites eo quod temporaliter divites sint, vituperatur. Sed si in officiis sint constituti, sunt utique propter dignitatem officii, tanquam Dei vicarii honorandi. De hac re, utputa qualiter pauperes non sint inhonorandi, nec divitibus postponendi, multa narrat apostolus Jacobus, ut est illud : Si introierit in conventum vestrum vir aureum annulum habens et in veste candida, introierit autem et pauper in sordido habitu, et intendatis in eum qui indutus est veste præclara, et dixeritis ei, Tu sede hic bene; pauperi autem dicatis, Tu sta illic, aut, Sede sub scabello pedum meorum : nonne judicatis apud vos ipsos, et facti estis judices cogitationum iniquarum?
paras.en: [[19:6|Many honour|Multi colunt]], that is, show honour to, [[19:6|the person|personam]] of the rich man [the Vulgate has *potentis*, "of him that is mighty"]: which can be taken of the rich man in body or in spirit, as has just been shown; [[19:6|and are friends of him that giveth gifts|et amici sunt dona tribuentis]]. And so they love him for his benefits, which is not evil in itself; yet to honour the rich because they are rich in temporal things is blamed. But if they are set in offices, they are certainly to be honoured for the dignity of the office, as vicars of God. Of this matter, namely how the poor are not to be dishonoured nor put after the rich, the apostle James says much, as in this: [[Jas 2:2|if there shall come into your assembly a man having a golden ring, in fine apparel; and there shall come in also a poor man in mean attire|Si introierit in conventum vestrum vir aureum annulum habens et in veste candida, introierit autem et pauper in sordido habitu]], [[Jas 2:3|And you have respect to him that is clothed with the fine apparel and shall say to him: Sit thou here well: but say to the poor man: Stand thou there, or: Sit under my footstool|et intendatis in eum qui indutus est veste præclara, et dixeritis ei, Tu sede hic bene; pauperi autem dicatis, Tu sta illic, aut, Sede sub scabello pedum meorum]]: [[Jas 2:4|Do you not judge within yourselves, and are become judges of unjust thoughts?|nonne judicatis apud vos ipsos, et facti estis judices cogitationum iniquarum?]]?

paras.t: Fratres hominis pauperis oderunt eum : quia putant se confundi et vilipendi eo quod habeant talem fratrem. Insuper et amici procul recesserunt ab eo, ne ex ejus præsentia incurrant gravamen. Hoc sanctus Job depauperatus sibi accidisse fatetur, dicendo : Fratres mei elongaverunt a me, et noti mei quasi alieni recesserunt a me. Quod item de Christo propter nos paupere facto, potest intelligi, a quo etiam tempore passionis fugerunt Apostoli.
paras.en: [[19:7|The brethren of the poor man hate him|Fratres hominis pauperis oderunt eum]]: because they think themselves shamed and made cheap by having such a brother. [[19:7|Moreover also his friends have departed far from him|Insuper et amici procul recesserunt ab eo]], lest they incur some burden from his presence. Holy Job, made poor, confesses that this happened to him, saying: My brethren have gone far from me[[Job 6:15||]], [[Job 19:13|and my acquaintance like strangers have departed from me|et noti mei quasi alieni recesserunt a me]] [the margin gives Job vi, 15 and xix, 13; Denis's words are those of Job 19:13]. This can likewise be understood of Christ, made poor for our sake, from whom the Apostles fled at the time of his passion[[Matt 26:56||]].

paras.t: Qui tantum verba sectatur, id est loquacitatem aut verborum ornatum, non sensum eorum, nec implet documenta ac jussa Scripturæ, nihil habebit gratiæ ac salutis. Nempe, ut ait Apostolus, Non auditores legis justi sunt apud Deum, sed factores legis justificabuntur.
paras.en: [[19:7|He that followeth after words only|Qui tantum verba sectatur]], that is, talkativeness or the ornament of words, not their sense, and does not fulfil the teachings and commands of Scripture, [[19:7|shall have nothing|nihil habebit]] of grace and salvation. For, as the Apostle says, [[Rom 2:13|not the hearers of the law are just before God: but the doers of the law shall be justified|Non auditores legis justi sunt apud Deum, sed factores legis justificabuntur]].

paras.t: Qui autem possessor est mentis, id est, rationem habet illæsam ac liberam, ita quod per virtutes morales, parti sensitivæ efficaciter dominatur, nec passionibus vulneratur; diligit animam suam spirituali amore, quia vult et procurat animæ suæ ea in quibus salus sua consistit. Quocontra dicitur de iniquo in Psalmo : Qui autem diligit iniquitatem, odit animam suam. Et custos prudentiæ inveniet bona.
paras.en: [[19:8|But he that possesseth a mind|Qui autem possessor est mentis]], that is, has his reason unharmed and free, so that through the moral virtues he effectively rules the sensitive part and is not wounded by the passions, [[19:8|loveth his own soul|diligit animam suam]] with a spiritual love, because he wills and procures for his soul those things in which its salvation consists. Against which it is said of the wicked man in the Psalm: [[Ps 10:6|but he that loveth iniquity, hateth his own soul|Qui autem diligit iniquitatem, odit animam suam]]. [[19:8|And he that keepeth prudence, shall find good things|Et custos prudentiæ inveniet bona]].

paras.t: Falsus testis non erit impunitus : et qui loquitur mendacia peribit.
paras.en: [[19:9|A false witness shall not be unpunished: and he that speaketh lies, shall perish|Falsus testis non erit impunitus : et qui loquitur mendacia peribit]].

paras.t: Non decent stultum divitiæ : quia abutitur eis. Similiter infidelem et hæreticum non decent naturales scientiæ, aut notitia Scripturarum, quibus fidem impugnant catholicam. Nec servum dominari principibus : quoniam hoc contrariatur ordini recto, qui exigit inferiorem subesse, et superiorem præesse. Servi quoque ad dominationem promoti, communiter sunt superbi et sævi. Similiter servum peccati et iniquum non decet dominari principibus, id est, his qui ratione ac virtutibus regunt se ipsos.
paras.en: [[19:10|Delicacies are not seemly for a fool|Non decent stultum divitiæ]] [Denis reads *divitiæ*, "riches", for the Vulgate's *deliciæ*, "delicacies"]: because he abuses them. Likewise the natural sciences, or knowledge of the Scriptures, are not seemly for the unbeliever and the heretic, for with them they attack the Catholic faith. [[19:10|Nor for a servant to have rule over princes|Nec servum dominari principibus]]: because this is contrary to right order, which requires the inferior to be subject and the superior to be over him. Servants raised to lordship are also commonly proud and cruel. Likewise it is not seemly for the servant of sin, the wicked man, to rule over princes, that is, over those who govern themselves by reason and the virtues.

paras.t: Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur : id est, si ipse qui docet, sit veraciter patiens, constat quod dignus sit alios informare, utputa virtuosus, quoniam patientia omnium est virtutum probatrix. Qui enim agit quod docet, reverenter est audiendus. Sed cujus vita juste despicitur, ejus quoque doctrina contemnitur. Ideo, teste Gregorio, Tanto unusquisque convincitur minus doctus, quanto minus patiens. Hinc ait Ambrosius : Ante vita, quam doctrina, quærenda est. Bona vita sine doctrina, gratiam habet; doctrina sine laudabili vita et vera patientia, gratia caret. Spiritualiter autem, Christi et Apostolorum et aliorum ejus discipulorum doctrina, innotuit esse vera ex eorumdem patientia : quia pro suæ doctrinæ veritate tuenda, æquanimiter sunt perpessi tot et tanta tormenta, imo et acerbissima genera mortis, nec aliquod præsentis vitæ commodum, aut honorem exquisierunt. Unde ostenditur, quod de futura alterius vitæ remuneratione fuerant certi. Et gloria ejus est iniqua prætergredi : id est, præclarum meritum et honor viri patientis consistit in hoc, ut aliorum improbitatem ac perversitatem æquanimiter ferat, et dum eam corrigere nequit, dissimulet, nec scelus scelere ulciscatur : sicut ait Apostolus, Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum. Unde Joannes monet : Noli imitari quod malum est. Hinc Seneca : Ridiculum (inquit) est, odio innocentiam perdere ; et iterum, Nunquam scelus scelere vindicandum ; itemque, Nihil magnum in rebus humanis, nisi animus magna vel mala despiciens.
paras.en: [[19:11|The learning of a man is known by patience|Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur]]: that is, if he who teaches is truly patient, it is plain that he is worthy to instruct others, being virtuous, since patience is the proof of all the virtues. For he who does what he teaches is to be heard with reverence; but he whose life is rightly despised, his teaching too is scorned. Therefore, as Gregory witnesses, Each man is shown to be the less learned, the less patient he is. Hence Ambrose says: Life is to be sought before learning. A good life without learning has grace; learning without a praiseworthy life and true patience lacks grace. Spiritually, the teaching of Christ, of the Apostles and of his other disciples was made known to be true by their patience: because, to defend the truth of their teaching, they bore with an even mind so many and such great torments, and even the bitterest kinds of death, and sought no advantage or honour of the present life. From this it is shown that they were certain of the reward of the other life to come. [[19:11|And his glory is to pass over wrongs|Et gloria ejus est iniqua prætergredi]]: that is, the splendid merit and honour of the patient man consists in this, that he bears the wickedness and perversity of others with an even mind, and, while he cannot correct it, overlooks it, and does not avenge crime with crime: as the Apostle says, [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good|Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]]. Hence John warns: [[3 John 1:11|follow not that which is evil|Noli imitari quod malum est]]. Hence Seneca: It is ridiculous, he says, to lose one's innocence through hatred; and again, Crime is never to be avenged by crime; and also, There is nothing great in human affairs but a mind that looks down on great things, or on evil ones.

paras.t: Sicut fremitus leonis est valde terribilis aliis bestiis : quarum multæ ex rugitu leonis ita terrentur, quod gradum mox figunt, non valentes fugere neque procedere. Unde scriptum est : Leo rugiet, quis non timebit? Ita et regis ira metuenda est subditis suis, quemadmodum dictum est : Nuntii mortis, ira regis. Et maxime ira Regis cœlestis, est incomparabiliter formidanda : qui ait, Ecce ego stridebo super vos, sicut stridet plaustrum onustum fœno. Et sicut ros super herbam valde conveniens est, ita et hilaritas ejus jucunda est subditis, præsertim Regis supremi in hora judicii.
paras.en: [[19:12|As the roaring of a lion|Sicut fremitus leonis]] is very terrible to the other beasts, many of which are so terrified by the lion's roar that they at once stand fixed, unable to flee or to go forward. Hence it is written: [[Amos 3:8|The lion shall roar, who will not fear|Leo rugiet, quis non timebit]]? [[19:12|So also is the anger of a king|Ita et regis ira]] to be feared by his subjects, as has been said: [[Prov 16:14|The wrath of a king is as messengers of death|Nuntii mortis, ira regis]]. And above all the anger of the heavenly King is beyond comparison to be dreaded, who says: [[Amos 2:13|Behold, I will screak under you as a wain screaketh that is laden with hay|Ecce ego stridebo super vos, sicut stridet plaustrum onustum fœno]]. And [[19:12|as the dew upon the grass|sicut ros super herbam]] is very welcome, so also [[19:12|his cheerfulness|hilaritas ejus]] is pleasant to his subjects, above all the cheerfulness of the supreme King in the hour of judgment.

paras.t: Dolor patris, filius stultus : quia de filio insipiente, vitioso, rebelli, pater tristatur, tam carnalis quam spiritualis, sicut expositum est ; et tecta jugiter perstillantia est litigiosa mulier, id est similis tecto fracto : quoniam sicut per tale tectum cadunt assidue stillæ pluviales, eos qui in domo sunt affligentes ; ita ex foramine oris rixosæ feminæ, jugiter erumpunt verba domesticos inquietantia, afflictiva, turbantia. Spiritualiter, per litigiosam mulierem intelligitur sensualitas incitans contra rationem, seu hæreticorum ecclesia garriens contra Catholicos, seu dialectica contra ea quæ fidei sunt loquax.
paras.en: [[19:13|A foolish son is the grief of his father|Dolor patris, filius stultus]]: because a father, carnal as well as spiritual, is saddened by an unwise, vicious, rebellious son, as has been explained; [[19:13|and a wrangling wife is like a roof continually dropping through|et tecta jugiter perstillantia est litigiosa mulier]], that is, she is like a broken roof: for as through such a roof the drops of rain fall without ceasing, distressing those who are in the house, so from the opening of a quarrelsome woman's mouth words burst out continually that disquiet, distress and trouble the household. Spiritually, by the wrangling wife is understood sensuality stirring up against reason, or the church of the heretics chattering against the Catholics, or dialectic, talkative against the things of faith.

paras.t: Domus et divitiæ dantur a parentibus : qui soboli suæ sua temporalia bona, tempore nuptiarum pro parte dant, et tempore mortis relinquunt ; a Domino autem proprie uxor prudens : id est, divinæ providentiæ donum est, prudentem acquirere conjugem, juxta illud : Pars bona, mulier bona ; in parte bona timentium Deum, dabitur viro pro factis bonis. Spiritualiter, uxor prudens, est mater Ecclesia, sapientia vera, ratio recta.
paras.en: [[19:14|House and riches are given by parents|Domus et divitiæ dantur a parentibus]], who give their temporal goods to their offspring, in part at the time of marriage, and leave them at the time of death; [[19:14|but a prudent wife is properly from the Lord|a Domino autem proprie uxor prudens]]: that is, it is a gift of divine providence to gain a prudent spouse, according to that saying: [[Ecclus 26:3|A good wife is a good portion, she shall be given in the portion of them that fear God, to a man for his good deeds|Pars bona, mulier bona ; in parte bona timentium Deum, dabitur viro pro factis bonis]]. Spiritually, the prudent wife is mother Church, true wisdom, right reason.

paras.t: Pigredo immittit soporem, id est mentis fastidium ac torporem ad ea quæ Dei sunt et salutis ; corpori quoque somnolentiam ingerit, præcipue in divinis, et tempore sermocinationis ; et anima dissoluta esuriet, id est, spiritualibus refectionibus indigebit, vanitates voluptatesque appetet, quia non consolatur a Domino, qui locutus est per Prophetam : Usquequo deliciis dissolveris, filia vaga?
paras.en: [[19:15|Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep|Pigredo immittit soporem]], that is, weariness and torpor of mind towards the things of God and of salvation; it also brings drowsiness on the body, especially in divine things and at the time of preaching; [[19:15|and an idle soul shall suffer hunger|et anima dissoluta esuriet]] [*dissoluta*, here "idle", is literally "loosened", "dissolute": the same word as in the verse of Jeremias that follows], that is, it will lack spiritual refreshment and will crave vanities and pleasures, because it is not consoled by the Lord, who has spoken through the Prophet: [[Jer 31:22|How long wilt thou be dissolute in deliciousness, O wandering daughter?|Usquequo deliciis dissolveris, filia vaga?]]?

paras.t: Qui custodit mandatum per memoriam et effectum, custodit animam suam a laqueis inimici, a potestate diaboli, a devoratione inferni ; qui autem negligit viam suam, id est, arctam viam salutis sibi præfixam ac jussam non ambulat, mortificabitur per peccata mortalia et gehennæ supplicia.
paras.en: [[19:16|He that keepeth the commandment|Qui custodit mandatum]] by memory and in deed [[19:16|keepeth his own soul|custodit animam suam]] from the snares of the enemy, from the power of the devil, from being devoured by hell; [[19:16|but he that neglecteth his own way|qui autem negligit viam suam]], that is, does not walk the strait way of salvation set before him and commanded him[[Matt 7:14||]] [the margin gives Matt. vii, 13; the strait way is in v. 14], [[19:16|shall die|mortificabitur]] through mortal sins and the punishments of hell.

paras.t: Fœneratur, id est accommodat, Domino, qui miseretur pauperis, subveniendo eidem : quia hoc Dominus reputat sibi factum, sicut in Evangelio protestatur : Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Et vicissitudinem suam reddet ei, id est copiosam remunerationem, sicut promisit : Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur. Imo centuplum reddet in præsenti, et vitam gloriæ in futuro.
paras.en: [[19:17|He that hath mercy on the poor|qui miseretur pauperis]], by coming to his aid, [[19:17|lendeth|Fœneratur]], that is, gives on loan, [[19:17|to the Lord|Domino]]: because the Lord counts this as done to himself, as he declares in the Gospel: [[Matt 25:40|as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me|Quod uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis]]. [[19:17|And he will repay him|Et vicissitudinem suam reddet ei]], that is, with abundant reward, as he promised: [[Matt 5:7|Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy|Beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordiam consequentur]]. Indeed he will repay a hundredfold in the present, and the life of glory in the future[[Matt 19:29||]].

paras.t: Erudi filium tuum carnalem ac spiritualem in scientia atque virtutibus, et ne desperes cito de profectu illius, quamvis forsan ad tempus videatur indocilis : ideo non faciliter cesses ab informatione illius. Ad internecionem autem ejus, ne ponas animam tuam : id est, non extendas te ad scandalizandum cum verbo aut facto, sed modeste redargue, et facto ædifica ; nec corporalem ejus mortem procures, ex timore gravioris ruinæ ipsius si diutius vixerit. Verumtamen in Deuteronomio scriptum est, qualiter filius contumax, incorrigibilis, comessationi atque luxuriæ vacans, poterat a parentibus morti tradi.
paras.en: [[19:18|Chastise thy son|Erudi filium tuum]] [*erudi*, literally "instruct"], carnal and spiritual, in knowledge and virtues, and [[19:18|despair not|ne desperes]] too soon of his progress, though perhaps for a time he seems unteachable: so do not lightly cease from instructing him. [[19:18|But to the killing of him set not thy soul|Ad internecionem autem ejus, ne ponas animam tuam]] [Denis reads *internecionem*; the margin notes the Vulgate's *interfectionem*]: that is, do not go so far as to scandalize him by word or deed, but reprove him with moderation and edify him by example; nor procure his bodily death for fear of a heavier fall of his if he should live longer. Yet in Deuteronomy it is written how a stubborn, incorrigible son, given to revelling and debauchery, could be handed over to death by his parents[[Deut 21:18||]].

paras.t: Qui enim impatiens est, id est, ex filii sui peccato ad impatientiam concitatur, sicque illum impetuose redarguit, sustinebit damnum : quia se ipsum graviter lædit in anima, et subditum magis exasperat, scandalizat, perturbat, quam sanet. Ideo ait Apostolus : Patres, nolite ad iracundiam provocare filios vestros, ut non pusillo animo fiant ; sed educate illos in disciplina et correptione Domini. Hinc asserit Augustinus : Quidquid lacerato animo dixeris, punientis est impetus, non caritas corrigentis. Et Prosper : Leviter castigatus, exhibet reverentiam castiganti ; asperitate autem nimiæ increpationis offensus, nec increpationem, nec salutem recipit. Et quum rapuerit, id est, aliquem violenter tractaverit, aut alicui sua subtraxerit, aliud apponet, id est, majus damnum incurret. Taliter igitur studeamus delinquentem curare in anima, ut non per iram, impatientiam, aut alio modo lædamus, aut perimamus propria corda, quum dicat Salvator : Quid proficit homo, si lucretur universum mundum, se autem ipsum perdat, et detrimentum sui faciat?
paras.en: For [[19:19|he that is impatient|Qui enim impatiens est]], that is, is roused to impatience by his son's sin and so rebukes him violently, [[19:19|shall suffer damage|sustinebit damnum]]: because he gravely hurts himself in his soul, and exasperates, scandalizes and upsets his subject more than he heals him. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Eph 6:4|fathers, provoke not your children to anger|Patres, nolite ad iracundiam provocare filios vestros]], [[Col 3:21|lest they be discouraged|ut non pusillo animo fiant]]; [[Eph 6:4|but bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord|sed educate illos in disciplina et correptione Domini]] [Denis joins Eph. vi, 4 and Col. iii, 21]. Hence Augustine declares: Whatever thou sayest with a torn mind is the onrush of one who punishes, not the charity of one who corrects. And Prosper: One who is gently chastised shows reverence to the one who chastises him; but one offended by the harshness of an excessive rebuke receives neither the rebuke nor salvation. [[19:19|And when he shall take away|Et quum rapuerit]], that is, when he has treated someone violently or taken someone's goods from him, [[19:19|he shall add another thing|aliud apponet]], that is, he will incur greater damage. Let us therefore so strive to heal the soul of one who does wrong that we do not wound or kill our own hearts through anger, impatience or in some other way, since the Saviour says: [[Luke 9:25|what is a man advantaged, if he gain the whole world and lose himself and cast away himself?|Quid proficit homo, si lucretur universum mundum, se autem ipsum perdat, et detrimentum sui faciat?]]?

paras.t: Audi consilium auribus mentis et corporis, consilium autem sapientium, virtuosorum et expertorum ; et suscipe disciplinam, id est increpationem verborum ac verberum, sive a Deo, sive a prælato infligantur, ut sis sapiens in novissimis tuis, id est, in extremis sapiens inveniaris ac justus. Qui enim tempore juventutis et sanitatis sapientiam et virtutes, consilium et disciplinam non suscipit, nec custodit, vix aut non invenietur sapiens in extremis.
paras.en: [[19:20|Hear counsel|Audi consilium]] with the ears of mind and body, the counsel, that is, of the wise, the virtuous and the experienced; [[19:20|and receive instruction|et suscipe disciplinam]], that is, the rebuke of words and of blows, whether they are dealt by God or by a superior, [[19:20|that thou mayst be wise in thy latter end|ut sis sapiens in novissimis tuis]], that is, that thou mayest be found wise and just at the last. For he who in the time of youth and health does not receive or keep wisdom and the virtues, counsel and instruction, will hardly, or not at all, be found wise at the last.

paras.t: Multæ cogitationes in corde viri, id est, assidue variantur in corde ex instabilitate fragilitatis humanæ, juxta illud : Cogitationes meæ variæ succedunt sibi, et mens in diversa rapitur. Voluntas autem Domini, quæ est ipsemet Deus volens, in æternum permanet una atque incommutabilis.
paras.en: [[19:21|There are many thoughts in the heart of a man|Multæ cogitationes in corde viri]], that is, they vary constantly in the heart from the instability of human frailty, according to that saying: [[Job 20:2|various thoughts succeed one another in me, and my mind is hurried away to different things|Cogitationes meæ variæ succedunt sibi, et mens in diversa rapitur]]. [[19:21|But the will of the Lord|Voluntas autem Domini]], which is God himself willing, [[19:21|shall stand firm|in æternum permanet]] for ever, one and unchangeable.

paras.t: Homo indigens misericors est : quia ex propriæ paupertatis et indigentiæ experientia commonetur ac discit aliis misereri. Unde de Christo dicit Apostolus : Debuit per omnia fratribus assimilari, ut misericors fieret. Aristoteles quoque in Politicis ait, quod et senes proni sunt ad compassionem, quia sunt pluribus indigentes ; similiter feminæ. Denique omnis homo proprias defectuositates, culpas, indigentias, quantum ad bona animæ, rite perpendens, misericors est. Et melior est pauper, ut talis, quam vir mendax : quia paupertas non tantum malificat personam sicut mendacium.
paras.en: [[19:22|A needy man is merciful|Homo indigens misericors est]]: because from the experience of his own poverty and need he is reminded and learns to have mercy on others. Hence the Apostle says of Christ: [[Heb 2:17|it behoved him in all things to be made like unto his brethren|Debuit per omnia fratribus assimilari]], that he might become merciful. Aristotle too says in the Politics that old men are prone to compassion, because they are in need of many things; and women likewise. Lastly, every man who duly weighs his own defects, faults and needs as regards the goods of the soul is merciful. [[19:22|And better is the poor|Et melior est pauper]], as such, [[19:22|than the lying man|quam vir mendax]]: because poverty does not make a person bad as much as lying does.

paras.t: Timor Domini ad vitam, id est, timor filialis ad vitam deducit beatam ; et in plenitudine, id est plena beatitudine, commorabitur absque visitatione pessimi, id est diaboli, cui ad Beatos nullus patet accessus.
paras.en: [[19:23|The fear of the Lord is unto life|Timor Domini ad vitam]], that is, filial fear leads to the blessed life; and [[19:23|in the fulness|in plenitudine]], that is, in full beatitude, [[19:23|he shall abide|commorabitur]] [[19:23|without being visited with evil|absque visitatione pessimi]] [Denis reads *pessimi*, "of the worst one", for the Vulgate's *pessima*], that is, by the devil, to whom there is no access to the Blessed.

paras.t: Abscondit piger manum suam sub ascella, nec ad os suum applicat eam : id est, ab operatione bona se retrahit, et manum capiti suo supponit ad apodiandum et dormiendum ex torpore ; nec ducit eam ad os suum, id est, ea quæ docet et scit, non facit, nec providet ori de necessariis laborando. Secundum Lyram, in Hebræo habetur, Sub caldaria : ut sit sensus, quod piger tempore frigido comestionem interrumpit, manus suas calefaciendo ad ignem, sub olla super ignem pendente, vel ad ascellam. Sed hoc videtur etiam ab aliis fieri.
paras.en: [[19:24|The slothful hideth his hand under his armpit, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth|Abscondit piger manum suam sub ascella, nec ad os suum applicat eam]]: that is, he draws back from good work and puts his hand under his head to prop it up and sleep from torpor; and he does not bring it to his mouth, that is, he does not do what he teaches and knows, nor provide for his mouth the necessaries by labouring. According to Lyra, the Hebrew has "under the cauldron": so that the sense is that the slothful man in cold weather breaks off his eating to warm his hands at the fire, under the pot hanging over the fire, or under his armpit. But this seems to be done by others too.

paras.t: Pestilente flagellato, id est impio, qui alios verbo aut exemplo scandalizat et inficit, debite punito et correcto, stultus sapientior erit : quia ex pœna alterius oritur sibi timor, quo a quibusdam malis retrahitur, et ita sapientior fit quam fuit. Unde Apostolus ait : Peccantes coram omnibus argue, ut et ceteri timorem habeant. Et Seneca loquitur : Sapiens, ex correctione peccati alterius, emendat suum. Si autem corripueris sapientem, intelliget disciplinam, id est, correptionem illam gratanter tanquam beneficium acceptabit, considerando quod sit disciplina quædam medicinaque animæ.
paras.en: [[19:25|The wicked man being scourged|Pestilente flagellato]] [*pestilens*, literally "the pestilent man"], that is, the impious man who scandalizes and infects others by word or example, being duly punished and corrected, [[19:25|the fool shall be wiser|stultus sapientior erit]]: because from another's punishment fear arises in him, by which he is drawn back from certain evils, and so he becomes wiser than he was. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 5:20|Them that sin reprove before all that the rest also may have fear|Peccantes coram omnibus argue, ut et ceteri timorem habeant]]. And Seneca says: The wise man corrects his own sin from the correction of another's. [[19:25|But if thou rebuke a wise man, he will understand discipline|Si autem corripueris sapientem, intelliget disciplinam]], that is, he will accept that rebuke gladly as a benefit, considering that it is a kind of discipline and medicine of the soul.

paras.t: Qui affligit patrem et fugit matrem, ignominiosus erit et infelix : quia ingratissimus est parentibus, et reddit mala pro bonis. Similiter qui spiritualem patrem seu prælatum affligit sua rebellione, aut perversitate, vel negligentia, et a matre sua Ecclesia sancta discedit, abominabilis est, et peribit. Verumtamen, si quis desiderio perfectionis, invitis parentibus competentiam habentibus, fugiat eos, religionem intrando, laudabile est.
paras.en: [[19:26|He that afflicteth his father, and chaseth away his mother|Qui affligit patrem et fugit matrem]] [Denis reads *fugit*, "flees from", for the Vulgate's *fugat*, "chases away"], [[19:26|is infamous and unhappy|ignominiosus erit et infelix]]: because he is most ungrateful to his parents and returns evil for good. Likewise he who afflicts his spiritual father or superior by his rebellion, perversity or negligence, and departs from his mother, holy Church, is abominable and will perish. Yet if anyone, from the desire of perfection, flees from his parents against their will by entering religion, when they have sufficient means [that is, are not in need of his support], it is praiseworthy.

paras.t: Non cesses tempore opportuno audire, fili, doctrinam : quia indesinenter studere debemus incremento scientiæ ac virtutum ; nec ignores sermones scientiæ, id est, ne contingat te non intelligere doctrinalia et sapientialia verba.
paras.en: [[19:27|Cease not|Non cesses]], at the fitting time, [[19:27|O my son, to hear instruction|audire, fili, doctrinam]]: because we must study unceasingly for the increase of knowledge and virtues; [[19:27|and be not ignorant of the words of knowledge|nec ignores sermones scientiæ]], that is, let it not happen that thou dost not understand the words of doctrine and wisdom.

paras.t: Testis iniquus deridet judicium, id est justam sententiæ prolationem : quia præsumit se falsitate testimonii sui posse impedire ne proferatur ; nec etiam timet judicium Dei, quem tam intimorate offendit. Et os impiorum devorat iniquitatem, id est, in verbis mendosis et testimoniis falsis delectatur, quasi in cibo, et ea in cor suum deglutit. In quorum persona fertur in Isaia : Posuimus mendacium spem nostram, et mendacio protecti sumus. Quibus et Amos propheta dicit : Væ qui lætamini in nihilo, qui convertistis in amaritudinem judicium, et fructum justitiæ in absinthium. Denique, Os impiorum devorat iniquitatem, id est bona impie acquisita, quia frequenter accipiunt munera ad perhibendum testimonia falsa.
paras.en: [[19:28|An unjust witness scorneth judgment|Testis iniquus deridet judicium]], that is, the just pronouncing of the sentence: because he presumes that by the falsehood of his testimony he can prevent its being pronounced; nor does he even fear the judgment of God, whom he offends so fearlessly. [[19:28|And the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity|Et os impiorum devorat iniquitatem]], that is, he delights in lying words and false testimony as in food, and swallows them down into his heart. In whose person it is said in Isaias: [[Is 28:15|we have placed our hope in lies, and by falsehood we are protected|Posuimus mendacium spem nostram, et mendacio protecti sumus]]. To whom the prophet Amos too says: Woe to you [[Amos 6:14|that rejoice in a thing of nought|qui lætamini in nihilo]], you that [[Amos 6:13|have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of justice into wormwood|convertistis in amaritudinem judicium, et fructum justitiæ in absinthium]] [Denis joins Amos vi, 14 and 13]. Lastly, the mouth of the wicked devoureth iniquity, that is, goods wickedly gained, because they often take gifts for bearing false witness.

paras.t: Parata sunt derisoribus veritatis et æquitatis, judicia : quoniam Deus paratus est eos judicare et condemnare, juxta illud : Stat ad judicandum Dominus. Et Judas ait : Ecce venit Dominus facere judicium, et arguere impios. In lege quoque divina ac positiva, instituta sunt justa judicia contra tales. Et mallei percutientes parati sunt stultorum, id est impiorum, corporibus : quibus etiam in hac vita pro diversis flagitiis, varia et amara infliguntur tormenta, ut flagellationes, mutilationes, suspendia, rotationes, ac consimilia genera mortis : infernalia quoque supplicia impœnitentibus, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi dicitur. Timidis et incredulis et exsecratis, et omnibus mendacibus, pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure.
paras.en: [[19:29|Judgments|judicia]] [[19:29|are prepared for scorners|Parata sunt derisoribus]] of truth and equity: because God is ready to judge and condemn them, according to that saying: [[Is 3:13|The Lord standeth up to judge|Stat ad judicandum Dominus]]. And Jude says: [[Jude 1:14|Behold, the Lord cometh|Ecce venit Dominus]] [[Jude 1:15|To execute judgment|facere judicium]], [[Jude 1:15|and to reprove all the ungodly|et arguere impios]]. In the divine and positive law, too, just judgments are established against such men. [[19:29|And striking hammers|Et mallei percutientes]] are prepared [[19:29|for the bodies of fools|stultorum]], that is, of the wicked: on whom even in this life various and bitter torments are inflicted for divers crimes, such as scourgings, mutilations, hangings, breakings on the wheel and like kinds of death; and the punishments of hell, too, on the impenitent, as is said in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:8|the fearful and unbelieving and the abominable|Timidis et incredulis et exsecratis]], [[Apoc 21:8|and all liars, they shall have their portion in the pool burning with fire and brimstone|et omnibus mendacibus, pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne et sulfure]].

20.title: DECLARATIO CAPITULI NONIDECIMI : MELIOR EST PAUPER QUI AMBULAT, ETC.
20.title_en: Declaration of the nineteenth chapter: Better is the poor man that walketh, etc.

paras.t: LUXURIOSA res vinum. Sicut sol dicitur calidus, non formaliter, sed effective, quia ex radiorum suorum repercussione gignitur calor; sic vinum vocatur res luxuriosa, quia causat calorem, et calidum efficit sanguinem, qui incitat cito ad luxum; immoderate quoque lætificat, et causat audaciam, rationisque lucem obscurat: quibus peractis, quid nisi venereorum imminet amor? Ideo dictum est ab uno prudentium sæculi hujus : Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus. Et tumultuosa, id est garrulosa et inquieta, est ebrietas. Ideo ait Salvator : Attendite vobis, ne graventur corda vestra in crapula vel ebrietate. Apostolus quoque : Nolite, inquit, inebriari vino, in quo est luxuria.
paras.en: [[20:1|Wine is a luxurious thing|LUXURIOSA res vinum]]. As the sun is called hot, not formally but effectively [that is, not because heat is in it as its form, but because it produces heat], since heat is produced by the reflection of its rays; so wine is called a luxurious thing because it causes heat and makes the blood hot, which quickly stirs to lust [*luxus*: the Latin *luxuriosa* means "lustful" as well as "luxurious"]; it also gladdens immoderately, causes boldness, and darkens the light of reason: and when these things are done, what threatens but the love of venereal things? Therefore it was said by one of the wise of this world: Without Ceres and Bacchus Venus grows cold [Terence, *Eunuchus*, as the margin notes; that is, without bread and wine love cools]. And [[20:1|riotous|tumultuosa]], that is, talkative and restless, is [[20:1|drunkenness|ebrietas]]. Therefore the Saviour says: [[Luke 21:34|take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness|Attendite vobis, ne graventur corda vestra in crapula vel ebrietate]]. The Apostle also: [[Eph 5:18|be not|Nolite]], he says, [[Eph 5:18|drunk with wine, wherein is luxury|inebriari vino, in quo est luxuria]].

paras.t: Quicumque his delectatur, non erit sapiens. Certum est quod nequaquam liceat ebrietate delectari, quum sit vitium in se. Vinum vero quum sit nobilis, vigorosa et utilis creatura, in usum et commodum hominum facta, juxta illud in Psalmo, Ut educas panem de terra, et vinum cor hominis lætificet; de cujus proprietatibus atque effectibus in apocryphis Esdræ multa leguntur; quod in Judicum libro dicitur lætificare Deum et homines: hinc vino delectari, non est in se vitiosum, nec sapientiæ impeditivum, præsertim quum vinum naturaliter delectet suo sapore gustum. Itaque, sicut licitum est vino moderate uti, vel causa medicinæ (prout Timotheo scribit Apostolus, Modico vino utere propter stomachum tuum, et frequentes tuas infirmitates), vel ob alias naturales ac rationabiles causas; sic licitum est vino delectari, naturali ac ordinata delectatione, quæ scilicet ad debitum finem refertur. Delectari autem in vino superfluo, vel in ipso sapore propter se, est illicitum. Qui igitur his, scilicet vino immoderato, aut immoderate in vino (quamvis modico) et ebrietate, sive (ut quidam exponunt) qui his, utpote luxuria et ebrietate, delectatur, non erit sapiens sapientia infusa, quæ donum est, nec in sapientia naturali et acquisita solet esse abundans. Imo quamdiu actualiter occupatur et delectatur his vitiis, usu et actu sapientiæ caret, quoniam rationem absorbent, juxta illud : Fornicatio et ebrietas et vinum auferunt cor. Ideo Isaias inducit : Væ qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem sectandam, et potandum usque ad vesperam.
paras.en: [[20:1|whosoever is delighted therewith, shall not be wise|Quicumque his delectatur, non erit sapiens]]. It is certain that it is in no way lawful to take delight in drunkenness, since it is a vice in itself. But wine is a noble, vigorous and useful creature, made for the use and benefit of men, according to that in the Psalm, [[Ps 103:14|That thou mayst bring bread out of the earth|Ut educas panem de terra]]: [[Ps 103:15|And that wine may cheer the heart of man|et vinum cor hominis lætificet]]; of its properties and effects much is read in the apocryphal Esdras [the margin gives III Esdr. iii, 18–24: the apocryphal Third Book of Esdras, which is not in the Douay-Rheims]; and in the book of Judges it is the wine [[Judg 9:13|that cheereth God and men|lætificare Deum et homines]]: hence to take delight in wine is not vicious in itself, nor a hindrance to wisdom, especially since wine naturally delights the taste by its savour. And so, as it is lawful to use wine moderately, either for medicine's sake (as the Apostle writes to Timothy, [[1 Tim 5:23|use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thy frequent infirmities|Modico vino utere propter stomachum tuum, et frequentes tuas infirmitates]]), or for other natural and reasonable causes; so it is lawful to take delight in wine with a natural and ordered delight, that is, one referred to its due end. But to take delight in superfluous wine, or in its very savour for its own sake, is unlawful. He therefore who is delighted with these, namely with immoderate wine, or immoderately with wine (though it be little) and with drunkenness, or (as some expound it) he who is delighted with these, namely with lust and drunkenness, [[20:1|shall not be wise|non erit sapiens]] with infused wisdom, which is a gift, nor is he wont to abound in natural and acquired wisdom. Nay, as long as he is actually occupied with and delighting in these vices, he lacks the use and act of wisdom, since they swallow up the reason, according to that: [[Osee 4:11|Fornication, and wine, and drunkenness, take away the understanding|Fornicatio et ebrietas et vinum auferunt cor]]. Therefore Isaias brings in: [[Is 5:11|Woe to you that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness, and to drink in the evening|Væ qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem sectandam, et potandum usque ad vesperam]].

paras.t: Hinc quoque philosophi, ut studio philosophiæ essent apti, a vinolentia, gula, luxuria, diligenter abstinuerunt. Atque, ut in Phædone asserit Plato, Nequaquam est philosophi, circa delectationes gustus et tactus versari. Unde quum quidam interrogasset Platonem, Unde tibi sapientia tanta? respondit: Quia plus consumpsi de oleo in lampade, quam de vino in calice. Aristoteles quoque in Problematibus suis fatetur, quod amatores dulcium sunt fatui. Nec dissonat inde, quod de sapientia scriptum est in Job, Non invenitur in terra suaviter viventium. Hinc quarto Proverbiorum suorum libro sanctus scribit Cyrillus : Vinum mel ori est, sed fel capiti venenosum : sapit in ore, ardet in ventre, fumat in capite, contundit sensus, vigorem confundit, imaginationem destruit, tollit mentem; visum obnubilat, nervos laxat, linguam balbificat et inhonestat, manus mobilitat, pectus inflammat; spumat luxuriam, vim gignitivam enervat, gressus inordinat, totumque corpus vastat, ita quod a planta usque ad verticem non est in eo sanitas.
paras.en: Hence the philosophers too, to be fit for the study of philosophy, carefully abstained from much wine, gluttony and lust. And, as Plato asserts in the *Phaedo*, It is in no way the part of a philosopher to busy himself about the delights of taste and touch. Hence when someone asked Plato, Whence hast thou so great wisdom? he answered: Because I have spent more oil in the lamp than wine in the cup. Aristotle too, in his *Problems*, admits that lovers of sweet things are foolish. Nor is that out of tune with this, which is written of wisdom in Job: [[Job 28:13|neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights|Non invenitur in terra suaviter viventium]]. Hence Saint Cyril writes in the fourth book of his Proverbs: Wine is honey to the mouth, but poisonous gall to the head: it is savoury in the mouth, burns in the belly, fumes in the head; it bruises the senses, confounds vigour, destroys the imagination, takes away the mind; it clouds the sight, slackens the sinews, makes the tongue stammer and shames it, makes the hands unsteady, inflames the breast; it foams with lust, weakens the power of generation, disorders the steps, and lays waste the whole body, so that from [[Is 1:6|the sole of the foot unto the top of the head, there is no soundness therein|a planta usque ad verticem non est in eo sanitas]].

paras.t: Sicut rugitus leonis, ita et terror regis. Hoc est quod præcedenti capitulo habetur, Sicut fremitus leonis, ita et regis ira. Qui provocat eum, scilicet regem ad iram per excessum verborum aut operum, peccat in animam suam, id est, sibi ipsi acquirit malum seu mortem, quemadmodum Adonias offendendo Salomonem.
paras.en: [[20:2|As the roaring of a lion, so also is the dread of a king|Sicut rugitus leonis, ita et terror regis]]. This is what is had in the preceding chapter: [[Prov 19:12|As the roaring of a lion, so also is the anger of a king|Sicut fremitus leonis, ita et regis ira]]. [[20:2|he that provoketh him|Qui provocat eum]], namely the king, to anger by excess of words or deeds, [[20:2|sinneth against his own soul|peccat in animam suam]]: that is, gains evil or death for himself, as Adonias did by offending Solomon[[3 Kings 2:13||]].

paras.t: Honor est homini coram Deo sapientibusque hominibus, qui separat se a contentionibus: quoniam inhonestum est valde contentioni servire. Ideo vir modestus, pacificus, mitis, exemplaris et sapiens, vitat contendere, ceditque improbitati, et secundum ordinem juris, suam prosequitur causam. Ideo ait Apostolus: Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium. Itemque: Si quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, neque Ecclesia Dei. Porro, ut ait Ambrosius, Contentio est impugnatio veritatis cum confidentia clamoris. Qui rursus fatetur: Melius est cum pace et gratia emigrare, quam cum contentione atque discordia cohabitare; melius est sine lite abire, quam cum jurgio resistere. Specialissime autem vitandum est, ne quis cum illo contendat, cum quo ante familiariter vixit, quum Seneca dicat: Turpius nihil est, quam cum eo bellum gerere, cum quo familiariter vixeris. Postremo hoc vitium in religiosis est maxime detestandum. Ad cujus detestationem satis nos debet inducere, quod Jacobus ait apostolus in sua Canonica: Si zelum amarum habetis, et contentiones sunt inter vos, nolite gloriari et mendaces esse adversus veritatem: non est sapientia ista desursum descendens, sed terrena, animalis et diabolica. Ubi enim zelus et contentio, ibi inconstantia et omne opus pravum. Ecce quid terribilius dici potest? Hinc de beatissimo viro illo Francisco narratur, quod ex ingenita probitate ac honestate, etiam dum adhuc erat in sæculo, a contentionibus se retraxit.
paras.en: [[20:3|It is an honour for a man|Honor est homini]] before God and wise men [[20:3|to separate himself from quarrels|qui separat se a contentionibus]]: since it is very dishonourable to be the servant of contention. Therefore the modest, peaceable, meek, exemplary and wise man avoids contending, gives way to the wickedness of others, and pursues his cause according to the order of law. Therefore the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words|Noli verbis contendere]]: [[2 Tim 2:14|for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers|ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium]]. And again: [[1 Cor 11:16|if any man seem to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor the Church of God|Si quis videtur contentiosus esse, nos talem consuetudinem non habemus, neque Ecclesia Dei]] [the margin gives no reference here; the words are those of 1 Cor 11:16]. Moreover, as Ambrose says, Contention is the assailing of the truth with the confidence of clamour. And again he declares: It is better to depart with peace and grace than to dwell together with contention and discord; it is better to go away without strife than to resist with wrangling. Most especially must one beware of contending with him with whom one has lived before on familiar terms, since Seneca says: Nothing is more shameful than to wage war with him with whom you have lived familiarly. Lastly, this vice is most of all to be detested in religious. To detest it we should be moved enough by what the apostle James says in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 3:14|if you have bitter zeal, and there be contention in your hearts: glory not and be not liars against the truth|Si zelum amarum habetis, et contentiones sunt inter vos, nolite gloriari et mendaces esse adversus veritatem]]: [[Jas 3:15|For this is not wisdom, descending from above: but earthly, sensual, devilish|non est sapientia ista desursum descendens, sed terrena, animalis et diabolica]]. [[Jas 3:16|For where envying and contention is: there is inconstancy and every evil work.|Ubi enim zelus et contentio, ibi inconstantia et omne opus pravum]] Behold, what more terrible thing can be said? Hence it is told of that most blessed man Francis that, from an inborn uprightness and decency, even while he was still in the world, he drew back from quarrels.

paras.t: Omnes autem stulti, id est vitiosi et contentiosi, miscentur contumeliis, contumeliam aliis inferendo per verba aut facta, vel his qui sibi invicem contumeliose injuriantur, communicando, seu uni eorum favendo et adsistendo. Proprie tamen consistit contumelia in verbis, quum quis dicit alteri verba injuriosa, per quæ ejus honor minuitur vel aufertur: quod, secundum Thomam, non est minus peccatum, quam rapina seu furtum, prout in secunda secundæ, quæstione 72, declarat. His ergo qui taliter nobis loquuntur, non est respondendum. Unde, ut quarto Regum habetur, Ezechias servis suis præcepit, ne contumeliosissimo Rabsaci responderent. Propter quod ait Valerius: Plena victoria est, ad clamantem tacere, nec respondere provocanti; habes enim mercedem de tua patientia, et de fratris medela. Sicut nihil deformius est quam respondere furentibus, sic nihil utilius quam tacere provocatis. Denique sapiens sciens verum esse quod Seneca asserit, A malis vituperari, laudari est, non movetur ex contumeliæ verbis. Quanquam denuo fassus est Seneca: Contumeliam generosus animus ferre non potest.
paras.en: [[20:3|but all fools|Omnes autem stulti]], that is, the vicious and contentious, [[20:3|are meddling with reproaches|miscentur contumeliis]]: by inflicting reproach on others by words or deeds, or by taking part with those who wrong one another with reproaches, or by favouring and standing by one of them. Properly, however, reproach [*contumelia*, an insult to a man's honour] consists in words, when one says to another injurious words by which his honour is lessened or taken away: which, according to Thomas, is no less a sin than robbery or theft, as he shows in the Secunda Secundae, question 72. To those, then, who speak to us in this way, no answer is to be given. Hence, as is had in the fourth book of Kings, Ezechias commanded his servants not to answer the most insolent Rabsaces[[4 Kings 18:36||]]. On which account Valerius says: It is a full victory to be silent before one who shouts, and not to answer one who provokes; for you have the reward of your patience and of your brother's cure. As nothing is more unseemly than to answer the raging, so nothing is more profitable than to be silent when provoked. Lastly, the wise man, knowing that what Seneca asserts is true, To be blamed by the wicked is to be praised, is not moved by words of reproach. Although Seneca again admitted: A noble mind cannot bear reproach.

paras.t: Propter frigus piger arare noluit tempore suo, ne frigore affligeretur; mendicabit ergo æstate, et non dabitur ei. Hoc in corporalibus quandoque ita contingit. Spiritualiter autem piger, propter frigus, id est ex sua desidia et caritatis infrigidatione, non vult arare, id est agrum cordis sui excolere, et examinando se ipsum evertere, aut sibi commissos sollicite exercere. Mendicabit ergo æstate, id est die judicii sui particularis aut universalis, quum venerit tempus recipiendi fructum eorum quæ seminavit: quia tunc dicet, Domine, Domine, aperi mihi; et non dabitur ei, quia tunc non patet precum meritorumve locus.
paras.en: [[20:4|Because of the cold the sluggard would not plough|Propter frigus piger arare noluit]] in his season, lest he be afflicted by the cold; [[20:4|he shall beg therefore in the summer, and it shall not be given him|mendicabit ergo æstate, et non dabitur ei]]. This sometimes happens so in bodily things. But spiritually the sluggard, [[20:4|because of the cold|propter frigus]], that is, from his sloth and the cooling of charity, will not plough, that is, cultivate the field of his heart and turn it over by examining himself, or diligently exercise those committed to him. [[20:4|he shall beg therefore in the summer|mendicabit ergo æstate]], that is, on the day of his particular or of the universal judgment, when the time has come to receive the fruit of what he has sown: for then he will say, [[Matt 25:11|Lord, Lord, open|Domine, Domine, aperi]] to me [the Gospel has "open to us"]; [[20:4|and it shall not be given him|et non dabitur ei]], for then there is no room for prayers or merits.

paras.t: Sicut aqua profunda, sic consilium in corde viri: quoniam sicut fundus profundæ aquæ facile sciri non valet, nec cernuntur quæ natant in ea ; ita consilium viri, quamdiu manet in abdito cordis, ignotum est aliis ; sed homo sapiens exhauriet illud, humiliter, benevole, et prudenter inquirendo a tali viro quid gerat in corde, et quæstionem movendo de his, de quibus ille intra se consulit.
paras.en: [[20:5|Counsel in the heart of a man is like deep water|Sicut aqua profunda, sic consilium in corde viri]]: for as the bottom of deep water cannot easily be known, nor are the things that swim in it seen, so a man's counsel, as long as it stays hidden in the heart, is unknown to others; [[20:5|but a wise man will draw it out|sed homo sapiens exhauriet illud]], by inquiring humbly, kindly and prudently of such a man what he bears in his heart, and by raising questions about the things on which he takes counsel within himself.

paras.t: Multi homines misericordes vocantur : quia in corporalibus condolent et succurrunt ; virum autem fidelem quis inveniet? qui scilicet vere et discrete misericors sit, sic ut justitiam non relinquat, sicque corporalia misericordiæ exhibeat opera, ut et spirituales misericordiæ actus exsequatur idonee, corripiendo et corrigendo proximum de malis culpæ, de quibus plus condolendum est proximo quam de malis pœnalibus. Unde loquitur Augustinus : Annon sunt in te viscera pietatis christianæ, ut plangas corpus a quo recessit anima, et non plangas animam a qua recessit Deus? Quasi dicat : Rarus est vir ita fidelis, amicum suum non palpans, nec veritatem relinquens.
paras.en: [[20:6|Many men are called merciful|Multi homines misericordes vocantur]], because they have compassion and give succour in bodily things; [[20:6|but who shall find a faithful man?|virum autem fidelem quis inveniet?]] that is, one who is truly and discreetly merciful, so as not to abandon justice, and so performs the bodily works of mercy as also to carry out fittingly the spiritual acts of mercy, rebuking and correcting his neighbour for the evils of fault, for which we must grieve with our neighbour more than for the evils of punishment. Hence Augustine says: Are there not in thee the bowels of Christian pity, that thou shouldst bewail the body from which the soul has departed, and not bewail the soul from which God has departed? As if to say: Rare is the man so faithful that he does not flatter his friend and does not abandon the truth.

paras.t: Justus qui ambulat in simplicitate sua columbina, non asinina, beatos post se filios derelinquet, id est filios carnales aut spirituales suis doctrinis et exemplis instructos, seu quoscumque suarum virtutum imitatores condignos, nunc beatos in spe, postmodum in re.
paras.en: [[20:7|The just that walketh in his simplicity|Justus qui ambulat in simplicitate sua]], the simplicity of the dove, not of the ass [that is, a wise innocence, not dullness], [[20:7|shall leave behind him blessed children|beatos post se filios derelinquet]]: that is, children of the flesh or of the spirit, instructed by his teachings and examples, or any worthy imitators of his virtues, blessed now in hope, afterwards in reality.

paras.t: Rex qui sedet in solio judicii, id est, qui justum in omnibus exercet judicium, dissipat omne malum intuitu suo, id est, subditos suos reformat, et vitia eorum exstirpat, ipsos sollicite intuendo in quibus reformatione indigeant. Porro Christus, Rex regum, reprobat et condemnat omne malum mortale.
paras.en: [[20:8|The king, that sitteth on the throne of judgment|Rex qui sedet in solio judicii]], that is, who exercises just judgment in all things, [[20:8|scattereth away all evil with his look|dissipat omne malum intuitu suo]]: that is, he reforms his subjects and roots out their vices, looking carefully into the things in which they need reforming. Moreover Christ, the King of kings, reproves and condemns every mortal evil.

paras.t: Quis potest dicere vere et sine jactantia : Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato? Quamvis enim ex gratia possit quis esse a mortali culpa immunis, sicque aliqualiter corde mundus (juxta quod scriptum est, Beati mundo corde; et, Beati immaculati in via; itemque, Innocens manibus et mundo corde); tamen in venialibus omnes sumus culpabiles, et paucissimi inveniuntur qui non fuerunt aut sunt mortali culpa fœdati. Ideo Jacobus ait apostolus : In multis offendimus omnes. Et S. Joannes : Si dixerimus, inquit, quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus. Unde et in Job legitur : Quid est homo, ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere? Itaque scripturæ quæ de hac re videntur diversimode loqui, per distinctionem faciliter solvi queunt et concordari : quoniam multis modis dicitur quis mundus, et justus, et sanctus. Primo, quoniam nulli unquam peccato fuit obnoxius, nec originali, nec personali aut actuali : quod competit Christo ; secundo, quoniam nulli personali, nec mortali, nec veniali ; tertio, quoniam nulli mortali ; quarto, quia etsi fuit, tamen modo non est.
