paras.en: [[20:9|Who can say|Quis potest dicere]] truly and without boasting: [[20:9|My heart is clean, I am pure from sin?|Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato?]] For although by grace one may be free of mortal sin, and so in some way clean of heart (according to what is written, [[Matt 5:8|Blessed are the clean of heart|Beati mundo corde]]; and, [[Ps 118:1|Blessed are the undefiled in the way|Beati immaculati in via]]; and again, [[Ps 23:4|The innocent in hands, and clean of heart|Innocens manibus et mundo corde]]), yet in venial sins we are all guilty, and very few are found who have not been or are not stained with mortal sin. Therefore the apostle James says: [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|In multis offendimus omnes]]. And Saint John: [[1 John 1:8|If we say|Si dixerimus]], he says, [[1 John 1:8|that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves|quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus]] [the margin gives Joann. i, 8; the words are in the First Epistle of John]. Hence also we read in Job: [[Job 15:14|What is man that he should be without spot, and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just?|Quid est homo, ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere?]] So the Scriptures which seem to speak of this matter in different ways can easily be resolved and brought into agreement by a distinction: for one is called clean, and just, and holy in many ways. First, because he was never liable to any sin, neither original, nor personal or actual: which belongs to Christ; secondly, because liable to no personal sin, neither mortal nor venial; thirdly, because liable to no mortal sin; fourthly, because, though he was, yet now he is not.

paras.t: Pondus et pondus, mensura et mensura, utrumque abominabile est apud Deum. Hoc lectum est supra, Statera dolosa abominatio est apud Deum : et ex dictis ibidem patet hujus intelligentia verbi. Denique qui propria facta et verba quærit semper justificare aut excusare, proximorumque verba et opera vituperare, seu in pejus interpretari, iniquis utitur pondere et mensura. Quocontra Seneca loquitur : Justus judex non aliter de alienis, quam de propriis judicat gestis. Qui et in suis ait Proverbiis : Æquus judex non aliam de sua, aliam de alia causa profert sententiam.
paras.en: [[20:10|Diverse weights and diverse measures, both are abominable before God|Pondus et pondus, mensura et mensura, utrumque abominabile est apud Deum]] [literally "weight and weight, measure and measure"]. This was read above: [[Prov 11:1|A deceitful balance is an abomination before the Lord|Statera dolosa abominatio est apud Deum]]; and from what was said there the meaning of this saying is plain. Further, he who always seeks to justify or excuse his own deeds and words, and to blame his neighbours' words and works or to interpret them for the worse, uses unjust weight and measure. Against which Seneca says: A just judge judges no otherwise of others' doings than of his own. And he says also in his Proverbs: A fair judge does not give one sentence in his own cause and another in another's.

paras.t: Ex studiis suis intelligitur puer. Si per puerum intelligamus parvulum corpore et ætate, potest ita exponi, quod ex studiis et occupationibus quibus innititur puer in pueritia sua, potest conjecturari qualis erit in virili ætate. Pueri enim bonæ indolis, cito incipiunt hoc monstrare per actus quosdam. Unde subjungitur : si munda et recta sunt opera ejus, id est honestatem quamdam prætendentia et virtutes ; vel si opera ejus postea erunt munda et justa : secundum quod ait Philosophus, quod pueros egregiæ indolis beatificamus in spe futuræ virtuositatis. Si autem per puerum intelliguntur quicumque fideles et servi Dei (qui in Scripturis multoties pueri appellantur, sicut et Christus ait discipulis : Pueri, numquid pulmentarium habetis ?) iste est sensus, quod de exterioribus talium operibus advertere possumus quod vere sint sincera et justa, si viderimus eos intentos studiis sapientiæ et virtutum, seu libenter audire verba salubria, atque ex corde zelari in omnibus pro Dei honore et justitia ac communi salute, esseque custoditos in verbis et sensibus, et coram Deo sollicitos, ac proximis exemplares.
paras.en: [[20:11|By his inclinations a child is known|Ex studiis suis intelligitur puer]] [*studia*: the pursuits a person applies himself to]. If by child we understand one who is little in body and age, it can be expounded thus: that from the pursuits and occupations to which a child applies himself in his childhood, one can guess what he will be in manhood. For children of good disposition soon begin to show it by certain acts. Hence is added: [[20:11|if his works be clean and right|si munda et recta sunt opera ejus]], that is, if they show forth a certain honesty and virtues; or, if his works will afterwards be clean and just: according to what the Philosopher says, that we call children of excellent disposition blessed in the hope of future virtue. But if by child are understood any faithful men and servants of God (who in the Scriptures are many times called children, as Christ too says to the disciples: [[John 21:5|Children, have you any meat?|Pueri, numquid pulmentarium habetis]]), this is the sense: that from the outward works of such men we can discern that they are truly sincere and just, if we see them intent on the pursuits of wisdom and virtue, or gladly hearing wholesome words, and zealous from the heart in all things for God's honour and justice and the common salvation, and guarded in words and senses, careful before God, and an example to their neighbours.

paras.t: Aurem audientem, id est obedienter suscipientem ac adimplentem ea quæ audit salubria, et oculum videntem, id est intellectum illuminatum seu alios instruentem, vel bona aliorum exempla ad sectandum inspicientem ; Dominus fecit utrumque : quia utrumque istorum est opus gratiæ Dei. Quocontra Moyses in Deuteronomio filiis Israel : Vos, inquit, vidistis universa magnalia quæ coram vobis fecit Dominus : et non dedit vobis Dominus cor intelligens, et oculos videntes, et aures quæ possint audire usque in præsentem diem.
paras.en: [[20:12|The hearing ear|Aurem audientem]], that is, one that obediently receives and fulfils the wholesome things it hears, [[20:12|and the seeing eye|et oculum videntem]], that is, an enlightened understanding, or one instructing others, or one looking at the good examples of others in order to follow them: [[20:12|the Lord hath made them both|Dominus fecit utrumque]], for each of these is the work of God's grace. On the other hand Moses in Deuteronomy says to the children of Israel: You, he says, [[Deut 29:2|have seen all the things that the Lord did before you|vidistis universa magnalia quæ coram vobis fecit Dominus]] [Denis has *universa magnalia*, "all the mighty works"]: [[Deut 29:4|And the Lord hath not given you a heart to understand, and eyes to see, and ears that may hear, unto this present day|et non dedit vobis Dominus cor intelligens, et oculos videntes, et aures quæ possint audire usque in præsentem diem]].

paras.t: Noli diligere somnum corporalem superfluum, nec somnum ignorantiæ, peccati sive teporis, ne te egestas opprimat, id est spiritualium temporaliumve bonorum defectus. Aperi oculos tuos, id est, vigilans esto ac providus in actibus bonis, et saturare panibus, id est refectione mentis ad abundantiam, ac corporis ad competentiam.
paras.en: [[20:13|Love not sleep|Noli diligere somnum]], bodily sleep beyond need, nor the sleep of ignorance, of sin or of lukewarmness, [[20:13|lest poverty oppress thee|ne te egestas opprimat]], that is, the want of spiritual or temporal goods. [[20:13|open thy eyes|Aperi oculos tuos]], that is, be watchful and provident in good acts, [[20:13|and be filled with bread|et saturare panibus]], that is, with refreshment of the mind to abundance, and of the body to sufficiency.

paras.t: Malum est, malum est, dicit omnis emptor : id est, ementes communiter dicunt rem emendam minus valere, quam venditor dicit aut veritas habet, ut minori pretio emant eam ; et quum recesserit re empta, tunc gloriabitur, quod modicum pro ea exposuit. Verumtamen sunt quidam tam justi, caritativi ac timorati, quod nequaquam scienter volunt mentiri, neque pro re venali minus dare quam valet : quia nec licet (secundum conscientiam) fallere aut damnificare vendentem, minuendo de pretio justo, quamvis secundum jura civilia hoc liceat, vel potius non puniatur, dummodo citra medium justi valoris id fiat. Hinc in libro de Trinitate recitat Augustinus, qualiter quidam volens propositionem exprimere, in qua universi concordant, dixit : Omnes vultis carius vendere, et vilius emere. Et ostendit Augustinus, hoc pati instantiam apud ministros Dei perfectos, qui utrumque horum abhorrent.
paras.en: [[20:14|It is naught, it is naught, saith every buyer|Malum est, malum est, dicit omnis emptor]]: that is, buyers commonly say that the thing to be bought is worth less than the seller says or than the truth holds, so as to buy it at a lower price; [[20:14|and when he is gone away|et quum recesserit]] with the thing bought, [[20:14|then he will boast|tunc gloriabitur]] that he paid little for it. Yet there are some so just, charitable and God-fearing that they will in no way knowingly lie, nor give less for a thing on sale than it is worth: for it is not lawful (in conscience) to deceive or damage the seller by lessening the just price, although by civil law this is allowed, or rather not punished, provided it be done within half the just value [the civil law let a sale be undone only when the price fell short of half the just value]. Hence in the book On the Trinity Augustine tells how someone wishing to state a proposition on which all agree, said: You all wish to sell dear and to buy cheap. And Augustine shows that this admits an exception among perfect ministers of God, who abhor both of these things.

paras.t: Est aurum, et multitudo gemmarum, et vas pretiosum, labia scientiæ : id est, labia alios sapienter salubriterque instruentia, ob dignitatem scientiæ et boni operis sui, merito comparantur, imo et præferuntur omni auro, gemmis, ac pretiosissimis vasis.
paras.en: [[20:15|There is gold and a multitude of jewels: but the lips of knowledge are a precious vessel|Est aurum, et multitudo gemmarum, et vas pretiosum, labia scientiæ]]: that is, lips that instruct others wisely and wholesomely are rightly compared, nay preferred, to all gold, jewels and most precious vessels, because of the dignity of their knowledge and of their good work.

paras.t: Tolle vestimentum ejus qui fidejussor exstitit alieni : id est, si quis fidejussit tibi pro alio, potes ab illo fidejussore accipere vestem suam tempore opportuno, quousque satisfaciat tibi. Verumtamen, sicut habetur in Exodo, si fidejussor tam pauper fuisset, quod noctu ad operiendum se indiguisset illa veste, reddenda sibi fuisset de sero, et rursus accipi potuisset de mane. Similiter si indiguisset ea in die, et non de nocte, poterat tolli de nocte, et reddenda erat de mane, poteratque resumi ad vesperam. Unde quibusdam Amos propheta improperat, quod super vestes pignoratas requiescebant. Et pro extraneis pro quibus fidejussit, aufer pignus ab eo : sicut de hoc erant judicialia quædam præcepta in Exodo ac Deuteronomio data : quæ in evangelica lege ex illa institutione non ligant, prout in prima secundæ Thomas declarat.
paras.en: [[20:16|Take away the garment of him that is surety for a stranger|Tolle vestimentum ejus qui fidejussor exstitit alieni]]: that is, if anyone has gone surety to thee for another, thou mayest take his garment from that surety at a fitting time, until he satisfies thee. Yet, as is had in Exodus, if the surety was so poor that he needed that garment to cover himself at night[[Ex 22:27||]], it had to be given back to him in the evening[[Ex 22:26||]], and could be taken again in the morning. Likewise, if he needed it by day and not by night, it could be taken at night and had to be given back in the morning, and could be taken back again in the evening. Hence the prophet Amos reproaches some because they rested upon garments taken in pledge[[Amos 2:8||]]. And [[20:16|for strangers|Et pro extraneis]], for whom he went surety, [[20:16|take a pledge from him|aufer pignus ab eo]]: as there were certain judicial precepts about this given in Exodus and Deuteronomy[[Deut 24:6||]][[Deut 24:10||]][[Deut 24:17||]], which in the law of the Gospel do not bind by virtue of that institution, as Thomas shows in the Prima Secundae [that is, the judicial precepts of the Old Law ceased with it, and bind only if they are enacted anew].

paras.t: Suavis est homini panis mendacii, id est cibus mendacio seu contra justitiam acquisitus, quasi faciliter et lucrose adeptus : et postea implebitur os ejus calculo, id est gravi confusione et pœna, dum crimen suum fateri compellitur, et justas luere pœnas : dum per quæ peccavit, per hæc punitur, quemadmodum dives epulo specialiter affligebatur in lingua. Istud intelligendum est de homine vitioso : cui delectabile est operari secundum inclinationem vitiosi habitus sui ; in quo non est timor Dei, et conscientiæ remorsus parvus aut nullus.
paras.en: [[20:17|The bread of lying is sweet to a man|Suavis est homini panis mendacii]], that is, food got by a lie or against justice, as if obtained easily and with gain: [[20:17|but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel|et postea implebitur os ejus calculo]], that is, with grievous confusion and punishment, when he is compelled to confess his crime and to pay the just penalties: when [[Wis 11:17|by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented|per quæ peccavit, per hæc punitur]], as the rich glutton was specially afflicted in his tongue[[Luke 16:24||]]. This is to be understood of the vicious man, to whom it is pleasant to act according to the inclination of his vicious habit; in whom [[Ps 13:3|there is no fear of God|non est timor Dei]], and little or no remorse of conscience.

paras.t: Præterea hæreticis, et pseudoprophetis, ac deceptoribus cunctis, dulcis est panis mendacii, id est doctrina hæretica, assertio fallax, sermo sophisticus : quorum ora implebuntur calculo, qui est lapis ignitus, id est infernalium globis incendiorum, sicut in Job de tali homine fertur : Cibos quos sumpserat, evomet, et de ventre illius extrahet illos Deus.
paras.en: Moreover, to heretics, false prophets and all deceivers the [[20:17|bread of lying|panis mendacii]] is sweet, that is, heretical doctrine, false assertion, sophistical speech: whose mouths shall be filled with gravel [*calculus*, a small stone], which is a fiery stone, that is, with the balls of the fires of hell; as is said in Job of such a man: The food which he had taken [[Job 20:15|he shall vomit up, and God shall draw them out of his belly|evomet, et de ventre illius extrahet illos Deus]] [Denis has *Cibos quos sumpserat*, "the food which he had taken", where the Vulgate has "the riches which he hath swallowed"].

paras.t: Cogitationes consiliis roborantur, id est, diriguntur ut bonæ sint, et prosperum sortiantur effectum ; et gubernaculis, id est prudentialibus ordinationibus ac providentiis, tractanda, id est inchoanda, disponenda, exercenda sunt bella : in quibus plus valet prudentia et dispositio exercituum apta, quam fortitudo corporea, prout Ægidius de Roma, libro de Regimine principum, tractat diffuse, Vegetius quoque compendiose in libro de Re militari. Nec minus caute, imo et cautius pugnandum est contra invisibiles hostes, ubi incomparabiliter majus præmium datur victoribus, graviusque periculum imminet victis.
paras.en: [[20:18|Designs are strengthened by counsels|Cogitationes consiliis roborantur]], that is, are directed so as to be good and to gain a prosperous outcome; and [[20:18|by governments|et gubernaculis]] [*gubernacula*, literally "rudders": the helm], that is, by prudent orderings and provisions, [[20:18|wars are to be managed|tractanda]], that is, begun, set in order and carried on: in which prudence and a fit disposition of the armies avails more than bodily strength, as Giles of Rome treats at length in his book On the Government of Princes, and Vegetius briefly in his book On Military Matters. And no less carefully, nay more carefully still, must we fight against invisible enemies, where an incomparably greater reward is given to the victors, and a graver danger threatens the vanquished.

paras.t: Ei qui revelat mysteria, id est secreta celanda, et sibi in fide manifestata : quemadmodum secundo Machabæorum Rhodocus legitur mysteria sui exercitus hostibus revelasse ; et ambulat fraudulenter, ostendens se quasi fidelem, quum sit adversarius et deceptor, et dilatat labia sua, in præsentia blandiendo, seu prospera promittendo, et loquacitati vacando ; ne commiscearis per societatem, consensum, vel tua secreta ei credendo.
paras.en: [[20:19|with him that revealeth secrets|Ei qui revelat mysteria]], that is, secrets that should be kept hidden and were disclosed to him in confidence, as Rhodocus, in the second book of Machabees, is read to have revealed the secrets of his army to the enemy[[2 Mach 13:21||]]; [[20:19|and walketh deceitfully|et ambulat fraudulenter]], showing himself as if faithful, though he is an adversary and deceiver, [[20:19|and openeth wide his lips|et dilatat labia sua]], by flattering to one's face, or promising prosperity, and giving himself to talkativeness: [[20:19|Meddle not|ne commiscearis]] by fellowship, by consent, or by entrusting your secrets to him.

paras.t: Qui maledicit patri suo et matri, exstinguetur lumen ejus in mediis tenebris, id est, occidetur : sicque lux vitæ auferetur in mediis tenebris, id est in præsenti exsilio, quando maxime desiderabit manere in lumine vitæ hujus. Talis namque jubetur occidi in Levitico. Dicimur autem in vita ista sedere in tenebris et umbra mortis, juxta illud : Illuminare his qui in tenebris et in umbra mortis sedent. Denique lux rationis et splendor legis naturalis, exstinguitur in maledicente suis parentibus : similiter in his qui maledicunt patri spirituali, et matri Ecclesiæ; præsertim in his qui Patri omnium creatori impiissime maledicunt. Unde apud Job dicitur : Nonne lux impii exstinguetur, et præcipitabit eum consilium suum?
paras.en: [[20:20|He that curseth his father, and mother|Qui maledicit patri suo et matri]], [[20:20|his lamp shall be put out in the midst of darkness|exstinguetur lumen ejus in mediis tenebris]] [Denis reads *lumen*, "light", where the Vulgate has *lucerna*, "lamp"]: that is, he shall be slain; and so the light of life shall be taken away in the midst of darkness, that is, in this present exile, when he will most desire to remain in the light of this life. For such a one is commanded in Leviticus to be put to death[[Lev 20:9||]]. Now we are said in this life to sit in darkness and the shadow of death, according to that: [[Luke 1:79|To enlighten them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death|Illuminare his qui in tenebris et in umbra mortis sedent]]. Further, the light of reason and the splendour of the natural law is put out in one who curses his parents: likewise in those who curse their spiritual father, and their mother the Church; above all in those who most impiously curse the Father, the Creator of all. Hence it is said in Job: [[Job 18:5|Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished|Nonne lux impii exstinguetur]], [[Job 18:7|and his own counsel shall cast him down headlong|et præcipitabit eum consilium suum?]]?

paras.t: Hereditas ad quam festinatur in principio : id est, qui patrimonium suum ante congruum tempus conatur accipere, aut alia bona ex avaritia cupit acquirere ; in novissimo benedictione carebit, id est, non benedicetur a Deo, neque augebitur sic agenti; nec ipse per hoc salutem, sed condemnationem incurret. Hoc præcipue respicit eos, qui patres suos expellunt de regno aut domo, ut ipsimet regnent, aut patresfamilias sint : quibus male solet succedere. Spiritualiter quoque, qui antequam idonei sint, et subesse didicerint, festinant præesse, et patrimonia Ecclesiæ obtinere, atque ecclesiasticas acquirere dignitates, in novissimo maledicentur, nec salubriter præsunt. Nam et Philosophus ait : Non bene decet principari eum, qui non sub principe fuerit. Seneca quoque : Nemo, inquit, regere potest, nisi qui et regi.
paras.en: [[20:21|The inheritance gotten hastily in the beginning|Hereditas ad quam festinatur in principio]]: that is, he who tries to receive his patrimony before the fitting time, or desires to acquire other goods out of avarice, [[20:21|in the end shall be without a blessing|in novissimo benedictione carebit]]: that is, he shall not be blessed by God, nor shall he who acts so be prospered; nor will he gain salvation by it, but condemnation. This regards chiefly those who drive their fathers out of the kingdom or the house, so that they themselves may reign or be heads of the household: with such it usually goes ill. Spiritually also, those who, before they are fit and have learned to be subject, hasten to be over others, and to obtain the patrimonies of the Church and acquire ecclesiastical dignities, in the end shall be cursed, and do not rule to salvation. For the Philosopher too says: He is not fit to rule who has not been under a ruler. Seneca also: No one, he says, can rule, unless he can also be ruled.

paras.t: Ne dicas : Reddam malum pro malo, id est, me ipsum inordinate ulciscar, vel scelus scelere vindicabo : quum et Apostolus dicat, Nulli malum pro malo reddentes ; atque Psalmista, Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala. Verumtamen judicis est pro malo culpæ infligere malum pœnæ. In lege quoque, pœna talionis fuit præfixa, juxta illud Levitici : Qui irrogaverit maculam cuilibet civium suorum, sicut fecit, sic fiet ei : fracturam pro fractura, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente. Sed hoc secundum ordinem juris fuit servandum, nec zelo vindictæ, sed justitiæ, adimplendum. Laudabilius tamen fuisse censetur, remittere pœnam, quando sine derogatione boni communis fieri potuit, nec aliud obstitit : quoniam scriptum est, Non quæres ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. Expecta Dominum : qui ait, Mihi vindictam, et ego retribuam ; et liberabit te. Imo et pro tua te patientia coronabit. De quo ait Psalmista : Facit judicium injuriam patientibus.
paras.en: [[20:22|Say not: I will return evil|Ne dicas : Reddam malum]] for evil: that is, I will take revenge for myself inordinately, or avenge crime with crime; since the Apostle too says, [[Rom 12:17|To no man rendering evil for evil|Nulli malum pro malo reddentes]]; and the Psalmist, [[Ps 7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils|Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala]]. Yet it belongs to a judge to inflict the evil of punishment for the evil of fault. In the Law too the penalty of retaliation was laid down, according to that of Leviticus: [[Lev 24:19|He that giveth a blemish to any of his neighbours: as he hath done, so shall it be done to him:|Qui irrogaverit maculam cuilibet civium suorum, sicut fecit, sic fiet ei]] [[Lev 24:20|Breach for breach, eye for ere, tooth for tooth|fracturam pro fractura, oculum pro oculo, dentem pro dente]]. But this was to be kept according to the order of law, and carried out not from zeal for revenge but from zeal for justice. Yet it is judged to have been more praiseworthy to remit the penalty, when it could be done without harm to the common good and nothing else stood in the way: since it is written, [[Lev 19:18|Seek not revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|Non quæres ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. [[20:22|wait for the Lord|Expecta Dominum]], who says, [[Rom 12:19|Revenge is mine, I will repay|Mihi vindictam, et ego retribuam]]; [[20:22|and he will deliver thee|et liberabit te]]. Nay, he will even crown thee for thy patience. Of which the Psalmist says: [[Ps 145:7|who executeth judgment for them that suffer wrong|Facit judicium injuriam patientibus]].

paras.t: Abominatio est apud Deum pondus et pondus ; et statera dolosa non est bona. Idem hoc eodem capitulo jam semel dictum est, ac supra etiam capitulo undecimo.
paras.en: [[20:23|Diverse weights are an abomination before the Lord|Abominatio est apud Deum pondus et pondus]] [Denis has *apud Deum*, "before God"]; [[20:23|a deceitful balance is not good|et statera dolosa non est bona]]. The same has been said already once in this same chapter[[20:10||]], and also above in chapter eleven[[Prov 11:1||]].

paras.t: A Domino diriguntur gressus, id est actus interiores exterioresque, viri (qui a vigore virtutum vir nuncupatur) ad supernaturalem finem, sicut jam sæpe præhabitum est. Unde et Isaias fatetur: Omnia opera nostra operatus es nobis: Apostolus quoque, Deus est qui operatur in vobis velle et perficere. Hinc merita nostra sunt Dei dona. Quis autem hominum intelligere potest viam suam? id est, nemo absque revelatione potest certo scire actionem seu conversationem suam esse meritoriam, ac Deo absolute placentem, quum nesciat an sit in caritate et dignus amore, prout de hoc in Ecclesiaste diffusius est tractandum. Ideo Job ait: Etiam si simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea.
paras.en: [[20:24|The steps|gressus]], that is, the inward and outward acts, [[20:24|of men|viri]] (man, *vir*, is so named from the vigour, *vigor*, of the virtues), [[20:24|are guided by the Lord|A Domino diriguntur]] to a supernatural end, as has often been said before[[Prov 3:6||]][[Prov 16:9||]]. Hence Isaias too confesses: [[Is 26:12|thou hast wrought all our works for us|Omnia opera nostra operatus es nobis]]; and the Apostle, [[Phil 2:13|it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus est qui operatur in vobis velle et perficere]]. Hence our merits are God's gifts. [[20:24|but who is the man that can understand his own way?|Quis autem hominum intelligere potest viam suam?]] that is, no one without revelation can know for certain that his action or conduct is meritorious and absolutely pleasing to God, since he knows not whether he be in charity and worthy of love[[Eccles 9:1||]], as is to be treated more fully in Ecclesiastes. Therefore Job says: [[Job 9:21|Although I should be simple, even this my soul shall be ignorant of|Etiam si simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]].

paras.t: Ruina, id est magnum peccatum, est homini devotare Sanctos, id est, aliquid et frequenter Sanctis vovere, et post vota rationabiliter facta retractare, id est, eadem revocare, non adimplere pro posse, quum necessitatis sit vota implere: imo majus peccatum est, secundum Thomam, fractio voti, quam juramenti.
paras.en: [[20:25|It is ruin|Ruina]], that is, a great sin, [[20:25|to a man|est homini]] to devote to the Saints [Denis reads *devotare*, "to vow to", where the Vulgate has *devorare*, "to devour"], that is, to vow something, and often, to the Saints, [[20:25|and after vows|et post vota]] reasonably made [[20:25|to retract|retractare]], that is, to revoke them and not fulfil them as far as one can, since fulfilling vows is a matter of necessity: nay, according to Thomas, the breaking of a vow is a greater sin than the breaking of an oath.

paras.t: Dissipat impios rex sapiens, eos debellando aut corrigendo; et incurvat super eos fornicem, id est, arcum triumphalem eis intentat, in signum victoriae super eos. Unde et Saul primo Regum fornicem triumphalem sibi legitur erexisse.
paras.en: [[20:26|A wise king scattereth the wicked|Dissipat impios rex sapiens]], by subduing or correcting them; [[20:26|and bringeth over them the wheel|et incurvat super eos fornicem]] [*fornix*, an arch or vault, where the Douay-Rheims has "the wheel"], that is, he raises over them a triumphal arch, in sign of victory over them. Hence Saul too, in the first book of Kings, is read to have erected for himself a triumphal arch[[1 Kings 15:12||]].

paras.t: Lucerna Domini spiraculum hominis, id est, spiritus seu anima hominis est lucerna Domini, id est res illuminata a Deo lumine intellectuali, continens in se lumen ingenii atque synderesis. De quo lumine fertur in Psalmo, Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine: quia hoc lumen naturale, est quoddam signaculum atque impressio increatæ lucis in anima. Porro anima appellatur spiraculum, juxta illud Geneseos: Inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitæ. Unde in Isaia Dominus ait: Flatus ego faciam. Quæ lucerna investigat omnia secreta ventris. Nam homo per rationem et intellectum intelligit proprios actus, et ea quæ in mente ipsius sunt, cogitationes et affectiones: quas vel certo vel probabiliter potest cognoscere esse ex caritate, si bonæ sint. Unde ait Apostolus: Quis hominum scit quæ sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est? Intellectus namque, quum sit inorganica vis et immaterialis potentia, est reditivus ad se ipsum, et reflexivus super proprios actus, secundum Philosophum: quod nulli materiali et organicæ potentiæ potest competere, prout subtilissime in Elementatione sua theologica probat Proclus Platonicus philosophus.
paras.en: [[20:27|The spirit of a man is the lamp of the Lord|Lucerna Domini spiraculum hominis]], that is, the spirit or soul of man is the lamp of the Lord, that is, a thing enlightened by God with intellectual light, containing in itself the light of the mind and of synderesis [that is, the natural grasp of the first principles of moral action, the spark of conscience]. Of which light it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]]: for this natural light is a kind of seal and impression of the uncreated light in the soul. Now the soul is called *spiraculum* [a breathing; "spirit" in the Douay-Rheims of this verse], according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 2:7|breathed into his face the breath of life|Inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitæ]]. Hence the Lord says in Isaias: [[Is 57:16|breathings I will make|Flatus ego faciam]]. Which lamp [[20:27|searcheth all the hidden things of the bowels|investigat omnia secreta ventris]]. For man by reason and intellect understands his own acts and the things that are in his mind, his thoughts and affections: which he can know, either certainly or probably, to be from charity, if they are good. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:11|what man knoweth the things of a man, but the spirit of a man that is in him?|Quis hominum scit quæ sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est?]] For the intellect, since it is an inorganic power and an immaterial potency, returns upon itself and reflects upon its own acts, according to the Philosopher: which can belong to no material and organic power, as Proclus the Platonic philosopher proves most subtly in his *Elements of Theology*.

paras.t: Insuper potest et sic exponi: Lucerna Domini, spiraculum hominis, id est, illuminatio divinæ inspirationis facta in homine, est lucerna Dei in anima, faciens eam diligenter investigare ac noscere semetipsam, et mala sua quæ antea non cognovit: qua quo homo copiosius desuper illustratur, eo subtilius interiora sua scrutatur. Hinc in Job asseritur: Ut video, spiritus est in homine, et inspiratio Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam.
paras.en: It can also be expounded thus: [[20:27|The spirit of a man is the lamp of the Lord|Lucerna Domini, spiraculum hominis]], that is, the enlightening of divine inspiration made in man is the lamp of God in the soul, making it diligently search out and know itself, and its own evils which before it did not know: and the more abundantly a man is enlightened from above, the more subtly he searches his inward parts. Hence it is asserted in Job: [[Job 32:8|as I see, there is a spirit in men, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth understanding|Ut video, spiritus est in homine, et inspiratio Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam]] [Denis has *in homine*, "in man", for "in men"].

paras.t: Misericordia et veritas custodiunt regem in gratia Dei, et præservant eum a diversis periculis ac morte æterna, faciuntque cum Deo atque hominibus amabilem, complacentem, acceptum: intelligendo nomine veritatis justitiam: quibus debet prudentia esse admixta, ut utraque per discretionem contemperetur. Specialiter tamen misericordia ornat ac stabilit regem. Unde subjungitur: et roboratur clementia thronus ejus. Est autem clementia, virtus qua pœna dimittitur aut laxatur: quod in dubiis, et peccatis quæ ex ignorantia aut infirmitate commissa sunt, magis agendum est. Hinc Tullius in laudibus Julii ait: Nulla te virtus tam acceptabilem reddit, ut tua clementia.
paras.en: [[20:28|Mercy and truth preserve the king|Misericordia et veritas custodiunt regem]] in the grace of God, and keep him from various dangers and from eternal death, and make him lovable, pleasing and acceptable to God and men: by the name of truth is understood justice; and with these prudence must be mixed, so that each may be tempered by discretion. Yet mercy especially adorns and establishes the king. Hence is added: [[20:28|and his throne is strengthened by clemency|et roboratur clementia thronus ejus]]. Now clemency is the virtue by which punishment is remitted or relaxed: which is to be done the more in doubtful cases, and in sins committed out of ignorance or weakness. Hence Tully says in praise of Julius: No virtue makes thee so acceptable as thy clemency.

paras.t: Exsultatio juvenum, fortitudo eorum, id est, de sua corporali fortitudine præcipue solent lætari; quam et per diversa exercitia solent mutuo experiri ac demonstrare. Spiritualiter vero, qui renovati sunt mente, et veterem cum suis actibus hominem exuerunt, de fortitudine gratiæ ac virtutum eis collata regratiantur ac gloriantur in Domino, secundum quod unus illorum dixit, Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat; et alius, In Deo meo transgrediar murum. Et dignitas senum est canities, id est maturitas ac sapientia cordis juncta canitiei capitis, juxta illud Sapientis : Senectus venerabilis est : cani enim sunt sensus hominis, etc. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur : Quam speciosa veteranis sapientia ! Hinc in Levitico jussum est : Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis.
paras.en: [[20:29|The joy of young men is their strength|Exsultatio juvenum, fortitudo eorum]], that is, they are wont to rejoice chiefly in their bodily strength, which they are also wont to try and show to one another through various exercises. But spiritually, those who are renewed in mind[[Eph 4:23||]] and have put off the old man with his acts[[Eph 4:22||]] give thanks and glory in the Lord for the strength of grace and of the virtues bestowed on them, according as one of them said, [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]]; and another, [[Ps 17:30|through my God I shall go over a wall|In Deo meo transgrediar murum]]. [[20:29|and the dignity of old men, their grey hairs|Et dignitas senum est canities]], that is, maturity and wisdom of heart joined to grey hairs of the head, according to that of the Wise Man, that old age is venerable[[Wis 4:8||]]: for [[Wis 4:8|the understanding of a man is grey hairs|cani enim sunt sensus hominis]], etc.[[Wis 4:9||]] Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 25:7|how comely is wisdom for the aged|Quam speciosa veteranis sapientia]]! Hence it is commanded in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:32|Rise up before the hoary head, and honour the person of the aged man|Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis]].

paras.t: Livor vulneris absterget mala : id est, læsio foris illata aufert peccata, dummodo æquanimiter toleretur pœna illa pro culpis. Talis quoque pœna reducit homini ad memoriam vitia sua, sicque vexatio tribuit intellectum, et commovet hominem adversitas sua ad pœnitendum. Hinc, ut Seneca docet, Nimius favor fortunæ, mentem excæcat. Propter quod iterum ait : Miserum te judico, qui nunquam miser fuisti. Prosperitas enim assidua, fovet hominem in peccatis. Ideo plus expedit habere adversa, quæ providentia Dei suis concedit electis. Et plagæ in secretioribus ventris : id est, interna contritio et pudor de vitiis, abstinentia, jejunium, et similes afflictiones pœnitentiales ac satisfactoriæ, etiam, imo et maxime, abstergent peccata, quoad culpam totaliter, et quoad pœnam in parte vel in toto, secundum quod magis aut minus vigent in homine.
paras.en: [[20:30|The blueness of a wound shall wipe away evils|Livor vulneris absterget mala]]: that is, a hurt inflicted from outside takes away sins, provided that punishment be borne with equanimity for one's faults. Such punishment also brings a man's vices back to his memory, and so vexation gives understanding[[Is 28:19||]], and his adversity moves a man to repent. Hence, as Seneca teaches, Too much favour of fortune blinds the mind. For which reason he says again: I judge thee wretched, who hast never been wretched. For constant prosperity fosters a man in his sins. Therefore it is more expedient to have adversities, which the providence of God grants to his elect. [[20:30|and stripes in the more inward parts of the belly|Et plagæ in secretioribus ventris]]: that is, inward contrition and shame for one's vices, abstinence, fasting, and like penitential and satisfactory afflictions, also, nay most of all, wipe away sins: as to the guilt wholly, and as to the punishment in part or in whole, according as they flourish more or less in a man.

20.note: This article treats chapters 19 and 20 together; its commentary on chapter 19 is shown under that chapter.

paras.t: Sicut divisiones aquarum, ita cor regis in manu Domini : id est, sicut in potestate Creatoris est, aquas ad libitum suum dividere et per terras diffundere (quemadmodum in exordio mundi divisit aquas quæ erant super firmamentum, ab his quæ erant sub firmamento, atque quotidie nubes circumducit, et pluere facit ubi sibi placuerit, juxta illud Job, Nubes lustrant universa per circuitum, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit, ad omne quod præcipit illis super faciem orbis terrarum, sive in una tribu, sive in terra sua, sive in quocumque loco misericordiæ suæ eas jusserit inveniri); ita cor regis in manu Domini, qui juxta omne beneplacitum suum, potest cor regum afficere, alterare, animare, roborare, debilitare. Ideo subditur : quocumque voluerit, inclinabit illud, id est, vertit et dirigit illud ad agendum, appetendum seu abhorrendum, quidquid voluerit Conditor ipse. Unde in Jeremia, Ezechiele, et alibi sæpe testatur, se assumere et vocare regem Babylonis ad impugnandum filios Israel atque Ægyptios. Nec solum cor regum, sed et hominum universorum, ita in manu est Creatoris, in cujus manu sunt omnes fines terræ. Sed specialiter exprimit regem tanquam ceteris potentiorem, ad innuendum quod et inferiorum corda non minus sint in manu Omnipotentis, in cujus ditione cuncta sunt posita, nec est qui ejus queat resistere voluntati ; et etiam quoniam circa reges tanquam circa publicas personas, est specialis providentia Dei, propter bonum commune. Propter quod Pharaoni tempore Joseph, et Nabuchodonosor regi sub Daniele, monstravit in somnis futura.
paras.en: [[21:1|As the divisions of waters, so the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord|Sicut divisiones aquarum, ita cor regis in manu Domini]]: that is, just as it is in the power of the Creator to divide the waters at his pleasure and to spread them over the lands (as in the beginning of the world he divided the waters that were above the firmament from those that were under the firmament[[Gen 1:7||]], and daily leads the clouds about and makes it rain wherever he pleases, according to that saying of Job: The clouds [[Job 37:12|go round about, whithersoever the will of him that governeth them shall lead them, to whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth|lustrant universa per circuitum, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit, ad omne quod præcipit illis super faciem orbis terrarum]], [[Job 37:13|Whether in one tribe, or in his own land, or in what place soever of his mercy he shall command them to be found|sive in una tribu, sive in terra sua, sive in quocumque loco misericordiæ suæ eas jusserit inveniri]]); [[21:1|so the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord|ita cor regis in manu Domini]], who according to all his good pleasure can affect, alter, animate, strengthen or weaken the heart of kings. Therefore it is added: [[21:1|whithersoever he will, he shall turn it|quocumque voluerit, inclinabit illud]], that is, he turns and directs it to do, to desire or to shun whatever the Maker himself wills. Hence in Jeremias, in Ezechiel and often elsewhere he declares that he takes and calls the king of Babylon to make war on the children of Israel and on the Egyptians[[Jer 43:10||]][[Ezech 29:19||]][[Ezech 30:11||]]. And not only the heart of kings but that of all men is thus in the hand of the Creator: [[Ps 94:4|For in his hand are all the ends of the earth|in cujus manu sunt omnes fines terræ]]. But he names the king in particular, as more powerful than the rest, to hint that the hearts of lesser men are no less in the hand of the Almighty, in whose power all things are placed, and there is none that can resist his will[[Esth 13:9||]]; and also because over kings, as over public persons, there is a special providence of God, for the sake of the common good. For this reason he showed things to come in dreams to Pharao in the time of Joseph[[Gen 41:1||]], and to King Nabuchodonosor under Daniel[[Dan 2:1||]][[Dan 4:1||]].

paras.t: Denique, per regem potest intelligi omnis justus bene regens se ipsum, non propria potestate, sed ope divina : ideo cor ejus in manu Dei consistit, qui inclinat illud ad omne bonum quod vult. Et sicut divisiones aquarum, ita divisiones gratiarum in Dei sunt manu : a quo unusquisque habet, ut ait Apostolus, donum suum. Præterea, iste est ordo rerum in causalitate et influentia, quod corpus hominis subjicitur influentiis cœlestium corporum; sensus autem interiores, et appetitus sensitivus, a dæmonibus possunt immutari : intellectus vero ab angelis sanctis potest illuminari. Deo autem proprium est, directe et immediate agere, et imprimere in voluntatem et apicem ejus, et omne obstaculum gratiæ inde auferre. Hinc apud Job legitur : Deus immutat cor principum terræ. Hoc Esther advertens, in oratione sua locuta est : Transfer cor regis (scilicet Assueri) in odium hostis nostri; nos autem libera. Itaque Dominum jugiter exoremus, ut sua pietate dulcissima dignetur semper corda nostra gratiose afficere, prout Salomon legitur exorasse : Sit Dominus Deus noster nobiscum, et inclinet corda nostra ad se.
paras.en: Lastly, by the king may be understood every just man who rules himself well, not by his own power but by God's help: therefore his heart rests in the hand of God, who inclines it to every good he wills. And [[21:1|as the divisions of waters|sicut divisiones aquarum]], so the divisions of graces are in the hand of God, from whom [[1 Cor 7:7|every one hath|unusquisque habet]], as the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 7:7|his proper gift|donum suum]]. Moreover, this is the order of things in causality and influence: the body of man is subject to the influences of the heavenly bodies; the interior senses and the sensitive appetite can be changed by the demons; the intellect can be enlightened by the holy angels. But it is proper to God to act directly and immediately upon the will and its apex [that is, its highest point], to make his impression there, and to take away from it every obstacle to grace. Hence we read in Job: God [[Job 12:24|changeth the heart of the princes|immutat cor principum]] of the earth. Esther, mindful of this, said in her prayer: Turn the heart of the king (namely Assuerus) [[Esth 14:13|to the hatred of our enemy|in odium hostis nostri]]; [[Esth 14:14|But deliver us|nos autem libera]]. Let us therefore pray the Lord unceasingly that in his most sweet goodness he may deign always to move our hearts by his grace, as Solomon is read to have prayed: [[3 Kings 8:57|The Lord our God be with us|Sit Dominus Deus noster nobiscum]], and [[3 Kings 8:58|may he incline our hearts to himself|inclinet corda nostra ad se]].

paras.t: Omnis via viri, id est actio cujuslibet hominis, recta sibi videtur : quia, ut divinus Dionysius docet, malum non appetitur sub ratione mali, sed sub specie et apparentia boni. Bonum etenim est appetitus objectum. Ideo nullus respiciendo ad malum, cepit aut operatur illud, nisi sub apparentia alicujus boni, utilis, delectabilis vel honesti : et quamvis sciat in generali quod malum sit, tamen in particulari errat ejus judicium. Imo, dato quod cum remorsu faciat illud, et in particulari judicet malum esse, tamen illud judicium est imperfectum et mixtum, ita quod ex una radice seu consideratione judicat quod sit malum, et ex alia, quod sit bonum, et prævalet illud errans judicium trahente affectu. Unde dixit Apostolus : Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, et captivantem me in lege peccati. Hinc ait Philosophus, quod omnis peccans est ignorans; et rursus, Qualis unusquisque est, talis sibi finis videtur. Impleamus ergo quod Seneca ait : Noli sequi affectionem, sed rationem : hoc est, non passionis impulsum, sed rationis imitare judicium. Appendit autem corda Dominus, id est, in statera seu judicio sapientiæ atque justitiæ suæ ponit et pensat ea, dando unicuique quod meretur. Hinc ait Apostolus : Est autem Deus verax, omnis vero homo mendax : quia videlicet judicium Dei est secundum infallibilem veritatem, quamvis homines devient judicando. Unde dictum est supra : Spirituum ponderator est Dominus.
paras.en: [[21:2|Every way of a man|Omnis via viri]], that is, the action of any man, [[21:2|seemeth right to himself|recta sibi videtur]]: because, as the divine Dionysius teaches, evil is not desired under the aspect of evil, but under the appearance and semblance of good. For the good is the object of the appetite. So no one, looking to evil, undertakes or does it except under the appearance of some good, useful, pleasant or honourable [the three kinds of good distinguished in the schools]; and though he know in general that it is evil, yet in the particular case his judgment errs. Nay, granted that he does it with remorse, and judges in the particular case that it is evil, yet that judgment is imperfect and mixed, so that from one root or consideration he judges that it is evil, and from another that it is good; and that erring judgment prevails, as the affection draws it. Hence the Apostle said: [[Rom 7:23|I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and captivating me in the law of sin|Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, et captivantem me in lege peccati]]. Hence the Philosopher says that every sinner is ignorant; and again: As each one is, such the end seems to him. Let us then fulfil what Seneca says: Follow not affection, but reason; that is, imitate not the impulse of passion but the judgment of reason. [[21:2|But the Lord weigheth the hearts|Appendit autem corda Dominus]], that is, he places and weighs them in the balance or judgment of his wisdom and justice, giving each what he deserves. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 3:4|But God is true and every man a liar|Est autem Deus verax, omnis vero homo mendax]]: because, namely, God's judgment is according to infallible truth, though men go astray in judging. Hence it was said above: [[Prov 16:2|the Lord is the weigher of spirits|Spirituum ponderator est Dominus]].

paras.t: Facere misericordiam, id est opera pietatis corporalia ac spiritualia ex caritate, et judicium discretionis, seu etiam justæ punitionis in subditos et in se ipsum per disciplinam, magis placet Domino, quam victimæ, id est sacrificia legis, quæ non erant placita Deo in se ipsis, sed solum ex offerentium fide et devotione, ut plenius dictum est supra. Circa hoc aliqui dicunt hujus causam fuisse, quia victimis non indiguit Deus, sed operibus misericordiæ indiget in membris suis. Ad quod poterit dici, quod etiam victimis indiguit in suis ministris, sacerdotibus ac Levitis, qui sacrificiis sustentabantur, ut in Levitico patet. Denique et juxta istam sententiam Michæas quoque ait : Numquid placari potest Dominus in millibus arietum, aut in multis millibus hircorum pinguium? Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te : utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam. Ubi et additur : Et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo.
paras.en: [[21:3|To do mercy|Facere misericordiam]], that is, the corporal and spiritual works of piety done out of charity, [[21:3|and judgment|et judicium]] of discretion, or also of just punishment, upon one's subjects and upon oneself by discipline, [[21:3|pleaseth the Lord more than victims|magis placet Domino, quam victimæ]], that is, the sacrifices of the Law, which were not pleasing to God in themselves but only through the faith and devotion of those who offered them, as was said more fully above. On this some say that the reason for it was that God had no need of victims, but does need works of mercy in his members. To which it may be answered that he had need of victims too, in his ministers, the priests and Levites, who were maintained by the sacrifices, as is plain in Leviticus. Lastly, in agreement with this sense Micheas also says: [[Mich 6:7|May the Lord be appeased with thousands of rams, or with many thousands of fat he goats?|Numquid placari potest Dominus in millibus arietum, aut in multis millibus hircorum pinguium?]] [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily to do judgment, and to love mercy|Indicabo tibi, homo, quid sit bonum, aut quid Dominus requirat a te : utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam]]. Where it is also added: [[Mich 6:8|and to walk solicitous with thy God|Et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo]].

paras.t: Exaltatio oculorum est dilatatio cordis : id est, ex cordis dilatatione, qua se longe ac late extendit ad magna in sæculo isto, ut scilicet dominetur, præsit, abundet, fametur, procedit causa exaltationis seu superbiæ, quæ apparet in oculis, in quibus (ut dictum est sæpe) evidenter apparere solet dispositio cordis. Lucerna, id est prudentia, impiorum, qua se dirigunt, quasi in lumine suo, ad obtinendum ea quæ cupiunt, est peccatum : quia, ut ait Apostolus, Prudentia carnis mors est. Impii equidem ad vitia utuntur sua prudentia, vel magis versutia. De quibus asserit Jeremias : Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt.
paras.en: [[21:4|Haughtiness of the eyes is the enlarging of the heart|Exaltatio oculorum est dilatatio cordis]]: that is, from the enlarging of the heart, by which it stretches itself far and wide toward great things in this world (namely, to rule, to be set over others, to abound, to be talked of), there proceeds haughtiness or pride [literally, "the cause of haughtiness"], which shows in the eyes, in which (as has often been said) the disposition of the heart is wont to show plainly. [[21:4|the lamp|Lucerna]], that is, the prudence [[21:4|of the wicked|impiorum]], by which they guide themselves, as if in their own light, to obtain what they covet, [[21:4|is sin|est peccatum]]: because, as the Apostle says, [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the flesh is death|Prudentia carnis mors est]] [the Latin word here, *prudentia*, is the one Denis has just used for the "lamp"]. The wicked indeed use their prudence, or rather their cunning, for vices. Of whom Jeremias declares: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge|Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt]].

paras.t: Cogitationes robusti semper in abundantia ; omnis autem piger in egestate, id est spiritualium divitiarum carentia, est : nisi pœnitentiam agens, pigritiam in fervorem mutaverit.
paras.en: [[21:5|The thoughts of the industrious always bring forth abundance|Cogitationes robusti semper in abundantia]]: [[21:5|but every sluggard is always in want|omnis autem piger in egestate]], that is, in lack of spiritual riches, unless by doing penance he change his sloth into fervour.

paras.t: Qui congregat thesauros lingua mendacii, id est per verba dolosa, fraudulenta, mendosa seu blanda, vanus et exors est : quia injustus, a summo bono aversus, menteque excæcatus, propter temporalia tam graviter peccans, et tantis periculis se exponens ; et impingetur ad laqueos mortis, id est æternæ damnationis, tum quia mendosus, tum quia aliorum deceptor, tum quia injustus alienorum bonorum possessor.
paras.en: [[21:6|He that gathereth treasures by a lying tongue|Qui congregat thesauros lingua mendacii]], that is, by deceitful, fraudulent, lying or flattering words, [[21:6|is vain and foolish|vanus et exors est]] [Denis's text has *exors*, "having no share", where the Vulgate has *excors*, "senseless"; his gloss fits either]: because he is unjust, turned away from the highest good and blinded in mind, sinning so grievously for temporal things and exposing himself to such great dangers; [[21:6|and shall stumble upon the snares of death|et impingetur ad laqueos mortis]], that is, of eternal damnation: both because he is a liar, and because he deceives others, and because he unjustly holds what belongs to others.

paras.t: Rapinæ impiorum detrahent eos in profundum inferni : qui locus debetur raptoribus. Nam et rapina ex suo genere, est gravior culpa quam furtum, ut in secunda secundæ Thomas declarat. Raptor enim majorem infert injuriam et contemptum quam fur : quoniam evidenter, non occulte, violentiam infert. Quia noluerunt facere judicium discretionis, id est, actus suos noluerunt dijudicare atque discernere, considerando quam pravi sint, et sic eos deserere. Unde habetur in Psalmo : Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio, id est, a peccatis suis per pœnitentiam non resurgunt judicando se ipsos, sicut ait Apostolus : Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Noluerunt etiam facere judicium, id est justam determinationem cum proximis, quorum bona sic congregant. Imo irrationabiliter ac injuste agunt cum ipsis.
paras.en: [[21:7|The robberies of the wicked shall be their downfall|Rapinæ impiorum detrahent eos]] [*detrahent eos*, literally "shall drag them down"] into the depth of hell, the place that is due to robbers. For robbery is by its kind a graver fault than theft, as Thomas declares in the Secunda Secundæ [the second part of the second part of his *Summa*]. For the robber inflicts greater injury and contempt than the thief, since he uses violence openly, not in secret. [[21:7|because they would not do judgment|Quia noluerunt facere judicium]] of discretion: that is, they would not judge and discern their own acts, considering how wicked they are, and so forsake them. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 1:5|Therefore the wicked shall not rise again in judgment|Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio]], that is, they do not rise again from their sins by penance, by judging themselves, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. Again, they would not [[21:7|do judgment|facere judicium]], that is, deal by just determination with their neighbours, whose goods they thus gather; rather they deal with them unreasonably and unjustly.

paras.t: Perversa via viri, id est vitiosa conversatio seu actio hominis, aliena est, id est innaturalis, et contraria legi æternæ, divinæ, positivæ ac naturali. Virtus enim est secundum naturam; vitium, contra vel præter naturam. Nam et ratio deprecatur ad optima. Et Tullius ait : Virtus est habitus mentis, rationi ac naturæ consentaneus. Ideo Dominus ait in Psalmo : Filii alieni mentiti sunt mihi, filii alieni inveterati sunt. Hinc asserit Glossa : Juste coram Domino vivere, proprium est conditioni humanæ. Unde ait Scriptura : Deum time, et mandata ejus observa : hoc est omnis homo. At qui perverse vivit, alienam ab humana natura incedit viam : idcirco perversa actio, est aliena et contra naturam. Qui autem mundus est, rectum opus ejus.
paras.en: [[21:8|The perverse way of a man|Perversa via viri]], that is, a man's vicious conduct or action, [[21:8|is strange|aliena est]], that is, unnatural, and contrary to the eternal, divine, positive and natural law [*aliena*, "strange", also means "foreign, alien": alien to man's nature, as Denis goes on to explain]. For virtue is according to nature; vice is against or beside nature. For reason too pleads for what is best. And Tully says: Virtue is a habit of the mind in accord with reason and nature. Therefore the Lord says in the Psalm: [[Ps 17:46|The children that are strangers have lied to me, strange children have faded away|Filii alieni mentiti sunt mihi, filii alieni inveterati sunt]]. Hence the Gloss declares: To live justly before the Lord is proper to man's condition. Hence the Scripture says: [[Eccles 12:13|Fear God, and keep his commandments|Deum time, et mandata ejus observa]]: [[Eccles 12:13|this is all man|hoc est omnis homo]]. But he that lives perversely walks a way alien to human nature: therefore perverse action is alien and against nature. [[21:8|but as for him that is pure, his work is right|Qui autem mundus est, rectum opus ejus]].

paras.t: Melius est sedere in angulo domatis, id est in loco secreto tecti seu domus, in quo potest homo quiete insistere orationi, meditationi, et aliis exercitiis bonis, secundum illud Psalmi, Factus sum sicut passer solitarius in tecto ; quam cum muliere litigiosa, et in domo communi tibi ac conjugi tali ; aut in taberna, vel societate multorum in quibus non viget compunctio. Imo tranquillitas, devotio, et omnis spiritualis profectus, per mulierem rixosam et communem societatem præsertim impediuntur. Ideo dixit Propheta : Elongavi fugiens, et mansi in solitudine.
paras.en: [[21:9|It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop|Melius est sedere in angulo domatis]], that is, in a secret place of the roof or house, where a man can quietly give himself to prayer, meditation and other good exercises, according to that of the Psalm: I [[Ps 101:8|am become as a sparrow all alone on the housetop|Factus sum sicut passer solitarius in tecto]]; [[21:9|than with a brawling woman|quam cum muliere litigiosa]], [[21:9|and in a common house|et in domo communi]], shared by thee and such a wife, or in a tavern, or in the company of many among whom compunction does not thrive. Indeed tranquillity, devotion and all spiritual progress are hindered above all by a quarrelsome woman and by common company. Therefore the Prophet said: [[Ps 54:8|I have gone far off flying away; and I abode in the wilderness|Elongavi fugiens, et mansi in solitudine]].

paras.t: Anima impii desiderat malum, id est peccare, aliena auferre, proximisque nocere ; non miserebitur proximo suo : imo potius aufert ei quod habet. Viscera enim impiorum crudelia. De quibus sanctus Job : Nudos, inquit, dimittunt homines, vestimenta tollentes.
paras.en: [[21:10|The soul of the wicked desireth evil|Anima impii desiderat malum]], that is, to sin, to take what belongs to others, and to harm his neighbours; [[21:10|he will not have pity on his neighbour|non miserebitur proximo suo]]: rather he takes from him what he has. For [[Prov 12:10|the bowels of the wicked are cruel|Viscera enim impiorum crudelia]]. Of whom holy Job says: [[Job 24:7|They send men away naked|Nudos, inquit, dimittunt homines]] (so he says), [[Job 24:7|taking away their clothes|vestimenta tollentes]].

paras.t: Mulctato, id est punito seu flagellato, pestilente, sapientior erit parvulus. Hoc est quod supra legitur : Pestilente flagellato, stultus sapientior erit. Et si sectetur sapientiam, id est notitiam divinorum, sumet scientiam, id est notitiam creaturarum : quoniam ex cognitione Creatoris, discit bene judicare de creaturis.
paras.en: When [[21:11|a pestilent man|pestilente]] [[21:11|is punished|Mulctato]], that is, chastised or scourged, [[21:11|the little one will be wiser|sapientior erit parvulus]]. This is what we read above: [[Prov 19:25|The wicked man being scourged, the fool shall be wiser|Pestilente flagellato, stultus sapientior erit]]. [[21:11|And if he follow|Et si sectetur]] wisdom [Denis reads *sapientiam*, "wisdom", where the Vulgate has *sapientem*, "the wise"], that is, the knowledge of divine things, [[21:11|he will receive knowledge|sumet scientiam]], that is, the knowledge of creatures: since from the knowledge of the Creator he learns to judge rightly of creatures.

paras.t: Excogitat justus de domo impii, id est, vir justus, præsertim bonus prælatus, sollicitus est de conversione et salute hominum iniquorum, ut detrahat impios a malo, id est, ut a peccatis revocet eos, quia spiritualiter diligit eos.
paras.en: [[21:12|The just considereth seriously the house of the wicked|Excogitat justus de domo impii]], that is, the just man, especially a good prelate, is concerned for the conversion and salvation of wicked men, [[21:12|that he may withdraw the wicked from evil|ut detrahat impios a malo]], that is, that he may call them back from their sins, because he loves them spiritually.

paras.t: Qui obturat aurem suam ad clamorem pauperis petentis sibi spiritualem aut corporalem eleemosynam dari, et ipse clamabit, misericordiam invocando tempore suæ angustiæ, et non exaudietur a Deo vel suis electis, nisi pœniteat interim. Ideo Jacobus ait : Judicium sine misericordia ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam. Hinc diviti epuloni negata est gutta aquæ, quoniam inopem Lazarum non advertit.
paras.en: [[21:13|He that stoppeth his ear against the cry of the poor|Qui obturat aurem suam ad clamorem pauperis]], who asks that spiritual or bodily alms be given him, [[21:13|shall also cry himself|et ipse clamabit]], calling for mercy in the time of his distress, [[21:13|and shall not be heard|et non exaudietur]] by God or by his elect, unless he repent in the meantime. Therefore James says: [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy|Judicium sine misericordia ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam]]. Hence a drop of water was denied to the rich glutton[[Luke 16:24||]], because he paid no heed to the poor man Lazarus[[Luke 16:25||]].

paras.t: Munus absconditum exstinguit iras : id est, dum quis occulte largitur munus notabile ei quem offendit, vel qui contra eum irascitur, vel mediatori alicui medianti inter eos ad pacificandum, placat iram illius; et donum in sinu, id est occulte positum in alterius gremio, exstinguit indignationem maximam. Hinc dixit Jacob de Esau : Placabo illum muneribus.
paras.en: [[21:14|A secret present quencheth anger|Munus absconditum exstinguit iras]]: that is, when someone secretly bestows a notable present on him whom he has offended, or who is angry with him, or on some mediator who goes between them to make peace, he appeases that man's anger; [[21:14|and a gift in the bosom|et donum in sinu]], that is, put secretly in the other's lap, quenches [[21:14|the greatest wrath|indignationem maximam]]. Hence Jacob said of Esau: [[Gen 32:20|I will appease him with the presents|Placabo illum muneribus]].

paras.t: Vel iste est sensus : Munus absconditum, id est eleemosyna data secrete intuitu Dei, non ad laudem humanam, exstinguit iram Judicis summi; et donum in sinu, id est beneficium pium clam datum, tollit indignationem maximam : sicut alibi scriptum est : Abscondite eleemosynam in sinu pauperum, et ipsa orabit pro vobis ad Dominum : quia sicut aqua exstinguit ignem, ita eleemosyna exstinguit peccatum. Unde Salvator : Quum facis eleemosynam, nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua.
paras.en: Or this is the sense: [[21:14|A secret present|Munus absconditum]], that is, alms given secretly with an eye to God, not for human praise, quenches the anger of the supreme Judge; [[21:14|and a gift in the bosom|et donum in sinu]], that is, a pious kindness given in secret, takes away [[21:14|the greatest wrath|indignationem maximam]]; as it is written elsewhere: [[Ecclus 29:15|Shut up alms in the heart of the poor, and it shall obtain help for thee|Abscondite eleemosynam in sinu pauperum, et ipsa orabit pro vobis ad Dominum]] [Denis's wording runs: "Hide alms in the bosom of the poor, and it shall pray for you to the Lord"]: because as water quenches fire, so alms quenches sin[[Ecclus 3:33||]] [the margin gives "Cf. Ibid. xxxiii, 33"; the passage is Ecclus 3:33]. Hence the Saviour: [[Matt 6:3|when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth|Quum facis eleemosynam, nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua]].

paras.t: Gaudium justo est facere judicium, id est se ipsum et subditos judicio discretionis discutere, disciplinare, et quæ justa sunt operari : quia delectatur in actu virtutum. Delectatio namque bona fiens in opere, est signum virtutis et ejus effectus; habitus quoque instar naturæ, inclinat ad operandum suaviter : et quamvis interdum sit difficultas in opere, et intus renisio sive tentatio, mens tamen promptam exhibere se studet, condelectaturque legi Dei, secundum Apostolum. Verumtamen virtutibus acquisitis, similiter virtutibus infusis, consummatis et exercitatis (quæ non solum tollunt peccata, sed et eorum reliquias) delectationes præsertim annexæ sunt; incipientibus vero labor, difficultas, amari[…]tudo, tentatio solent misceri. Sed quo magis proficiunt, et virtuosæ consuetudini appropinquant, eo omnia illa plus minuuntur, et consolatio atque alacritas intenduntur. Hinc ait Leo Papa : Nihil arduum humilibus, nihil asperum mitibus, et facile cuncta præcepta veniunt in effectum, quando et gratia prætendit auxilium, et obedientia mollit imperium : nec dura necessitate servitur, ubi diligitur quod jubetur. Et pavor operantibus iniquitatem : id est, iniquis, operariisque malignis durum et pavidum videtur insistere actibus virtuosis, quia inclinantur ad vitia, nec amant bona vere honesta. Vel, Pavor, id est inordinata formido, inest operantibus iniquitatem, ac pavor damnationis æternæ. Semper enim præsumit sæva, conscientia perturbata.
paras.en: [[21:15|It is joy to the just to do judgment|Gaudium justo est facere judicium]], that is, to examine and discipline himself and his subjects with the judgment of discretion, and to do what is just: because he delights in the act of the virtues. For good delight arising in the work is a sign of virtue and its effect; and the habit, like a nature, inclines one to act with ease; and though there is at times difficulty in the work, and resistance or temptation within, yet the mind strives to show itself ready, and is delighted with the law of God, according to the Apostle[[Rom 7:22||]]. Yet delights are joined above all to the acquired virtues, and likewise to the infused virtues, when they are perfected and exercised (and these take away not only sins but also their remnants); while in beginners labour, difficulty, bitterness [part of this word is lost in the print (*amari…tudo*); it is surely *amaritudo*, "bitterness"] and temptation are wont to be mingled. But the more they advance and draw near to a virtuous habit, the more all those things lessen, and consolation and eagerness grow. Hence Pope Leo says: Nothing is hard to the humble, nothing harsh to the meek, and all the commandments are readily fulfilled when grace lends its help and obedience softens the command; nor is service rendered under hard necessity where what is commanded is loved. [[21:15|and dread to them that work iniquity|Et pavor operantibus iniquitatem]]: that is, to the wicked and to evil workers it seems hard and fearful to apply themselves to virtuous acts, because they are inclined to vices and do not love goods that are truly honourable. Or, [[21:15|dread|Pavor]], that is, inordinate fear, is in [[21:15|them that work iniquity|operantibus iniquitatem]], and the dread of eternal damnation. For [[Wis 17:10|a troubled conscience always forecasteth grievous things|Semper enim præsumit sæva, conscientia perturbata]].

paras.t: Vir qui erraverit a via doctrinæ salubris, in cœtu gigantum commorabitur, id est, inter superbos, magnos et violentos homines, seu dæmones, in æternum damnabitur. De quibus in libro Job fertur : Ecce gigantes gemunt sub aquis, et qui habitant cum eis. Baruch quoque ait : Ibi fuerunt gigantes nominati. Interdum tamen gigantes sumuntur in bono, pro magnis et fortibus in sapientia et virtute. Unde de Christo habetur in Psalmo : Exsultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam. Ambrosius quoque in hymno dixit de ipso : Geminæ gigas substantiæ, alacris ut currat viam.
paras.en: [[21:16|A man that shall wander out of the way of doctrine|Vir qui erraverit a via doctrinæ salubris]] [Denis's text adds *salubris*: "of wholesome doctrine"] [[21:16|shall abide in the company of the giants|in cœtu gigantum commorabitur]], that is, shall be damned for ever among proud, great and violent men, or among the demons. Of whom it is said in the book of Job: [[Job 26:5|Behold the giants groan under the waters, and they that dwell with them|Ecce gigantes gemunt sub aquis, et qui habitant cum eis]]. Baruch too says: [[Bar 3:26|There were the giants, those renowned men|Ibi fuerunt gigantes nominati]]. Yet giants are sometimes taken in a good sense, for those great and strong in wisdom and virtue. Hence it is said of Christ in the Psalm: [[Ps 18:6|Hath rejoiced as a giant to run the way|Exsultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam]]. Ambrose too said of him in a hymn: Giant of twofold substance, eager to run his course [from the Advent hymn *Veni, Redemptor gentium*].

paras.t: Qui diligit epulas, id est gulosus et delicatus, qui in cibo et potu voluptatem quærit magis quam necessariam refectionem, in egestate erit, id est, virtutum opulentia destituetur; tales etiam solent, sua immoderate consumendo, depauperari. Hinc Seneca in libro de Quatuor virtutibus scripsit : Nec præsentibus deliciis inhærebis, nec desiderabis absentes. Victus sit tibi ex facili re, nec ad voluptatem, sed ad cibum accede : palatum tuum fames excitet, non sapores; desideria tua parvo redime, quia hoc tantum curare debes, ut desinant; atque ita quasi ad exemplar divinum compositus, a corpore ad spiritum, quantum potes, abducere. Præterea, juxta Cyrillum, sicut pinguia fovent ignem quousque consumantur, sic qui amant vinum et pinguia, cibus erunt infernalis incendii. Ideo subditur : Qui amat vinum et pinguia propter voluptatem et immoderate, non ditabitur : imo pauper erit in anima, et temporalia expendet superflue.
paras.en: [[21:17|He that loveth good cheer|Qui diligit epulas]], that is, the glutton and the man of dainty tastes, who seeks pleasure in food and drink more than needful refreshment, [[21:17|shall be in want|in egestate erit]], that is, shall be stripped of the wealth of the virtues; such men are also wont to become poor by consuming their goods without measure. Hence Seneca wrote in the book On the Four Virtues: Thou shalt not cling to present delights, nor long for those that are absent. Let thy living come from what is easily had; and go to table not for pleasure but for food: let hunger stir thy palate, not flavours; buy off thy desires cheaply, for thou shouldst care only that they cease; and so, ordered as it were after the divine pattern, withdraw thyself from the body to the spirit as far as thou canst. Moreover, according to Cyril, as fat things feed a fire until they are consumed, so those who love wine and fat things will be food for the fire of hell. Therefore it is added: [[21:17|he that loveth wine, and fat things|Qui amat vinum et pinguia]] for pleasure and without measure [[21:17|shall not be rich|non ditabitur]]: rather he will be poor in soul, and will spend temporal goods superfluously.

paras.t: Pro justo datur vir impius, et pro recto iniquus. Justus et rectus, pro eodem accipi solent ; similiter impius et iniquus. Sed hic per justum intelligi potest, qui circa Deum juste se habet; et per rectum, qui circa proximos habet se recte : per impium vero, qui peccat in Deum ; et per iniquum, qui peccat in proximum. Ut sit sensus : Pro justo datur vir impius, etc., id est, pro peccato quod impius committit in justum, datur impius damnationi æternæ, et quandoque temporali pœnæ aut morti : sic tyranni pro martyribus dati sunt. Et propter peccata commissa in hominem rectum, punitur et damnatur iniquus qui peccavit in illum : sic et Aman pro Mardochæo. Hinc per Isaiam Dominus loquitur Israeli : Dabo homines pro te, et populos pro anima tua.
paras.en: [[21:18|The wicked is delivered up for the just|Pro justo datur vir impius]], [[21:18|and the unjust for the righteous|et pro recto iniquus]]. *Just* and *righteous* are usually taken for the same thing, and likewise *wicked* and *unjust*. But here by the just may be understood him who bears himself justly toward God, and by the righteous him who bears himself rightly toward his neighbours; by the wicked [*impius*, literally "ungodly"] him who sins against God, and by the unjust him who sins against his neighbour. So that the sense is: [[21:18|The wicked is delivered up for the just|Pro justo datur vir impius]], etc.: that is, for the sin that the wicked man commits against the just, the wicked man is delivered up to eternal damnation, and sometimes to temporal punishment or death: so tyrants were delivered up for the martyrs. And for the sins committed against the righteous man, the unjust man who sinned against him is punished and condemned: so too Aman for Mardochai[[Esth 7:10||]]. Hence the Lord speaks to Israel through Isaias: [[Is 43:4|I will give men for thee, and people for thy life|Dabo homines pro te, et populos pro anima tua]].

paras.t: Melius est habitare in terra deserta, quam cum muliere rixosa et iracunda. Hoc est quod dictum est paulo ante : Melius est sedere in angulo domatis, quam cum muliere litigiosa. Porro alibi plus dicitur, utpote : Commorari leoni et draconi placebit, quam habitare cum muliere nequam.
paras.en: [[21:19|It is better to dwell in a wilderness, than with a quarrelsome and passionate woman|Melius est habitare in terra deserta, quam cum muliere rixosa et iracunda]]. This is what was said a little before: [[21:9|It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman|Melius est sedere in angulo domatis, quam cum muliere litigiosa]]. And elsewhere still more is said, namely: [[Ecclus 25:23|It will be more agreeable to abide with a lion and a dragon, than to dwell with a wicked woman|Commorari leoni et draconi placebit, quam habitare cum muliere nequam]].

paras.t: Thesaurus desiderabilis, id est opulentia meritorum, et oleum pietatis ac caritatis, sunt in habitaculo justi, id est in corde ipsius, vel in ejus domesticis bene rectis et obedientibus sibi; vel in sanctorum Ecclesia; et imprudens homo dissipabit illud, id est, habitaculum justi scandalizabit et destruet, quantum in se est, et si potuerit.
paras.en: [[21:20|There is a treasure to be desired|Thesaurus desiderabilis]] (that is, wealth of merits) [[21:20|and oil|et oleum]] (of piety and charity) [[21:20|in the dwelling of the just|in habitaculo justi]], that is, in his heart, or in his household when they are well ordered and obedient to him, or in the Church of the saints; [[21:20|and the foolish man shall spend it|et imprudens homo dissipabit illud]] [*dissipabit* means both "shall squander" and "shall scatter, destroy"; Denis takes the second sense], that is, he will scandalize and destroy the dwelling of the just, as far as in him lies, and if he can.

paras.t: Qui sequitur, id est, apprehendit, amat et exercet, judicium et misericordiam, inveniet vitam gratiæ, et justitiam, id est justam a Deo remunerationem, et gloriam claritatis cœlestis.
paras.en: [[21:21|He that followeth|Qui sequitur]], that is, lays hold of, loves and practises, judgment [Denis reads *judicium*, "judgment", where the Vulgate has *justitiam*, "justice"] [[21:21|and mercy|et misericordiam]], [[21:21|shall find life|inveniet vitam]] of grace, and [[21:21|justice|justitiam]], that is, a just reward from God, and [[21:21|glory|gloriam]] of heavenly brightness.

paras.t: Civitatem fortium ascendit sapiens, et destruxit robur fiduciæ ejus. Sic Moyses, Josue, David, ac alii justi reges, ac Machabæi, fortissima adversariorum suorum oppida obsederunt et expugnaverunt. Ideo ait Apostolus : Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna. Christus quoque per beatissimos suos apostolos Petrum et Paulum, ascendit dominam mundi Romam, eamque fidei suæ subjecit, quemadmodum Isaias prædixit : Civitatem sublimem humiliabit; humiliabit eam usque ad terram. Potest item per civitatem fortium, intelligi mundus positus in maligno, in quo dæmones dominabantur : quem Christus per se et sanctos Apostolos ab idololatria convertit ad fidem.
paras.en: [[21:22|The wise man hath scaled the city of the strong, and hath cast down the strength of the confidence thereof|Civitatem fortium ascendit sapiens, et destruxit robur fiduciæ ejus]]. So Moses, Josue, David and other just kings, and the Machabees, besieged and stormed the strongest towns of their enemies. Therefore the Apostle says: The saints [[Heb 11:33|by faith conquered kingdoms|per fidem vicerunt regna]]. Christ too, through his most blessed apostles Peter and Paul, scaled Rome, the mistress of the world, and subjected her to his faith, as Isaias foretold: [[Is 26:5|the high city he shall lay low. He shall bring it down even to the ground|Civitatem sublimem humiliabit; humiliabit eam usque ad terram]]. By the city of the strong may also be understood the world [[1 John 5:19|seated in wickedness|positus in maligno]], in which the demons held sway, and which Christ, by himself and by the holy Apostles, converted from idolatry to the faith.

paras.t: Qui custodit os suum ab immoderantia cibi et potus, et linguam suam a verborum excessu, custodit ab angustiis animam suam : quas gulosi incidunt et verbosi. Iste versiculus expositione non indiget, sed exhortatione et adimpletione. Qui ergo cupit a multis præservari angustiis, periculis et peccatis, custodiat os et linguam. Etenim vir verbosus non dirigetur in terra. Et sicut Jacobus ait apostolus, Si quis putat se religiosum esse, non refrenans linguam suam, hujus vana est religio. Atque, ut Seneca protestatur : Qui nescit tacere, nescit loqui. Hinc abbas Agathon lapidem diu portavit in ore, ut disceret os suum custodire.
paras.en: [[21:23|He that keepeth his mouth|Qui custodit os suum]] from immoderation in food and drink, [[21:23|and his tongue|et linguam suam]] from excess of words, [[21:23|keepeth his soul from distress|custodit ab angustiis animam suam]], into which gluttons and talkers fall. This little verse needs no exposition, but exhortation and fulfilment. Let him then who desires to be preserved from many distresses, dangers and sins keep his mouth and his tongue. For [[Ps 139:12|A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth|vir verbosus non dirigetur in terra]]. And as James the apostle says: [[Jas 1:26|if any man think himself to be religious, not bridling his tongue|Si quis putat se religiosum esse, non refrenans linguam suam]], [[Jas 1:26|this man's religion is vain|hujus vana est religio]]. And as Seneca declares: He who knows not how to be silent knows not how to speak. Hence Abbot Agathon carried a stone in his mouth for a long time, to learn to keep his mouth.

paras.t: Superbus et arrogans vocatur indoctus, qui in ira operatur superbiam, id est, ex impetu iræ procedit in opus superbum, injuriosum seu contumeliosum. Talis enim est fatuus, dono sapientiæ carens, nec unctus seu doctus a Spiritu Sancto, quando ita se habet, quamvis ante forsitan fuerit bonus et sapiens, et quamvis humana instructione sit eruditus.
paras.en: [[21:24|The proud and the arrogant is called ignorant|Superbus et arrogans vocatur indoctus]], [[21:24|who in anger worketh pride|qui in ira operatur superbiam]], that is, who from an outburst of anger goes on to a proud, injurious or insulting deed.
