For such a man is a fool, lacking the gift of wisdom, neither anointed nor taught by the Holy Ghost while he behaves so [*indoctus*, "ignorant", is literally "untaught"], though before he was perhaps good and wise, and though he be learned by human instruction.

paras.t: Desideria occidunt pigrum. Habet enim desideria vitiosa, quibus spiritualiter mortificatur. Cupit quoque adipisci terrena, non tamen vult laborare pro illis : sicque desideria ipsum affligunt, dum rebus caret optatis. Unde subjungitur : noluerunt enim quidquam manus ejus operari : id est, vires ejus practicæ noluerunt aggredi actus virtutum, neque laborem honestum.
paras.en: [[21:25|Desires kill the slothful|Desideria occidunt pigrum]]. For he has vicious desires, by which he is put to death spiritually. He also desires to obtain earthly things, yet will not labour for them; and so his desires afflict him, while he goes without the things he longs for. Hence it is added: [[21:25|for his hands have refused to work at all|noluerunt enim quidquam manus ejus operari]]: that is, his practical powers [the powers of acting, as distinct from those of knowing] would not take up acts of virtue, nor honest labour.

paras.t: Tota die concupiscit et desiderat temporalia bona, et interdum etiam spiritualia, remisso affectu, sed abhorret laborem; qui autem justus est, tribuet ea quæ rationabiliter postulantur ab eo pro posse, sicut ait Salvator : Omni petenti te tribue; et non cessabit tempore opportuno sua communicare et agere bene.
paras.en: [[21:26|He longeth and desireth all the day|Tota die concupiscit et desiderat]] temporal goods, and sometimes spiritual ones too, but with slack affection, and he shrinks from labour; [[21:26|but he that is just, will give|qui autem justus est, tribuet]] what is reasonably asked of him, as far as he can, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:30|Give to every one that asketh thee|Omni petenti te tribue]]; [[21:26|and will not cease|et non cessabit]] at the fitting time to share his goods and to do good.

paras.t: Hostiæ impiorum abominabiles, quia offeruntur ex scelere, id est ex rapina aut furto, aut mercede prostibulari. Hostiæ namque legales non erant acceptæ in se, sed ex offerentium fide et devotione : ideo displicuerunt Deo, quando ex injustitia et vitio aut turpitudine offerebantur.
paras.en: [[21:27|The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, because they are offered of wickedness|Hostiæ impiorum abominabiles, quia offeruntur ex scelere]], that is, of robbery or theft, or of a harlot's hire. For the sacrifices of the Law were not acceptable in themselves, but through the faith and devotion of those who offered them: therefore they displeased God when they were offered out of injustice and vice or foulness.

paras.t: Testis mendax peribit. Unde dictum est supra : Testis mendax non erit impunitus. Vir obediens loquetur victorias : id est, ipso facto ostendet se fortem ac victoriosum, dabitque aliis materiam loquendi de hoc; vel, ad laudem Dei ædificationemque proximi, narrabit qualiter obediendo prævaluit adversariis suæ salutis, et carnem ac sensualitatem rationi subjecerit, et suo dominatus sit animo, viceritque se ipsum. Vel, Loquetur victorias, id est, humilia et obedientialia dabit responsa præcipientibus sibi, per quæ adversariis gratiæ prævalebit. Loquetur quoque libenter victorias, id est aliorum electorum gloriosos triumphos, quibus de mundo, carne atque diabolo triumpharunt.
paras.en: [[21:28|A lying witness shall perish|Testis mendax peribit]]. Hence it was said above: [[Prov 19:5|A false witness shall not be unpunished|Testis mendax non erit impunitus]] [the same words stand in Prov 19:5 and 19:9; Denis has *mendax*, "lying", for the Vulgate's *falsus*, "false"]. [[21:28|an obedient man shall speak of victory|Vir obediens loquetur victorias]] [Denis reads *victorias*, "victories", where the Vulgate has *victoriam*]: that is, by the very deed he will show himself strong and victorious, and will give others matter to speak of it; or, to the praise of God and the edification of his neighbour, he will tell how by obeying he prevailed over the enemies of his salvation, subjected the flesh and sensuality to reason, mastered his own mind and conquered himself. Or, he [[21:28|shall speak of victory|Loquetur victorias]], that is, he will give humble and obedient answers to those who command him, by which he will prevail over the enemies of grace. He also [[21:28|shall speak of victory|Loquetur quoque libenter victorias]] gladly, that is, of the glorious triumphs of the other elect, by which they triumphed over the world, the flesh and the devil.

paras.t: Vir impius procaciter obfirmat vultum suum, id est, interiorem suam indurationem impudenter ostendit facie torva, et quasi se armat vultu feroci ad non recipiendum exhortationem, correptionem, emollitionemve aliquam. Sic Laban obfirmavit vultum suum adversus Jacob, et Saul contra David, quem non recte oculis intuebatur. Qui autem rectus est, corrigit viam suam, id est, quotidie studet venialia peccata bonis actibus suis admixta, emendare, vitare, delere, et accusat se ipsum.
paras.en: [[21:29|The wicked man impudently hardeneth his face|Vir impius procaciter obfirmat vultum suum]], that is, he shows his inward hardness shamelessly with a grim face, and as it were arms himself with a fierce countenance so as not to receive any exhortation, rebuke or softening. So Laban hardened his face against Jacob, and Saul against David, whom he did not look upon with right eyes. [[21:29|but he that is righteous, correcteth his way|Qui autem rectus est, corrigit viam suam]], that is, he strives daily to amend, avoid and blot out the venial sins mingled with his good acts, and he accuses himself.

paras.t: Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum : id est, nec per cognitionem divinorum, nec per notitiam creaturarum, nec per investigationem agibilium potest quis Deo resistere, et ejus propositum impedire, aut voluntatem ipsius ab effectu absolute volito retardare : quoniam ipse per Prophetam testatur : Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet; et per alium : Quis similis mei, et quis sustinebit me? et quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo? Ideo sanctus Job fassus est : Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest; et quodcumque voluit, fecit. Imo sæpe per ea quæ homines agunt ad impediendum id quod Deus decrevit, illud amplius adimpletur.
paras.en: [[21:30|There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord|Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum]]: that is, neither by the knowledge of divine things, nor by the knowledge of creatures, nor by the investigation of things to be done [*agibilia*, matters of action, the field of prudence: Denis matches the verse's wisdom, prudence and counsel to these three] can anyone resist God and hinder his purpose, or hold back his will from the effect that he absolutely wills: since he himself declares by the Prophet: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]]; and by another: [[Jer 49:19|who is like to me? and who shall abide me? and who is that shepherd that can withstand my countenance?|Quis similis mei, et quis sustinebit me? et quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo?]] [the same words stand in Jer 50:44]. Therefore holy Job confessed: [[Job 23:13|For he is alone, and no man can turn away his thought|Deus solus est, et cogitationem ejus nemo avertere potest]]; [[Job 23:13|and whatsoever his soul hath desired, that hath he done|et quodcumque voluit, fecit]]. Indeed, often by the very things men do to hinder what God has decreed, it is fulfilled all the more.

paras.t: Insuper potest et ita exponi, quod nulla sapientia hæreticorum, nulla scientia philosophorum, nullum consilium tyrannorum, potuit evangelicæ legis ac fidei veritatem reprobare, exstirpare, aut ejus diffusionem per mundum impedire, quoniam Deus decrevit eam disseminare et confirmare in mundo.
paras.en: It can also be expounded thus: that no wisdom of heretics, no knowledge of philosophers, no counsel of tyrants could reject or root out the truth of the Gospel law and faith, or hinder its spread through the world, since God decreed to sow it and to establish it in the world.

paras.t: Equus paratur ad diem belli. Dominus autem salutem tribuet : id est, quamvis pugnaturi ad prœliandum se muniant equitatura et armatura, faciendo quod in ipsis est, ne videantur Deum tentare; tamen ex divina providentia et omnipotentia Dei, conceditur huic aut illi victoria. Ideo in Deo principaliter est sperandum, et ejus auxilium est petendum. Unde in Psalmo dicitur : Fallax equus ad salutem : et alibi, Victoria de cœlo est. Hinc legitur in libro Verborum dierum : Si putas in robore exercitus bella consistere, superare te faciet Dominus.
paras.en: [[21:31|The horse is prepared for the day of battle|Equus paratur ad diem belli]]: [[21:31|but the Lord giveth safety|Dominus autem salutem tribuet]]: that is, although those about to fight arm themselves for battle with horses and weapons, doing what lies in them, lest they seem to tempt God, yet it is by the divine providence and the omnipotence of God that victory is granted to this one or that. Therefore our hope must be placed chiefly in God, and his help must be asked. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:17|Vain is the horse for safety|Fallax equus ad salutem]]; and elsewhere: Victory is from heaven[[1 Mach 3:19||]] [no margin reference; compare 1 Mach 3:19, "strength cometh from heaven"]. Hence we read in the book of Words of the Days [*Verba dierum*, the Hebrew title of Paralipomenon]: [[2 Par 25:8|if thou think that battles consist in the strength of the army|Si putas in robore exercitus bella consistere]], [[2 Par 25:8|God will make thee to be overcome|superare te faciet Dominus]] [Denis's text has *superare*, "to overcome", where the Vulgate has *superari*, "to be overcome"].

22.title: [CAPITULUM VICESIMUM SECUNDUM : MELIUS EST NOMEN BONUM]
22.title_en: [The twenty-second chapter: A good name is better than great riches]
22.note: The printed heading of this article is missing from the transcription; the title in brackets is supplied from the chapter's first verse.

paras.t: Melius est nomen bonum, id est fama honesta et exemplaris, quam divitiæ multæ : quoniam magis propinquat ad spiritualia bona, et magis est ad Dei honorem, proximiorumque ædificationem, quam facultates ; estque de numero bonorum honorabilium, divitiæ autem de numero bonorum utilium, quæ inferioris sunt gradus. Hinc dixit Apostolus : Christi bonus odor sumus in omni loco. Denique Deo debemus conscientiam puram, proximis famam bonam, ne scilicet scandalizentur in nobis. Ideo jussit Salvator : Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus. Hinc asserit Augustinus : Duo sunt necessaria, scilicet conscientia et fama : conscientia, propter te ; fama, propter proximum. Qui conscientiæ suæ confidens, famam negligit, crudelis est. Super argentum enim et aurum valet gratia bona : per quam homo acceptus est proximis propter suas virtutes ; et maxime valet gratia Dei apud homines. Etiam plus prodest homini gratia quam invenit coram eis, quam opes. Idcirco in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Curam habe de bono nomine ; hoc enim plus prodest tibi, quam thesauri. Unde et Seneca : Bona, inquit, opinio (id est fama hominum) est tutior quam pecunia ; et rursus, Bona fama in tenebris suum habet splendorem.
paras.en: [[22:1|A good name is better|Melius est nomen bonum]], that is, an honourable and exemplary reputation, [[22:1|than great riches|quam divitiæ multæ]]: because it comes nearer to spiritual goods, and serves more for the honour of God and the edification of our neighbours than wealth does; and it is of the number of honourable goods [that is, goods worth having for their own excellence], whereas riches are of the number of useful goods, which are of a lower rank. Hence the Apostle said: [[2 Cor 2:15|we are the good odour of Christ|Christi bonus odor sumus]] [[2 Cor 2:14|in every place|in omni loco]]. In short, we owe God a pure conscience, and our neighbours a good name, so that they be not scandalized in us. Therefore the Saviour commanded: [[Matt 5:16|let your light shine before men|Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus]]. Hence Augustine declares: Two things are necessary, namely conscience and reputation: conscience for thy own sake, reputation for thy neighbour's. He who, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation, is cruel. For [[22:1|good favour is above silver and gold|Super argentum enim et aurum valet gratia bona]]: the favour by which a man is accepted by his neighbours for his virtues; and above all the grace of God avails with men. Moreover the favour a man finds before them profits him more than wealth. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 41:15|Take care of a good name|Curam habe de bono nomine]]; for this profiteth thee more than treasures [so Denis; the Vulgate has "this shall continue with thee more than a thousand treasures"]. Whence Seneca too says: A good opinion (that is, men's good report) is safer than money; and again: A good name has its splendour even in darkness.

paras.t: Dives et pauper obviaverunt sibi : utriusque operator est Dominus. Ideo, sicut dives non est propter divitias honorandus, ita nec pauper ob suam pauperiem contemnendus. Nec dives debet despicere pauperem, nec pauper dijudicare divitem. Imo dives debet pauperem honorare in corde suo, tanquam ad misericordiam et gratiam Dei magis dispositum. Pauperes enim elegit Deus. Et, sicut ait Gregorius, hos elegit Deus, quos despicit mundus. Unde S. Joannes Eleemosynarius, patriarcha Alexandrinus, pauperes semper vocavit dominos suos. At vero Deus quosdam divites, quosdam pauperes fecit, ut divites temporalia bene dispensando, et ea pauperibus communicando, bonæ dispensationis meritis consequantur salutem ; pauperes vero, suæ paupertatis purgatorium æquanimiter tolerando, per patientiam coronentur.
paras.en: [[22:2|The rich and poor have met one another: the Lord is the maker of them both.|Dives et pauper obviaverunt sibi: utriusque operator est Dominus.]] Therefore, as the rich man is not to be honoured for his riches, so neither is the poor man to be despised for his poverty. The rich man ought not to despise the poor, nor the poor man to judge the rich. Rather, the rich man ought to honour the poor man in his heart, as one better disposed for the mercy and grace of God. For God hath [[Jas 2:5|chosen the poor|Pauperes enim elegit]] [the margin gives James ii, 3; the words are at Jas 2:5]. And, as Gregory says, God has chosen those whom the world despises. Hence St John the Almoner, patriarch of Alexandria, always called the poor his lords. But God made some rich and some poor, so that the rich, by dispensing temporal things well and sharing them with the poor, may attain salvation by the merits of good stewardship; and the poor, by bearing with an even mind the purgatory of their poverty, may be crowned through patience.

paras.t: Callidus videt malum, id est imminens periculum, damnum, tormentum, et abscondit se, id est, retrahit se, ne incidat illud : quod licitum est, nisi ex præcepto teneatur veritatem fateri, seu aliquid facere, ex quo indubitanter malum illud incideret : sicut in certis casibus requirunt caritas atque justitia, ut propter fidei ac veritatis defensionem homo periculis se exponat. Innocens pertransiit locum periculi, seu opus bonum publice continuando, et afflictus est damno. Sic multi ex principibus Judæorum credebant in Christum ; sed quia videbant sibi ex hoc imminere periculum, non confitebantur, ut ait evangelista Joannes. Apostoli vero innocentes, et eorum consortes, processerunt in publica fidei confessione, et passi sunt persecutiones diversas.
paras.en: [[22:3|The prudent man saw the evil|Callidus videt malum]], that is, the danger, loss or torment that threatens, [[22:3|and hid himself|et abscondit se]], that is, draws himself back so as not to fall into it: which is lawful, unless he is bound by a precept to confess the truth, or to do something from which he would without doubt fall into that evil: as in certain cases charity and justice require that a man expose himself to dangers for the defence of the faith and of the truth. [[22:3|The simple passed on|Innocens pertransiit]] through the place of danger, or by carrying on a good work in public, [[22:3|and suffered loss|et afflictus est damno]]. Thus many of the chief men of the Jews believed in Christ; but because they saw that danger threatened them from it, they did not confess him[[John 12:42||]], as John the Evangelist says. But the Apostles, who were simple [Latin *innocentes*, the word of the verse], and their companions went forward in the public confession of the faith, and suffered various persecutions.

paras.t: Finis modestiæ : de qua loquitur Paulus, Modestia vestra nota sit omnibus hominibus ; est timor Domini. Modestia interdum est specialis virtus, prout in secunda secundæ, quæstione 160, Thomas declarat. Sed nunc accipi potest pro moderamine observando in omni virtute morali, ad quam spectat passionem reformare. Omnes autem virtutes morales tendunt ad hoc, ut passionibus reformatis, ad eam sinceritatem et rectitudinem homo perveniat, quod jugiter timeat filiali timore Deum etiam quantumlibet modice inhonorare sive offendere. Et non solum timor Domini est finis modestiæ, sed item divitiæ, id est spiritualis opulentia in donis virtutibusque theologicis, et gloria æternalis, et vita beatificæ fruitionis.
paras.en: [[22:4|The fruit of humility|Finis modestiæ]] [Latin *finis modestiæ*, "the end of modesty"; Denis takes *modestia* as moderation], that modesty of which Paul speaks: [[Phil 4:5|Let your modesty be known to all men|Modestia vestra nota sit omnibus hominibus]], is [[22:4|the fear of the Lord|timor Domini]]. Modesty is sometimes a special virtue, as Thomas explains in the Secunda Secundæ, question 160. But here it can be taken for the moderation to be kept in every moral virtue, to which it belongs to bring passion into order. Now all the moral virtues tend to this: that with the passions brought into order, a man may come to such sincerity and uprightness that he constantly fears, with filial fear, to dishonour or offend God even in the least degree. And not only is the fear of the Lord the end of modesty, but also [[22:4|riches|divitiæ]], that is, spiritual wealth in the gifts and the theological virtues, [[22:4|and glory|et gloria]] eternal, [[22:4|and life|et vita]] of blessed enjoyment.

paras.t: Arma et gladii in via superbi, id est, superbia in viis et factis suis ad bella et bellica instrumenta convertitur, quibus frequenter abutitur, non advertens nec metuens quod ait Salvator : Quicumque acceperit gladium, gladio peribit. Custos autem animæ suæ, ne peccet, longe recedit ab eis, id est a prætacta armorum tyrannide et abusu.
paras.en: [[22:5|Arms and swords are in the way|Arma et gladii in via]] of the proud [Denis reads *superbi*, "of the proud", where the Vulgate has *perversi*], that is, pride in its ways and deeds turns to wars and the instruments of war, which it often abuses, not heeding or fearing what the Saviour says: [[Matt 26:52|all that take the sword shall perish with the sword|Quicumque acceperit gladium, gladio peribit]]. [[22:5|But he that keepeth his own soul|Custos autem animæ suæ]], lest he sin, [[22:5|departeth far from them|longe recedit ab eis]], that is, from the tyranny and abuse of arms just mentioned.

paras.t: Proverbium est : Adolescens juxta viam suam, id est secundum modum suum conversans, etiam quum senuerit, non recedet ab ea : juxta illud metricum, Quod nova testa capit, inveterata sapit. Ideo versiculus ille repudiatur : Angelicus juvenis senibus satanescit in annis. Imo et ait Philosophus Ethicorum primo, non parum prodesse, juvenes assuefieri virtutum operibus. Et Seneca in suis ait Proverbiis : Facile est teneros adhuc annos componere.
paras.en: [[22:6|It is a proverb: A young man according to his way|Proverbium est : Adolescens juxta viam suam]], that is, living after his own manner, [[22:6|even when he is old, he will not depart from it|etiam quum senuerit, non recedet ab ea]]: according to that verse, What the new jar takes in, the old one tastes of. Therefore that little verse is rejected: The angelic youth turns satanic in his old years. Indeed the Philosopher too says, in the first book of the Ethics, that it profits not a little for the young to be accustomed to the works of the virtues. And Seneca says in his Proverbs: It is easy to set in order years that are still tender.

paras.t: Dives pauperibus imperat, id est, imperiose loquitur eis, præsertim servientibus sibi, et indigentibus sui. Dives quoque in sapientia atque virtutibus, præcipit discipulis suis adhuc pusillis. Et qui accipit mutuum, servus est fenerantis, id est ejus qui sibi accommodat mutuum : quia tenetur accommodanti rependere vicem, et indiget se illi subjicere. Unde et Seneca dixit : Beneficium accipere, est vendere libertatem.
paras.en: [[22:7|The rich ruleth over the poor|Dives pauperibus imperat]], that is, speaks to them imperiously, especially to those who serve him and are in need of him. So too he who is rich in wisdom and virtues gives commands to his disciples who are still little ones. [[22:7|And the borrower is servant to him that lendeth|Et qui accipit mutuum, servus est fenerantis]], that is, to him who lends to him: because he is bound to make a return to the lender, and has need to submit himself to him. Whence Seneca too said: To accept a kindness is to sell one's liberty.

paras.t: Qui seminat iniquitatem, id est discordiam aut falsam doctrinam, metet mala, id est, damnationem et tormenta recipiet pro mercede, dicente Apostolo, Quæ seminaverit homo, hæc et metet ; et virga iræ suæ, id est tribulatio quam ex ira aliis infert, consummabitur, id est, finem accipiet ; vel ipse consummabitur virga iræ suæ, id est, punitio qua æternaliter punietur propter iram et injuriam quas intulit aliis, erit finis et consummatio seu damnatio ejus finalis. Hinc scriptum est : Arastis impietatem, iniquitatem messuistis, et comedistis frugem mendacii.
paras.en: [[22:8|He that soweth iniquity|Qui seminat iniquitatem]], that is, discord or false doctrine, [[22:8|shall reap evils|metet mala]], that is, shall receive damnation and torments for his wages, as the Apostle says: [[Gal 6:8|what things a man shall sow, those also shall he reap|Quæ seminaverit homo, hæc et metet]]. [[22:8|And with the rod of his anger|et virga iræ suæ]], that is, the tribulation which he inflicts on others out of anger, [[22:8|he shall be consumed|consummabitur]], that is, shall come to an end [*consummabitur* can mean "shall be ended" or "shall be consumed"; Denis reads it both ways]; or, he himself shall be consumed by the rod of his anger, that is, the punishment with which he will be punished eternally for the anger and injury he did to others will be his end and consummation, or his final damnation. Hence it is written: [[Osee 10:13|You have ploughed wickedness, you have reaped iniquity, you have eaten the fruit of lying|Arastis impietatem, iniquitatem messuistis, et comedistis frugem mendacii]].

paras.t: Qui pronus est ad misericordiam, non solum ex inclinatione ingenita et naturali complexione, sed ex exercitatione assidua, benedicetur : quia a Deo dona gratiæ et gloriæ sortietur, et homines eum laudabunt, bona imprecando eidem. Talis fuit sanctus Job, qui ait : Ab infantia crevit mecum miseratio. De panibus enim suis dedit pauperi.
paras.en: [[22:9|He that is inclined to mercy|Qui pronus est ad misericordiam]], not only from an inborn inclination and natural temperament but from constant practice, [[22:9|shall be blessed|benedicetur]]: because he will receive from God the gifts of grace and glory, and men will praise him, wishing him good things. Such was holy Job, who says: [[Job 31:18|from my infancy mercy grew up with me|Ab infantia crevit mecum miseratio]]. [[22:9|For of his bread he hath given to the poor|De panibus enim suis dedit pauperi]].

paras.t: Victoriam et honorem acquiret qui dat munera. Talis enim a multis diligitur et juvatur, et si ex caritate egenis largitur, gratiam prævalendi hostibus suæ salutis a Deo sortitur. Animam autem aufert accipientium : id est, corda accipientium munera sua allicit sibi, benevolentiam eorum captando, quasi furatur ea ipsis, et transformat in se. Verumtamen iste versus non est in Hebræo.
paras.en: [[22:9|He that maketh presents, shall purchase victory and honour|Victoriam et honorem acquiret qui dat munera]]. For such a man is loved and helped by many; and if he gives freely to the needy out of charity, he receives from God the grace to prevail over the enemies of his salvation. [[22:9|But he carrieth away the souls of the receivers|Animam autem aufert accipientium]]: that is, he draws to himself the hearts of those who receive his gifts, capturing their goodwill; he as it were steals them from them, and changes them into himself. However, this verse is not in the Hebrew.

paras.t: Ejice derisorem, tu qui auctoritative et apte potes hoc facere, et exibit cum eo jurgium, cujus ipse est incitator et causa, cessabuntque causæ, id est lites, et contumeliæ : quarum ipse incitator est. Ideo, causa remota, removebitur et effectus. Sic et hæreticus incorrigibilisque transgressor, et communitatis turbator, sunt ab Ecclesia et congregatione ejiciendi.
paras.en: [[22:10|Cast out the scoffer|Ejice derisorem]], thou who canst do this with authority and fittingly, [[22:10|and contention shall go out with him|et exibit cum eo jurgium]], of which he is the instigator and cause, and [[22:10|quarrels|cessabuntque causæ]] shall cease, that is, lawsuits, [[22:10|and reproaches|et contumeliæ]], of which he is the instigator. For when the cause is removed, the effect too will be removed. So too the heretic, the incorrigible transgressor, and the disturber of the community are to be cast out of the Church and of the congregation.

paras.t: Qui diligit cordis munditiam, ita quod habet, amplectitur et custodit eam in corde suo, propter gratiam labiorum suorum, id est propter gratiam suæ puritatis quæ redundat in labiis suis, quibus libenter de munditia loquitur ; vel, Propter gratiam labiorum suorum, id est gratiosam efficaciam suæ sermocinationis, venientis ex puritate interna : ex qua sermocinatione innotescit cordis sui munditia : habebit amicum regem Deum omnipotentem essentialiter sanctum et purum. Similitudo enim est causa amoris. Talis quoque placet omni regi terreno et bono.
paras.en: [[22:11|He that loveth cleanness of heart|Qui diligit cordis munditiam]], so that he has it, embraces it and keeps it in his heart, [[22:11|for the grace of his lips|propter gratiam labiorum suorum]], that is, for the grace of his purity, which overflows into his lips, with which he gladly speaks of cleanness; or, for the grace of his lips, that is, for the gracious power of his speech, which comes from inward purity, and by which the cleanness of his heart becomes known, [[22:11|shall have the king for his friend|habebit amicum regem]]: almighty God, who is holy and pure in his essence. For likeness is the cause of love. Such a man also pleases every earthly king who is good.

paras.t: Oculi Domini custodiunt scientiam : id est, divinæ pietatis respectus conservat in mente salubrem notitiam, et præsertim scientiam quæ est donum ; et supplantantur verba iniqui : quia a Deo falsa esse monstrantur, et sæpe ab optato impediuntur effectu.
paras.en: [[22:12|The eyes of the Lord preserve knowledge|Oculi Domini custodiunt scientiam]]: that is, the regard of the divine goodness preserves wholesome knowledge in the mind, and especially the knowledge which is a gift [that is, the gift of knowledge, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost]; [[22:12|and the words of the unjust are overthrown|et supplantantur verba iniqui]]: because God shows them to be false, and they are often hindered from the effect they hoped for.

paras.t: Dicit piger : Leo est foris, in medio platearum occidendus sum : id est, calvas, vanas et leves quærit occasiones et excusationes, quibus evadat aggredi et exercere opera bona. Sic tempore persecutionis, imperfecti ac timidi subterfugiunt fidem publice confiteri, dicentes quod adsint tyranni.
paras.en: [[22:13|The slothful man saith: There is a lion without, I shall be slain in the midst of the streets|Dicit piger : Leo est foris, in medio platearum occidendus sum]]: that is, he looks for bald, empty and trifling pretexts and excuses by which to escape setting about and doing good works. So in time of persecution the imperfect and fearful shrink from confessing the faith in public, saying that tyrants are at hand.

paras.t: Fovea profunda, os alienæ : id est, verba lasciva et oscula feminæ adulteræ et fornicariæ, seu dogmata deceptricis scientiæ, assimilantur foveæ profundæ, in quam merguntur et pereunt corruentes : sic os tale trahit ad enormitatem peccati et tormentorum voraginem. Cui iratus est Dominus, id est, quem justo relinquit judicio, juxta illud, Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum ; incidet in eam. Quum enim destitutus fuerit miser homo gratia Creatoris, mox labitur in profunditatem criminum et erroris, quemadmodum per Prophetam loquitur Dominus : Averti faciem meam ab eo, et abiit vagus in via cordis sui. Unde et idem Propheta dicit Deo : Ecce tu iratus es, et peccavimus.
paras.en: [[22:14|The mouth of a strange woman is a deep pit|Fovea profunda, os alienæ]]: that is, the wanton words and kisses of an adulterous and fornicating woman, or the teachings of a deceitful learning, are like a deep pit, into which those who fall are swallowed up and perish: so such a mouth draws men into enormity of sin and into the abyss of torments. [[22:14|He whom the Lord is angry with|Cui iratus est Dominus]], that is, whom he leaves to his just judgment, according to that word: [[Ps 80:13|So I let them go according to the desires of their heart|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum]] [the margin gives Ps. lxxx, 3; the words are at Ps 80:13], [[22:14|shall fall into it|incidet in eam]]. For when a wretched man has been forsaken by the grace of the Creator, he soon slips into the depth of crimes and of error, as the Lord says by the Prophet: [[Is 57:17|I hid my face|Averti faciem meam]] from him [Denis reads *Averti faciem meam ab eo*, "I turned away my face from him"; the Vulgate has *Abscondi a te faciem meam*], [[Is 57:17|and he went away wandering in his own heart|et abiit vagus in via cordis sui]]. Whence the same Prophet says to God: [[Is 64:5|behold thou art angry, and we have sinned|Ecce tu iratus es, et peccavimus]].

paras.t: Stultitia colligata est in corde pueri nondum adultæ ætatis : quia ad ludicra jugiter inclinatur, nec habet acquisitam prudentiam, experientiam, rationemve fortem : similiter in corde pueri sensu, quamvis forte sit centum annorum ; et virga disciplinæ, per quam fit correctio, fugabit eam : non enim amore virtutis et rationabili persuasione, sed timore et pœna reprimuntur, instruunturque pueri circa exordium discretionis.
paras.en: [[22:15|Folly is bound up in the heart of a child|Stultitia colligata est in corde pueri]] not yet of grown age: because he is always inclined to play, and has not acquired prudence, experience or strong reason; and likewise in the heart of one who is a child in understanding, though he be perhaps a hundred years old[[Is 65:20||]] [the margin gives "Ibid. lxv" (Isaias) with an unclear verse; Is 65:20 speaks of the child a hundred years old]; [[22:15|and the rod of correction|et virga disciplinæ]], by which correction is made, [[22:15|shall drive it away|fugabit eam]]: for children are restrained and taught, at the beginning of discretion [that is, the age at which they begin to tell right from wrong], not by love of virtue and reasonable persuasion, but by fear and punishment.

paras.t: Qui calumniatur pauperem, ut augeat divitias suas, per ea quæ abstrahit pauperi, vel quæ capit ab impio, ut propter ejus preces ac munera opprimat pauperem ; dabit ipse ditiori, id est, a judice superiori adjudicabitur pecuniariæ satisfactioni, et privabitur rebus male adeptis, et egebit. Similiter qui pauperi spiritu et humili detrahit, ut ipse ex hoc melior videatur, cogetur reddere rationem Christo, et miser probatus damnabitur.
paras.en: [[22:16|He that oppresseth the poor, to increase his own riches|Qui calumniatur pauperem, ut augeat divitias suas]], by what he takes from the poor man, or by what he takes from a wicked man so as to oppress the poor at his prayers and for his gifts, [[22:16|shall himself give to one that is richer|dabit ipse ditiori]], that is, he will be sentenced by a higher judge to make satisfaction in money, and will be deprived of what he got wickedly, [[22:16|and shall be in need|et egebit]]. Likewise he who disparages one who is poor in spirit and humble, so as to seem the better himself by it, will be forced to render an account to Christ, and, proved a wretch, will be damned.

paras.t: Fili mi, inclina aurem tuam, etc. Circa hæc ait Glossa : Hucusque titulus Parabolarum Salomonis, qui supra est positus illo loco ex quo cœpit novo loquendi genere loqui, non ad eum quem docuit, sed secum ratiocinando : quod incipit ibi, Filius sapiens lætificat patrem ; et finitur hic, Dabit ipse ditiori, et egebit. Hic ad priorem loquendi modum revertitur, dirigendo verba ad eum quem docet. Cui jam ait : Fili mi, inclina aurem tuam, id est, humiliter et ardenter applica aures cordis et corporis : quod est signum egregiæ indolis ; et audi verba sapientium, id est ad verba sapientium. Appone autem cor tuum ad doctrinam meam.
paras.en: My son, [[22:17|Incline thy ear|inclina aurem tuam]], etc. [Denis's text adds *Fili mi*, "My son", which the Vulgate does not have here]. On this the Gloss says: Thus far the title "Parables of Solomon", which was set above at the place where he began to speak in a new manner, not addressing the one he taught but reasoning with himself: which begins there, [[Prov 10:1|A wise son maketh the father glad|Filius sapiens lætificat patrem]], and ends here, [[22:16|shall himself give to one that is richer, and shall be in need|Dabit ipse ditiori, et egebit]]. Here he returns to his former manner of speaking, directing his words to the one he teaches. To whom he now says: My son, incline thy ear, that is, humbly and eagerly apply the ears of the heart and of the body, which is the sign of an excellent disposition; [[22:17|and hear the words of the wise|et audi verba sapientium]], that is, listen to the words of the wise. [[22:17|And apply thy heart to my doctrine|Appone autem cor tuum ad doctrinam meam]].

paras.t: Quæ pulchra erit tibi : quia admixtione caret erroris et vitii, et luce veritatis resplendet ; quum servaveris eam per memoriam et effectum, in ventre tuo, id est in mente, in qua animæ fercula suscipiuntur, digeruntur et conservantur ; et redundabit in labiis tuis, ut sit in Domino fiducia tua. Unde et ostendam eam tibi hodie : quia instructio ista est sæpius iteranda.
paras.en: [[22:18|Which shall be beautiful for thee|Quæ pulchra erit tibi]]: because it is free of any admixture of error and vice, and shines with the light of truth; [[22:18|if thou keep it|quum servaveris eam]] by memory and by deed, [[22:18|in thy bowels|in ventre tuo]] [Latin *venter*, "belly"], that is, in the mind, in which the dishes of the soul are received, digested and kept; [[22:18|and it shall flow in thy lips|et redundabit in labiis tuis]]: [[22:19|That thy trust may be in the Lord|ut sit in Domino fiducia tua]]. [[22:19|Wherefore I have also shewn it to thee this day|Unde et ostendam eam tibi hodie]] [Denis reads *ostendam*, "I will shew"]: because this instruction is to be repeated often.

paras.t: Ecce descripsi eam tibi tripliciter : utpote anagogice, symbolice, historice. Vel, Tripliciter, id est litteraliter seu historice, et tropologice seu moraliter, et allegorice. His enim modis Scriptura exponitur, et triplex theologia assignatur. Vel, Tripliciter, id est proportionabiliter juxta triplicem hominum statum, videlicet incipientium, proficientium, et perfectorum. Nam et in isto Proverbiorum volumine, doctrina seu sapientia quandoque traditur tam subtiliter ac profunde, ut solum perfectis conveniat ; quandoque mediocriter, prout proficientibus competit ; aliquando ita simpliciter, ut incipientium congruat capacitati. Vel, Tripliciter, quia, sicut circa exordium operis hujus inductum est, Salomon in tribus suis voluminibus de sapientia tripliciter tractat, ac triformem tradit doctrinam. Aliqui autem dicunt, Salomonem hic loqui in persona Dei, qui sapientiam descripsit per Sanctos suos tripliciter, secundum tres partes Scripturæ : quia descripsit eam in lege, in Prophetis, atque in libris hagiographis. Porro, quod subditur, in cogitationibus et scientia, intelligendum est quod sapientia seu sacra doctrina consistit in actuali consideratione, et in habituali notitia : et quantum ad horum utrumque, tripliciter est descripta : nam et habitualis notitia, ad actualem finaliter ordinatur.
paras.en: [[22:20|Behold I have described it to thee three manner of ways|Ecce descripsi eam tibi tripliciter]]: namely anagogically, symbolically and historically. Or, three manner of ways, that is, literally or historically, tropologically or morally, and allegorically. For in these ways Scripture is expounded, and a threefold theology is assigned. Or, three manner of ways, that is, in proportion to the threefold state of men, namely of beginners, of the proficient, and of the perfect. For in this volume of Proverbs too, doctrine or wisdom is sometimes handed down so subtly and profoundly that it suits only the perfect; sometimes in a middle way, as befits the proficient; and at times so simply that it fits the capacity of beginners. Or, three manner of ways, because, as was set out at the beginning of this work, Solomon treats of wisdom in three ways in his three volumes, and hands down a threefold doctrine. Some, however, say that Solomon speaks here in the person of God, who described wisdom in three ways through his Saints, according to the three parts of Scripture: for he described it in the Law, in the Prophets, and in the books of the Hagiographa [that is, the "holy writings", the third part of the Hebrew Bible]. Further, as to what follows, [[22:20|in thoughts and knowledge|in cogitationibus et scientia]], it is to be understood that wisdom or sacred doctrine consists in actual consideration and in habitual knowledge [that is, in the act of thinking on it, and in the abiding knowledge of it]; and as to each of these it has been described in three ways: for habitual knowledge too is ordered in the end to the actual.

paras.t: Ut ostenderem tibi firmitatem, id est firmam Scripturæ intelligentiam, quæ tot modis exponitur, virtutum quoque stabilitatem, ad quam doctrina moralis refertur ac tendit, et qualiter mente robusta inhærendum sit summo bono, et eloquia veritatis, id est sermones divinæ Scripturæ, per quos te in omnibus possis dirigere : respondere ex his illis qui miserunt te, id est ad respondendum ex horum notitia sapienter majoribus tuis, potissime Deo in suo judicio, et angelis ac prælatis, a quibus ad diversa agenda dirigeris. In Hebræo tamen fertur haberi, Respondere ex his interrogantibus te : et sic textus est planior. Nam et beatissimus Archiapostolus in sua prima hortatur Canonica : Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem de ea quæ in vobis est, fide et spe. Porro, qui interrogat alium, mittit eum quodammodo ad interiora sua, ad cogitandum et deliberandum de sibi proposita quæstione : et sic translatio nostra redit in idem.
paras.en: [[22:21|That I might shew thee the certainty|Ut ostenderem tibi firmitatem]] [Latin *firmitas*, "firmness"], that is, a firm understanding of Scripture, which is expounded in so many ways; and also the stability of the virtues, to which moral doctrine is referred and tends; and how one must cleave with a strong mind to the highest good; [[22:21|and the words of truth|et eloquia veritatis]], that is, the discourses of divine Scripture, by which thou canst direct thyself in all things: [[22:21|to answer out of these to them that sent thee|respondere ex his illis qui miserunt te]], that is, so as to answer wisely, from the knowledge of these, those set over thee: above all God in his judgment, and the angels and prelates by whom thou art directed to the various things to be done. In the Hebrew, however, it is said to read: To answer out of these them that question thee; and so the text is plainer. For the most blessed Prince of the Apostles also exhorts in his first canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 3:15|being ready always to satisfy every one that asketh you a reason|Parati semper ad satisfactionem omni poscenti vos rationem]] of that which is in you, faith and hope [Denis's text adds faith; the Vulgate has "of that hope which is in you"]. Moreover, he who questions another sends him in a manner into his own inward parts, to think and deliberate on the question put to him: and so our translation comes to the same thing.

paras.t: Non facias violentiam pauperi, quia pauper est. Hoc dupliciter potest exponi. Primo sic : Eo ipso quo pauper est, non facias violentiam ei : nam quamvis illicitum et crudele sit alicui violentiam inferre, præcipue tamen impotenti et pauperi, miserabilibusque personis. Secundo sic : Non facias violentiam pauperi quia pauper est, id est ob hoc quod inops et impotens est ad resistendum. Neque conteras egenum in porta, id est in foro judicii, quod antiquitus fiebat in urbium portis, sicut in Deuteronomio Dominus jubet : Judices constitues in omnibus portis tuis. Hinc Job dicit : Si levavi super pupillum manum meam, etiam quum viderem me in porta superiorem. Et per Prophetam Dominus loquitur : Quare atteritis populum meum, et facies pauperum commolitis?
paras.en: [[22:22|Do no violence to the poor, because he is poor|Non facias violentiam pauperi, quia pauper est]]. This can be expounded in two ways. First thus: by the very fact that he is poor, do him no violence: for though it is unlawful and cruel to do violence to anyone, it is so above all to the powerless and the poor, and to persons in distress. Second thus: do no violence to the poor man because he is poor, that is, for the reason that he is needy and powerless to resist. [[22:22|And do not oppress the needy in the gate|Neque conteras egenum in porta]], that is, in the court of judgment, which in ancient times was held in the gates of cities, as the Lord commands in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 16:18|Thou shalt appoint judges|Judices constitues]] [[Deut 16:18|in all thy gates|in omnibus portis tuis]]. Hence Job says: [[Job 31:21|If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, even when I saw myself superior in the gate|Si levavi super pupillum manum meam, etiam quum viderem me in porta superiorem]]. And the Lord says by the Prophet: [[Is 3:15|Why do you consume my people, and grind the faces of the poor?|Quare atteritis populum meum, et facies pauperum commolitis?]]

paras.t: Quia Dominus judicabit causam ejus : quia male judicata Dominus rejudicabit, et ipse omnium judex est. Specialiter vero pauperum est protector, quorum injuriam gravius vindicat ; cui in Psalmo cantatur : Tibi derelictus est pauper ; et denuo, Facit judicium injuriam patientibus. Quibus ipse locutus est per Zachariam : Qui tetigerit vos, tangit pupillam oculi mei. Et configet eos puncturis æternæ damnationis, qui confixerunt animam ejus, id est, animam pauperis afflixerunt injuste.
paras.en: [[22:23|Because the Lord will judge his cause|Quia Dominus judicabit causam ejus]]: because what has been judged ill the Lord will judge again, and he is the judge of all. But he is in a special way the protector of the poor, whose wrongs he avenges more heavily; to whom it is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 9:35|To thee is the poor man left|Tibi derelictus est pauper]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 14, "according to the Hebrew"; in the Vulgate numbering Ps 9:35]; and again, [[Ps 145:7|who executeth judgment for them that suffer wrong|Facit judicium injuriam patientibus]]. To them he spoke by Zacharias: [[Zach 2:8|he that toucheth you, toucheth the apple of my eye|Qui tetigerit vos, tangit pupillam oculi mei]]. And he [[22:23|will afflict them|Et configet eos]] with the piercings of eternal damnation [*configere*, "to pierce through": hence "piercings"], [[22:23|that have afflicted his soul|qui confixerunt animam ejus]], that is, who have unjustly afflicted the soul of the poor man.

paras.t: Noli esse amicus, id est familiaritatem aut societatem habens, homini iracundo : quem tamen debes ex caritate diligere ; neque ambules libenter, aut solus, aut sæpe, cum viro furioso, ne forte discas semitas ejus, id est, ne provoceris ex ira et impatientia ac furore ejus, sicque assuescas faciliter ad iram impatientiamque moveri, contendere, perturbari : quemadmodum scriptum est, Cum perverso perverteris ; et alibi rursus, Amicus stultorum efficietur similis. Et sumas scandalum, id est occasionem ruinæ, animæ tuæ, ex tali societate et communione. Quærenda est ergo amicitia, familiaritas atque societas hominis mansueti, virtuosi, fidelis. Sed pensandum quod in Proverbiis suis Seneca ait : Quam multi amicos tales habere voluerunt, et ipsimet tales esse non potuerunt! Ideo rursus optime docet et consulit : Te ipsum primo exhibe bonum, et sic quære alterum similem. Verumtamen istud de imperfectis intelligendum videtur : quibus periculosa est amicitia et familiaritas iracundorum, quia adhuc proni sunt scandalizari. Perfecti autem, ut ait Hieronymus, scandala non recipiunt : qui adeo virtuosi et fortes sunt, quod sua mansuetudine, pietate, patientia, caritate et exemplo, iracundos et alios passionatos possunt ad reformationem allicere.
paras.en: [[22:24|Be not a friend|Noli esse amicus]], that is, one having familiarity or fellowship, [[22:24|to an angry man|homini iracundo]], whom nevertheless thou oughtest to love out of charity; [[22:24|and do not walk|neque ambules]] willingly, or alone, or often, [[22:24|with a furious man|cum viro furioso]]: [[22:25|Lest perhaps thou learn his ways|ne forte discas semitas ejus]], that is, lest thou be provoked by his anger, impatience and fury, and so grow used to being easily moved to anger and impatience, to quarrelling and to being disturbed: as it is written, [[Ps 17:27|with the perverse thou wilt be perverted|Cum perverso perverteris]]; and again elsewhere, [[Prov 13:20|a friend of fools shall become like to them|Amicus stultorum efficietur similis]]. [[22:25|And take scandal|Et sumas scandalum]], that is, an occasion of ruin, [[22:25|to thy soul|animæ tuæ]], from such fellowship and company. The friendship, familiarity and fellowship to be sought, then, is that of a man who is gentle, virtuous and faithful. But we should weigh what Seneca says in his Proverbs: How many have wished to have such friends, and could not be such themselves! Therefore he teaches and counsels again, most excellently: First show thyself good, and then seek another like thee. Yet this seems to be understood of the imperfect, for whom friendship and familiarity with angry men is dangerous, because they are still prone to be scandalized. But the perfect, as Jerome says, do not take scandal: they are so virtuous and strong that by their gentleness, kindness, patience, charity and example they can draw the angry and others ruled by their passions to amendment.

paras.t: Noli esse cum his qui defigunt, id est obligant, manus suas, extendendo eas ad promittendum pro aliis, et qui vades, id est fidejussores, se offerunt pro debitis alienis. Si enim non habet ille pro quo fidem facis, et satisfactionem in casu promittis, unde restituat, id est, debitum suum persolvat, et fidejussori satisfacere queat, quid causæ est, id est quæ ratio sive utilitas, ut tollas vestimentum de cubili tuo, id est, vestem tuam des in pignus pro illo? quasi dicat : Sine necessitate ingeris tibi damnum atque molestiam. Tamen in necessitate et ex rationabili causa ac caritate, pium est cum discretione pro amico fidejubere.
paras.en: [[22:26|Be not with them that fasten down|Noli esse cum his qui defigunt]], that is, bind, [[22:26|their hands|manus suas]], stretching them out to make promises for others, [[22:26|and that offer themselves sureties|et qui vades]], that is, guarantors, [[22:26|for debts|se offerunt pro debitis]] of others. For if he [[22:27|have not|non habet]], for whom thou givest thy pledge and promisest satisfaction should the case arise, [[22:27|wherewith to restore|unde restituat]], that is, to pay his debt and to satisfy his surety, [[22:27|what cause is there|quid causæ est]], that is, what reason or profit, that thou shouldst take thy garment [[22:27|from thy bed|de cubili tuo]], that is, give thy clothing in pledge for him? [Denis's text reads *non habet … restituat*, of the debtor, and *ut tollas vestimentum*, "that thou take the garment"; the Vulgate has *non habes … restituas … ut tollat operimentum*] As if to say: without necessity thou bringest loss and trouble on thyself. Yet in necessity, and for a reasonable cause and out of charity, it is a kindly thing to stand surety for a friend, with discretion.

paras.t: Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui : id est, bona et confinia aliorum non invadas, nec cupide quæras, sed esto contentus hereditate patrum tuorum. Spiritualiter vero, non debemus transgredi regulas et præcepta, institutiones et documenta, a patribus nostris nobis præfixa ac derelicta ; nec intromittere nos de his quæ statum, gradum, vires et auctoritatem nostram transcendunt, sed juxta nostræ vocationis et professionis exigentiam ac tenorem, Omnipotenti sollicite deservire ; nec terminos obedientiæ nostræ exire, quemadmodum libro de Angelica hierarchia divinus et magnus Dionysius docet et asserit, quod nullus angelicorum spirituum legem sibi divinitus præfixam audet transcendere. Hinc in Deuteronomio scriptum est : Non transferes terminos quos fixerunt priores in possessione tua.
paras.en: [[22:28|Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set|Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui]]: that is, do not invade the goods and borders of others, nor covet them, but be content with the inheritance of thy fathers. Spiritually, we must not pass beyond the rules and precepts, the institutions and teachings, laid down for us and left to us by our fathers; nor meddle in things that go beyond our state, rank, strength and authority, but serve the Almighty with care according to the demands and tenor of our calling and profession; nor go beyond the bounds of our obedience: as the divine and great Dionysius teaches and declares in the book of the Angelic Hierarchy, that none of the angelic spirits dares to pass beyond the law divinely laid down for it. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 19:14|Thou shalt not take nor remove|Non transferes]] the bounds [[Deut 19:14|which thy predecessors have set in thy possession|quos fixerunt priores in possessione tua]].

paras.t: Vidisti virum velocem, id est expeditum, strenuum, agilem, in opere suo bono? Coram regibus stabit, id est, aptus erit regibus obsequi : tales enim ministri regibus placent, quoniam volunt sibi prompte atque velociter obediri ; nec erit ante ignobiles : id est, non decet cum ignobilibus ministrare, nec ipse libenter hoc faceret.
paras.en: [[22:29|Hast thou seen a man swift|Vidisti virum velocem]], that is, ready, vigorous, nimble, [[22:29|in his work|in opere suo]], a good one? [[22:29|He shall stand before kings|Coram regibus stabit]], that is, he will be fit to serve kings: for such servants please kings, since they wish to be obeyed promptly and swiftly; [[22:29|and shall not be before those that are obscure|nec erit ante ignobiles]]: that is, it is not fitting for him to serve with men of low degree, nor would he gladly do so.

paras.t: Spiritualiter vero, qui velox et fervens est in actibus virtuosis, coram regibus regni cœlestis, id est sanctis Apostolis et apostolicis viris, stabit, puta ad dexteram Judicis in die judicii, et cum ipsis æternaliter Regem sæculorum immortalem, invisibilem, intuebitur ac laudabit. Nec erit ante ignobiles, qui a sinistris consistent. Itaque cum moderata velocitate, et discreta alacritate, ac caritativa festinantia, serviendum est Deo, quemadmodum in Genesi narratur de Abraham, quod tribus angelis hospitio susceptis, festinavit, et dixit ad Saram, Accelera ; et ipse ad armentum cucurrit, deditque puero vitulum, qui festinavit et coxit illum. Ubi loquitur Origenes : Vide quomodo in domo sapientis omnes festinant, et nihil cum torpore aut negligentia agitur : festinavit Abraham, et cucurrit ; festinavit Sara, et azymos panes paravit ; festinavit et puer, vitulum coquens. Hinc in Ecclesiaste inducitur : Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare.
paras.en: Spiritually, he who is swift and fervent in virtuous acts shall stand [[22:29|before kings|coram regibus]] of the heavenly kingdom, that is, the holy Apostles and apostolic men: namely at the right hand of the Judge[[Matt 25:33||]] on the day of judgment; and with them he will eternally behold and praise the [[1 Tim 1:17|king of ages, immortal, invisible|Regem sæculorum immortalem, invisibilem]]. [[22:29|And shall not be before those that are obscure|Nec erit ante ignobiles]], who will stand on the left[[Matt 25:33||]]. God, then, is to be served with measured swiftness, discreet eagerness and charitable haste, as is told in Genesis of Abraham: when he had received three angels as guests[[Gen 18:2||]], he made haste and said to Sara: [[Gen 18:6|Make haste|Accelera]]; and [[Gen 18:7|he himself ran to the herd|ipse ad armentum cucurrit]], and gave the calf [[Gen 18:7|to a young man, who made haste and boiled it|puero vitulum, qui festinavit et coxit illum]]. On which Origen says: See how in the house of the wise man all make haste, and nothing is done with sloth or negligence: Abraham made haste and ran; Sara made haste and prepared unleavened loaves; the servant too made haste, cooking the calf. Hence it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly|Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare]].

23.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI VICESIMI TERTII : QUANDO SEDERIS UT COMEDAS CUM PRINCIPE, ETC.
23.title_en: Exposition of the twenty-third chapter: When thou shalt sit to eat with a prince, etc.

paras.t: QUANDO sederis ut comedas cum principe, diligenter attende quæ posita sunt ante faciem tuam, et statue cultrum in gutture tuo. Potest hic locus primo superficialiter accipi de modo habendi se in mensa corporalis refectionis cum principe : cum quo modeste ac sobrie est edendum, ita ut proposita alimenta diligenter pensentur, ne de eis aliquid inordinate aut immoderate sumatur. Sicque culter in gutture est ponendus, id est, guttur virtute temperantiæ, quæ instar cultelli rescindit superflua, refrenandum est a voluptuosa et gulosa alimentorum acceptione. Nempe, ut in Job scriptum est, Guttur escas gustu dijudicat. Istud ergo agendum est, si tamen habes in potestate animam tuam, id est, si ratione et virtute eam regere atque reprimere potes.
paras.en: [[23:1|When thou shalt sit to eat with a prince|QUANDO sederis ut comedas cum principe]], [[23:1|consider diligently what is set before thy face|diligenter attende quæ posita sunt ante faciem tuam]], [[23:2|And put a knife to thy throat|et statue cultrum in gutture tuo]]. This passage can first be taken at the surface, of how one should behave at a table of bodily refreshment with a prince: with him one must eat modestly and soberly, so that the food set out is carefully weighed, lest anything of it be taken in a disorderly or immoderate way. And so the knife is to be put to the throat: that is, the throat is to be reined in from the pleasure-seeking and gluttonous taking of food by the virtue of temperance, which like a little knife cuts away what is superfluous. For, as is written in Job: [[Job 34:3|the mouth discerneth meats by the taste|Guttur escas gustu dijudicat]] [the Latin has *guttur*, the same word as "throat" in our verse]. This, then, is to be done, [[23:2|if it be so that thou have thy soul in thy own power|si tamen habes in potestate animam tuam]], that is, if thou canst rule and restrain it by reason and virtue.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur sic : Quando sederis ad mensam sapientiæ et sacræ Scripturæ, id est, verbum Dei audieris, aut sacræ fueris lectioni intentus, ut comedas cum principe, id est, cum prælato seu doctore reficiaris sensu verborum cœlestium, diligenter attende quæ posita sunt, id est documenta, præcepta, consilia et exempla quæ audis seu legis, ut ea intelligas et observes. Scienti enim bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi. Et Scriptura tanquam sermo et epistola Spiritus Sancti, cum omni diligentia est legenda ac audienda, ut secundum eam vivatur. Et statue cultrum, id est discretionem superflua resecantem, in gutture tuo, id est in interiori palato, quo dulcedo verborum Dei percipitur; vel, in gutture tuo, id est locutione, quæ per guttur formatur, quatenus non velis plus sapere, profundius perscrutari, subtilius loqui quam expedit et capere vales.
paras.en: Secondly, it is expounded thus: [[23:1|When thou shalt sit|Quando sederis]] at the table of wisdom and of holy Scripture, that is, when thou hearest the word of God, or art intent on sacred reading, [[23:1|to eat with a prince|ut comedas cum principe]], that is, when thou art refreshed with the sense of the heavenly words together with a prelate or teacher, [[23:1|consider diligently what is set|diligenter attende quæ posita sunt]], that is, the teachings, precepts, counsels and examples which thou hearest or readest, so as to understand and keep them. For [[Jas 4:17|who knoweth to do good and doth it not, to him it is sin|Scienti enim bonum et non facienti, peccatum est illi]]. And Scripture, as being the discourse and letter of the Holy Ghost, must be read and heard with all diligence, so that one may live according to it. [[23:2|And put a knife|Et statue cultrum]], that is, discretion that cuts away what is superfluous, [[23:2|to thy throat|in gutture tuo]], that is, to the inner palate by which the sweetness of the words of God is tasted; or, [[23:2|to thy throat|in gutture tuo]], that is, to thy speech, which is formed in the throat: so that thou wish not to be wiser, to search deeper, or to speak more subtly than is expedient and than thou art able to grasp[[Eccles 7:17||]][[Rom 12:3||]].

paras.t: Præterea præinductam auctoritatem Augustinus in quodam sermone exponit de mensa Christi, in qua corpus ejus et sanguis proponuntur, ejusque passio, virtutes et opera recitantur : quæ omnia sunt diligentissime advertenda, ac pro viribus imitanda, et devotissime suscipienda.
paras.en: Moreover, Augustine in a certain sermon expounds the text cited above of the table of Christ, on which his body and blood are set before us, and his passion, virtues and works are recounted: all of which are to be heeded most diligently, imitated as far as our strength allows, and received most devoutly.

paras.t: Ne desideres de cibis ejus in quo est panis mendacii : id est, nec corporaliter nec spiritualiter cupias refici ab eo, qui vel fallacem proponit doctrinam, vel alimenta mendaciter aut injuste adepta habet et exhibet.
paras.en: [[23:3|Be not desirous of his meats, in which is the bread of deceit|Ne desideres de cibis ejus in quo est panis mendacii]]: that is, do not desire to be refreshed, either bodily or spiritually, by one who either sets forth a deceitful teaching, or has and serves food gained by deceit or injustice.

paras.t: Noli laborare ut diteris in rebus terrenis ultra qualitatem et dispositionem tui status : quia, ut ait Apostolus, Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli. Sed prudentiæ tuæ pone modum, ne vertatur in vitium quærendo superflua.
paras.en: [[23:4|Labour not to be rich|Noli laborare ut diteris]] in earthly things beyond the quality and condition of thy state: for, as the Apostle says, [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil|Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli]]. [[23:4|but set bounds to thy prudence|Sed prudentiæ tuæ pone modum]], lest it turn into vice by seeking superfluous things.

paras.t: Ne erigas oculos tuos ex aviditate acquirendi, ad opes quas habere non potes, quia facient sibi pennas quasi aquilæ, et volabunt in cælum : id est, sua pretiositate tuam effugiunt capacitatem, sicut aquila sua velocitate volat in altum; atque ad Creatoris cedunt honorem, qui ex suis creaturis ostenditur honorandus. Potestque istud de spiritualibus accipi opibus, ut scilicet homo nequaquam præsumat Deitatis penetrare secreta, nec incomprehensibilia perscrutari conetur, nec ad perfectionem virtutum, stabilitatemque cordis viatoribus impossibilem conetur in hac vita pertingere, quum scriptum sit : Quia plus fecit quam potuit, idcirco periit; et alibi : Noli esse justus multum, neque plus sapias quam oportet, ne obstupescas.
paras.en: [[23:5|Lift not up thy eyes|Ne erigas oculos tuos]] out of greed for getting, [[23:5|to riches which thou canst not have|ad opes quas habere non potes]], [[23:5|because they shall make themselves wings like those of an eagle, and shall fly towards heaven|quia facient sibi pennas quasi aquilæ, et volabunt in cælum]]: that is, by their preciousness they escape thy grasp, as the eagle by its swiftness flies on high; and they go to the honour of the Creator, who is shown by his creatures to be worthy of honour. And this can be taken of spiritual riches too: namely, that a man should by no means presume to pierce the secrets of the Godhead, nor try to search out things incomprehensible, nor try to reach in this life a perfection of virtue and a steadfastness of heart that is impossible for wayfarers [that is, those still on the way in this life, not yet in the homeland]; since it is written: [[Jer 48:36|because he hath done more than he could, therefore they have perished|Quia plus fecit quam potuit, idcirco periit]]; and elsewhere: [[Eccles 7:17|Be not over just: and be not more wise than is necessary, lest thou become stupid.|Noli esse justus multum, neque plus sapias quam oportet, ne obstupescas]].

paras.t: Ne comedas cum homine invido, quem scis talem esse et te odire; et ne desideres cibos ejus; quoniam in similitudinem arioli et conjectoris æstimat quod ignorat : id est, sicut divinator, et qui conjecturis intentus est, aut somnia exponit, sæpe suspicatur aut asserit quod non scit; sic invidiosus putat variis modis nocere, quod tamen quandoque non valet implere. Similiter cum hæreticis et fallacibus doctoribus non est communicandum in mensa sapientiæ, quia Scripturas false interpretantur, aut ad finem retorquent perversum, de futuris quoque pronosticare usurpant.
paras.en: [[23:6|Eat not with an envious man|Ne comedas cum homine invido]], whom thou knowest to be such and to hate thee, [[23:6|and desire not his meats|et ne desideres cibos ejus]]; [[23:7|Because, like a soothsayer, and diviner, he thinketh that which he knoweth not|quoniam in similitudinem arioli et conjectoris æstimat quod ignorat]]: that is, as a diviner, and one who is bent on conjectures or expounds dreams, often suspects or asserts what he does not know, so the envious man thinks to do harm in various ways, which yet he is sometimes not able to carry out. In the same way, one must not share the table of wisdom with heretics and deceitful teachers, for they interpret the Scriptures falsely, or twist them to a perverse end, and also take it upon themselves to foretell things to come.

paras.t: Comede et bibe, dicet tibi, invitando te ficto amore : et mens ejus non est tecum, id est tibi conjuncta per verum et spiritualem amorem. Cibos quos comederas, evomes : id est, non commodum, sed magis dispendium ex comestione cum illo habita, consequeris; et perdes pulchros sermones tuos, id est, fructum non habebis ex verbis peritis seu caritativis quæ habuisti cum tali, quia decipiet te, si potest. Deus tamen nullum bonum irremuneratum relinquit.
paras.en: [[23:7|Eat and drink, will he say to thee|Comede et bibe, dicet tibi]], inviting thee with feigned love: [[23:7|and his mind is not with thee|et mens ejus non est tecum]], that is, joined to thee by true and spiritual love. [[23:8|The meats which thou hadst eaten, thou shalt vomit up|Cibos quos comederas, evomes]]: that is, thou shalt get not profit but rather loss from the meal had with him; [[23:8|and shalt loose thy beautiful words|et perdes pulchros sermones tuos]], that is, thou shalt have no fruit from the skilled or charitable words which thou hadst with such a man, for he will deceive thee if he can. Yet God leaves no good unrewarded.

paras.t: In auribus insipientium, quos scis aut experiris incorrigibiles esse, ne loquaris, eos docendo aut increpando; quia despicient doctrinam eloquii tui, et ita non emendantur, sed pejorantur. Unde ait Salvator : Nolite sanctum dare canibus. Et in Ecclesiastico legitur : Ubi non est auditus, non effundas sermonem. Ezechieli quoque Dominus dixit : Non eris quasi vir objurgans, quia domus exasperans est.
paras.en: [[23:9|Speak not|ne loquaris]] [[23:9|in the ears of fools|In auribus insipientium]], whom thou knowest or findest to be incorrigible, by teaching or rebuking them; [[23:9|because they will despise the instruction of thy speech|quia despicient doctrinam eloquii tui]], and so they are not amended but made worse. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:6|Give not that which is holy to dogs|Nolite sanctum dare canibus]]. And we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 32:6|Where there is no hearing, pour not out words|Ubi non est auditus, non effundas sermonem]] [the margin gives Eccli. xxii, 6; the words are Ecclus 32:6]. To Ezechiel too the Lord said: [[Ezech 3:26|not as a man that reproveth: because they are a provoking house|Non eris quasi vir objurgans, quia domus exasperans est]].

paras.t: Ne attingas terminos parvulorum, id est, nihil de terra et possessione illorum invadas, aut subtrahas eis; et agrum pupillorum ne introeas ad vastandum. Propinquus enim eorum, scilicet judex terrenus, ejusdem cum illis naturæ exsistens, vel potius Deus omnipotens, pater spirituum, et specialis miserabilium personarum patronus (cui fertur in Psalmo, Orphano tu eris adjutor; et rursus, Pupillum et viduam suscipiet; itemque, Custodiens parvulos Dominus), fortis est, et ipse judicabit contra te causam illorum, id est, causam illorum justam ostendet, et tuam injustitiam vindicabit : juxta illud, Facit judicium pupillo et viduæ.
paras.en: [[23:10|Touch not the bounds of little ones|Ne attingas terminos parvulorum]], that is, seize nothing of their land and possession, nor take it from them; [[23:10|and enter not into the field of the fatherless|et agrum pupillorum ne introeas]] to lay it waste. [[23:11|For their near kinsman|Propinquus enim eorum]], namely the earthly judge, who is of the same nature as they, or rather God almighty, the Father of spirits[[Heb 12:9||]], and the special patron of persons in misery (to whom it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 9:35|thou wilt be a helper to the orphan|Orphano tu eris adjutor]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 14, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate this is Ps 9:35]; and again: [[Ps 145:9|he will support the fatherless and the widow|Pupillum et viduam suscipiet]]; and likewise: [[Ps 114:6|The Lord is the keeper of little ones|Custodiens parvulos Dominus]]), [[23:11|is strong: and he will judge their cause against thee|fortis est, et ipse judicabit contra te causam illorum]], that is, he will show their cause to be just, and will punish thy injustice: according to the words: [[Deut 10:18|He doth judgment to the fatherless and the widow|Facit judicium pupillo et viduæ]].

paras.t: Ingrediatur ad doctrinam cor tuum, et aures tuæ ad verba scientiæ : id est, ad audiendum doctrinalia et salubria verba accede.
paras.en: [[23:12|Let thy heart apply itself to instruction and thy ears to words of knowledge.|Ingrediatur ad doctrinam cor tuum, et aures tuæ ad verba scientiæ]]: that is, draw near to hear words of teaching and of salvation.

paras.t: Noli subtrahere a puero, id est a filio tuo carnali adhuc juveniculo, vel a subdito indisciplinato ac puero sensibus, disciplinam, id est correctionem. Si enim percusseris eum virga corporali aut spirituali, non morietur, nisi percussio esset prorsus immoderata. Tu virga percuties eum, et animam ejus de inferno liberabis, id est de vitiis et erroribus, quos incideret nisi eum disciplinares, et per quos tandem corrueret in gehennam.
paras.en: [[23:13|Withhold not|Noli subtrahere]] [[23:13|from a child|a puero]], that is, from thy son after the flesh while he is still a youngster, or from a subject who is undisciplined and a child in understanding, [[23:13|correction|disciplinam]], that is, chastisement. [[23:13|for if thou strike him with the rod|Si enim percusseris eum virga]], bodily or spiritual, [[23:13|he shall not die|non morietur]], unless the beating were altogether immoderate. [[23:14|Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and deliver his soul from hell.|Tu virga percuties eum, et animam ejus de inferno liberabis]], that is, from the vices and errors into which he would fall unless thou didst discipline him, and through which he would at last plunge headlong into hell.

paras.t: Fili mi, si sapiens fuerit animus, id est spiritus seu intellectus tuus, gaudebit tecum, id est, congratulabitur tibi, cor meum ex caritate qua diligo te, et exsultabunt renes mei, id est, interior lætitia cordis mei redundabit in corpus, et sensitivus etiam appetitus lætabitur, quum locuta fuerint rectum, id est justum et prudentem sermonem, labia tua.
paras.en: [[23:15|My son, if thy mind be wise|Fili mi, si sapiens fuerit animus]], that is, thy spirit or understanding, [[23:15|shall rejoice with thee|gaudebit tecum]], that is, shall share thy joy, [[23:15|my heart|cor meum]], out of the charity with which I love thee; [[23:16|And my reins shall rejoice|et exsultabunt renes mei]], that is, the inward gladness of my heart shall overflow into the body, and the sense appetite too shall be glad, [[23:16|when thy lips shall speak what is right|quum locuta fuerint rectum]], that is, a just and prudent word.

paras.t: Non æmuletur cor tuum peccatores, id est, eos non imitetur in vitiis, nec odiat eos, in quantum sunt homines ac viatores, pœnitentiæ et salutis capaces; sed in timore Domini filiali esto tota die, id est assidue et omni tempore gratiæ Christi. De qua die ait Apostolus : Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit; et rursus, Nos qui diei sumus, sobrii simus. Quia habebis spem efficacem in novissimo, id est in fine vitæ præsentis, et præstolatio tua non auferetur, id est, exspectatio qua beatitudinem præstolaris, non privabitur suo effectu.
paras.en: [[23:17|Let not thy heart envy sinners|Non æmuletur cor tuum peccatores]], that is, let it not imitate them in their vices, nor hate them, in so far as they are men and wayfarers, capable of penance and salvation; [[23:17|but be thou in the fear of the Lord|sed in timore Domini]], a filial fear, [[23:17|all the day long|esto tota die]], that is, constantly and through the whole time of the grace of Christ. Of which day the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:12|The night is passed And the day is at hand|Nox præcessit, dies autem appropinquavit]]; and again: [[1 Thess 5:8|let us, who are of the day, be sober|Nos qui diei sumus, sobrii simus]]. [[23:18|Because thou shalt have hope|Quia habebis spem]] that is effectual [[23:18|in the latter end|in novissimo]], that is, at the end of the present life, [[23:18|and thy expectation shall not be taken away|et præstolatio tua non auferetur]], that is, the expectation with which thou awaitest beatitude shall not be deprived of its fulfilment.

paras.t: Audi, fili mi, et esto sapiens, et dirige in viam gratiæ ac salutis oculos tuos interiores, scilicet ad considerandum divina præcepta, juxta illud : Dirige cor tuum in viam directam.
paras.en: [[23:19|Hear thou, my son, and be wise|Audi, fili mi, et esto sapiens]], [[23:19|and guide|et dirige]] [[23:19|in the way|in viam]] of grace and salvation thy inward eyes [Denis reads *oculos tuos*, "thy eyes", where the Vulgate has *animum tuum*, "thy mind"], namely to consider the divine precepts, according to the words: [[Jer 31:21|direct thy heart into the right way|Dirige cor tuum in viam directam]].

paras.t: Noli esse in conviviis potatorum, nec in comessationibus eorum qui carnes ad vescendum conferunt : quia vacantes potibus, et dantes symbola, id est collationem pecuniæ in prædictis, consumentur : quia corpus et animam destruunt, vitam abbreviant, depauperantur et condemnantur; et vestietur pannis dormitatio : id est, dormitio mortis eorum erit despecta, seu ipse qui talis est, viliter operietur in morte. Vel sensus est, quod ad tantam deveniet paupertatem, ut dormiendo non habeat sufficiens, sed tenue operimentum.
paras.en: [[23:20|Be not in the feasts of great drinkers, nor in their revellings, who contribute flesh to eat:|Noli esse in conviviis potatorum, nec in comessationibus eorum qui carnes ad vescendum conferunt]]: [[23:21|Because they that give themselves to drinking, and that club together|quia vacantes potibus, et dantes symbola]], that is, a pooling of money for the things just named [*symbola*, a share or contribution towards a common meal], [[23:21|shall be consumed|consumentur]]: for they destroy body and soul, shorten their life, are impoverished and condemned; [[23:21|and drowsiness shall be clothed with rags|et vestietur pannis dormitatio]]: that is, their sleep of death will be despised, or he who is such will be meanly covered in death. Or the sense is that he will come to such poverty that in sleeping he will have no sufficient covering, but only a thin one.

paras.t: Audi in rebus licitis patrem tuum qui genuit te, et ne contemnas, quum senuerit mater tua. Imo in senectute et necessitate debes eis magis caritative ac pie adsistere, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico legitur : Fili, suscipe senectam patris tui, et non contristes eum in vita illius.
paras.en: [[23:22|Hearken to|Audi]] in lawful things [[23:22|thy father, that begot thee|patrem tuum qui genuit te]]: [[23:22|and despise not thy mother when she is old|et ne contemnas, quum senuerit mater tua]]. Nay, in their old age and need thou oughtest to stand by them all the more charitably and dutifully, as we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:14|Son, support the old age of thy father, and grieve him not in his life|Fili, suscipe senectam patris tui, et non contristes eum in vita illius]].

paras.t: Veritatem eme : non dando directe pro ea pecuniam, aut aliquod temporale tanquam pretium rei; sed emenda est a Deo, oratione et opere virtuoso, et a doctoribus, seu ex libris, studio et labore. Et sicut dantur temporalia, ut oretur pro dantibus, non pro oratione, sed ut orantes inclinentur ex beneficio corporali ad recompensandum in spiritualibus; sic potest temporale dari magistro, ut provocetur ad laborandum pro informatione discipuli. De hujusmodi emptione scriptum est in Isaia : Emite absque argento, et absque ulla commutatione. Et alibi dicitur : Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum probatum, id est caritatem. Et noli vendere sapientiam, quæ est notitia divinorum, et doctrinam, moralium, et intelligentiam speculabilium : quæ non sunt sub pretio corporalium rerum ponendæ; nihilo minus docens potest accipere pro suo labore sustentaculum vitæ.
paras.en: [[23:23|Buy truth|Veritatem eme]]: not by giving money directly for it, or any temporal thing as the price of the thing; but it is to be bought from God by prayer and virtuous work, and from teachers or from books by study and labour. And just as temporal things are given so that prayer may be made for the givers, not in payment for the prayer, but so that those who pray may be inclined by the bodily benefit to make a return in spiritual things, so a temporal thing may be given to a master to stir him to labour for the instruction of his pupil [that is, without the sin of simony, the buying of spiritual things for a price]. Of buying of this kind it is written in Isaias: [[Is 55:1|come ye, buy|Emite]] [[Is 55:1|without money, and without any price|absque argento, et absque ulla commutatione]]. And it is said elsewhere: [[Apoc 3:18|I counsel thee to buy|Suadeo tibi emere]] [[Apoc 3:18|gold, fire tried|aurum ignitum probatum]], that is, charity. [[23:23|and do not sell wisdom|Et noli vendere sapientiam]], which is the knowledge of divine things, [[23:23|and instruction|et doctrinam]], of moral things, [[23:23|and understanding|et intelligentiam]], of speculative things: which are not to be set at the price of bodily things; none the less one who teaches may receive for his labour the support of life.

paras.t: Exsultat gaudio pater justi, id est pater ejus carnalis, seu spiritualis, si tamen sit bonus et spiritualiter amans : nam quidam sunt ita perversi, quod de spirituali et virtuosa filiorum suorum conversatione tristantur. Qui sapientem genuit, lætabitur in eo.
paras.en: [[23:24|The father of the just rejoiceth greatly|Exsultat gaudio pater justi]], that is, his father after the flesh or in the spirit, provided he be good and love in a spiritual way: for some are so perverse that they are saddened by the spiritual and virtuous life of their children. [[23:24|he that hath begotten a wise son, shall have joy in him|Qui sapientem genuit, lætabitur in eo]].

paras.t: Gaudeat pater tuus et mater tua, et exsultet quæ genuit te : id est, tam sapienter et virtuose te habe, ut merito de te glorientur carnales ac spirituales tui parentes.
paras.en: [[23:25|Let thy father and thy mother be joyful, and let her rejoice that bore thee.|Gaudeat pater tuus et mater tua, et exsultet quæ genuit te]]: that is, bear thyself so wisely and virtuously that thy parents, after the flesh and in the spirit, may rightly glory in thee.

paras.t: Præbe, fili mi, cor tuum mihi, ut instruatur a me ad vitandum vitia carnis, et oculi tui vias meas custodiant.
paras.en: [[23:26|My son, give me thy heart|Præbe, fili mi, cor tuum mihi]], that it may be instructed by me to shun the vices of the flesh, [[23:26|and let thy eyes keep my ways|et oculi tui vias meas custodiant]].

paras.t: Fovea enim profunda est meretrix, quoniam trahit in voraginem vitiorum, et puteus angustus, aliena, id est adultera : quia sicut in puteo arcto cadens, ita demergitur ut vix extrahi queat; ita qui in adulterium labitur, difficulter curatur. Unde apud Job inducitur : Si ad ostium amici mei insidiatus sum, scortum sit alteri uxor mea : hoc enim nefas est et iniquitas maxima, ignis est usque ad perditionem devorans.
paras.en: [[23:27|For a harlot is a deep ditch|Fovea enim profunda est meretrix]], since she drags into the whirlpool of vices, [[23:27|and a strange woman is a narrow pit|et puteus angustus, aliena]], that is, an adulteress: for as one who falls into a narrow well sinks so deep that he can hardly be drawn out, so he who slips into adultery is hard to heal. Hence it is brought in in Job: [[Job 31:9|if I have laid wait at my friend's door|Si ad ostium amici mei insidiatus sum]], [[Job 31:10|Let my wife be the harlot of another|scortum sit alteri uxor mea]]: [[Job 31:11|For this is a heinous crime, and a most grievous iniquity|hoc enim nefas est et iniquitas maxima]], [[Job 31:12|It is a fire that devoureth even to destruction|ignis est usque ad perditionem devorans]].
