paras.t: Insidiatur in via quasi latro : nam sicut latro vult corpus occidere, et occisi bona diripere; sic fornicaria et adultera quærit occidere animam, ac per hoc spiritualia gratiæ dona ac merita ei auferre; et quos incautos viderit, id est faciliter deceptibiles, qui pericula vitiorum non pensant, nec vitant prudenter, interficiet morte culpæ, trahendo eos ad concupiscendum ac commiscendum.
paras.en: [[23:28|She lieth in wait in the way as a robber|Insidiatur in via quasi latro]]: for as a robber wishes to kill the body and plunder the goods of the man he has killed, so the fornicating and adulterous woman seeks to kill the soul, and thereby to take from it the spiritual gifts of grace and its merits; [[23:28|and him whom she shall see unwary|et quos incautos viderit]], that is, easily deceived, who do not weigh the dangers of the vices nor prudently shun them, [[23:28|she will kill|interficiet]] with the death of sin, by drawing them to lust and to intercourse.

paras.t: Cui væ æternæ damnationis et præsentis afflictionis? Cujus patri væ tristitiæ et doloris? Cui rixæ? cui foveæ? cui sine causa vulnera? cui suffusio, id est debilitatio et quædam lacrimatio oculorum? Nonne his qui commorantur in vino, et student calicibus epotandis? id est, omnia mala hæc imminent et contingunt vinolentis : qui et parentes suos sæpe contristant, et rixari, pugnare, vulnerari solent in locis potationum suarum : propter quod incarcerantur : et ambulando cadere solent ex cerebri perturbatione propter ascendentes fumositates ad caput : quorum et visus obscuratur, et oculi humore defluente quasi lacrimis humectantur.
paras.en: [[23:29|Who hath woe?|Cui væ]] of eternal damnation and of present affliction? [[23:29|whose father hath woe?|Cujus patri væ]] of sadness and sorrow? [[23:29|who hath contentions?|Cui rixæ?]] [[23:29|who falls into pits?|cui foveæ?]] [[23:29|who hath wounds without cause?|cui sine causa vulnera?]] [[23:29|who hath redness|cui suffusio]], that is, a weakening and a kind of watering, [[23:29|of eyes|oculorum]]? [[23:30|Surely they that pass their time in wine, and study to drink off their cups|Nonne his qui commorantur in vino, et student calicibus epotandis?]]? That is, all these evils hang over and befall drunkards: who both often grieve their parents, and are wont to quarrel, fight and be wounded in the places of their drinking; for which they are put in prison [the "pits" of the verse]; and in walking they are wont to fall, from the disturbance of the brain caused by the fumes rising to the head; and their sight is darkened, and their eyes are wet with a running humour as if with tears.

paras.t: Ne intuearis vinum, quando flavescit, id est, flavum et quasi aureum quemdam colorem ostendit in se, quum splenduerit in vitro color ejus : id est, ex carnali affectu non facias hoc, ne provoceris ad potum illicitum; tamen ad cognoscendum vini valorem, justumque pretium, poterit ita videri. Ingreditur blande, quia dulciter sapit; sed in novissimo, id est, antequam consumatur in corpore, mordebit ut coluber, id est, calefactiones pœnales, puncturas et multas incommoditates causabit in homine vinolento; et sicut regulus, qui est pessimus serpens, venena diffundet : quia non solum corpus sic læsit, sed animam quoque ad concupiscentias, et vitia eas sequentia, incitat. Hinc in Ecclesiastico habetur : Vigilia et cholera et tortura viro infrunito. Vinum multum potatum, irritationem, iram et ruinas multas facit.
paras.en: [[23:31|Look not upon the wine when it is yellow|Ne intuearis vinum, quando flavescit]], that is, when it shows in itself a yellow and as it were golden colour, [[23:31|when the colour thereof shineth in the glass|quum splenduerit in vitro color ejus]]: that is, do not do this out of fleshly desire, lest thou be provoked to unlawful drinking; yet it may be looked at so in order to know the worth of the wine and its just price. [[23:31|it goeth in pleasantly|Ingreditur blande]], because it tastes sweet; [[23:32|But in the end|sed in novissimo]], that is, before it is used up in the body, [[23:32|it will bite like a snake|mordebit ut coluber]], that is, it will cause painful heats, prickings and many discomforts in the drunken man; and [[23:32|like a basilisk|sicut regulus]], which is the worst of serpents, [[23:32|will spread abroad poison|venena diffundet]]: for not only has it harmed the body thus, but it also stirs up the soul to lusts and to the vices that follow them. Hence we have in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:23|Watching, and choler, and gripes, are with an intemperate man|Vigilia et cholera et tortura viro infrunito]]. [[Ecclus 31:38|Wine drunken with excess raiseth quarrels, and wrath, and many ruins|Vinum multum potatum, irritationem, iram et ruinas multas facit]] [the margin gives no reference here].

paras.t: Oculi tui, quum fueris vino ingurgitatus, videbunt extraneas, id est feminas tibi legitime non unitas, ad peccandum cum eis, et cor tuum loquetur, id est, intra se cogitabit et ore proferet, perversa, id est verba lasciva, procatoria, vitiosa : et eris sicut dormiens in medio mari. Nam sicut qui dormit in mari, periculis multis exponitur, fluctibusque marinis jactatur : sic vino repletus, in somnum cito resolvitur, et humoribus intus exæstuat, ac variis inquietudinibus agitatur; imo periculosissime stat, quantum ad animam. Et quasi sopitus gubernator, amisso clavo. Nam sicut gubernator dormiens, et clavum quo gubernaculum regitur, perdens, negligit ac mergi permittit navem; sic talis vinolentus corpus suum non regit per rationis judicium. Unde Plato dixit, animam se habere ad corpus sicut nauta ad navem.
paras.en: [[23:33|Thy eyes|Oculi tui]], when thou hast been gorged with wine, [[23:33|shall behold strange women|videbunt extraneas]], that is, women not lawfully joined to thee, so as to sin with them, [[23:33|and thy heart shall utter|et cor tuum loquetur]], that is, shall think within itself and bring forth with the mouth, [[23:33|perverse things|perversa]], that is, wanton, wooing, sinful words: [[23:34|And thou shalt be as one sleeping in the midst of the sea|et eris sicut dormiens in medio mari]]. For as one who sleeps at sea is exposed to many dangers and tossed by the waves of the sea, so one full of wine quickly sinks into sleep, and boils within with humours, and is shaken by various disquiets; nay, as regards the soul he stands in the greatest danger. [[23:34|and as a pilot fast asleep when the stern is lost|Et quasi sopitus gubernator, amisso clavo]] [*clavus*, the tiller or helm, which Denis explains as that by which the rudder is steered]. For as a pilot who sleeps and loses the tiller by which the rudder is steered neglects the ship and lets it sink, so such a drunkard does not rule his body by the judgment of reason. Hence Plato said that the soul stands to the body as a sailor to a ship.

paras.t: Et dices, ad mentem aliqualiter rediens post vitia gulæ atque luxuriæ : Verberaverunt me : id est, pravæ affectiones, seu dæmones, ad præfata peccata me instigaverunt, ex quibus multas afflictiones incurri; et non dolui : id est, passionibus, voluptatibus et vitiis excæcatus, non percepi neque deflevi læsiones præteritas corporis ac animæ meæ. Traxerunt me de uno peccato ac tormento in aliud, et non sensi : ex causa præhabita. Sic et Jeremias asserit : Percussisti eos, et non doluerunt. Et alius Propheta dicit : Comederunt alieni robur ejus, et ipse ignoravit. Attamen ista dices, non ex vera et stabili contritione, sed ex lumine rationis, seu fide informi, vel ex ipsa experientia incommodorum tuorum inductus. Idcirco subjungitur : Quando evigilabo, id est, ad pristinam vigoris mei habitudinem redibo, et rursus vina reperiam ad potandum solito more? Qui enim vitiosa consuetudine gulæ et immunditiæ sunt infecti, quamvis ad horam sua advertunt incommoda, pericula et peccata, mox tamen concupiscentiis inflammati redeunt ad vitia consueta.
paras.en: [[23:35|And thou shalt say|Et dices]], coming somewhat to thy senses after the vices of gluttony and lust: [[23:35|They have beaten me|Verberaverunt me]]: that is, evil affections, or demons, have urged me on to the sins named above, from which I have incurred many afflictions; [[23:35|but I was not sensible of pain|et non dolui]] [the margin gives the reading *sed*, "but", for *et*]: that is, blinded by passions, pleasures and vices, I did not perceive or bewail the past injuries of my body and soul. [[23:35|they drew me|Traxerunt me]] from one sin and torment into another, [[23:35|and I felt not|et non sensi]]: for the reason already given. So too Jeremias declares: [[Jer 5:3|thou hast struck them, and they have not grieved|Percussisti eos, et non doluerunt]]. And another Prophet says: [[Osee 7:9|Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knew it not|Comederunt alieni robur ejus, et ipse ignoravit]]. Yet thou wilt say these things not out of true and steadfast contrition, but led by the light of reason, or by unformed faith [that is, faith without charity], or by the very experience of thy troubles. Therefore it is added: [[23:35|when shall I awake|Quando evigilabo]], that is, return to the former condition of my vigour, [[23:35|and find wine again|et rursus vina reperiam]] to drink in my usual way? For those who are infected by a sinful habit of gluttony and uncleanness, though for the moment they notice their troubles, dangers and sins, yet soon, inflamed by their lusts, go back to their accustomed vices.

paras.t: Ecce hic docuit Salomon, quanta mala pœnæ et culpæ ex vinolentia oriantur, et quam detestanda sint gulæ atque luxuriæ inquinamenta. Fugienda sunt ergo hæc scelera, in quibus brutale ac turpissimum est jacere. Ideo ait Ambrosius : Ebriosus quum vinum absorbet, absorbetur a vino, abominatur a Deo, despicitur ab angelis, et ab hominibus irridetur, virtutibus spoliatur, a dæmonibus conculcatur. Econtra de sobrietate loquitur Augustinus : Sobrietas temeritatem fugit et fugat, pericula cuncta declinat, mutuis officiis obtemperat, superbiam detestatur, domum atque familiam cum moderatione gubernat. Et rursus : Sobrietas, inquit, est mentis et sensus membrorumque omnium cautela, castitatis ac pudicitiæ munimentum, pudori proxima, amicitiæ ac pacis conservativa, honestati semper conjuncta, vitiorumque omnium profuga.
paras.en: See here how Solomon has taught what great evils of punishment and of guilt arise from drunkenness, and how detestable are the defilements of gluttony and lust. These crimes, then, are to be fled, in which it is brutish and most shameful to lie. Therefore Ambrose says: The drunkard, while he swallows wine, is swallowed by wine; he is abhorred by God, despised by the angels and mocked by men, stripped of the virtues, trampled on by the demons. On the other hand Augustine speaks of sobriety: Sobriety flees and puts to flight rashness, turns aside from all dangers, complies with mutual duties, detests pride, governs house and household with moderation. And again: Sobriety, he says, is the safeguard of the mind and the senses and of all the members, the bulwark of chastity and modesty, the neighbour of shamefastness, the keeper of friendship and peace, ever joined to honesty, and the fugitive from all vices.

24.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI VICESIMI QUARTI : NE ÆMULERIS VIROS MALOS, NEC DESIDERES ESSE CUM EIS.
24.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-fourth chapter: Be not emulous of evil men, neither desire to be with them.

paras.t: Ne æmuleris, id est, nec mente nec corpore sequaris, viros malos, gulæ atque luxuriæ deditos: de quibus præcedenti capitulo facta est mentio; nec desideres esse cum eis: quia rapinas meditatur mens eorum, id est, bona aliorum cupiunt rapiendo acquirere, quum dissipaverint substantiam suam gulose et immunde vivendo. Qui autem furatur aut rapit ut gulæ aut luxuriæ vacet, magis dicendus est gulosus aut luxuriosus, quam raptor aut fur, ut ait Philosophus. A fine enim denominatio sumitur. Atque, ut ait Ambrosius, intentio imprimit speciem operi. Et fraudes, id est verba dolosa, labia eorum loquuntur, ut dolo acquirant, quæ per rapinam acquirere nequeunt.
paras.en: [[24:1|Seek not to be like|Ne æmuleris]], that is, follow neither in mind nor in body, [[24:1|evil men|viros malos]], given to gluttony and lust, of whom mention was made in the preceding chapter[[Prov 23:20||]][[Prov 23:27||]] [the margin gives Prov. xxiii, 20, 27–30]; [[24:1|neither desire to be with them|nec desideres esse cum eis]]: [[24:2|Because their mind studieth robberies|quia rapinas meditatur mens eorum]], that is, they long to get the goods of others by robbery, since they have squandered their own substance by living gluttonously and impurely. But he who steals or robs so as to give himself to gluttony or lust is rather to be called a glutton or a lecher than a robber or a thief, as the Philosopher says; for a thing takes its name from its end. And, as Ambrose says, the intention stamps its species on the work. And [[24:2|deceits|Et fraudes]], that is, deceitful words, [[24:2|their lips speak|labia eorum loquuntur]], so that they may get by guile what they cannot get by robbery.

paras.t: Sapientia ædificabitur domus, et prudentia roborabitur. Per sapientiam ædificata est Ecclesia, et discretione boni regiminis roborata. Similiter per sapientiam ædificatur quæcumque congregatio, familia, cognatio ac politia. Per sapientiam enim instituitur ad bene vivendum, ad credendum, ad proficiendum: in quibus omnibus per prudentiam roboratur. Unde Apostolus: Ut sapiens (inquit) architectus, fundamentum posui. Sed et domus materialis, per sapientiam seu prudentiam est ædificanda, sicut in Evangelio ait Salvator: Quis ex vobis volens turrim ædificare, non prius sedens computat sumptus qui necessarii sunt? Domus quoque conscientiæ, et habitaculum cordis, juxta Christi doctrinam, id est per evangelicæ legis sapientiam atque prudentiam, sunt ædificanda ac roboranda. Propter quod loquitur Veritas: Omnis qui audit verba mea hæc, et facit ea, assimilabitur viro sapienti, qui ædificavit domum suam supra petram.
paras.en: [[24:3|By wisdom the house shall be built, and by prudence it shall be strengthened.|Sapientia ædificabitur domus, et prudentia roborabitur.]] By wisdom the Church was built, and strengthened by the discretion of good government. Likewise by wisdom every community, household, kindred and commonwealth is built; for by wisdom it is set in order for living well, for believing and for making progress, and in all these it is strengthened by prudence. Hence the Apostle: [[1 Cor 3:10|as a wise|Ut sapiens]] (he says) [[1 Cor 3:10|architect, I have laid the foundation|architectus, fundamentum posui]]. But a material house too is to be built by wisdom or prudence, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 14:28|which of you, having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down and reckon the charges that are necessary|Quis ex vobis volens turrim ædificare, non prius sedens computat sumptus qui necessarii sunt?]]? The house of the conscience also, and the dwelling of the heart, are to be built and strengthened according to Christ's teaching, that is, by the wisdom and prudence of the law of the Gospel. For which reason the Truth says: [[Matt 7:24|Every one therefore that heareth these my words, and doth them, shall be likened to a wise man that built his house upon a rock|Omnis qui audit verba mea hæc, et facit ea, assimilabitur viro sapienti, qui ædificavit domum suam supra petram]].

paras.t: In doctrina, id est per doctrinam observantiamque legis divinæ, replebuntur cellaria, id est corda fidelium, per gratiarum charismata, sublimata et elevata a terra, universa substantia pretiosa et pulcherrima, id est cunctis spiritualibus ac internis divitiis, in quibus est maximus decor et splendor. Scriptura etenim docet omnem virtutum perfectionem, et lex Christi dat gratiam pertingendi ad eam. Hinc Corinthiis scribit Apostolus: In omnibus divites facti estis in illo, in omni verbo et in omni scientia. Alibi quoque ait Scriptura: Replebimur in bonis domus tuæ; et, Nihil deest timentibus Deum. Denique in veteri Testamento per observantiam legis dabatur Judæis opulentia prosperitasque terrena, ut patet in David, Salomone ad tempus, Asa, Josaphat, Ezechia. Unde de Josaphat fertur in secundo libro Paralipomenon: Factæ sunt ei infinitæ divitiæ.
paras.en: [[24:4|By instruction|In doctrina]], that is, through the teaching and the keeping of the divine law, [[24:4|the storerooms shall be filled|replebuntur cellaria]], that is, the hearts of the faithful, raised and lifted up from the earth by the gifts of the graces, [[24:4|with all precious and most beautiful wealth|universa substantia pretiosa et pulcherrima]], that is, with all spiritual and inward riches, in which there is the greatest beauty and splendour. For Scripture teaches all the perfection of the virtues, and the law of Christ gives the grace to attain to it. Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 1:5|in all things you are made rich in him, in all utterance and in all knowledge|In omnibus divites facti estis in illo, in omni verbo et in omni scientia]]. Elsewhere too Scripture says: [[Ps 64:5|We shall be filled with the good things of thy house|Replebimur in bonis domus tuæ]]; and, [[Ps 33:10|there is no want to them that fear him|Nihil deest timentibus Deum]] [Denis's wording, *Nihil deest timentibus Deum*, "nothing is wanting to them that fear God", is freer than the Vulgate's]. Lastly, in the Old Testament earthly wealth and prosperity were given to the Jews for keeping the law, as is plain in David[[2 Kings 23:5||]], in Solomon for a time[[3 Kings 3:13||]][[3 Kings 4:1||]][[3 Kings 10:1||]], in Asa[[2 Par 14:6||]], Josaphat[[2 Par 17:5||]][[2 Par 17:10||]][[2 Par 18:1||]][[2 Par 20:30||]] and Ezechias[[2 Par 32:27||]]. Hence it is said of Josaphat in the second book of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 17:5|he acquired immense riches|Factæ sunt ei infinitæ divitiæ]].

paras.t: Vir sapiens fortis est, ad minus in anima, cujus præcipua fortitudo est sapientia, maxime illa quæ est donum. Propter quod scriptum est: Omnium potentior est sapientia. Facit enim mentem Deo firmiter inhærere, contemplari divina, et per internum summi boni saporem, aspernari carnalia: sicque contra invisibilium hostium pugnas roborat sapientem. Et vir doctus, præsertim qui unctus est desuper, et quem unctio docet de omnibus (de quo ait Psalmista, Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum), est robustus intellectu, contra perfidiam et errores, et validus voluntate, per caritatem, quæ tali unctioni et illuminationi semper conjuncta est. Sunt autem nonnulli, quos scientia inflat, et qui solum acquisitam habent sapientiam et doctrinam, seu eam quæ est donum gratiæ gratis datæ; qui infirmi sunt corde, tentationibusque vincuntur, et vitiorum sunt servi. Quibus dicit Propheta: Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te. Et Christus ait Patri: Abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus.
paras.en: [[24:5|A wise man is strong|Vir sapiens fortis est]], at least in soul, whose chief strength is wisdom, above all the wisdom that is a gift [that is, wisdom as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost]. For which reason it is written: [[Wis 10:12|wisdom is mightier than all|Omnium potentior est sapientia]]. For it makes the mind cleave firmly to God and contemplate divine things, and, through the inward savour of the highest good, despise the things of the flesh; and so it strengthens the wise man against the assaults of invisible enemies. [[24:5|and a knowing man|Et vir doctus]], especially one who is anointed from above and whom the unction teaches of all things[[1 John 2:27||]] (of whom the Psalmist says, [[Ps 93:12|Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord: and shalt teach him out of thy law|Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum]]), is [[24:5|stout|robustus]] in understanding, against faithlessness and errors, [[24:5|and valiant|et validus]] in will, through charity, which is always joined to such an unction and enlightenment. But there are some whom knowledge puffs up[[1 Cor 8:1||]], and who have only acquired wisdom and learning, or that which is a gift of grace freely given [*gratia gratis data*: a grace given for the good of others, such as prophecy or the word of wisdom, which does not of itself make its bearer holy]; who are weak of heart, are overcome by temptations, and are slaves of vices. To these the Prophet says: [[Is 47:10|Thy wisdom, and, thy knowledge, this hath deceived thee|Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te]]. And Christ says to the Father: [[Matt 11:25|thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent|Abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus]].

paras.t: Quia cum dispositione, id est provida præparatione et congrua ordinatione, initur bellum, id est, ineundum ac committendum est prælium, tam contra invisibiles quam contra visibiles hostes. Et in utroque multitudo ac persona improvida, inordinata, impræparata, non est nisi hostium victima; sicque in bello utroque, plus valent sapientia et doctrina quam fortitudo corporea. Ideo scriptum est: Melior est sapientia quam vires; et vir prudens, quam fortis. Denique, si quis perpessus sit vulnera, damna, seu quæcumque adversa, multum valet sapientia et doctrina ad consolandum eumdem, et ad patientiam amplectendam. Unde et ait Philosophus, quod homo contemplativus seu sapiens, plenus est jucundis theorematibus, id est sapientialibus considerationibus, per quas potest se consolari, nec extra se in rebus fœdis ac vilibus expetit delectari aut consolari. Et erit salus ubi multa consilia sunt: quia per inquisitionem consiliarem vitantur pericula. Istud superius diffuse expositum est.
paras.en: [[24:6|Because|Quia]] [[24:6|by due ordering|cum dispositione]], that is, with provident preparation and fitting arrangement, [[24:6|war is managed|initur bellum]], that is, battle is to be entered on and joined, against invisible as much as against visible enemies. And in either, a multitude or a person that is improvident, disordered and unprepared is nothing but a victim for the enemy; and so in both kinds of war wisdom and learning avail more than bodily strength. Therefore it is written: [[Wis 6:1|Wisdom is better than strength: and a wise man is better than a strong man.|Melior est sapientia quam vires; et vir prudens, quam fortis]] Lastly, if anyone has suffered wounds, losses, or any adversity whatever, wisdom and learning avail much to console him and to make him embrace patience. Hence the Philosopher too says that the contemplative or wise man is full of delightful *theoremata*, that is, considerations of wisdom, by which he can console himself, and does not seek delight or consolation outside himself in foul and vile things. [[24:6|and there shall be safety where there are many counsels|Et erit salus ubi multa consilia sunt]]: for by seeking counsel dangers are avoided. This was expounded at length above[[Prov 2:11||]][[Prov 11:14||]][[Prov 13:16||]].

paras.t: Excelsa stulto sapientia, id est, in alto sita est, seu qualitas valde præclara: sicque stultus nequit eam attingere. Si tamen exemplo Zachæi, ascendat in arborem sycomorum, id est, humilitatem crucis Christi intueatur et amplexetur, sapientiam veram attinget, sicut præhabitum est: Ubi humilitas, ibi et sapientia. In porta non aperiet os suum, id est, in foro judicii (quod in portis fieri consuevit, juxta illud Prophetæ, Constituite in porta judicium) non poterit rationabiliter respondere. In porta quoque, id est in exitu ab hac vita, præsentatus summo Judici, obmutescet.
paras.en: [[24:7|Wisdom is too high for a fool|Excelsa stulto sapientia]], that is, it is set on high, or is a very excellent quality, and so the fool cannot reach it. Yet if, after the example of Zacheus, he climbs up into the sycamore tree[[Luke 19:4||]], that is, looks upon and embraces the humility of the cross of Christ, he will reach true wisdom, as was said before: [[Prov 11:2|where humility is, there also is wisdom|Ubi humilitas, ibi et sapientia]]. [[24:7|in the gate he shall not open his mouth|In porta non aperiet os suum]], that is, in the court of judgment (which used to be held in the gates, according to that of the Prophet, [[Amos 5:15|establish judgment in the gate|Constituite in porta judicium]]) he will not be able to answer reasonably. In the gate too, that is, at the going out from this life, when he is set before the supreme Judge, he will be struck dumb.

paras.t: Sed quia in verbis proverbiorum istorum Salomon sæpissime utitur nomine stulti, ne quis nomine stulti intelligendos putet eos dumtaxat, qui ex indispositione sensuum interiorum aut cerebri, ratione nequeunt uti, subjungit quem nominet stultum. Qui cogitat mala facere cum consensu, id est, quicumque proponit transgredi Dei præceptum, stultus vocabitur: quia revera stultus est valde, quum occidat animam suam, et Creatori suo rebellis sit et ingratus, ac summo bono et donis gratiæ privet se, pessimo quoque hosti suo consentiat, vitiis ac dæmonibus obsequatur, atque æternæ damnationis se exponat periculis.
paras.en: But since in the words of these proverbs Solomon very often uses the name of *fool*, lest anyone should think that by that name are to be understood only those who cannot use their reason through some disorder of the inner senses or of the brain, he adds whom he calls a fool. [[24:8|He that deviseth to do evils|Qui cogitat mala facere]] with consent, that is, whoever purposes to transgress the commandment of God, [[24:8|shall be called a fool|stultus vocabitur]]: for he is truly very foolish, since he slays his own soul, is rebellious and ungrateful to his Creator, deprives himself of the highest good and of the gifts of grace, consents to his worst enemy, obeys vices and demons, and exposes himself to the dangers of eternal damnation.

paras.t: Cogitatio stulti, qua cum consensu cogitat facere malum, aut omittere debitum bonum, peccatum est; et abominatio hominum, detractor, id est, abominabilis est hominibus oblocutor, peccans contra legem naturalem, faciendo proximis quod non vult fieri sibi, et contra legem divinam, hoc detestabile vitium multoties prohibentem. Hinc ait Bernardus: Non veniat anima mea in consilio detractorum, quoniam Deus odit eos. Nec mirum, quoniam vitium istud caritatem (quæ Deus est) acrius persequi et impugnare cognoscitur. Et ipse qui detrahit, primo prodit se ipsum, quod sit vacuus caritate. Quid demum aliud detrahendo intendit, nisi ut is cui obloquitur, veniat in odium aut contemptum apud eos, coram quibus venenum detractionis effundit? Ferit ergo caritatem in omnibus, quantum in se est, apud quos detrahit.
paras.en: [[24:9|The thought of a fool|Cogitatio stulti]], by which with consent he thinks to do evil or to leave undone a good that he owes, [[24:9|is sin|peccatum est]]; [[24:9|and the detractor is the abomination of men|et abominatio hominum, detractor]], that is, the slanderer is abominable to men, sinning against the natural law, by doing to his neighbours what he would not have done to himself[[Tob 4:16||]][[Matt 7:12||]][[Luke 6:31||]], and against the divine law, which forbids this detestable vice many times over. Hence Bernard says: Let not my soul come into the counsel of detractors, for God hates them. Nor is it any wonder, since this vice is known to persecute and assail charity (which is God[[1 John 4:8||]][[1 John 4:16||]] [the margin reads 1 Joann. iv, 3, 16; for *3* read *8*]) more bitterly than others. And he who detracts first betrays himself, that he is empty of charity. What else, in short, does he aim at by detracting, but that the one he speaks against should come into hatred or contempt with those before whom he pours out the poison of detraction? He strikes at charity, then, as far as in him lies, in all those before whom he detracts.

paras.t: Si desperaveris lapsus in die angustiæ tuæ: id est, si in peccatum aut damnum, aut aliam adversitatem dilapsus tempore tribulationis, desperaveris de venia, consolatione, evasione, aut damni recuperatione; imminuetur fortitudo tua, id est, mente et corpore eris debilior. Nil ergo desperatione exsecrabilius: quæ etiam ponitur inter peccata in Spiritum Sanctum. Sequamur ergo sanctum Job asserentem, Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo; et Abraham patriarcham, qui contra spem in spem credidit, hoc est contra spem naturæ, in spem gratiæ.
paras.en: [[24:10|If thou lose hope, being weary in the day of distress|Si desperaveris lapsus in die angustiæ tuæ]] [Denis reads *lapsus*, "fallen", where the Vulgate has *lassus*, "weary"]: that is, if, having fallen into sin or loss or some other adversity in the time of tribulation, thou despair of pardon, of consolation, of escape, or of recovering the loss, [[24:10|thy strength shall be diminished|imminuetur fortitudo tua]], that is, thou wilt be weaker in mind and in body. Nothing, then, is more accursed than despair, which is even reckoned among the sins against the Holy Ghost. Let us follow, then, holy Job, who declares: [[Job 13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiam si occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]; and the patriarch Abraham, [[Rom 4:18|Who against hope believed in hope|qui contra spem in spem credidit]], that is, against the hope of nature, in the hope of grace.

paras.t: Erue eos qui ducuntur ad mortem; et qui trahuntur ad interitum liberare ne cesses. Hoc primo exponitur de his qui contra justitiam trahuntur ad corporalem occisionem; secundo, de his qui ab hæreticis aut perfidis trahuntur ad vitia infidelitatis: qui per sanam informationem et signa sunt reducendi; tertio, de his qui a prava societate quacumque, aut diabolica tentatione, trahuntur ad peccatum mortale: quos pro posse debemus revocare atque convertere; quarto, de his qui fame, siti, nuditate, frigore, tendunt ad mortem: quos debemus eruere necessaria impendendo. Hinc non solum Seneca, sed et sancti doctores Basilius Ambrosiusque testantur: Tot homines occidis, quot succurrere potes, et negligis.
paras.en: [[24:11|Deliver them that are led to death: and those that are drawn to death, forbear not to deliver.|Erue eos qui ducuntur ad mortem; et qui trahuntur ad interitum liberare ne cesses]] This is expounded, first, of those who are dragged against justice to bodily slaughter; second, of those who are drawn by heretics or the faithless into the vices of unbelief, who are to be brought back by sound instruction and by signs; third, of those who are drawn into mortal sin by any wicked company or by the temptation of the devil, whom we ought to call back and convert as far as we can; fourth, of those who are going to their death through hunger, thirst, nakedness and cold, whom we ought to rescue by giving them what they need. Hence not only Seneca but also the holy doctors Basil and Ambrose testify: As many men as thou canst succour and dost neglect, so many thou slayest.

paras.t: Si dixeris, Vires non suppetunt: id est, si per impotentiam tuam excusare te velis, et dissimulare; qui inspector est cordis, utpote Deus, de se ipso loquens: Non juxta intuitum hominis ego judico; homo enim videt ea quæ parent, Dominus autem intuetur cor; ipse intelligit an te vere excuses, et servatorem animæ tuæ nihil fallit: id est, Deum omnia conservantem in esse, et qui animam servat in gratia ac virtute, nullus potest decipere; reddetque homini juxta opera sua, ita quod eruit eos a periculis, et a morte culpæ ac gehennæ, qui prætactis modis eruunt proximos suos.
paras.en: [[24:12|If thou say: I have not strength enough|Si dixeris, Vires non suppetunt]]: that is, if thou wouldst excuse thyself by thy want of power, and look the other way, [[24:12|he that seeth into the heart|qui inspector est cordis]], namely God, who says of himself: [[1 Kings 16:7|nor do I judge according to the look of man: for man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart|Non juxta intuitum hominis ego judico; homo enim videt ea quæ parent, Dominus autem intuetur cor]]; [[24:12|he understandeth|ipse intelligit]] whether thou art truly excusing thyself, [[24:12|and nothing deceiveth the keeper of thy soul|et servatorem animæ tuæ nihil fallit]]: that is, no one can deceive God, who keeps all things in being, and who keeps the soul in grace and virtue; [[24:12|and he shall render to a man according to his works|reddetque homini juxta opera sua]], in this way, that he delivers from dangers, and from the death of guilt and of hell, those who deliver their neighbours in the ways touched on above.

paras.t: Comede, fili mi, mel, quia bonum est; tamen, si immoderate sumatur, nocet; et favum dulcissimum gutturi tuo, cui dulciter valde sapit.
paras.en: [[24:13|Eat honey, my son, because it is good|Comede, fili mi, mel, quia bonum est]]; yet if it is taken immoderately, it does harm; [[24:13|and the honeycomb most sweet to thy throat|et favum dulcissimum gutturi tuo]], to which it tastes very sweet.

paras.t: Sic et doctrina sapientiæ dulcissima ac convenientissima refectio est animæ tuæ: quæ hoc invisibili utitur cibo, sine quo aret et sitit, juxta illud Psalmi: Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi. Atque per mel, quod in promptu est, literalis accipitur sensus; per favum, ubi mel in cera, spiritualis ac mysticus intellectus. Hinc Augustinus: Pinguissimus, inquit, est sermo divinus: omnes in se habet delicias; quidquid volueris, ex divino sermone nascitur, sicut manna ad uniuscujusque sapuit voluntatem. Quàm sapientiam salutarem, quum inveneris, habebis in novissimis spem æternæ salutis, dummodo usque ad finem vitæ in sapientia ista permanseris. Neminem enim diligit Deus, nisi eum qui cum sapientia inhabitat. Et spes tua non peribit, id est, effectus spei tuæ tibi præstabitur, scilicet beatitudo cœlestis: qua adepta, spes cessat, sicut et fides, beatifica fruitione adepta.
paras.en: [[24:14|So also is the doctrine of wisdom|Sic et doctrina sapientiæ]] the sweetest and most fitting refreshment [[24:14|to thy soul|animæ tuæ]], which feeds on this invisible food, without which it is parched and thirsts, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 142:6|my soul is as earth without water unto thee|Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi]]. And by the honey, which is ready to hand, the literal sense is understood; by the honeycomb, where the honey is in the wax, the spiritual and mystical understanding. Hence Augustine: The divine word, he says, is most rich; it holds all delights in itself; whatever thou wilt springs from the divine word, as the manna tasted according to the will of each[[Wis 16:21||]]. This saving wisdom, [[24:14|when thou hast found|quum inveneris]] it, [[24:14|thou shalt have hope in the end|habebis in novissimis spem]], the hope of eternal salvation, provided thou abide in this wisdom to the end of life. [[Wis 7:28|For God loveth none but him that dwelleth with wisdom.|Neminem enim diligit Deus, nisi eum qui cum sapientia inhabitat]] [[24:14|and thy hope shall not perish|Et spes tua non peribit]], that is, the effect of thy hope shall be granted thee, namely heavenly beatitude; and when that is gained, hope ceases, as faith does too, once the beatific enjoyment is gained.

paras.t: Ne insidieris et quæras iniquitatem * in * impietatem domo justi: id est, contra justum et justos ejus domesticos, non quæras occasionem accusandi aut obloquendi; neque vastes requiem ejus, id est, pacem ejus non inquietes, nec ipsum perturbes propter venialia et quotidiana ejus peccata, quia de eis quotidie pœnitet.
paras.en: [[24:15|Lie not in wait, nor seek after wickedness|Ne insidieris et quæras iniquitatem]] [Denis has *iniquitatem*, "iniquity"; the edition adds the Vulgate's *impietatem* between asterisks] [[24:15|in the house of the just|domo justi]]: that is, against the just man and the just members of his household, seek not occasion to accuse or to speak against them; [[24:15|nor spoil his rest|neque vastes requiem ejus]], that is, do not trouble his peace, nor disturb him on account of his venial and daily sins, since he repents of them daily.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Septies enim in die cadet justus, id est frequenter, præsertim in venialia: sicque ponitur numerus determinatus pro indeterminato, quemadmodum apud Job habetur: Ecce hæc omnia operatur Deus tribus vicibus per singulos, ut revocet animas eorum a corruptione, et illuminet luce viventium. Unde subjungitur: et resurget per pœnitentiam. Propter quod ait Propheta: Quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam. Condolendum est igitur tali ruinæ, quæ ex fragilitate et humana necessitudine oritur. Hinc Plato loquitur in Phædone: Quamdiu corpus habuerit, et conglutinata fuerit anima huic malo, numquam plene sufficienterque adipiscemur quod exoptamus. Decies enim millena vacationum (id est contemplationum ac spiritualium studiorum) impedimenta nobis inde proveniunt, propter corporis necessitatem. Verum sunt quidam perversi, qui proprias negligentias et iniquitates palliare optantes, assidue quærunt, observant, recondunt, quod melioribus se opponant. Impii autem corruent in malum: id est, sic peccant, quod non student resurgere, sed manent prostrati in vitiis. Aliqui tamen hujusmodi interdum, Omnipotente miserante ac præveniente, resurgunt.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[24:16|For a just man shall fall seven times|Septies enim in die cadet justus]] [Denis's text adds *in die*, "in a day"], that is, often, especially into venial sins; and so a definite number is put for an indefinite one, as is found in Job: [[Job 33:29|Behold, all these things God worketh three times within every one.|Ecce hæc omnia operatur Deus tribus vicibus per singulos]] [[Job 33:30|That he may withdraw their souls from corruption, and enlighten them with the light of the living.|ut revocet animas eorum a corruptione, et illuminet luce viventium]] Hence it is added: [[24:16|and shall rise again|et resurget]] by penance. For which reason the Prophet says: [[Ps 36:24|When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, for the Lord putteth his hand under him.|Quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam]] We should therefore feel compassion for such a fall, which arises from frailty and human necessity. Hence Plato says in the Phædo: As long as we have the body, and the soul is glued to this evil, we shall never fully and sufficiently attain what we long for; for ten thousand hindrances to our leisure (that is, to contemplation and spiritual pursuits) come to us from it, because of the needs of the body. But there are certain perverse men who, wishing to cloak their own negligences and iniquities, are always seeking out, watching for and storing up something to set against their betters. [[24:16|but the wicked shall fall down into evil|Impii autem corruent in malum]]: that is, they so sin that they do not strive to rise again, but remain prostrate in their vices. Yet some of this kind do at times rise again, by the mercy of the Almighty, whose grace goes before them.

paras.t: Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas: præsertim si in malum culpæ corruerit, de quo nunquam licet gaudere. Si autem in malum pœnæ labatur, et capitur, infirmetur, puniatur aut occidatur per viam justitiæ, non licet inde gaudere ex odio, ira, aut simili prava radice, sed bene ex caritate et zelo justitiæ, in quantum malum illud pœnale, est pro salute animæ patientis, et expediens bono communi, et alios revocans ab excessu. Et in ruina ejus non exsultet cor tuum. Unde David mortem Saulis deplanxit. Julius quoque, viso capite Pompeii adversarii sui, lacrimas fudit.
paras.en: [[24:17|When thy enemy shall fall, be not glad|Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas]]: above all if he has fallen into the evil of guilt, at which it is never lawful to rejoice. But if he falls into the evil of punishment, and is taken, falls sick, is punished or slain by way of justice, it is not lawful to rejoice at it out of hatred, anger, or some like wicked root, but it is right to rejoice out of charity and zeal for justice, in so far as that penal evil serves the salvation of the sufferer's soul, is expedient for the common good, and calls others back from excess. [[24:17|and in his ruin let not thy heart rejoice|Et in ruina ejus non exsultet cor tuum]]. Hence David lamented the death of Saul[[2 Kings 1:17||]]. Julius too, when he saw the head of Pompey his adversary, shed tears.

paras.t: Ne forte videat Dominus. Dominus indubitanter omnia videt bona et mala. Ideo sic exponendum est: Ne forte videat Dominus, id est, per vindictam se videre demonstret tuam vitiosam lætitiam. Vel ait, Ne forte, ad insinuandum nostræ voluntatis libertatem ad bona et mala: quia si non agimus malum, nec Deus id videt; qui tamen æternaliter ineffabiliterque cuncta prævidit, sed ob hoc necessitatem non imposuit rebus actibusque humanis. Et displiceat ei, cui displicet omnis culpa: non per displicentiam beatæ voluntati contrariam, quæ habet quidquid vult, et quidquid non vult, eo caret; sed displicentia illa non est nisi detestatio, qua Deus detestatur omne quod bonitati ac virtuti opponitur. Et auferat ab eo iram suam. Non gaudere de ruina alterius, ne Dominus ab illo auferat iram suam, non esset caritatis, sed odii. Ideo sensus est: Et auferat ab eo iram suam, id est, te ipsum juste permittat in mala corruere, sic quod ira Dei ab illo ablata, super te cadat, et ille te lapsum juste irrideat, de cujus ruina gaudebas injuste. Juxta quem modum ait Apostolus: Quod si aliqui ex ramis fracti sunt, tu autem quum oleaster esses, insertus es in illis, et socius radicis et pinguedinis olivæ factus, noli gloriari adversus ramos.
paras.en: [[24:18|Lest the Lord see|Ne forte videat Dominus]]. The Lord beyond doubt sees all things, good and evil[[Heb 4:13||]]. It is therefore to be expounded thus: [[24:18|Lest the Lord see|Ne forte videat Dominus]], that is, lest he show by punishment that he sees thy sinful gladness. Or he says *lest perhaps* [*ne forte*, which the Douay-Rheims renders simply "lest"] to suggest the freedom of our will for good and for evil: for if we do not do evil, neither does God see it; who nonetheless foresaw all things eternally and ineffably, but did not on that account lay necessity on things and on human acts. [[24:18|and it displease him|Et displiceat ei]], to whom all guilt is displeasing: not by a displeasure contrary to his blessed will, which has whatever it wills and is without whatever it does not will; but that displeasure is nothing but detestation, by which God detests all that is opposed to goodness and virtue. [[24:18|and he turn away his wrath from him|Et auferat ab eo iram suam]]. Not to rejoice at another's fall lest the Lord take his wrath away from him would be a mark not of charity but of hatred. The sense, therefore, is: [[24:18|and he turn away his wrath from him|Et auferat ab eo iram suam]], that is, lest he justly let thee fall into evils, so that the wrath of God, taken away from him, falls upon thee, and he justly mocks thee in thy fall, at whose ruin thou didst unjustly rejoice. In the same way the Apostle says: [[Rom 11:17|And if some of the branches be broken and thou, being a wild olive, art ingrafted in them and art made partaker of the root and of the fatness of the olive tree|Quod si aliqui ex ramis fracti sunt, tu autem quum oleaster esses, insertus es in illis, et socius radicis et pinguedinis olivæ factus]], [[Rom 11:18|Boast not against the branches|noli gloriari adversus ramos]].

paras.t: Ne contendas cum pessimis, id est induratis et incorrigibilibus, quos nec corripiendo, nec exhortando, nec disceptando poteris emendare. Idcirco pro illis orandum est. Verumtamen præsidentium et judicum est, tales per pœnas reprimere. Nec æmuleris, id est, non sequaris, impios in vitiis, nec diligas, secundum quod tales; quia non habent futurorum spem mali: quoniam ultimum finem sibi constituunt in rebus præsentibus et caducis, sicque futuram beatitudinem non exspectant; et si dicantur eam sperare, intelligendum est de spe informi, non formata, sicut et credunt eam; et lucerna impiorum, id est prosperitas, memoria, scientia informis, et lux naturalis ingenii, exstinguetur: quia per vitia obscuratur, aut in morte finitur, deinde putrescit. Istud supra plenius fuit expositum.
paras.en: [[24:19|Contend not with the wicked|Ne contendas cum pessimis]], that is, with the hardened and incorrigible, whom thou canst not amend by rebuking, by exhorting, or by disputing. Therefore we must pray for them. Yet it belongs to those in authority and to judges to restrain such men by punishments. [[24:19|nor seek to be like|Nec æmuleris]], that is, do not follow, [[24:19|the ungodly|impios]] in their vices, nor love them as such; [[24:20|For evil men have no hope of things to come|quia non habent futurorum spem mali]]: since they set their last end in present and perishing things, and so do not look for the beatitude to come; and if they are said to hope for it, this is to be understood of an unformed hope, not a formed one, just as they also believe in it [an *unformed* hope or faith is one not quickened by charity]; [[24:20|and the lamp of the wicked|et lucerna impiorum]], that is, prosperity, memory, unformed knowledge, and the natural light of the mind, [[24:20|shall be put out|exstinguetur]]: for it is darkened by vices, or ended in death, and then rots. This was expounded more fully above[[Prov 13:9||]].

paras.t: Time Dominum, fili mi, et regem, id est Deum regem universorum, vel Deum et ejus vicarios præsidentes, qui propter Deum timendi sunt; et cum detractoribus ne commiscearis, approbando aut libenter audiendo detractoria verba eorum, aut etiam non resistendo eis aliquo modo, videlicet corripiendo eos de tanto peccato, vel pie hortando ut cessent, aut tristem vultum monstrando, sicut in Ecclesiaste habetur: Per tristitiam vultus corrigitur animus delinquentis; et alibi, Ventus aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem.
paras.en: [[24:21|My son, fear the Lord, and the king|Time Dominum, fili mi, et regem]], that is, God the King of all things, or God and his vicars in authority, who are to be feared for God's sake; [[24:21|and have nothing to do with detractors|et cum detractoribus ne commiscearis]], by approving or by willingly hearing their detracting words, or even by not resisting them in some way, namely by rebuking them for so great a sin, or by kindly urging them to stop, or by showing a sad face, as is found in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 7:4|by the sadness of the countenance the mind of the offender is corrected|Per tristitiam vultus corrigitur animus delinquentis]]; and elsewhere, [[Prov 25:23|The north wind driveth away rain, as doth a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.|Ventus aquilo dissipat pluvias, et facies tristis linguam detrahentem]]

paras.t: Quoniam repente consurget perditio, id est damnatio, eorum, videlicet detrahentis, et commiscentis se ei. Unde ait Bernardus: Non facile dixerim, quis gravius peccet, detrahens, detrahentemve audiens. Et ruinam utriusque quis novit? id est, quam districte damnandi sint, ignoramus. Detractor enim, quantum in se est, non modo occidit se ipsum in anima, sed et cunctos qui audiunt eum, quibus mortis poculum præbet. Unde ait Bernardus, quod lingua detractoris crudelior est gladio persecutoris: estque gladius ex utraque parte acutus, interficiens, quantum in se est, ad minus animas duas, utpote detrahentis, et audientis; imo et ejus cui detrahitur, qui quum audierit qualiter sibi detractum sit, incitatur in obloquentem. Ecce quam rigorose et seriose, imo et sæpe, loquitur Salomon contra hoc vitium; et tamen multi valde incaute se habent circa facinus tantum, et jugiter proni sunt ad obloquendum, etiam ex sola et levi suspicione: quod est utique ineffabiliter periculosum. Quorum lingua (ut Jacobus ait apostolus) est inquietum malum, plena veneno mortifero, inflammata a gehenna, id est diabolo, cujus instrumentum est ad internecionem animarum multarum. Ideo sapientissimus Augustinus juxta mensam suam scripsit hos versus: Quisquis amat dictis absentum carpere vitam, Hanc mensam vetitam noverit esse sibi.
paras.en: [[24:22|For their destruction shall rise suddenly|Quoniam repente consurget perditio]], that is, their damnation, namely that of the detractor and of him who mixes with him. Hence Bernard says: I would not easily say which sins more grievously, the detractor or the one who listens to the detractor. [[24:22|and who knoweth the ruin of both?|Et ruinam utriusque quis novit?]] that is, we do not know how strictly they are to be condemned. For the detractor, as far as in him lies, slays not only himself in his soul but also all who hear him, to whom he offers the cup of death. Hence Bernard says that the tongue of the detractor is crueller than the sword of the persecutor; and it is a sword sharp on both sides, killing, as far as in it lies, at least two souls, namely the detractor's and the hearer's; nay, and that of the one detracted as well, who, when he hears how he has been detracted, is stirred up against the one who spoke against him. See how strictly and seriously, and how often too, Solomon speaks against this vice; and yet many are very heedless about so great a crime, and are always ready to speak against others, even on a mere slight suspicion, which is indeed unspeakably dangerous. Their tongue (as the apostle James says) is [[Jas 3:8|an unquiet evil, full of deadly poison|inquietum malum, plena veneno mortifero]], [[Jas 3:6|being set on fire by hell|inflammata a gehenna]], that is, by the devil, whose instrument it is for the slaughter of many souls. Therefore the most wise Augustine wrote these verses by his table: Whoever loves to pick at the life of the absent with his words, let him know that this table is forbidden him.

paras.t: Hæc quoque sapientibus: id est, jam dicta atque dicenda, sunt sapientibus observanda. Cognoscere personam in judicio non est bonum. Minus dicit, et majus significat: quia personarum acceptio, præsertim in judicio, est grande et mortale peccatum, et contra veritatem atque justitiam, ut supra jam dictum est plenius. Cognoscendæ ergo et intuendæ sunt causæ in judicio, non personæ, quantum ad ea quæ ad rem non pertinent in tali negotio.
paras.en: [[24:23|These things also to the wise|Hæc quoque sapientibus]]: that is, the things already said and still to be said are to be observed by the wise. [[24:23|It is not good to have respect to persons in judgment|Cognoscere personam in judicio non est bonum]]. He says less and means more: for respect of persons, especially in judgment, is a great and mortal sin, and against truth and justice, as was said more fully above[[Prov 18:5||]]. In judgment, therefore, it is the cases that are to be known [*cognoscendæ*, taking up *cognoscere personam*, literally "to know the person"] and looked to, not the persons, as regards the things that do not bear on the matter in such business.

paras.t: Qui dicunt impio, Justus es, præsertim in foro judicii, maledicent eis populi, et detestabuntur eos tribus, quum cognoverint crimen hoc.
paras.en: [[24:24|They that say to the wicked man: Thou art just|Qui dicunt impio, Justus es]], especially in the court of judgment, [[24:24|shall be cursed by the people, and the tribes shall abhor them|maledicent eis populi, et detestabuntur eos tribus]], when they come to know of this crime.

paras.t: Qui arguunt eum, laudabuntur: id est, qui peccantem caritative, discrete, juste corripiunt, falsaque reprobant, et pro defensione legis divinæ ac fidei disputant, laude sunt digni, et commendabuntur a Deo ac Sanctis; et super eos veniet benedictio, id est largitio et multiplicatio donorum gratiæ in præsenti, deinde salus æterna. Tales etenim zelatores justitiæ secundum scientiam, Deus præcipue diligit, ditat, felicitat; a bonis quoque hominibus benedicuntur et laudantur. Illi quoque qui arguuntur, si probi sint, eis regratiantur, et dato quod indignentur ad tempus, tamen ad mentem reversi, gratias agunt, sicut et infra habetur: Qui corripit hominem, gratiam postea inveniet apud eum.
paras.en: [[24:25|They that rebuke him shall be praised|Qui arguunt eum, laudabuntur]]: that is, those who rebuke the sinner charitably, discreetly and justly, and disprove falsehoods, and dispute in defence of the divine law and of the faith, are worthy of praise, and will be commended by God and the Saints; [[24:25|and a blessing shall come upon them|et super eos veniet benedictio]], that is, the bestowal and multiplying of the gifts of grace in the present, and then eternal salvation. For such zealots of justice according to knowledge God especially loves, enriches and makes happy; and they are blessed and praised by good men too. Those also who are rebuked, if they are upright, thank them; and granted that they are indignant for a time, yet when they come to themselves they give thanks, as is found below too: [[Prov 28:23|He that rebuketh a man, shall afterward find favour with him|Qui corripit hominem, gratiam postea inveniet apud eum]] [the margin also gives Prov. xxviii, 26, which does not bear on this].

paras.t: Labia deosculabitur, id est, caritatem et pacem reformabit, fovebit, perficiet, qui recta verba respondet, id est, discrete se habet loquendo, et ea dicendo, quæ pro causa, loco et tempore magis expediunt: quia per hoc fit amabilis bonis hominibus, et discordantes pacificat. Porro deosculatio labiorum, signum est caritatis et pacis, prout in libro de Officiis pulchre de hoc scribit Ambrosius.
paras.en: [[24:26|He shall kiss the lips|Labia deosculabitur]], that is, he will restore, cherish and perfect charity and peace, [[24:26|who answereth right words|qui recta verba respondet]], that is, who bears himself discreetly in speaking, and says what is most expedient for the cause, the place and the time: for by this he becomes lovable to good men, and makes peace between those at variance. Moreover the kissing of the lips is a sign of charity and peace, as Ambrose writes finely of this in his book On Duties.

paras.t: Præpara foris opus tuum: id est, aliis exemplarem te exhibe, nec aliquem scandalizes, ut juxta doctrinam Apostoli, provideas bona non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus. Unde jussit Salvator: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra. Et diligenter exerce agrum tuum, id est, campum cordis tui, et eos qui tibi commissi sunt, a vitiis purga, virtutum seminibus semina, virtuosis exercitiis cole, meritisque fecunda; et postea ædifices domum tuam: id est, fabricam virtutum sublimium construe in habitaculo mentis tuæ, atque in grege tibi commisso. Nempe qui præest aut prædicat, debet in primis se ipsum purgare, exercere, perficere, deinde ad aliorum instructionem præsidentiamque procedere, ne ei dicatur, Medice, cura te ipsum; itemque, Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces?
paras.en: [[24:27|Prepare thy work without|Præpara foris opus tuum]]: that is, show thyself an example to others, and scandalize no one, so as to follow the Apostle's teaching, [[Rom 12:17|Providing good things, not only in the sight of God but also in the sight of all men|provideas bona non solum coram Deo, sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus]]. Hence the Saviour commanded: [[Matt 5:16|let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works|Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra]]. [[24:27|and diligently till thy ground|Et diligenter exerce agrum tuum]], that is, the field of thy heart, and those who are committed to thee: purge them of vices, sow them with the seeds of virtues, cultivate them with virtuous exercises, and make them fruitful with merits; [[24:27|that afterward thou mayst build thy house|et postea ædifices domum tuam]]: that is, raise the building of the lofty virtues in the dwelling of thy mind, and in the flock committed to thee. For he who presides or preaches ought first of all to purge, exercise and perfect himself, and then go on to instruct and govern others, lest it be said to him: [[Luke 4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]]; and again: [[Rom 2:21|Thou therefore, that teachest another, teachest not thyself|Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces?]]?

paras.t: Ne sis testis frustra, id est inaniter et sine idonea causa, contra proximum tuum: tamen si innocentis liberatio, aut judicis præceptum, aut similis rationabilis exigat causa, testimonium est ferendum; nec lactes quemquam labiis tuis, id est, nemini adulteris, nec foveas aliquem in peccatis: quemadmodum scriptum est, Laudatur peccator in desideriis animæ suæ. Istud supra magis expositum est.
paras.en: [[24:28|Be not witness without cause|Ne sis testis frustra]], that is, idly and without fitting cause, [[24:28|against thy neighbour|contra proximum tuum]]: yet if the deliverance of an innocent man, or the command of a judge, or some like reasonable cause requires it, testimony is to be given; [[24:28|and deceive not any man with thy lips|nec lactes quemquam labiis tuis]], that is, flatter no one [*lactare*, literally to give milk, hence to coax or beguile], nor cherish anyone in his sins, as it is written: [[Ps 9:24|the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul|Laudatur peccator in desideriis animæ suæ]] [the margin gives Ps. x, 3, according to the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate this is Ps 9:24]. This was explained more fully above[[Prov 1:10||]].

paras.t: Ne dicas: Quomodo fecit mihi, inferendo injurias, sic faciam ei, et reddam unicuique mihi forefacienti, secundum opus suum, quo peccat in me. Hoc est quod dictum est supra: Ne dicas: Reddam malum pro malo. Porro injurias vindicare, et inter proximos æqualitatem servare justitiæ, ac mala culpæ per mala pœnæ recuperare, ad publicam spectat auctoritatem, hoc est ad præsidentem et judicem: ad quos tanquam ad vivam legem ac animatam justitiam confugere, pertinet ad subjectos, secundum Philosophum, vel injuriam penitus indulgere. Unde in Proverbiis suis Seneca ait: Optimum est semper ignoscere, tanquam si ipse quotidie pecces; et iterum: Turpe est vincere suos; satis pœnarum est, potuisse puniri. Tullius quoque: Nobile, inquit, victoriæ genus est, potuisse vindicare.
paras.en: [[24:29|Say not|Ne dicas]]: [[24:29|as he hath done to me|Quomodo fecit mihi]], by inflicting injuries, [[24:29|I will do to him|sic faciam ei]]; [[24:29|I will render to every one|reddam unicuique]] who wrongs me [[24:29|according to his work|secundum opus suum]], by which he sins against me. This is what was said above: [[Prov 20:22|Say not: I will return evil|Ne dicas: Reddam malum]] for evil. Now to avenge injuries, to keep the equality of justice among neighbours, and to make good the evils of guilt by the evils of punishment, belongs to public authority, that is, to the ruler and the judge; and it is for subjects, according to the Philosopher, to take refuge with these as with a living law and justice ensouled, or else to forgive the injury altogether. Hence Seneca says in his Proverbs: It is best always to forgive, as though thou thyself didst sin daily; and again: It is shameful to conquer one's own; it is punishment enough to have been able to be punished. Tully too: It is a noble kind of victory, he says, to have been able to take vengeance.

paras.t: Per agrum hominis pigri transivi, et per vineam viri stulti; et ecce totum replerant urticæ, operuerant superficiem ejus spinæ, et maceria lapidum destructa erat. Istud in corporalibus et exterioribus ita est. Spiritualiter vero, ager hominis pigri, et vinea viri stulti, est cor peccatoris acediosi, seu populus ei commissus: in quibus ex negligentia et torpore pravi prælati seu hominis vitiosi, prædominantur tribuli vitiorum, punctura crudelium passionum, videlicet iræ, impatientiæ, invidiæ, indignationis, amaritudinis. Et maceria, id est opera bona ex genere aliquando inchoata, non erant ad complementum perducta, nec caritatis coagulo adunata. Maceria equidem vocatur murus absque cæmento. Hæc autem videre, est in aliis ista considerare.
paras.en: [[24:30|I passed by the field of the slothful man, and by the vineyard of the foolish man:|Per agrum hominis pigri transivi, et per vineam viri stulti]] [[24:31|And behold it was all filled with nettles, and thorns had covered the face thereof|et ecce totum replerant urticæ, operuerant superficiem ejus spinæ]], [[24:31|and the stone wall was broken down|et maceria lapidum destructa erat]]. So it is in bodily and outward things. But spiritually, the field of the slothful man and the vineyard of the foolish man is the heart of the slothful sinner [*acediosus*: given to acedia, the sloth that is weary of spiritual things], or the people committed to him: in whom, through the negligence and torpor of a wicked prelate or a vicious man, the briars of vices prevail, the stinging of cruel passions, namely of anger, impatience, envy, indignation and bitterness. [[24:31|and the stone wall|Et maceria]], that is, good works, good in their kind [that is, good as acts, though not yet quickened by charity], once begun, had not been brought to completion, nor bound together by the mortar of charity. For a *maceria* is a wall without cement. And to see these things is to consider them in others.

paras.t: Quod quum vidissem, posui in corde meo, id est, memoriter ea recolui, ne simili modo accideret mihi, et exemplo didici disciplinam, id est, ex aliorum facto reprehensibili me ipsum correxi, direxi, et cautior factus sum. Felix enim quem faciunt aliena damna peritum: quia quod in aliis reprehensibile judicamus, vitare debemus.
paras.en: [[24:32|Which when I had seen, I laid it up in my heart|Quod quum vidissem, posui in corde meo]], that is, I called them to mind, lest the like should happen to me, [[24:32|and by the example I received instruction|et exemplo didici disciplinam]], that is, by the blameworthy deeds of others I corrected and directed myself, and became more wary. For happy is he whom other men's losses make wise: since what we judge blameworthy in others we ought to avoid.

paras.t: Postremo totum residuum hujus capituli, supra scriptum est atque expositum. * ibi Tamen quod dicitur hic *, Usquequo, piger, dormies...? non est hic de textu, secundum Hebræos. Imo versus hic incipit: Parum, inquam, dormies.
paras.en: Lastly, all the rest of this chapter was written out and expounded above[[Prov 6:10||]][[Prov 6:11||]]. However, what is said here, [[Prov 6:9|How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?|Usquequo, piger, dormies]], is not part of the text here, according to the Hebrews [the edition sets asterisks round the words *ibi Tamen quod dicitur hic*, "there. However, what is said here", apparently an editorial mark]. Rather, the verse here begins: [[24:33|Thou wilt sleep a little, said I|Parum, inquam, dormies]].

25.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI VICESIMI QUINTI : HÆ QUOQUE PARABOLÆ SALOMONIS, QUAS TRANSTULERUNT VIRI, ETC.
25.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-fifth chapter: These are also parables of Solomon, which the men copied out, etc.

paras.t: Hæ quoque parabolæ Salomonis, id est, sequentes parabolæ a Salomone prolatæ sunt, quemadmodum præcedentes; quas transtulerunt: non de idiomate Hebræo in aliud; sed, Transtulerunt, id est, transposuerunt eas de schedulis ac rapiariis, in quibus hinc inde erant descriptæ, ac redegerunt eas in unum, et inseruerunt ac addiderunt eas huic volumini; viri Ezechiæ regis Juda, id est scribæ et docti viri, domestici seu ministri devotissimi Ezechiæ, qui cultum Dei reparavit in regno suo, ac populum suum inclyte reformavit, prout partim quarto Regum, et plenius secundo Paralipomenon recitatur: et forsan ex ejus commissione facta fuit translatio et additio ista. Nempe (ut circa principium expositionis istius super hunc librum inductum est) Salomon parabolas istas non conscripsit, nec librum hunc edidit; sed servi ipsius parabolas ex ore ejus auditas notaverunt, atque in schedulas redegerunt, quæ tandem per diversos ac diversis temporibus in unum librum collectæ sunt et redactæ.
paras.en: [[25:1|These are also parables of Solomon|Hæ quoque parabolæ Salomonis]]: that is, the following parables were uttered by Solomon, as were the preceding ones; [[25:1|which|quas]] they [[25:1|copied out|transtulerunt]]: not from the Hebrew tongue into another; but [[25:1|copied out|Transtulerunt]] [the Latin *transtulerunt* means literally "transferred", and is also the word for "translated"; hence Denis's remark] means that they transposed them from the slips and notebooks [*rapiaria*: notebooks of jotted extracts] on which they had been written down here and there, gathered them into one, and inserted and added them to this volume; [[25:1|the men of Ezechias, king of Juda|viri Ezechiæ regis Juda]], that is, the scribes and learned men, the household servants or ministers of the most devout Ezechias, who restored the worship of God in his kingdom and nobly reformed his people, as is related partly in the fourth book of Kings and more fully in the second of Paralipomenon: and perhaps this transferring and adding was done at his commission. For (as was set out near the beginning of this exposition of the book) Solomon did not write these parables down, nor did he publish this book; but his servants noted down the parables they heard from his mouth and put them on slips, which were at length collected and put together into one book by various persons and at various times.

paras.t: Gloria Dei est celare verbum: id est, ad Dei gloriam pertinet, aliqua tradere in Scripturis per verba obscura, velata et mystica, ne divina secreta pandantur indignis, et [ut] studiosis Catholicis detur occasio virtuosæ exercitationis, prout divinus Dionysius plenius docet. Sic quoque gloria Dei est, secretiora Scripturæ non manifestare, sed occultare rudibus, præsumptuosis, carnalibus et indignis, sicut ait Salvator: Nolite sanctum dare canibus. Et rursus Apostolis: Vobis, inquit, datum est nosse mysterium regni Dei, ceteris autem in parabolis, ut audientes non intelligant. Hinc primo mysticæ theologiæ capitulo magnus Dionysius præcepit Timotheo: Vide ut nullus indoctorum hæc videat. Hinc Vas electionis scribit se in raptu audisse arcana verba, quæ non licet homini loqui. Et angelus Raphael protestatur: Sacramentum regis abscondere, bonum est. Et ad Danielem angelus Gabriel: Clausi sunt, inquit, signatique sermones. Insuper gloria Dei est, ut ex fidelitate celetur verbum quod unus ab alio in secreto recepit. Allegorice, Gloria Dei est celare verbum, id est, gloria Unigeniti Patris æterni, propter homines incarnati, est celare Verbum, id est occultare se ipsum, Verbum æternum, in humanitate assumpta.
paras.en: [[25:2|It is the glory of God to conceal the word|Gloria Dei est celare verbum]]: that is, it belongs to the glory of God to hand down some things in the Scriptures in obscure, veiled and mystical words, so that the divine secrets be not laid open to the unworthy, and that earnest Catholics be given occasion for virtuous exercise, as the divine Dionysius teaches more fully. So too it is the glory of God not to make the more secret things of Scripture plain, but to hide them from the unlearned, the presumptuous, the carnal and the unworthy, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:6|Give not that which is holy to dogs|Nolite sanctum dare canibus]]. And again, to the Apostles: [[Luke 8:10|To you|Vobis]], he says, [[Luke 8:10|it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest in parables|datum est nosse mysterium regni Dei, ceteris autem in parabolis]], that [[Luke 8:10|hearing may not understand|audientes non intelligant]]. Hence, in the first chapter of the *Mystical Theology*, the great Dionysius charged Timothy: See that none of the uninstructed see these things. Hence the Vessel of election [that is, Paul, whom the Lord called "a vessel of election"] writes that in his rapture he heard [[2 Cor 12:4|secret words which it is not granted to man to utter|arcana verba, quæ non licet homini loqui]]. And the angel Raphael declares: [[Tob 12:7|it is good to hide the secret of a king|Sacramentum regis abscondere, bonum est]]. And the angel Gabriel to Daniel: [[Dan 12:9|the words are shut up|Clausi sunt]], he says, [[Dan 12:9|and sealed|signatique sermones]]. Moreover it is the glory of God that a word which one has received from another in secret be kept hidden out of faithfulness. Allegorically, [[25:2|It is the glory of God to conceal the word|Gloria Dei est celare verbum]]: that is, the glory of the Only-begotten of the eternal Father, made flesh for men's sake, is to conceal the Word, that is, to hide himself, the eternal Word, in the humanity he assumed.

paras.t: Et gloria regum, investigare sermonem: id est, regibus, et cunctis qui præsunt, specialiter commendabile honorificumque consistit, ut verba Scripturæ quæ non intelligunt, scrutentur, et sibi exponi deposcant, veritatem quoque verborum quæ audiunt, diligenter inquirant, sicut beatus Job fatetur, dicendo: Causam quam ignorabam, diligentissime investigabam. Sic gloria regum, id est Apostolorum, rectorum ac principum populi christiani, fuit investigare sermonem, id est expositionem verborum quæ audierunt a Christo, quem, ut in Evangelio innotescit, de talibus sæpe interrogaverunt; vel, Investigare sermonem, id est ipsum Christum, qui est increatus sermo Dei Patris: de quo ad Hebræos ait Apostolus, Vivus est sermo Dei. Sed et regum, id est universorum fidelium se bene regentium, gloria est investigare Scripturam, quantum ad eorum pertinet statum.
paras.en: [[25:2|and the glory of kings to search out the speech|Et gloria regum, investigare sermonem]]: that is, for kings, and for all who are set over others, it is especially praiseworthy and honourable that they search into the words of Scripture which they do not understand and ask to have them expounded to them, and also that they diligently inquire into the truth of the words they hear; as blessed Job confesses, saying: [[Job 29:16|the cause which I knew not, I searched out most diligently|Causam quam ignorabam, diligentissime investigabam]]. So [[25:2|the glory of kings|gloria regum]], that is, of the Apostles, the rulers and princes of the Christian people, was [[25:2|to search out the speech|investigare sermonem]], that is, the explanation of the words they heard from Christ, whom, as is made known in the Gospel, they often questioned about such things[[Matt 13:36||]][[Matt 15:15||]][[Mark 4:10||]][[Mark 10:10||]][[Mark 13:3||]]; or, [[25:2|to search out the speech|Investigare sermonem]], that is, Christ himself, who is the uncreated Word [*sermo*, the word rendered "speech" in the verse] of God the Father, of whom the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:12|the word of God is living|Vivus est sermo Dei]]. But it is also the glory of kings, that is, of all the faithful who govern themselves well, to search into Scripture, as far as befits their state.

paras.t: Cœlum sursum, et terra deorsum, et cor regum inscrutabile: id est, altitudo cœlorum imperscrutabilis nobis est, similiter terræ profunditas: sic et corda regum, de quibus jam dictum est, sunt nobis imperscrutabilia, solique cognita Creatori. Conformiter sapientia Apostolorum, quæ ex eorum corde nobis profluxit, plene a nobis perscrutari ac comprehendi non valet.
paras.en: [[25:3|The heaven above and the earth beneath, and the heart of kings is unsearchable|Cœlum sursum, et terra deorsum, et cor regum inscrutabile]]: that is, the height of the heavens is unsearchable to us, and likewise the depth of the earth: so too the hearts of kings, of whom we have just spoken, are unsearchable to us and known to the Creator alone. In the same way the wisdom of the Apostles, which has flowed to us from their heart, cannot be fully searched out and comprehended by us.

paras.t: Aufer rubiginem de argento, et egredietur vas purissimum; aufer impietatem de vultu regis, et firmabitur justitia thronus ejus: id est, sicut ex argento a rubigine et scoria depurato, formatur vas valde purum: ita si a corde regis ac præsidentis tollatur omnis iniquitas, auctoritas et præsidentia ejus roboratur æquitate atque virtutibus ejus, quoniam conservatur a Deo, et ad posteros ejus devolvitur. Spiritualiter, per argentum designatur naturalis ac philosophica scientia: a qua si rubigo, id est error admixtus, seu inflatio et abusus, tollantur, egreditur cor eruditum; sic enim deservit ad intelligendum divinam Scripturam.
paras.en: [[25:4|Take away the rust from silver, and there shall come forth a most pure vessel|Aufer rubiginem de argento, et egredietur vas purissimum]]; [[25:5|Take away wickedness from the face of the king, and his throne shall be established with justice|aufer impietatem de vultu regis, et firmabitur justitia thronus ejus]]: that is, as a very pure vessel is formed from silver cleansed of rust and dross, so, if all iniquity be taken from the heart of a king or ruler, his authority and rule are strengthened by his equity and virtues, since it is preserved by God and passes down to his posterity. Spiritually, silver signifies natural and philosophical knowledge: if the rust be taken from it, that is, the error mixed in with it, or the puffing up and the misuse of it, there comes forth a learned heart; for so it serves for understanding the divine Scripture.

paras.t: Ne gloriosus appareas coram rege: id est, coram regibus et præsidentibus non jactes nec extollas te, nec magnificare et ostentare te studeas, sed reverenter et modeste te habeas: præsertimque vitandum est [hoc] coram Rege cœlorum omnia intuente, sub cujus manu debemus nos semper humiliare. Et in loco magnorum ne steteris, id est, non ponas te in loco sublimiori quam decet gradum et statum tuum, sed magis in bassiori. Melius est enim ut dicatur tibi, Ascende huc, id est ad locum altiorem, quam ut humilieris, id est, ad inferiorem locum descendere compellaris, coram principe. Hoc est quod Dominus in Evangelio ait: Quum invitatus fueris ad nuptias, non discumbas in primo loco, etc. Advertant hæc superbi, ambitiosi et vani, qui nolunt sequi vestigia Christi, sed Scribarum ac Pharisæorum: de quibus ipse in Evangelio protestatur, quod ament primos recubitus in cœnis, et primas cathedras in synagogis, et salutationes in foro, et vocari ab hominibus Rabbi. O quam multi sunt modo tales!
paras.en: [[25:6|Appear not glorious before the king|Ne gloriosus appareas coram rege]]: that is, before kings and rulers do not boast or exalt thyself, nor be eager to magnify and show thyself off, but bear thyself reverently and modestly; and this is above all to be avoided before the King of heaven, who beholds all things, under whose hand we ought always to humble ourselves[[1 Pet 5:6||]]. [[25:6|and stand not in the place of great men|Et in loco magnorum ne steteris]], that is, do not put thyself in a higher place than befits thy rank and state, but rather in a lower one. [[25:7|For it is better that it should be said to thee: Come up hither|Melius est enim ut dicatur tibi, Ascende huc]], that is, to a higher place, [[25:7|than that thou shouldst be humbled|quam ut humilieris]], that is, be forced to go down to a lower place, [[25:7|before the prince|coram principe]]. This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: [[Luke 14:8|When thou art invited to a wedding, sit not down in the first place|Quum invitatus fueris ad nuptias, non discumbas in primo loco]], etc. Let the proud, the ambitious and the vain mark this, who will not follow the footsteps of Christ, but those of the Scribes and Pharisees, of whom he himself declares in the Gospel that [[Matt 23:6|they love the first places at feasts and the first chairs in the synagogues|ament primos recubitus in cœnis, et primas cathedras in synagogis]], and [[Matt 23:7|salutations in the market place, and to be called by men, Rabbi|salutationes in foro, et vocari ab hominibus Rabbi]]. O how many such there are now!

paras.t: Quæ viderunt oculi tui, id est, ea quæ nosti mala de alio, ne proferas in jurgio, id est contra alium litigando, vel in lite coram judice, cito, id est præcipitanter ex impetu passionis absque congrua deliberatione et rationabili causa, ne postea emendare, id est ea quæ sic propalasti revocare, non possis, et famam restituere proximo, quum dehonestaveris amicum tuum, id est, proximum tuum diffamaveris, culpam ejus taliter objiciendo, improperandove ei. Hoc dicitur contra homines passionatos, qui tam impetuosi irrationabilesque exsistunt, ut si quid reprehensibile noverint de proximo seu amico, mox illud ei objiciant et insultent, quum fuerint ab eo offensi, aut verbis contendere cœperint contra illum; et culpam illius sic manifestant, ac ipsum diffamant, contra præceptum de ordine observando in correptione fraterna: quem ordinem Christus docuit et præcepit, dicendo, Corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum, ut scilicet fama proximi non lædatur.
paras.en: [[25:8|The things which thy eyes have seen|Quæ viderunt oculi tui]], that is, the evil things thou knowest of another, [[25:8|utter not|ne proferas]] [[25:8|in a quarrel|in jurgio]], that is, in disputing against another, or in a lawsuit before a judge, [[25:8|hastily|cito]], that is, headlong, on the impulse of passion, without fitting deliberation and reasonable cause, [[25:8|lest afterward thou mayst not be able to make amends|ne postea emendare]], that is, to take back what thou hast thus spread abroad, and to restore thy neighbour's good name, [[25:8|when thou hast dishonoured thy friend|quum dehonestaveris amicum tuum]], that is, hast defamed thy neighbour by casting his fault in his face in this way, or reproaching him with it. This is said against passionate men, who are so impetuous and unreasonable that, if they know anything blameworthy of their neighbour or friend, they at once throw it in his face and taunt him with it when they have been offended by him, or have begun to quarrel with him in words; and so they make his fault known and defame him, against the precept about the order to be kept in fraternal correction, the order which Christ taught and commanded, saying: [[Matt 18:15|rebuke him between thee and him alone|Corripe eum inter te et ipsum solum]], so, that is, that the neighbour's good name be not hurt.

paras.t: Causam tuam tracta seorsum cum amico tuo fideli et familiari, de cujus fidelitate sis certus; et secretum tuum extraneo ne reveles: quia hoc esset valde periculosum et fatuum, sicut subjungitur: ne forte insultet tibi, quum audierit, et exprobrare non cesset. Secreta namque non nisi fidelissimo amico sunt revelanda, prout de hoc supra dictum est plenius. Gratia et amicitia liberant: quas tibi serva, ne exprobrabilis fias.
paras.en: [[25:9|Treat thy cause|Causam tuam tracta]] apart [[25:9|with thy friend|cum amico tuo]], a faithful and familiar one, of whose faithfulness thou art sure; [[25:9|and discover not the secret to a stranger|et secretum tuum extraneo ne reveles]]: for this would be very dangerous and foolish, as is added: [[25:10|Lest he insult over thee, when he hath heard it, and cease not to upbraid thee|ne forte insultet tibi, quum audierit, et exprobrare non cesset]]. For secrets are to be revealed only to a most faithful friend, as was said more fully above[[Prov 11:13||]]. [[25:10|Grace and friendship deliver a man: keep these for thyself, lest thou fall under reproach|Gratia et amicitia liberant: quas tibi serva, ne exprobrabilis fias]].

paras.t: Mala aurea in lectis argenteis, qui loquitur verbum in tempore suo: id est, proferens sermonem utilem tempore opportuno, assimilatur aureis pomis, quæ ad decorem affiguntur lectis argenteis. Talis etenim homo ornatur suis verbis, quemadmodum lectus argenteus aureis pomis, id est similitudinibus pomorum factis de auro. Et sicut in lecto argenteo dulciter quiescitur ac dormitur, sic sermo hujus facit auditores suaviter in se requiescere. Consueverunt autem antiquitus magnates lectis aureis atque argenteis uti, juxta illud libri Esther: Lectuli quoque aurei et argentei super pavimentum dispositi erant.
