paras.en: [[25:11|apples of gold on beds of silver|Mala aurea in lectis argenteis]], [[25:11|To speak a word in due time|qui loquitur verbum in tempore suo]]: that is, one who utters a profitable word at a fitting time is likened to golden apples, which are fixed to silver beds for ornament. For such a man is adorned by his words as a silver bed is by golden apples, that is, by likenesses of apples made of gold. And as one rests and sleeps sweetly in a silver bed, so this man's speech makes his hearers rest sweetly in it. Now in ancient times the great were accustomed to use beds of gold and silver, according to that of the book of Esther: [[Esth 1:6|The beds also were of gold and silver, placed in order upon a floor|Lectuli quoque aurei et argentei super pavimentum dispositi erant]].

paras.t: Inauris aurea et margaritum fulgens, qui arguit sapientem et aurem obedientem, id est vir caritative increpans sapientem, qui utique libenter suscipit correptionem, et aurem quæ exhortationi ac jussioni obedit. Quemadmodum enim inauris aurea aurem decorat, et splendida margarita vultum venustat; sic talis corrector et exhortator, verbis suis correctoriis ac informativis ornat se ipsum, et correptum, et obedientem. Suntque verba prudentiæ ejus splendentia instar argenti, et pretiosa ut margaritum, juxta illud Psalmi: Eloquia Domini argentum igne examinatum.
paras.en: [[25:12|As an earring of gold and a bright pearl, so is he that reproveth the wise, and the obedient ear|Inauris aurea et margaritum fulgens, qui arguit sapientem et aurem obedientem]], that is, a man who charitably rebukes the wise man, who indeed gladly receives correction, and the ear that obeys exhortation and command. For as a golden earring adorns the ear, and a shining pearl graces the face, so such a corrector and exhorter, by his words of correction and instruction, adorns himself, and the one corrected, and the obedient one. And the words of his prudence shine like silver and are precious as a pearl, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 11:7|The words of the Lord|Eloquia Domini]] are [[Ps 11:7|as silver tried by the fire|argentum igne examinatum]].

paras.t: Sicut frigus nivis in die messis, id est, sicut tempore messis acceptum est frigus aliquantulum simile frigori nivis ipsis messoribus, quia refrigerat eos; ita legatus fidelis ei qui misit eum, id est, conveniens et jucundus est domino, a quo directus est: animam illius requiescere facit.
paras.en: [[25:13|As the cold of snow in the time of harvest|Sicut frigus nivis in die messis]], that is, as in the time of harvest a coolness somewhat like the cold of snow is welcome to the reapers themselves, because it refreshes them, [[25:13|so is a faithful messenger to him that sent him|ita legatus fidelis ei qui misit eum]], that is, he is fitting and pleasing to the lord by whom he was sent: [[25:13|he refresheth his soul|animam illius requiescere facit]].

paras.t: Nubes et ventus, et pluviæ non sequentes, vir gloriosus, id est famosus, seu præclarum et virtuosum ac liberalem se fingens, magna promittendo, et promissa non complens. Nam sicut ventus et nubes, volantes sunt et sine optato effectu, ad quos non sequitur imber; sic homo promissa non implens, est corde levis, instabilis, et sine effectu virtutis, ac in suspenso tenens, magisque affligens quam lætificans eum cui promisit.
paras.en: [[25:14|As clouds, and wind, when no rain followeth|Nubes et ventus, et pluviæ non sequentes]], [[25:14|so is the man that boasteth|vir gloriosus]], that is, one famous, or feigning himself illustrious, virtuous and liberal by promising great things, [[25:14|and doth not fulfil his promises|et promissa non complens]]. For as wind and clouds fly past and are without the effect hoped for, when no shower follows them, so a man who does not fulfil his promises is light of heart, unstable, and without the effect of virtue, and keeps in suspense, and grieves rather than gladdens, the one to whom he made the promise.

paras.t: Patientia lenietur princeps: id est, per patientiam ejus quem princeps jubet puniri, mitigatur iracundia principis, nisi sit penitus ferox et inhumanus. Sic et Princeps altissimus, Dominus Deus, per patientiam sustinentium adversa eis reconciliatur. Ideo ait Michæas: Iram Domini portabo, quia peccavi ei. Unde in secundo Machabæorum habetur: Ira Domini in misericordiam conversa est. Et lingua mollis, id est responsio humilis, et recognitio propriæ culpæ, seu sermo suavis, confringet duritiam, id est, indignationem et rigorem offensi tollet et placabit: quemadmodum mulier Thecuitis et Abigail mentem David ad clementiam pertraxerunt.
paras.en: [[25:15|By patience a prince shall be appeased|Patientia lenietur princeps]]: that is, by the patience of the man whom the prince orders to be punished, the prince's anger is softened, unless he be utterly fierce and inhuman. So too the most high Prince, the Lord God, is reconciled to those who bear adversities with patience. Therefore Micheas says: [[Mich 7:9|I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him|Iram Domini portabo, quia peccavi ei]]. Hence it is found in the second book of Machabees: [[2 Mach 8:5|the wrath of the Lord was turned into mercy|Ira Domini in misericordiam conversa est]]. [[25:15|and a soft tongue|Et lingua mollis]], that is, a humble answer and acknowledgement of one's own fault, or a gentle word, [[25:15|shall break hardness|confringet duritiam]], that is, will take away and appease the indignation and severity of the one offended, as the woman of Thecua[[2 Kings 14:21||]] and Abigail[[1 Kings 25:33||]][[1 Kings 25:34||]] drew David's mind to clemency.

paras.t: Mel invenisti? comede quod sufficit tibi: id est, quidquid dulcis edulii habes, quantumcumque facile obtinueris illud, tamen non nisi moderate utere illo; ne forte satiatus evomas illud, et ita ex tua gula et carnalitate fiat tibi nocivum, quod ex se est suave ac aptum. Spiritualiter autem, Si mel invenisti, id est, Deum contemplari cœpisti, et Scripturarum dulcedinem aliqualiter degustasti, comede quod sufficit tibi, id est, juxta capacitatem intellectus tui te refice inde, nec incomprehensibilia comprehendere conitaris; ne forte satiatus evomas illud, id est, ex consideratione laboriosa repleto vertatur tibi in nocumentum summum illud primæ veritatis objectum, atque id ipsum quod cœpisti de eo salubriter degustare, amittas.
paras.en: [[25:16|Thou hast found honey|Mel invenisti]]? [[25:16|eat what is sufficient for thee|comede quod sufficit tibi]]: that is, whatever sweet food thou hast, however easily thou hast come by it, yet use it only in moderation; [[25:16|lest being glutted therewith thou vomit it up|ne forte satiatus evomas illud]], and so, through thy gluttony and carnality, that become harmful to thee which of itself is sweet and fitting. Spiritually, however: If [[25:16|thou hast found honey|mel invenisti]], that is, if thou hast begun to contemplate God and hast in some measure tasted the sweetness of the Scriptures, [[25:16|eat what is sufficient for thee|comede quod sufficit tibi]], that is, refresh thyself from it according to the capacity of thy understanding, and do not strive to comprehend things incomprehensible; [[25:16|lest being glutted therewith thou vomit it up|ne forte satiatus evomas illud]], that is, lest, when thou art overfilled by laborious consideration, that supreme object, the first truth, be turned to thy harm, and thou lose the very thing thou hadst begun to taste of it with profit.

paras.t: Subtrahe pedem tuum de domo proximi tui, id est, non nimis frequenter visites eum, nec apud eum nimis diu remaneas; nequando satiatus, id est de tua præsentia attædiatus, oderit te propter molestiam, vel expensas quas ingeris ei, vel ex suspicione qua putare posset quod uxorem aut filiam ejus turpiter ames. Melius est ergo, ut rarius veniendo facias eum tuum optare adventum, quam ut una vice tam diu secum permaneas, aut tam multoties eum accedas, ut fastidiat tuam præsentiam. Sed in hac re necessaria est discretio, qua homo prudenter perpendat an sua præsentia sit suo proximo onerosa, aut minus solito gratiosa: quo cognito, moderetur sive abstineat.
paras.en: [[25:17|Withdraw thy foot from the house of thy neighbour|Subtrahe pedem tuum de domo proximi tui]], that is, do not visit him too often, nor stay with him too long; [[25:17|lest having his fill|nequando satiatus]], that is, wearied of thy presence, [[25:17|he hate thee|oderit te]] because of the annoyance, or the expense thou puttest him to, or from a suspicion by which he might think that thou lovest his wife or daughter shamefully. It is better, then, by coming more seldom, to make him long for thy coming, than to stay with him so long at one time, or to go to him so many times, that he grows weary of thy presence. But in this matter discretion is needed, by which a man may prudently weigh whether his presence is burdensome to his neighbour, or less welcome than usual: and, knowing this, let him moderate his visits or keep away.

paras.t: Jaculum et gladius et sagitta acuta, id est, his rebus assimilatur, et instar earum nocet, lædit, et perforat, homo qui loquitur contra proximum suum falsum testimonium: per quod privat eum fama, substantia, aut etiam vita.
paras.en: [[25:18|a dart and a sword and a sharp arrow|Jaculum et gladius et sagitta acuta]]: that is, to these things is likened, and like them harms, wounds and pierces: [[25:18|A man that beareth false witness against his neighbour|homo qui loquitur contra proximum suum falsum testimonium]], by which he deprives him of his good name, his goods, or even his life.

paras.t: Dens putridus, et pes lassus, qui sperat super infideli in die angustiæ: id est, sicut dens putrefactus, et pes læsus ac lassus, valde affligunt, et tempore famis ac itinerationis non bene deserviunt; sic homo magnos incurrit dolores et cruciatus, confidendo de subsidio hominis infidelis, injusti, fallacis, præsertim tempore necessitatis; et amittit pallium, id est necessarium sibi amictum, in die frigoris, quando plus indiget pallio.
paras.en: [[25:19|a rotten tooth, and weary foot|Dens putridus, et pes lassus]], [[25:19|To trust in an unfaithful man in the time of trouble|qui sperat super infideli in die angustiæ]]: that is, as a decayed tooth and a hurt and weary foot afflict greatly, and serve but poorly in time of hunger and of journeying, so a man incurs great pains and torments by trusting in the help of an unfaithful, unjust, deceitful man, especially in a time of need; [[25:20|And one that looseth his garment|et amittit pallium]], that is, the cloak he needs, [[25:20|in cold weather|in die frigoris]], when he has most need of a cloak.

paras.t: Acetum in nitro, qui cantat carmina cordi pessimo: id est, qui cantica Scripturarum et divina eloquia proponit cordi incorrigibili et indurato, similis est ei qui acetum infundit nitro. Quemadmodum enim nitrum ex infusione aceti super se, fumat et crepitat, sicut et calx viva aqua infusa; sic pessima corda ex Scripturarum admonitione, correptione et castigatione, non quiescunt a vitiis suis, sed acrius indignantur, inquietantur, et fumum iræ emittunt. Circa hoc ait Glossa: Nitrum non multum a specie salis distat. Sicut enim fervor solis conficit salem in littore maris, durando aquas marinas in petras, quem salem vis ventorum, aut maris fervor seu agitatio projicit ad littus; ita in provincia Nitria in qua nascitur nitrum, ubi pluviæ longiores infuderint terram, succenditur ardor nimius, qui aquas durat et excoquit in petram simillimam glaciei aut sali, sed nihil gelidi frigoris, nihil salsi saporis habentem: quæ tamen petra juxta naturam salis solet durari in caumate, atque in nubiloso aere fluere ac liquefieri consuevit. Hæc petra, scilicet nitro, indigenæ ad lavandum utuntur, juxta illud in Jeremia: Si laveris te nitro, et multiplicaveris tibi herbam Borith, etc. Crepitat autem in aceto quasi calx viva, et deperit; sed aquam lotioni habilem reddit. Unde per nitrum quidam intelligunt speciem terræ, similem minuto sabulo: cui si aqua infundatur, fumigat. Denique de præfatis carminibus scriptum est in libro Job: Non dixit: Ubi est Deus qui fecit me, qui dedit carmina in nocte?
paras.en: [[25:20|As vinegar upon nitre|Acetum in nitro]], [[25:20|so is he that singeth songs to a very evil heart|qui cantat carmina cordi pessimo]]: that is, he who sets the songs of the Scriptures and the divine words before an incorrigible and hardened heart is like one who pours vinegar on nitre. For as nitre, when vinegar is poured on it, smokes and crackles, as quicklime does too when water is poured on it, so the worst hearts, at the admonition, correction and chastisement of the Scriptures, do not rest from their vices, but are the more bitterly indignant and disturbed, and give off the smoke of anger. On this the Gloss says: Nitre does not differ much from the species of salt. For as the heat of the sun makes salt on the seashore, hardening the sea water into stones, which salt the force of the winds, or the heaving or tossing of the sea, throws up on the shore, so in the province of Nitria, where nitre is produced, when long rains have soaked the ground, an excessive heat is kindled, which hardens and bakes the waters into a stone very like ice or salt, yet having nothing of icy cold and nothing of salty taste; which stone, however, as is the nature of salt, is wont to harden in hot weather and to flow and melt in cloudy air. This stone, namely nitre, the natives use for washing, according to that in Jeremias: [[Jer 2:22|Though thou wash thyself with nitre, and multiply to thyself the herb borith|Si laveris te nitro, et multiplicaveris tibi herbam Borith]], etc. But in vinegar it crackles like quicklime and perishes; yet it makes water fit for washing. Hence some understand by nitre a kind of earth like fine sand, which smokes if water is poured on it. Lastly, of the songs mentioned it is written in the book of Job: [[Job 35:10|he hath not said: Where is God, who made me, who hath given songs in the night?|Non dixit: Ubi est Deus qui fecit me, qui dedit carmina in nocte]]

paras.t: Sicut tinea vestimento, et vermis ligno; ita tristitia viri nocet cordi. Istud non est in Hebræo, neque de textu. Sed et sensus patet ex eo quod scriptum est supra, Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa.
paras.en: [[25:20|As a moth doth by a garment, and a worm by the wood: so the sadness of a man consumeth the heart|Sicut tinea vestimento, et vermis ligno; ita tristitia viri nocet cordi]]. This is not in the Hebrew, nor is it part of the text [that is, it is an addition found in the Latin, not part of the original text]. But its sense is plain from what is written above: [[Prov 17:22|a sorrowful spirit drieth up the bones|Spiritus tristis exsiccat ossa]].

paras.t: Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum; si sitierit, da ei aquam, id est aptum poculum, bibere: id est, redde ei bona pro malis, ut beneficiis vincas eum. Ideo subditur: prunas enim, id est caritatis fomenta et incentiva, congregabis super caput ejus, id est in corde ipsius, inducendo eum ad considerationem caritatis, pietatis, et beneficentiæ tuæ: ex quibus cor ejus rancorem abjiciet, et tuo accendetur amore. Sic enim vincitur malum in bono. Et Dominus reddet tibi copiosam mercedem. Quasi dicat: Dato quod ille in sua duritia inimicitiaque permanserit, tu tamen digno præmio non carebis. Hanc auctoritatem allegat Apostolus ad Romanos. Ex qua etiam elucescit, non fuisse intentionem legis Mosaicæ, quod inimicus absolute odiretur. Et consonat ista auctoritas cum eo quod dictum est supra: Ne dicas, Reddam malum pro malo. Porro, pro eo quod dicitur hic, Et Dominus reddet tibi, aliqui dicunt in Hebræo haberi: Et Dominus pacificabit tibi, id est, cor adversarii, cui sic benefacis, convertet ad habendam amicitiam tecum ac pacem.
paras.en: [[25:21|If thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat|Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum]]; [[25:21|if he thirst, give him water|si sitierit, da ei aquam]], that is, a fitting drink, [[25:21|to drink|bibere]]: that is, return him good for evil, so as to overcome him by kindnesses. Therefore it is added: [[25:22|For thou shalt heap hot coals|prunas enim]], that is, the kindlings and incentives of charity, [[25:22|upon his head|congregabis super caput ejus]], that is, in his heart, by leading him to consider thy charity, kindness and beneficence: from which his heart will cast off its rancour and be kindled with love of thee. For thus is evil overcome by good[[Rom 12:21||]]. [[25:22|and the Lord will reward thee|Et Dominus reddet tibi]] with an abundant recompense. As if to say: Granted that he remains in his hardness and enmity, thou nevertheless shalt not lack a worthy reward. The Apostle cites this authority to the Romans[[Rom 12:20||]]. From which it is also clear that it was not the intention of the law of Moses that an enemy should be hated absolutely[[Matt 5:43||]]. And this authority agrees with what was said above: [[Prov 20:22|Say not: I will return evil|Ne dicas, Reddam malum]] for evil. Further, for what is said here, [[25:22|and the Lord will reward thee|Et Dominus reddet tibi]], some say that the Hebrew has: And the Lord will make peace for thee; that is, he will turn the heart of the adversary to whom thou dost good in this way, so that he has friendship and peace with thee.

paras.t: Ventus Aquilo, id est aquilonaris seu septentrionalis, dissipat, id est impedit, pluvias. Est enim præcipue frigidus: ideo, ut frequenter, impedit copiosam vaporum elevationem, ac nubium resolutionem in imbrem, quamvis non semper. Et facies tristis, linguam detrahentem: id est, auditor detrahentis, mœstum vultum monstrando detractori, tacite admonet eum ut sileat. Dum enim detractor perpendit sua verba invite audiri, repercutitur in se ipso, et advertit se male loqui. Circa hoc asserit Glossa: Si hilari vultu audieris detrahentem, tu illi das fomitem detrahendi; si autem tristi eum vultu audieris, discit non libenter dicere quod didicerit non libenter audiri. (Aliqui asserunt in Hebræo haberi, Ventus Aquilo creat pluvias: ut sit sensus, quod sicut ventus australis generat pluvias versus partes aquilonares, sic ventus aquilonaris versus partes australes, prout etiam secundo Meteororum habetur; Et facies tristes lingua detrahens, id est, lingua detrahens provocat contra se iram divini respectus.) Itaque dum detrahentem quis increpare, vel ab eo non audet recedere, saltem mœstum et formidolosum ei ostendat vultum ac apparatum.
paras.en: [[25:23|The north wind|Ventus Aquilo]], that is, the northerly or septentrional wind, [[25:23|driveth away|dissipat]], that is, hinders, [[25:23|rain|pluvias]]. For it is especially cold: and so it frequently hinders the abundant rising of vapours and the dissolving of clouds into rain, though not always. [[25:23|as doth a sad countenance a backbiting tongue|Et facies tristis, linguam detrahentem]]: that is, the hearer of a backbiter, by showing the backbiter a sorrowful face, silently warns him to be quiet. For when the backbiter perceives that his words are heard unwillingly, he is struck back upon himself and notices that he is speaking ill. On this the Gloss declares: If thou hearest a backbiter with a cheerful face, thou givest him fuel for backbiting; but if thou hearest him with a sad face, he learns not to say willingly what he has learned is not willingly heard. (Some assert that the Hebrew has: The north wind bringeth forth rain: so that the sense is that, as the south wind produces rain towards the northern parts, so the north wind does towards the southern parts, as is also found in the second book of the *Meteorologica*; and: The face sad, the tongue backbiting; that is, the backbiting tongue provokes against itself the anger of the divine regard.) So when someone dares not rebuke a backbiter, or withdraw from him, let him at least show him a sorrowful and fearful face and bearing.

paras.t: Melius est sedere in angulo domatis, quam cum muliere litigiosa, et in domo communi. Hoc supra scriptum atque expositum est.
paras.en: [[25:24|It is better to sit in a corner of the housetop: than with a brawling woman, and in a common house|Melius est sedere in angulo domatis, quam cum muliere litigiosa, et in domo communi]]. This was written and explained above[[Prov 21:9||]].

paras.t: Aqua frigida animæ, id est personæ seu homini, sitienti, supple, suavis est; et nuntius bonus de terra longinqua apportans bona nova, jucundus est domino a quo erat missus. Sic Christus, secundum naturam assumptam, nuntius Dei Patris, veniens in hunc mundum a regione vivorum, et optima nova et dona ac promissa deferens secum, suavissimus factus est ferventibus animabus, quæ dicere possunt: Sicut desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus. Similiter Gabriel missus a cœlo ad Virginem benedictam, exhilaravit eamdem.
paras.en: [[25:25|As cold water|Aqua frigida]] to a [[25:25|soul|animæ]], that is, a person or man, [[25:25|thirsty|sitienti]], is (understand) sweet; [[25:25|so are good tidings from a far country|et nuntius bonus de terra longinqua]] [*nuntius* means both "tidings" and "messenger"; Denis takes it as the messenger], bringing good news, is pleasing to the lord by whom he was sent. So Christ, according to the nature he assumed, the messenger of God the Father, coming into this world from the land of the living, and bringing with him the best of news, and gifts and promises, has become most sweet to fervent souls, which can say: [[Ps 41:2|As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God|Sicut desiderat cervus ad fontes aquarum, ita desiderat anima mea ad te, Deus]]. Likewise Gabriel, sent from heaven to the blessed Virgin[[Luke 1:26||]][[Luke 1:27||]], gladdened her[[Luke 1:46||]].

paras.t: Fons turbatus pede, et vena corrupta: id est, quemadmodum aqua agitata suam amittit quietem et venustum adspectum, et sicut vena infecta est vitæ corruptiva; sic justus cadens coram impio, id est, oppressionem mortemve sustinens a persecutore iniquo: quia ex hoc multi insipientes judicant eum fuisse iniquum, et ipsum diffamant; vel, Cadens coram impio in peccatum: quoniam vitiosi homines proni sunt justos cadentes in culpam accusare, denigrare, et peccatum eorum exaggerare.
paras.en: [[25:26|a fountain troubled with the foot and a corrupted spring|Fons turbatus pede, et vena corrupta]]: that is, as stirred-up water loses its stillness and fair appearance, and as an infected vein [*vena*, the word rendered "spring", is also a vein of the body] corrupts life, so is [[25:26|A just man falling down before the wicked|justus cadens coram impio]], that is, suffering oppression or death from a wicked persecutor; for on this account many foolish people judge that he was wicked, and defame him; or, [[25:26|falling down before the wicked|Cadens coram impio]] into sin: for vicious men are prone to accuse just men who fall into sin, to blacken them and to exaggerate their sin.

paras.t: Sicut qui mel comedit multum, id est excessive, non est ei bonum, sed valde læsivum, ac fastidii mellis inductivum; sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, id est, ea quæ Dei sunt, irreverenter, intimorate, præsumptuose scrutari præsumit, videlicet occulta Dei judicia, et ea quæ prædestinationem præscientiamque concernunt, seu superbeatissimæ Trinitatis mysterium, opprimetur a gloria, id est, ab excellentia et incomprehensibilitate ac luce immensa tanti objecti vincetur, retundetur, et quodammodo excæcari videbitur. Nam sicut lux solis corporei, plenitudine suæ claritatis visum corporalem reverberat, et si diu sibi infigatur, excæcat; sic increata illa majestas sua infinita et incircumscriptibili excellentia, claritate, et actualitate, mentem humanam vincit, superat, et retundit in infinitum. Nempe, ut ait Boetius, quædam difficilia sunt ad intelligendum ex modicitate et imperfectione suæ entitatis, sicut materia prima, tempus et consimilia; quædam vero, ex eminentia suæ actualitatis et formalitatis, quemadmodum substantiæ separatæ, ad quarum notitiam ita se habet intellectus noster, sicut oculus vespertilionis ad lumen solis, secundum Philosophum. Quum ergo Deus excelsus et benedictus sit prorsus in infinitum perfectior, actualior, excellentior omni intelligentia, constat quod infinite nostram transcendat capacitatem. Propter quod ait et Plato in primo Timæi: Genitorem opificemque universi tam difficile invenire, quam inventum impossibile digne effari. Abstinendum est ergo ab omni incauto divinorum scrutinio; atque, ut divinus Dionysius ac Damascenus testantur, non est audendum aliquid de superessentiali dicere Deitate, præter ea quæ nobis in Scripturis sunt tradita. Moderata tamen humilisque scrutatio divinorum, auxilio gratiæ Dei innitens, est licita, dicente Propheta: Mirabilia testimonia tua, ideo scrutata est ea anima mea. Hinc quoque in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris.
paras.en: As [[25:27|for a man to eat much honey|Sicut qui mel comedit multum]], that is, to excess, [[25:27|it is not good|non est ei bonum]], but very harmful, and brings on a loathing of honey, [[25:27|so he that is a searcher of majesty|sic qui perscrutator est majestatis]], that is, who presumes to search into the things of God irreverently, without fear, presumptuously, namely the hidden judgements of God, and the things that concern predestination and foreknowledge, or the mystery of the most blessed Trinity, [[25:27|shall be overwhelmed by glory|opprimetur a gloria]], that is, he will be overcome and beaten back by the excellence and incomprehensibility and the boundless light of so great an object, and will seem in some way to be blinded. For as the light of the bodily sun by the fullness of its brightness dazzles bodily sight, and blinds it if it be fixed on it long, so that uncreated majesty, by its infinite and uncircumscribable excellence, brightness and actuality [that is, its being wholly in act, with nothing merely potential in it], overcomes, surpasses and beats back the human mind infinitely. For, as Boethius says, some things are hard to understand because of the slightness and imperfection of their being, such as prime matter, time and the like; others because of the eminence of their actuality and formality, such as the separated substances [that is, the angels and other spirits that exist apart from matter], to the knowledge of which our intellect is as the eye of a bat to the light of the sun, according to the Philosopher. Since, then, God, exalted and blessed, is altogether infinitely more perfect, more actual and more excellent than every intelligence, it is clear that he infinitely transcends our capacity. For which reason Plato too says in the first book of the *Timaeus*: To find the begetter and maker of the universe is as hard as, once he is found, it is impossible to speak of him worthily. We must therefore abstain from all incautious searching into divine things; and, as the divine Dionysius and Damascene testify, we must not dare to say anything of the superessential Godhead beyond what has been handed down to us in the Scriptures. Yet a moderate and humble searching into divine things, relying on the help of God's grace, is lawful, as the Prophet says: [[Ps 118:129|Thy testimonies are wonderful: therefore my soul hath sought them|Mirabilia testimonia tua, ideo scrutata est ea anima mea]]. Hence too it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:22|Seek not the things that are too high for thee, and search not into things above thy ability|Altiora te ne quæsieris, et fortiora te ne scrutatus fueris]].

paras.t: Sicut urbs patens, id est aperta, et absque murorum ambitu, ab hostibus citius expugnatur atque destruitur, et quid intra se habeat, introeuntibus manifestat; ita vir qui non potest, id est, non studet nec vult, in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum a verbis superfluis et incautis, ab invisibilibus hostibus faciliter superatur, læditur et necatur: quoniam ipsemet sua loquacitate contra se pugnat, suam quoque insipientiam, vanitatem, incustodiam, cogitationem et affectionem audientibus per propria verba pandit. Ideo ait Psalmista: Cohibe linguam tuam a malo. Et alia dicit scriptura: Verba prudentium statera ponderabuntur. Et alibi: Numquid vir verbosus justificabitur? Ponamus ergo custodiam ori nostro, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis nostris.
paras.en: [[25:28|As a city that lieth open|Sicut urbs patens]], that is, unguarded, [[25:28|and is not compassed with walls|et absque murorum ambitu]], is the sooner stormed and destroyed by enemies, and shows those who enter what it holds within, [[25:28|so is a man that cannot|ita vir qui non potest]], that is, does not strive or will to, [[25:28|refrain his own spirit in speaking|in loquendo cohibere spiritum suum]] from superfluous and incautious words: he is easily overcome, wounded and slain by invisible enemies, for by his own talkativeness he fights against himself, and by his own words lays bare to his hearers his folly, vanity, unguardedness, thoughts and affections. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 33:14|Keep thy tongue from evil|Cohibe linguam tuam a malo]]. And another scripture says: [[Ecclus 21:28|the words of the wise shall be weighed in a balance|Verba prudentium statera ponderabuntur]]. And elsewhere: [[Job 11:2|shall a man full of talk be justified?|Numquid vir verbosus justificabitur?]] Let us therefore set a watch before our mouth, and a door round about our lips[[Ps 140:3||]].

26.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI VICESIMI SEXTI : QUOMODO NIX IN ÆSTATE, ET PLUVIÆ IN MESSE, SIC INDECENS EST STULTO GLORIA.
26.title_en: Exposition of the twenty-sixth chapter: As snow in summer, and rain in harvest, so glory is not seemly for a fool.

paras.t: Quomodo nix in æstate inconveniens est, utpote contra solitum naturæ ac temporis cursum, eo quod nix generetur ex frigore magno, et pluvia in messe non congruunt, quia nociva sunt bladis : sic indecens est stulto gloria, id est fama clara, quia indignus est ea, vel honor manifestus, qui debetur virtutibus, non moralibus tantum, sed intellectualibus : vel, Gloria, id est lætitia : quum enim sit stultus, non habet in se unde ordinate ac spiritualiter jucundetur. Verumtamen, etsi stulto, ut tali, non congruat gloria, tamen si forsan prælatus sit, aut in aliqua eminentia constitutus, honorandus est ratione prælaturæ aut dignitatis. Unde sapientissimus princeps apostolici ordinis : Servi, inquit, subditi estote in omni timore dominis, non tantum bonis et modestis, sed et dyscolis.
paras.en: [[26:1|As snow in summer|Quomodo nix in æstate]] is unfitting, being against the usual course of nature and of the season, since snow is produced by great cold, [[26:1|and rain in harvest|et pluvia in messe]] are out of place, since they are harmful to the corn: [[26:1|so glory is not seemly for a fool|sic indecens est stulto gloria]], that is, bright fame, because he is unworthy of it; or open honour, which is owed to virtues, not only moral but also intellectual ones. Or, [[26:1|glory|Gloria]], that is, gladness: for since he is a fool, he has nothing in himself in which to rejoice in an ordered and spiritual way. Nevertheless, though glory does not befit a fool as such, yet if he happens to be a prelate, or set in some eminent position, he is to be honoured by reason of his prelacy or dignity. Hence the most wise prince of the apostolic order: [[1 Pet 2:18|Servants|Servi]], he says, [[1 Pet 2:18|be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle but also to the froward|subditi estote in omni timore dominis, non tantum bonis et modestis, sed et dyscolis]].

paras.t: Nam sicut avis ad alta transvolans, et passer quolibet vadens : id est, sicut avis volans in altum aeris locum, ad tempus in motu est, deinde alicubi requiescit, similiter passer vadens volando aut incedendo quolibet, id est ad aliquem locum in quo subsistit, vel, Quo libet, id est, quo sibi placuerit ; sic maledictum frustra prolatum, id est verbum maledictionis contra alterum injuste pronuntiatum, in quempiam superveniet, id est, in aliquem redundabit : quoniam etsi non noceat ei in quem profertur, vertitur tamen in crimen ei qui protulit illud, et in eos qui ei consentiunt. Ideo monet Apostolus : Benedicite persequentibus vos ; benedicite, et nolite maledicere. Nihilo minus quidam ad maledicendum aliis valde proni sunt, jamque impletum est quod Osee asserit : Maledictum et homicidium, mendacium, furtum et adulterium inundaverunt.
paras.en: For [[26:2|As a bird flying|sicut avis ad alta transvolans]] [Denis reads *ad alta*, "to the heights", where the Vulgate has *ad alia*, "to other places"], [[26:2|and a sparrow going here or there|et passer quolibet vadens]]: that is, as a bird flying up to a high place in the air is in motion for a time and then comes to rest somewhere, so likewise a sparrow going, by flying or by walking, *quolibet*, that is, to some place where it stops; or *quo libet*, that is, wherever it pleases [the one word *quolibet*, "anywhere", read as two, *quo libet*, "where it pleases"]; [[26:2|so a curse uttered without cause|sic maledictum frustra prolatum]], that is, a word of cursing pronounced unjustly against another, [[26:2|shall come upon a man|in quempiam superveniet]], that is, will rebound upon someone: for even if it does no harm to the one against whom it is uttered, yet it turns to the guilt of the one who uttered it, and of those who consent to him. Therefore the Apostle warns: [[Rom 12:14|Bless them that persecute you: bless, and curse not.|Benedicite persequentibus vos ; benedicite, et nolite maledicere]]. Nevertheless some are very prone to cursing others, and now that is fulfilled which Osee declares: [[Osee 4:2|Cursing, and lying, and killing, and theft, and adultery, have overflowed|Maledictum et homicidium, mendacium, furtum et adulterium inundaverunt]] [Denis puts killing before lying].

paras.t: Est autem maledicere, malum alicui imprecari : quod ex suo genere est mortale et caritati contrarium, quum et Apostolus fateatur, Neque maledici regnum Dei possidebunt : prout in secunda secundæ, quæstione 76, Thomas declarat. Attamen sancti viri leguntur quandoque maledixisse iniquis, quemadmodum quarto Regum Eliseus pueris pravis, et princeps Apostolorum Simoni mago ; sed talia facta sunt zelo justitiæ, non affectu iræ, invidiæ, aut similis malæ radicis. Vel imprecati sunt aliis mala poenalia, non in quantum sunt mala, sed ut justa supplicia, et purgantia a vitiis in præsenti : quemadmodum judex maledicit reo, in quem damnationis profert sententiam ; vel qui cupit alteri infirmitatem et adversitatem, ut per eas ab iniquitatibus retrahatur. Istud tamen non est proprie maledicere, quia non optatur malum ut tale.
paras.en: Now to curse is to call down evil upon someone: which is mortal by its kind [that is, of itself a mortal sin, though a slight or unconsidered curse may be venial] and contrary to charity, since the Apostle too declares: [[1 Cor 6:10|nor railers|Neque maledici]] [Latin *maledici*, "cursers"] [[1 Cor 6:10|shall possess the kingdom of God|regnum Dei possidebunt]]; as Thomas shows in the Second Part of the Second Part, question 76. Yet holy men are sometimes read to have cursed the wicked, as in the fourth book of Kings Eliseus cursed the wicked boys[[4 Kings 2:24||]], and the prince of the Apostles Simon Magus[[Acts 8:20||]]; but such things were done out of zeal for justice, not from a feeling of anger, envy, or some like evil root. Or they called down upon others penal evils, not inasmuch as they are evils, but as just punishments, and as purging from vices in the present life: as a judge curses a guilty man against whom he pronounces sentence of condemnation; or as one wishes another sickness and adversity, so that by them he may be drawn back from his iniquities. This, however, is not properly cursing, since the evil is not wished as such.

paras.t: Flagellum convenit equo pigro seu indomito, et camus asino, et virga in dorso imprudentium : id est, disciplina imprudentibus debetur, ut vel ipsi emendentur, quod si noluerint, alii eorum terreantur exemplo. Similiter indisciplinatis brutalibusque hominibus Deus misericordissime facit, dum per aspera et adversa, per infirmitates, terrores et damna eos compescit et reprimit a peccatis, sicut cuidam loquitur per Osee : Sepiam viam tuam spinis. Ideo orat Psalmista : In camo et freno maxillas eorum constringe, qui non approximant ad te. Unde et in libro Job inducitur : Pater mi, ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis, qui addit super peccata sua blasphemiam, id est, talem disciplinare non cesses, quousque resipiscens pœniteat.
paras.en: [[26:3|A whip for a horse|Flagellum convenit equo]], a lazy or untamed one, is fitting, [[26:3|and a snaffle for an ass, and a rod for the back of fools|et camus asino, et virga in dorso imprudentium]]: that is, correction is owed to fools, either that they themselves may be amended, or, if they will not, that others may be frightened by their example. In like manner God acts most mercifully with undisciplined and brutish men, when by hard and adverse things, by sicknesses, terrors and losses, He restrains them and holds them back from sins, as He says to someone through Osee: [[Osee 2:6|I will hedge up thy way with thorns|Sepiam viam tuam spinis]]. Therefore the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 31:9|With bit and bridle bind fast their jaws, who come not near unto thee|In camo et freno maxillas eorum constringe, qui non approximant ad te]] [*bit* here is *camus*, the "snaffle" of v. 3]. Hence in the book of Job too it is said: [[Job 34:36|My father|Pater mi]], [[Job 34:36|cease not from the man of iniquity|ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis]], [[Job 34:37|because he addeth blasphemy upon his sins|qui addit super peccata sua blasphemiam]]; that is, do not cease to correct such a man, until he comes to his senses and repents.

paras.t: Ne respondeas stulto, id est homini vitioso, juxta stultitiam suam : id est, quamvis ipse insipienter et injuriose loquatur aut quærat, non tamen insipienter et vitiose respondeas; ne efficiaris ei similis : quia hoc esset vinci a malo, et verbis contendere. Imo agendum est quod loquitur Paulus : Libenter suffertis insipientes, quum sitis ipsi sapientes.
paras.en: [[26:4|Answer not a fool|Ne respondeas stulto]], that is, a vicious man, [[26:4|according to his folly|juxta stultitiam suam]]: that is, though he himself speaks or asks foolishly and insultingly, yet do not answer foolishly and viciously; [[26:4|lest thou be made like him|ne efficiaris ei similis]]: for this would be to be [[Rom 12:21|overcome by evil|vinci a malo]], and to contend in words[[2 Tim 2:14||]]. Rather, we must do what Paul speaks of: [[2 Cor 11:19|you gladly suffer the foolish: whereas yourselves are wise|Libenter suffertis insipientes, quum sitis ipsi sapientes]].

paras.t: Responde stulto juxta stultitiam suam, ne sibi sapiens esse videatur. Istud videtur præfatæ doctrinæ contrarium, sed non est : quoniam sensus est : Responde stulto juxta stultitiam suam, id est, juxta exigentiam atque demeritum sui stulti sermonis, da ei aptam responsionem, vel ejus verba ironice repetendo, vel suam insipientiam ei declarando, aut eum increpatorie seu reprobative interrogando, seu verba justi rigoris et debitæ invectionis enuntiando ; ne putet se sapientem, sed suam advertat impietatem, imperitiam aut errorem : quemadmodum martyres sancti frequenter responderunt tyrannis, imo et præclarissimæ virgines, ut Agatha, Cæcilia et Lucia. Interdum etenim licet et expedit clavo clavum retundere, dum impii seu improbi homines aliter informari aut reprimi nequeunt. Unde et Christus a Pharisæis interrogatus, Cur discipuli tui transgrediuntur traditionem seniorum? respondit : Quare et vos transgredimini præceptum Dei, propter traditionem vestram? Verumtamen in hac re discretio valde est necessaria, ne sub colore zeli justitiæ, ira et impatientia admittantur. Ideo unusquisque conscientiam suam examinet, quo affectu, qua intentione, qua tranquillitate locutus sit.
paras.en: [[26:5|Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he imagine himself to be wise.|Responde stulto juxta stultitiam suam, ne sibi sapiens esse videatur]] This seems contrary to the teaching just given, but it is not: for the sense is: [[26:5|Answer a fool according to his folly|Responde stulto juxta stultitiam suam]], that is, according to what his foolish speech calls for and deserves, give him a fitting answer: either by repeating his words ironically, or by showing him his folly, or by questioning him in rebuke or reproof, or by uttering words of just severity and due invective; so that he may not think himself wise, but may notice his impiety, his unskilfulness or his error: as the holy martyrs often answered tyrants, and indeed the most glorious virgins too, such as Agatha, Cecilia and Lucy. For at times it is lawful and expedient to beat back a nail with a nail [a proverb: to meet like with like], when wicked or unprincipled men cannot otherwise be taught or checked. Hence Christ too, when asked by the Pharisees, [[Matt 15:2|Why do thy disciples transgress the tradition of the ancients?|Cur discipuli tui transgrediuntur traditionem seniorum?]] answered: [[Matt 15:3|Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for your tradition?|Quare et vos transgredimini præceptum Dei, propter traditionem vestram?]] Yet in this matter discretion is very necessary, lest under colour of zeal for justice, anger and impatience creep in. Therefore let each one examine his conscience, with what feeling, with what intention, with what calm he has spoken.

paras.t: Claudus pedibus, id est, claudicanti est similis, nec in via virtutum expedite procedit, et iniquitatem bibens, id est abundanter peccans, seu nocumentum quod est effectus iniquitatis, accipiens, est qui mittit verba per nuntium stultum, id est, indiscreto et malitioso legationem seu expeditionem arduæ rei committit, dummodo sciat nuntium esse hujusmodi. Talis etenim nuntius infideliter agit et imperite, et interdum sponte variat verba, et provocat jurgia, damnaque infert. Potissime autem peccat, qui homines vitiosos, diffames, hæreticos sive schismaticos, ad prædicandum et gubernandum alios mittit. Porro, qui graviter peccat, dicitur iniquitatem potare, juxta illud in libro Job : Bibens subsannationem quasi aquam.
paras.en: [[26:6|lame of feet|Claudus pedibus]], that is, like one who limps, and not going forward readily on the way of the virtues, [[26:6|and drinketh iniquity|et iniquitatem bibens]], that is, sinning abundantly, or receiving the harm that is the effect of iniquity, is [[26:6|He that sendeth words by a foolish messenger|qui mittit verba per nuntium stultum]]: that is, he who entrusts an embassy, or the carrying out of a difficult matter, to an indiscreet and malicious man, provided he knows the messenger to be such. For such a messenger acts unfaithfully and unskilfully, and at times changes the words of his own accord, and stirs up quarrels, and does harm. But he sins most of all who sends vicious, ill-famed, heretical or schismatic men to preach to and govern others. Further, one who sins gravely is said to drink iniquity, according to that saying in the book of Job: [[Job 34:7|drinketh up scorning like water|Bibens subsannationem quasi aquam]].

paras.t: Quomodo pulchras frustra habet claudus tibias, quia eis uti non valet ; sic indecens est in ore stultorum parabola, id est parabolica doctrina. Quum enim sint impii, docere alios sunt indigni, nec sapientialia verba decenter exponunt : imo ex eorum carnalitate et pravitate vilescit audientibus doctrina ipsorum.
paras.en: [[26:7|As a lame man hath fair legs in vain|Quomodo pulchras frustra habet claudus tibias]], since he cannot use them; [[26:7|so a parable is unseemly in the mouth of fools|sic indecens est in ore stultorum parabola]], that is, teaching in parables. For since they are wicked, they are unworthy to teach others, nor do they set forth the words of wisdom fittingly: indeed, through their carnality and depravity their teaching grows cheap to those who hear it.

paras.t: Sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii, id est, adjutorium præbet, et saxum apponit acervo materiæ, ex qua ædificatur templum Mercurio, uni deorum gentilium: sicut, inquam, talis reprehensibiliter facit, ita qui tribuit insipienti, ut tali, honorem : quia, ut sic, est honore indignus. Vel iste est sensus : Sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii, id est in cumulum lapillorum per quos computare solebant mercatores, Mercurium specialiter venerantes, perturbat eosdem; ita qui insipientem honorat, ordinem rerum conturbat.
paras.en: [[26:8|As he that casteth a stone into the heap of Mercury|Sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii]], that is, gives help and adds a stone to the heap of material from which a temple is being built to Mercury, one of the gods of the heathen: as, I say, such a man acts blameworthily, [[26:8|so is he that giveth honour to a fool|ita qui tribuit insipienti, ut tali, honorem]] as such: since, as such, he is unworthy of honour. Or this is the sense: [[26:8|As he that casteth a stone into the heap of Mercury|Sicut qui mittit lapidem in acervum Mercurii]], that is, into the pile of pebbles by which merchants, who especially worshipped Mercury, used to reckon, throws them into confusion; so he who honours a fool throws the order of things into confusion.

paras.t: Quomodo si spina nascatur in manu temulenti, id est ebrii, pungit et lædit tam temulentum, quam illos quos accipit manu spinosa; sic parabola in ore stultorum tam stultos fœdat et lædit doctores, quam eos qui audiunt, gravat, scandalizat, offendit.
paras.en: [[26:9|As if a thorn should grow in the hand of a drunkard|Quomodo si spina nascatur in manu temulenti]], that is, of a drunken man, it pricks and hurts both the drunkard and those whom he takes hold of with his thorny hand; [[26:9|so is a parable in the mouth of fools|sic parabola in ore stultorum]] both defiles and hurts the foolish teachers themselves, and burdens, scandalizes and offends those who hear.

paras.t: Judicium, id est sententia judicis, determinat causas, id est, expedit lites quæ coram tribunali ventilantur: et qui imponit stulto silentium, iras mitigat quæ ex loquacitate pravorum nascuntur.
paras.en: [[26:10|Judgment|Judicium]], that is, the sentence of the judge, [[26:10|determineth causes|determinat causas]], that is, settles the suits that are argued before the tribunal: [[26:10|and he that putteth a fool to silence, appeaseth anger|et qui imponit stulto silentium, iras mitigat]], the anger that arises from the talkativeness of the wicked.

paras.t: Sicut canis qui revertitur ad vomitum suum, id est, sæpius vomit, seu id quod vomuit resorbet, est fœdus et turpiter agens; sic imprudens qui iterat stultitiam suam, id est peccator recidivans, et quod per confessionem ejecit, denuo faciens. Huic consonat, quod in secunda sua ait epistola præstantissimus Petrus: Melius erat illis non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti. Contigit enim eis illud veri proverbii: Canis reversus ad vomitum suum.
paras.en: [[26:11|As a dog that returneth to his vomit|Sicut canis qui revertitur ad vomitum suum]], that is, vomits again and again, or swallows again what it has vomited, is foul and acts filthily; [[26:11|so is the fool that repeateth his folly|sic imprudens qui iterat stultitiam suam]], that is, the sinner who falls back, and does again what he cast out by confession. With this agrees what the most excellent Peter says in his second epistle: [[2 Pet 2:21|it had been better for them not to have known the way of justice than, after they have known it, to turn back|Melius erat illis non cognoscere viam justitiæ, quam post agnitionem retrorsum reverti]]. [[2 Pet 2:22|For, that of the true proverb has happened to them: The dog is returned to his vomit|Contigit enim eis illud veri proverbii: Canis reversus ad vomitum suum]].

paras.t: Vidisti hominem sapientem sibi videri in se et ex se, seu magis quam est? Magis illo spem habebit stultus, id est, curabilior illo erit peccator defectum suum perpendens, et insipientem se cognoscens. Ideo scriptum est: Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes. Paulus quoque: Nolite, inquit, prudentes esse apud vosmetipsos, id est propria reputatione. Nemo enim absque revelatione potest certo scire se sapientiam illam quæ est donum habere, quoniam caritati inseparabiliter est conjuncta. Qui autem noverunt se esse in caritate et desuper illustratos, ut sancti Apostoli, cognoscebant in Deo esse se sapientes, cum gratiarum actione et humilitate. Itaque non arbitremur nos sapientes, sed potius defectuosos et fatuos, quia revera multæ et magnæ sunt stoliditates peccantium; nec alios aspernemur ut stultos, imo magis pensemus peccata nostra præterita, et bona quæ desunt, quam quæ forsan habemus.
paras.en: [[26:12|Hast thou seen a man wise|Vidisti hominem sapientem]] [[26:12|in his own conceit|sibi videri]], in himself and of himself, or more than he is? [[26:12|there shall be more hope of a fool than of him|Magis illo spem habebit stultus]]: that is, a sinner who weighs his own failing and knows himself to be foolish will be easier to cure than he. Therefore it is written: [[Is 5:21|Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own conceits.|Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes]] Paul too: [[Rom 12:16|Be not|Nolite]], he says, [[Rom 12:16|wise in your own conceits|prudentes esse apud vosmetipsos]], that is, in your own estimation. For no one without a revelation can know for certain that he has that wisdom which is a gift [that is, wisdom as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost], since it is inseparably joined to charity. But those who knew that they were in charity and enlightened from above, as the holy Apostles, knew themselves to be wise in God, with thanksgiving and humility. Let us therefore not think ourselves wise, but rather faulty and foolish, since truly many and great are the stupidities of sinners; nor let us despise others as fools, but rather let us weigh our past sins, and the good things we lack, more than those we perhaps have.

paras.t: Dicit piger: Leo est in via, et leæna in itineribus. Hoc supra scriptum est atque expositum.
paras.en: [[26:13|The slothful man saith: There is a lion in the way, and a lioness in the roads.|Dicit piger: Leo est in via, et leæna in itineribus]] This was written and expounded above[[Prov 22:13||]].

paras.t: Sicut ostium vertitur in cardine suo, ita piger in lectulo suo. Unde præhabitum est: Pigredo immittit soporem. Et piger abhorret laborem, et repausationem diligit corporalem: sicque multa bona omittit.
paras.en: [[26:14|As the door turneth upon its hinges, so doth the slothful upon his bed.|Sicut ostium vertitur in cardine suo, ita piger in lectulo suo]] Hence it was said before: [[Prov 19:15|Slothfulness casteth into a deep sleep|Pigredo immittit soporem]]. And the slothful man shrinks from labour and loves bodily rest: and so he leaves many good things undone.

paras.t: Abscondit piger manus sub ascella sua, et laborat si ad os suum eas converterit. Hoc etiam supra expositum est.
paras.en: [[26:15|The slothful hideth his hand under his armpit, and it grieveth him to turn it to his mouth.|Abscondit piger manus sub ascella sua, et laborat si ad os suum eas converterit]] This too was expounded above[[Prov 19:24||]].

paras.t: Sapientior sibi piger videtur septem viris loquentibus sententias. Majoris enim putat esse prudentiæ quærere et servare repausationem carnalem, diu dormire, pericula negotiantium evitare, quam vigiliis, studiis, laboribusque insistere; suam ignaviam sæpe putat esse discretionem, ac peritum se arbitratur, quum excusaverit suum torporem; viros quoque sapientes ac fervidos, ardua virtutum exercitia edocentes, judicat indiscretos.
paras.en: [[26:16|The sluggard is wiser in his own conceit, than seven men that speak sentences.|Sapientior sibi piger videtur septem viris loquentibus sententias]] For he thinks it a mark of greater prudence to seek and keep bodily rest, to sleep long, and to avoid the dangers that those who do business run, than to apply himself to vigils, studies and labours; he often thinks his sloth to be discretion, and reckons himself skilful when he has excused his torpor; and men who are wise and fervent, who teach the hard exercises of the virtues, he judges indiscreet.

paras.t: Sicut qui apprehendit auribus canem acquirit morsum et læsionem a cane impatiente et iracundo: sic qui pertransit impatiens, et commiscetur rixæ alterius, id est, corrixantibus se immiscet, non ad pacificandum, sed adjuvando unam partem ex irrationabili causa: quia ex hoc vulnerationem sæpe incurrit.
paras.en: [[26:17|As he that taketh a dog by the ears|Sicut qui apprehendit auribus canem]] gets bitten and hurt by the dog, impatient and angry as it is: [[26:17|so is he that passeth by in anger, and meddleth with another man's quarrel|sic qui pertransit impatiens, et commiscetur rixæ alterius]], that is, mixes himself in with those who are quarrelling, not to make peace, but by helping one party for no reasonable cause: since from this he often gets wounded.

paras.t: Sicut noxius est, id est proximo valde nocivus, qui mittit lanceas et sagittas in mortem, id est ad alios occidendos: sic vir qui fraudulenter nocet amico suo: sicut impiissimus Tryphon occidit Antiochum regem adolescentem, virtuosumque Jonathan cepit, ac filios ejus procuravit sibi mitti, quos interfecit. Et quum fuerit deprehensus per opus iniquum, dicit: Ludens feci, id est, intentionem nocendi non habui, sed improvise sic contigit.
paras.en: [[26:18|As he is guilty|Sicut noxius est]], that is, very harmful to his neighbour, [[26:18|that shooteth arrows, and lances unto death|qui mittit lanceas et sagittas in mortem]], that is, to kill others: [[26:19|So is the man that hurteth his friend deceitfully|sic vir qui fraudulenter nocet amico suo]]: as the most impious Tryphon slew the young king Antiochus[[1 Mach 13:31||]], and took the virtuous Jonathan[[1 Mach 12:48||]], and procured that his sons be sent to him, and killed them[[1 Mach 13:23||]]. [[26:19|and when he is taken|Et quum fuerit deprehensus]] in a wicked deed, he [[26:19|saith: I did it in jest|dicit: Ludens feci]], that is, I had no intention of harming, but it happened so unawares.

paras.t: Quum defecerint ligna, extinguetur ignis, cujus materia ligna sunt. Nam causa deficiente, deficit et effectus. Et susurrone subtracto, qui scilicet in aure susurrando profert verba detractoria, aut discordiæ seminativa, ex quibus nascuntur contentiones et jurgia: jurgia conquiescunt. Juxta quem modum scriptum est supra: Ejice derisorem, et exibit cum eo jurgium, cessabuntque causæ et contumeliæ.
paras.en: [[26:20|When the wood faileth, the fire shall go out|Quum defecerint ligna, extinguetur ignis]], of which wood is the fuel. For when the cause fails, the effect fails too. [[26:20|and when the talebearer is taken away|Et susurrone subtracto]] [Latin *susurro*, "whisperer"], that is, he who, whispering in the ear, utters words of detraction, or words that sow discord, from which contentions and quarrels arise: [[26:20|contentions shall cease|jurgia conquiescunt]]. In this way it was written above: [[Prov 22:10|Cast out the scoffer, and contention shall go out with him, and quarrels and reproaches shall cease.|Ejice derisorem, et exibit cum eo jurgium, cessabuntque causæ et contumeliæ]]

paras.t: Sicut carbones ad prunas, quibus appositi accenduntur, et ligna ad ignem, quem nutriunt et augmentant; sic homo iracundus suscitat rixas, proferendo verba injuriosa, et alium invadendo desiderio ultionis.
paras.en: [[26:21|As coals are to burning coals|Sicut carbones ad prunas]], by which, laid beside them, they are kindled, [[26:21|and wood to fire|et ligna ad ignem]], which it feeds and increases; [[26:21|so an angry man stirreth up strife|sic homo iracundus suscitat rixas]], by uttering insulting words, and attacking another in the desire for revenge.

paras.t: Verba susurronis quasi simplicia, et ipsa perveniunt ad intima cordis. Hoc supra expositum est.
paras.en: [[26:22|The words of a talebearer are as it were simple, but they reach to the innermost parts of the belly|Verba susurronis quasi simplicia, et ipsa perveniunt ad intima cordis]] [Denis has *cordis*, "of the heart", where the Vulgate has *ventris*, "of the belly"]. This was expounded above[[Prov 18:8||]] [the margin reads Prov. xxviii, 8; the passage is 18:8].

paras.t: Quomodo si argento sordido, id est, in quo scoria manet, ornare velis vas fictile: qui ornatus non convenit; sic labia tumentia, quæ proferunt verba elata, cum pessimo corde sociata: quorum conjunctio est periculosa, quia quod latet in corde, mox per labia animosa profertur in medium.
paras.en: As if [[26:23|with silver dross|argento sordido]], that is, with silver in which the dross remains, thou wouldst adorn [[26:23|an earthern vessel|vas fictile]]: an adornment that is not fitting; so are [[26:23|Swelling lips|labia tumentia]], which utter proud words, [[26:23|joined with a corrupt heart|cum pessimo corde sociata]]: their union is dangerous, because what lies hidden in the heart is soon brought out into the open through bold lips.

paras.t: Unde subjungitur: Labiis suis intelligitur inimicus, id est, per verba superba et injuriosa, hostis occultus prodit se ipsum, quum in corde tractaverit dolos, id est, intra se excogitaverit modum et vias nocendi dolose et clam: sicque interdum contra propositum suum, ex impetu passionum pandit suam iniquitatem: de quo postea dolet, et cupit per verba ficta amicitiam demonstrare, ut non observantibus se acrius ac celerius noceat.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[26:24|An enemy is known by his lips|Labiis suis intelligitur inimicus]], that is, through proud and insulting words the hidden foe betrays himself, [[26:24|when in his heart he entertaineth deceit|quum in corde tractaverit dolos]], that is, when he has thought out within himself the manner and ways of doing harm craftily and secretly: and so at times, against his own purpose, he lays bare his iniquity in the rush of passion: which he afterwards regrets, and seeks by feigned words to show friendship, so as to harm more sharply and more quickly those who are not on their guard against him.

paras.t: Idcirco subjungitur: Quando submiserit vocem suam, bassius humiliusque loquendo ex fictione, ne credideris ei, sed observa te, quia abundans cautela non nocet, præcipue circa talem; quoniam septem nequitiæ sunt in corde illius: id est, omni modo sibi possibili machinatur tibi malum. Septenario quippe universitas designatur.
paras.en: Therefore it is added: [[26:25|When he shall speak low|Quando submiserit vocem suam]], speaking more softly and humbly out of pretence, [[26:25|trust him not|ne credideris ei]], but be on thy guard, since abundant caution does no harm, especially with such a man; [[26:25|because there are seven mischiefs in his heart|quoniam septem nequitiæ sunt in corde illius]]: that is, he plots evil against thee in every way possible to him. For by the number seven totality is signified.

paras.t: Qui operit odium fraudulenter, id est, rancorem suum contra alium dolose occultat, aut per amicitiæ signa oppositum simulat, quemadmodum Joab Amasam osculando; revelabitur malitia ejus in consilio, id est, per diligentem inquisitionem poterit deprehendi ex aliquibus factis aut signis, aut revelatione quorumdam: sicut in libro [primo] Machabæorum sæpe habetur, quod Judæ et fratribus ejus innotuit odium et machinatio adversariorum. Istud tamen quandoque fieri nequit per humanam industriam; sed in consilio atque judicio Dei omne malum, quantumcumque absconditum, manifestabitur, sicut in Evangelio asserit Christus: Nihil absconditum quod non reveletur.
paras.en: [[26:26|He that covereth hatred deceitfully|Qui operit odium fraudulenter]], that is, craftily hides his rancour against another, or feigns the opposite by signs of friendship, as Joab did in kissing Amasa[[2 Kings 20:9||]][[2 Kings 20:10||]]; [[26:26|his malice shall be laid open in the public assembly|revelabitur malitia ejus in consilio]], that is, it can be found out by careful inquiry, from some deeds or signs, or by the disclosure of certain persons: as we often find in the first book of Machabees, that the hatred and plotting of their adversaries became known to Judas and his brethren[[1 Mach 3:42||]][[1 Mach 5:10||]][[1 Mach 5:25||]][[1 Mach 7:30||]] [the margin gives 1 Mach. iii, 42; v, 10–15, 25–27; vii, 30]. Yet this sometimes cannot be done by human effort; but in the council [*consilium*, the word rendered "assembly" in the verse] and judgment of God every evil, however hidden, will be made manifest, as Christ declares in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:2|there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed|Nihil absconditum quod non reveletur]].

paras.t: Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam: id est, qui alteri molitur insidias, laqueosque extendit et parat ruinam, patietur pro suo facinore debitam pœnam; et iniquitas sua redundat in ipsum, magisque lædit se ipsum peccando, quam alium damna aut supplicia inferendo: imo frequenter in hac vita cadit in malum quod alteri præparavit, sicut Judæi Christum et ejus discipulos occidendo, fugando, despoliando, meruerunt a Romanis occidi, captivari, et toto orbe dispergi. Unde ait Salvator: Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit; et Psalmista, Lacum aperuit et effodit eum, et incidit in foveam quam fecit.
paras.en: [[26:27|He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it|Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam]]: that is, he who lays snares for another, and spreads nets and prepares his ruin, will suffer the punishment due for his crime; and his iniquity rebounds upon himself, and he harms himself more by sinning than he harms the other by inflicting losses or punishments: indeed, often in this life he falls into the evil he prepared for another, as the Jews, by killing, putting to flight and despoiling Christ and His disciples, deserved to be killed by the Romans, taken captive, and scattered through the whole world. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 26:52|all that take the sword shall perish with the sword|Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 7:16|He hath opened a pit and dug it: and he is fallen into the hole he made.|Lacum aperuit et effodit eum, et incidit in foveam quam fecit]]

paras.t: Atque ad idem spectat quod subditur: et qui volvit lapidem, revertetur ad eum: quia qui grave malum nititur superinducere alteri, meretur opprimi et perire; et frequenter ab eis vastatur, quos conabatur suppeditare, sicut et Balaam a filiis Israel fuit occisus, de quorum deceptione et morte dedit consilium. Simili modo perierunt Absalon atque Achitophel, qui contra David conspiraverunt. Hinc in Ecclesiaste legitur: Qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber. Et alibi dicitur: Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur. Attendant hæc qui suis vitiis ac passionibus sic obtenebrantur, ut quum detraxerint proximis, aut quamcumque injuriam intulerint eis, gloriantur et jactant se illis nocuisse, quum potius nocuerint sibimetipsis, illis vero, dummodo fuerint patientes, profuerint, et gloriæ coronam paraverint. Etenim nulla nocebit adversitas, si nulla dominetur iniquitas. Itaque uniuscujusque malum in proprium redundat auctorem. Ideo scriptum est: Væ impio in malum; retributio enim manuum ejus fiet ei.
paras.en: And to the same point looks what follows: [[26:27|and he that rolleth a stone, it shall return to him|et qui volvit lapidem, revertetur ad eum]]: because he who strives to bring a grave evil upon another deserves to be crushed and to perish; and often he is laid waste by those whom he was trying to trample underfoot, as Balaam too was slain by the children of Israel[[Num 31:8||]], for whose deceiving and death he had given counsel[[Num 31:16||]]. In like manner Absalom[[2 Kings 18:9||]][[2 Kings 18:14||]][[2 Kings 18:15||]] and Achitophel[[2 Kings 17:23||]] perished, who had conspired against David[[2 Kings 15:1||]] [the margin gives 2 Kings xv, 1–12]. Hence we read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:8|he that breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him|Qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber]]. And elsewhere it is said: [[Ecclus 27:30|A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back upon the author|Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur]]. Let those take heed of this who are so darkened by their vices and passions that, when they have detracted from their neighbours or done them any injury whatever, they glory and boast that they have harmed them, when rather they have harmed themselves, but have profited the others, provided these were patient, and have prepared a crown of glory for them. For no adversity will harm, if no iniquity holds sway. And so each one's evil rebounds upon its own author. Therefore it is written: [[Is 3:11|Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be given him.|Væ impio in malum; retributio enim manuum ejus fiet ei]]

paras.t: Lingua fallax non amat veritatem, sed dolosa mendosaque verba, ac testimonia falsa ; et os lubricum, id est libidinosum, seu faciliter labile ad verba illicita, operatur ruinas : quia ex verbis quæ profert, frequenter sequuntur facta injusta et opera vitiosa, sicque loquentem præcipitat ad inferni supplicia.
paras.en: [[26:28|A deceitful tongue loveth not truth|Lingua fallax non amat veritatem]], but crafty and lying words, and false testimonies; [[26:28|and a slippery mouth|et os lubricum]], that is, a lustful one, or one that slips easily into unlawful words, [[26:28|worketh ruin|operatur ruinas]]: because from the words it utters there often follow unjust deeds and vicious works, and so it casts the speaker headlong into the torments of hell.

27.title: ELUCIDATIO CAPITULI VICESIMI SEPTIMI : NE GLORIERIS IN CRASTINUM, IGNORANS QUID SUPERVENTURA PARIAT DIES.
27.title_en: Elucidation of the twenty-seventh chapter: Boast not for to-morrow, for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth.

paras.t: Ne glorieris in crastinum: id est, non præsumas pro certo te crastino die victurum, quia, ut ait Salvator, nescimus diem neque horam; nec differas vitæ tuæ emendationem, quasi velis eam emendare in posterum, sicque de crastino, id est futuro tempore glorieris, quasi bona operaturus in illo (solet enim cras, pro futuro accipi in Scripturis, sicut in Genesi Jacob ait, Cras respondebit mihi justitia mea); nec præsupponas te cras aut postea lucraturum; ignorans quid superventura pariat dies, id est, quid tibi in eo contingat, an scilicet vives in eo, et an sanus eris, an æger, an prospera habiturus, an adversa. Hinc contra præsumentes de crastino, scriptum est: Ecce qui nunc dicitis, Hodie aut crastino ibimus in illam civitatem, et faciemus quidem ibi annum, et mercabimur, et lucrum faciemus: qui ignoratis quid sit vobis in crastinum. Sic ergo vivamus, quasi quocumque die morituri: quia, ut ait Gregorius, qui tibi promisit de peccato, si pœniteas, veniam, non tibi promisit crastinum diem. Hinc in Proverbiis suis Seneca scripsit: Omnes vitam differentes, incerta mors prævenit. Omnis igitur dies tanquam ultimus ordinandus est.
paras.en: [[27:1|Boast not for to morrow|Ne glorieris in crastinum]]: that is, do not presume for certain that thou wilt live tomorrow, for, as the Saviour says, [[Matt 25:13|you know not the day nor the hour|nescimus diem neque horam]] [Denis has "we know not"]; and do not put off the amendment of thy life, as though thou wouldst amend it later, and so boast of tomorrow, that is, of time to come, as though thou wert going to do good works in it (for in the Scriptures *tomorrow* is often taken for the future, as when Jacob says in Genesis: [[Gen 30:33|And my justice shall answer for me tomorrow|Cras respondebit mihi justitia mea]]); and do not take it for granted that thou wilt make a gain tomorrow or afterwards; [[27:1|for thou knowest not what the day to come may bring forth|ignorans quid superventura pariat dies]]: that is, what may befall thee in it: whether thou wilt live in it, whether thou wilt be well or sick, whether thou wilt meet prosperity or adversity. Hence it is written against those who presume upon tomorrow: [[Jas 4:13|Behold, now you that say: To-day or to-morrow we will go into such a city, and there we will spend a year and will traffic and make our gain|Ecce qui nunc dicitis, Hodie aut crastino ibimus in illam civitatem, et faciemus quidem ibi annum, et mercabimur, et lucrum faciemus]]: [[Jas 4:14|Whereas you know not what shall be on the morrow|qui ignoratis quid sit vobis in crastinum]]. Let us therefore live as though we were to die on any day: for, as Gregory says, he who has promised thee pardon for sin if thou repent has not promised thee tomorrow. Hence Seneca wrote in his Proverbs: Uncertain death overtakes all who put off living. Every day, then, is to be ordered as though it were the last.

paras.t: Laudet te alienus: id est, sic vive, ut ab aliis sis dignus laudari: nam propter ea quæ insunt a natura, non meremur laudari, nec vituperari, secundum Philosophum. Et quamvis fueris laude dignus, et non tamen laudet te os tuum: quia laus propria sordet. Extraneus, et non labia tua: nam, ut ait Apostolus, Oportet etiam ab his qui foris sunt, testimonium bonum habere. Non tamen debemus humanam appetere laudem, sed potius abhorrere, quum simus valde defectuosi atque culpabiles, et ne aliquid mercedis recipiamus in vita præsenti, et quoniam certi non sumus quod opera nostra vere procedant ex caritate; sed taliter conversemur, ut digni existamus præconiis, sicut et Seneca loquitur: Quam magnum est, non laudari, et esse laudabilem! Et rursus: Quid sis inter est, non quid habeas.
paras.en: [[27:2|Let another praise thee|Laudet te alienus]]: that is, live in such a way that thou art worthy to be praised by others: for we do not merit praise or blame for what is in us by nature, according to the Philosopher. And although thou be worthy of praise, still [[27:2|and not thy own mouth|et non os tuum]] praise thee, for self-praise is mean. [[27:2|a stranger, and not thy own lips|Extraneus, et non labia tua]]: for, as the Apostle says, [[1 Tim 3:7|he must have a good testimony of them who are without|Oportet etiam ab his qui foris sunt, testimonium bonum habere]]. Yet we ought not to desire human praise, but rather to shrink from it, since we are very faulty and blameworthy, and lest we receive some of our reward in the present life, and because we are not sure that our works truly proceed from charity; but we should so live as to be worthy of praise, as Seneca too says: How great a thing it is not to be praised, and yet to be praiseworthy! And again: What matters is what thou art, not what thou hast.

paras.t: Nihilo minus sancti viri interdum pro confortatione suæ fiduciæ, aut pro aliorum ædificatione et perversorum confutatione, ad laudem et gloriam Dei, quandoque suas commemorant aut describunt virtutes ac merita, aut excellentiam gratiæ eis concessæ: quemadmodum Ezechias loquitur Deo, Memento quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et corde perfecto; Paulus quoque, præsertim in epistola ad Corinthios: qui etiam ad Romanos testatur, Nos ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes. Sic et interdum volunt honorari a subditis, in quantum sunt vicarii Dei: non propter se, sed ne Deus inhonoretur in eis, et ne subditi peccent, debitum eis honorem non tribuendo.
paras.en: Nevertheless holy men sometimes, to strengthen their own confidence, or to edify others and confute the perverse, for the praise and glory of God, now and then recall or describe their own virtues and merits, or the excellence of the grace granted them: as Ezechias says to God, [[4 Kings 20:3|remember how I have walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart|Memento quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et corde perfecto]]; and Paul too, especially in the epistle to the Corinthians[[2 Cor 11:22||]], who also testifies to the Romans: [[Rom 8:23|ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit|Nos ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes]]. So also they sometimes wish to be honoured by their subjects, inasmuch as they are God's vicars: not for their own sake, but lest God be dishonoured in them, and lest their subjects sin by not paying them the honour due.

paras.t: Grave est saxum, ut lapis molaris, seu quodcumque mortale peccatum, quod suo mox pondere trahit ad aliud, et impœnitentem præcipitat in gehennam; et onerosa arena conglutinata seu multiplicata, vel venialium multitudo. Sed ira stulti, id est hominis vitiosi, utpote ira per vitium, non per zelum, utroque est gravior ad portandum hominibus, nisi sapientibus ac perfectis. Multis enim mortalibus peccatis, non omnibus, ira est gravior coram Deo atque hominibus.
paras.en: [[27:3|A stone is heavy|Grave est saxum]], such as a millstone, or any mortal sin whatever, which by its weight soon drags a man to another, and hurls the impenitent into hell; [[27:3|and sand weighty|et onerosa arena]], massed together or multiplied, or the multitude of venial sins. [[27:3|but the anger of a fool|Sed ira stulti]], that is, of a vicious man, namely anger from vice, not from zeal, [[27:3|is heavier than them both|utroque est gravior]] for men to bear, except for the wise and perfect. For anger is heavier before God and men than many mortal sins, though not than all.

paras.t: Ira non habet misericordiam: loquendo de ira per vitium, rationem omnino obtenebrante, quæ ex suo genere est unum de septem peccatis mortalibus; nec erumpens furor: quia crudelitate, non pietate, utuntur ac agitantur. Et impetum concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit? Hinc, secundum Philosophum, ira est animæ ægritudo. Et consonat istud ei quod dictum est supra: Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere? Hinc in Proverbiis suis Seneca contestatur: Nihil minus quam irasci punientem decet, quum per hoc magis ad emendationem proficiat; itemque, Ira in temeritatem prona est, et periculum inferre non cavet. Hinc denuo loquitur: In vindicando criminosa est celeritas. Est autem ira hæc vehementer detestanda, ac diligentissime evitanda, quia per eam, quasi per canem, communitas inquietatur, gratia vitæ spiritualis aufertur, proximus scandalizatur, ratio obscuratur, mens Spiritum Sanctum repellit, et hominem bruto, imo furenti belluæ similem reddit. Sed, ut ait Ambrosius, Qui sibi ipsi irascitur quia iram admisit, desinit proximo suo irasci. Qui autem vult iram suam probare justam, magis inflammat eamdem. Ne ergo communitati aut domesticis graves importabilesque reddamur, impetum iræ prorsus superare et exstirpare conemur.
paras.en: [[27:4|Anger hath no mercy|Ira non habet misericordiam]]: speaking of anger from vice, which wholly darkens the reason, and which of its kind is one of the seven deadly sins; [[27:4|nor fury, when it breaketh forth|nec erumpens furor]]: for they are moved and driven by cruelty, not by mercy. [[27:4|and who can bear the violence of one provoked?|Et impetum concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit?]] [Denis reads *concitati spiritus*, "of a provoked spirit"]. Hence, according to the Philosopher, anger is a sickness of the soul. And this agrees with what was said above: [[Prov 18:14|a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere?]] Hence Seneca declares in his Proverbs: Nothing less becomes one who punishes than to be angry, since without it he does more toward amendment; and again: Anger is prone to rashness, and takes no care not to bring danger. And once more he says: In punishing, haste is criminal. This anger, then, is to be vehemently detested and most carefully avoided, for through it, as through a dog, the community is disturbed, the grace of the spiritual life is taken away, the neighbour is scandalized, the reason is darkened, the mind drives away the Holy Ghost, and it makes a man like a brute beast, or rather a raging one. But, as Ambrose says, he who is angry with himself for having given way to anger ceases to be angry with his neighbour; but he who wishes to prove his anger just inflames it the more. So, lest we become heavy and unbearable to the community or to our household, let us strive to master the onset of anger altogether and root it out.

paras.t: Melior est manifesta correctio, quæ est actus caritatis, et eleemosyna ac opus justitiæ, quam amor absconditus, id est dilectio habitualis, non procedens in actum: in qua meritum non consistit, nec proximo prodest. Aliqui tamen per amorem absconditum, intelligunt carnalem et sæcularem dilectionem, quæ non quærit animæ bonum, sed oblectamentum et proprium commodum. Hinc in Ecclesiastico legitur: Corripe amicum, ne forte non intellexerit, et dicat, Non feci; aut si fecerit, ne iterum addat facere.
paras.en: [[27:5|Open rebuke is better|Melior est manifesta correctio]], which is an act of charity, and an alms and a work of justice, [[27:5|than hidden love|quam amor absconditus]]: that is, love held as a habit [that is, as a settled disposition only], not going forth into act, in which there is no merit and which does the neighbour no good. Some, however, understand by hidden love carnal and worldly love, which seeks not the good of the soul but pleasure and its own advantage. Hence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:13|Reprove a friend, lest he may not have understood, and say: I did it not: or if he did it, that he may do it no more|Corripe amicum, ne forte non intellexerit, et dicat, Non feci; aut si fecerit, ne iterum addat facere]].

paras.t: Meliora sunt vulnera diligentis, id est verba et læsiones inflicta dilecto a spiritualiter diligente Deo, aut angelo sancto, vel homine bono, quum sint quædam remedia contra peccata futura, et medicamenta peccati præteriti vel præsentis, quam fraudulenta osculantis oscula: quæ non prosunt, sed fallunt. Hinc loquitur Augustinus: Magis amat objurgator castigans et sanans, quam adulator dissimulans; et rursus: Non semper osculatur pater filium, sed interdum castigat: ergo dum castigatur qui diligitur, tunc circa eum pietas exercetur. Itemque: Si me, inquit, posses docere quod nescio, non solum verbis reprehendentem, sed et pugnis cædentem deberem te patientissime sustinere.
paras.en: [[27:6|Better are the wounds of a friend|Meliora sunt vulnera diligentis]] [*diligentis*, literally "of one who loves"]: that is, the words and hurts inflicted on the beloved by one who loves spiritually, whether God, or a holy angel, or a good man, since they are remedies against future sins and medicines for sin past or present, [[27:6|than the deceitful kisses|quam fraudulenta osculantis oscula]] of one who kisses [Denis reads *osculantis*, "of one who kisses", where the Vulgate has *odientis*, "of an enemy"]: which do no good, but deceive. Hence Augustine says: The chider who chastises and heals loves more than the flatterer who dissembles; and again: A father does not always kiss his son, but sometimes chastises him: so when one who is loved is chastised, then love is being shown him. And again: If thou couldst teach me what I do not know, he says, I ought to bear with thee most patiently, not only when thou rebukest me with words, but even when thou strikest me with thy fists.

paras.t: Anima saturata calcabit favum: id est, homo cibo repletus, fastidit durante saturitate cibum quantumlibet dulcem. Anima autem esuriens, etiam amarum pro dulci sumet, id est, vilia et amara cibaria delectabiliter comedet, fame cogente: quæ amara judicat dulcia, juxta illud in Job, Animæ esurienti etiam amara dulcia esse videntur: quod tamen non est ibi de textu, quamvis textui inseratur; sed ex his quæ ibi dicuntur, elicitur: sicque pro glossa fuit primo inductum.
