Nam subdit ibidem sanctus Job: Quæ prius nolebat tangere anima mea, nunc præ angustia, cibi mei sunt. Spiritualius autem loquendo, Anima saturata calcabit favum, id est, corporaliter satiati et gulosi fastidiunt cœlestis regni dulcedinem, et contemplationis suavitatem. Talibus enim loquitur Dominus: Væ vobis divitibus, qui habetis consolationem vestram; væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esurietis. Anima autem esuriens sitiensque justitiam, pro obtinenda quiete æterna, libenter suffert adversa et pœnitentiæ opera. Posset itidem sic exponi: Anima saturata consolatione interna, ex contemplatione et gustu summi et incircumscriptibilis boni calcabit favum, id est terrena omnia oblectamenta.
paras.en: [[27:7|A soul that is full shall tread upon the honeycomb|Anima saturata calcabit favum]]: that is, a man full of food, while his fullness lasts, loathes food however sweet. [[27:7|and a soul that is hungry shall take even bitter for sweet|Anima autem esuriens, etiam amarum pro dulci sumet]]: that is, under the compulsion of hunger he will eat cheap and bitter foods with relish, and judges bitter things sweet, according to that saying in Job: To the hungry soul even bitter things seem sweet [these words stand in some copies of Job 6:7]; which however is not part of the text there, though it is inserted into the text, but is drawn from what is said there, and so was first brought in as a gloss. For holy Job adds in the same place: [[Job 6:7|The things which before my soul would not touch, now, through anguish, are my meats|Quæ prius nolebat tangere anima mea, nunc præ angustia, cibi mei sunt]]. But to speak more spiritually: [[27:7|A soul that is full shall tread upon the honeycomb|Anima saturata calcabit favum]]: that is, those who are bodily sated and gluttonous loathe the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom and the delight of contemplation. For to such the Lord says: [[Luke 6:24|woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation|Væ vobis divitibus, qui habetis consolationem vestram]]; [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that are filled: for you shall hunger|væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esurietis]]. But the soul that hungers and thirsts after justice gladly bears adversities and the works of penance to obtain eternal rest. It could also be expounded thus: the soul filled with inward consolation, from the contemplation and taste of the supreme and boundless good, will tread upon the honeycomb, that is, upon all earthly delights.

paras.t: Sicut avis transmigrans de nido suo, id est, nidum suum cum pullis seu ovis suis ibi contentis omnino relinquens; sic vir qui relinquit locum suum, id est congregationem seu familiam sibi commissam, et spiritualibus seu carnalibus filiis debitam subtrahit curam et educationem; vel, Locum suum, id est virtuosam exercitationem, in qua cœpit proficere. Unde in Ecclesiaste habetur: Si spiritus potestatem habentis ascenderit super te, locum tuum ne dimiseris: hoc est, si diaboli tentatio irruerit super te, non desistas a bono quod inchoasti. Vel, Locum suum, id est societatem et religiosum conventum, in quo Deo servire incepit. Unde ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Non deserentes collectionem nostram, sicut est moris quibusdam, sed consolantes. Hinc Seneca satis notabiliter ait: Primum argumentum compositæ mentis existimo, posse secum consistere et morari; ægri animi est ista jactatio, discurrere, et locorum varietatibus inquietari. Peregrinantes hospitia habent multa, amicitias nullas. Nec prodest cibus, nec corpori accedit, qui statim sumptus emittitur. Nihil æque sanitatem impedit, ut remediorum crebra mutatio; non convalescit planta, quæ sæpe transfertur. Nihil tam utile est, ut in transitu prosit. Fastidientis stomachi est, plura degustare, quæ ubi varia et diversa sunt, inquinant, non alunt.
paras.en: [[27:8|As a bird that wandereth from her nest|Sicut avis transmigrans de nido suo]]: that is, wholly abandoning her nest with the young or the eggs it holds; [[27:8|so is a man that leaveth his place|sic vir qui relinquit locum suum]]: that is, the congregation or household entrusted to him, and withdraws from his spiritual or carnal children the care and upbringing he owes them; or, *his place*, that is, the exercise of virtue in which he had begun to make progress. Hence we have in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:4|If the spirit of him that hath power, ascend upon thee, leave not thy place|Si spiritus potestatem habentis ascenderit super te, locum tuum ne dimiseris]]: that is, if the temptation of the devil rush upon thee, do not give up the good thou hast begun. Or, *his place*, that is, the fellowship and religious community in which he began to serve God. Hence the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:25|Not forsaking our assembly, as some are accustomed: but comforting|Non deserentes collectionem nostram, sicut est moris quibusdam, sed consolantes]]. Hence Seneca says, very notably: I hold the first proof of a well-ordered mind to be that it can stay in one place and abide with itself; this tossing about, running here and there and being unsettled by changes of place, belongs to a sick mind. Those who travel abroad have many lodgings, but no friendships. Food does no good and does not nourish the body if it is thrown up as soon as it is taken. Nothing hinders health so much as frequent change of remedies; a plant that is often moved does not thrive. Nothing is so useful that it can help in passing. It is the mark of a squeamish stomach to taste many things, which, when they are various and diverse, defile and do not nourish.

paras.t: Ecce ex his reprehenditur religiosorum quoque instabilitas aliquorum: qui quum in conventu et ordine laudabilis observantiæ sint, ex quadam phantastica apprehensione, aut diabolica illusione, aliam domum aut religionem ingredi cupiunt, et semper inconstantes sunt corde, ac animo fluctuantes; atque ex propria impatientia, inquietudine, irrefrenatione ac pertinacia potius incitantur, quam desiderio perfectionis majoris: cujus evidens signum est, quod in eo quo resident loco, male se habent, non dantes se ad obedientiam sanctam, ad propriæ voluntatis fractionem, ad mortificationem salubrem, ad diligentiam observantiæ regularis, ad jugem custodiam cordis. Verum, ut ait Chrysostomus, de majori perfectione potest inquirere, qui implevit minorem. Contra hanc pestem, multa in suis homiliis scribit Eusebius Emisenus. Quid prodest quod discedis, qui quocumque pergis, te tecum portas?
paras.en: See how by these words is rebuked the instability of some religious as well: who, though they are in a community and an order of praiseworthy observance, from some fanciful notion or illusion of the devil desire to enter another house or order, and are ever inconstant of heart and wavering of mind; and they are driven rather by their own impatience, restlessness, lack of restraint and obstinacy than by a desire for greater perfection. A plain sign of this is that in the place where they live they behave badly, not giving themselves to holy obedience, to the breaking of their own will, to wholesome mortification, to diligence in the observance of the rule, to the continual guarding of the heart. But, as Chrysostom says, he may seek after greater perfection who has fulfilled the lesser. Against this plague Eusebius of Emesa writes much in his homilies: What does it profit thee to go away, when wherever thou goest thou carriest thyself with thee?

paras.t: Unguento et variis odoribus dulcibus delectatur cor: ad quod redundant delectationes sensuum exteriorum; et bonis amici consiliis anima ejus cui datur tale consilium, dulcoratur, id est, consolationem et spem concipit, sive de malo vitando, sive de bono adipiscendo: per quod amaritudinem, desolationem, tristitiamque repellit. Nempe, ut Tullius protestatur, Non viribus, non velocitatibus, non celeritate corporum res magnæ geruntur, sed consilio antiquorum atque scientia, quibus non orbari, sed augeri solet senectus. Qualis vero debeat esse consiliarius, docet Ambrosius: Talis, inquiens, debet esse qui consilium dat, ut se ipsum ad exemplum bonorum exhibeat operum, in doctrina, in integritate, in gravitate, ut sit sermo ejus irreprehensibilis et salubris, consilium utile, vita honesta, sententiaque decora.
paras.en: [[27:9|Ointment and perfumes rejoice the heart|Unguento et variis odoribus dulcibus delectatur cor]] [Denis reads *variis odoribus dulcibus*, "various sweet perfumes"]: for the delights of the outward senses flow over into it; [[27:9|and the good counsels of a friend|et bonis amici consiliis]] the soul of him to whom such counsel is given is sweetened [*dulcoratur*; the Douay-Rheims has "are sweet to the soul"]: that is, it conceives consolation and hope, either of avoiding evil or of gaining good, and thereby drives away bitterness, desolation and sadness. For, as Tully declares, great things are done not by strength, nor by swiftness, nor by quickness of body, but by the counsel and knowledge of the old, of which old age is not wont to be robbed, but rather enriched. What sort of man a counsellor ought to be, Ambrose teaches: He who gives counsel, he says, ought to be such that he shews himself [[Tit 2:7|an example of good works, in doctrine, in integrity, in gravity|exemplum bonorum exhibeat operum, in doctrina, in integritate, in gravitate]], that his speech may be irreproachable[[Tit 2:8||]] and wholesome, his counsel useful, his life honest, and his judgement seemly.

paras.t: Amicum tuum et amicum patris tui ne dimiseris, et domum fratris tui ne ingrediaris in die afflictionis tuæ, ne tua præsentia ingerat illi mærorem, et ne videaris ab illo velle aliquid obtinere pro relevamine. Verumtamen ex rationabili causa potest oppositum fieri: præsertim si cogat necessitas, aut si quis graviter sit tentatus aut desolatus, vel angustiatus, debet pro salubri remedio, consilio, relevamine, ad sapientem et expertum, ad fidelem et familiarem amicum recurrere: quemadmodum primo Regum narratur, quod convenerunt ad David omnes qui erant in angustia constituti, et oppressi ære alieno, et amaro animo.
paras.en: [[27:10|Thy own friend, and thy father's friend, forsake not: and go not into thy brother's house in the day of thy affliction|Amicum tuum et amicum patris tui ne dimiseris, et domum fratris tui ne ingrediaris in die afflictionis tuæ]]: lest thy presence bring grief upon him, and lest thou seem to want to get something from him for thy relief. Yet for a reasonable cause the opposite may be done: especially if necessity compels, or if someone is grievously tempted or desolate or in distress, he ought to have recourse, for a wholesome remedy, counsel and relief, to a wise and experienced man, to a faithful and familiar friend: as is told in the first book of Kings, that there gathered to David [[1 Kings 22:2|all that were in distress, and oppressed with debt, and under affliction of mind|omnes qui erant in angustia constituti, et oppressi ære alieno, et amaro animo]].

paras.t: Melior est, id est ad succurrendum utilior, vicinus juxta, quam frater carnalis seu consanguineus procul: et hoc in casibus certis ac repentinis periculis. Melior quoque est vicinus, id est quicumque proximus caritate conjunctus, amicabiliterque convivens, quam frater procul, id est cognatus aut alter quicumque, mente aversus, ac dissimilitudine infidelitatis vitiorumque distans: quod concordat parabolæ quam Christus in Evangelio de Samaritano et Levita circa vulneratum inducit.
paras.en: [[27:10|Better is|Melior est]], that is, more useful for giving help, [[27:10|a neighbour that is near|vicinus juxta]], [[27:10|than a brother|quam frater carnalis]] according to the flesh, or kinsman, [[27:10|afar off|consanguineus procul]]: and this in certain cases and in sudden dangers. Better too is a neighbour, that is, anyone near to us, joined by charity and living with us in friendship, than a brother afar off, that is, a kinsman or anyone else who is turned away in mind and far off by the unlikeness of unbelief and vices: which agrees with the parable that Christ gives in the Gospel of the Samaritan[[Luke 10:33||]] and the Levite[[Luke 10:32||]] and the wounded man.

paras.t: Stude sapientiæ, fili mi, et lætifica cor meum, qui de tuo profectu quasi de proprio ex caritate exsulto, ut possis exprobranti, id est veritatem legis divinæ ac fidei, seu justitiam contemnenti, respondere sermonem, id est efficax dare responsum et ipsum rationabiliter confutare. Unde orat Propheta: Et veniat super me misericordia tua, Domine; et respondebo exprobrantibus mihi verbum. Hinc ait Apostolus: Sunt multi inobedientes et vaniloqui, quos oportet redargui. Et rursus: Oportet, inquit, episcopum sine crimine esse, amplectentem eum, qui secundum doctrinam est, fidelem sermonem, ut potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt, arguere.
paras.en: [[27:11|Study wisdom, my son, and make my heart joyful|Stude sapientiæ, fili mi, et lætifica cor meum]], for out of charity I rejoice at thy progress as at my own, [[27:11|that thou mayst|ut possis]] [[27:11|to him that reproacheth|exprobranti]], that is, him who despises the truth of the divine law and of the faith, or justice, [[27:11|give an answer|respondere sermonem]]: that is, give an effective answer and confute him by reason. Hence the Prophet prays: [[Ps 118:41|Let thy mercy also come upon me, O Lord|Et veniat super me misericordia tua, Domine]]; [[Ps 118:42|So shall I answer them that reproach me in any thing|et respondebo exprobrantibus mihi verbum]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[Tit 1:10|there are also many disobedient, vain talkers|Sunt multi inobedientes et vaniloqui]], [[Tit 1:11|Who must be reproved|quos oportet redargui]]. And again: [[Tit 1:7|a bishop must be without crime|Oportet, inquit, episcopum sine crimine esse]], he says, [[Tit 1:9|Embracing that faithful word which is according to doctrine, that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to convince the gainsayers|amplectentem eum, qui secundum doctrinam est, fidelem sermonem, ut potens sit exhortari in doctrina sana, et eos qui contradicunt, arguere]].

paras.t: Astutus videns malum, id est imminere periculum, absconditus est, id est, se ipsum subtraxit et inde celavit; parvuli transeuntes, id est innocentes, inexperti, improvidi, inde non fugientes, sustinuere dispendia, id est damna. Hoc consonat ei quod dictum est supra: Callidus videt malum, et abscondit se; innocens pertransiit, et afflictus est damno: ubi istud magis expositum est.
paras.en: [[27:12|The prudent man seeing evil|Astutus videns malum]], that is, danger threatening, [[27:12|hideth himself|absconditus est]]: that is, withdrew and hid himself from it; [[27:12|little ones passing on|parvuli transeuntes]], that is, the innocent, inexperienced and improvident, not fleeing from it, [[27:12|have suffered losses|sustinuere dispendia]], that is, damage. This agrees with what was said above: [[Prov 22:3|The prudent man saw the evil, and hid himself: the simple passed on, and suffered loss|Callidus videt malum, et abscondit se; innocens pertransiit, et afflictus est damno]]: where this is expounded more fully.

paras.t: Tolle, id est, accipere potes, vestimentum ejus qui spopondit, id est, satisfacere tibi promisit, pro extraneo tibi obligato; et pro alienis, pro quibus spopondit, aufer pignus ab eo. Qualiter autem, et in quo casu pignus seu vestimentum fuit fidejussori restituendum, de mane sive ad vesperam, juxta Moysis legem, dictum est supra.
paras.en: [[27:13|Take away|Tolle]], that is, thou mayest take, [[27:13|his garment that hath been surety|vestimentum ejus qui spopondit]], that is, who promised to make satisfaction to thee, [[27:13|for a stranger|pro extraneo]] bound to thee; and [[27:13|for strangers|pro alienis]], for whom he became surety, [[27:13|take from him a pledge|aufer pignus ab eo]]. But how, and in what case, the pledge or garment was to be given back to the surety, in the morning or toward evening, according to the law of Moses, has been said above[[Prov 20:16||]].

paras.t: Qui benedicit proximo suo voce grandi de nocte consurgens, id est tempore inconvenienti, hoc est, ex adulatione, vel intuitu proprii commodi aut præconii consequendi, laudat proximum suum hora inepta, vel tempore ad hoc sollicite exquisito, maledicenti similis erit: quoniam peccat, et potius quærit decipere proximum quam prodesse eidem.
paras.en: [[27:14|He that blesseth his neighbour with a loud voice, rising in the night|Qui benedicit proximo suo voce grandi de nocte consurgens]], that is, at an unfitting time; that is, he who out of flattery, or with an eye to his own advantage or to winning praise, praises his neighbour at an unsuitable hour, or at a time anxiously sought out for this, [[27:14|shall be like to him that curseth|maledicenti similis erit]]: for he sins, and seeks rather to deceive his neighbour than to do him good.

paras.t: Tecta perstillantia in die frigoris, et litigiosa mulier, comparantur: quia utrumque afflictivum est et molestum. Propter quod scriptum est supra: Melius est habitare in terra deserta, quam cum muliere litigiosa, rixosa et iracunda.
paras.en: [[27:15|Roofs dropping through in a cold day, and a contentious woman are alike|Tecta perstillantia in die frigoris, et litigiosa mulier, comparantur]]: for both are distressing and troublesome. On which account it is written above: [[Prov 21:19|It is better to dwell in a wilderness, than with a quarrelsome and passionate woman|Melius est habitare in terra deserta, quam cum muliere litigiosa, rixosa et iracunda]] [Denis adds *litigiosa*, "contentious"].

paras.t: Qui retinet eam, quasi qui ventum teneat, id est, qui eam apud se habet, verbositate ejus quasi vento duro affligitur, et oleum dextræ suæ evacuet, id est, pietatem sibi concessam tollat a se, tantam tribulationem apud se retinendo: quam tamen opportune non potest vitare in toto. Vel sic: Qui retinet eam, id est, eam retrahere a sua inquietudine nititur, quasi qui ventum teneat: id est, impossibile quid attentat, sicut qui conatur ventum a suo flatu compescere; et oleum dextræ suæ evacuet, id est, oleum in dextra sua tentum velit stringendo tenere: quod quanto plus stringitur, tanto magis elabitur, ita quod manus ejus evacuatur: sic quo mulier iracunda aut rixosa magis quæritur refrenari, eo plus suis passionibus inflammatur et agitatur. Potest autem per mulierem litigiosam, hæreticorum doctrina atque loquacitas, nullam verecundiam corrigibilitatemve habens, signari.
paras.en: [[27:16|He that retaineth her, is as he that would hold the wind|Qui retinet eam, quasi qui ventum teneat]]: that is, he who keeps her with him is afflicted by her wordiness as by a harsh wind, and empties [[27:16|the oil of his right hand|oleum dextræ suæ]] [Denis reads *evacuet*, "empties", where the Vulgate has *vocabit*, "shall call"]: that is, takes from himself the devotion granted him, by keeping so great a trouble with him; which, however, he cannot conveniently avoid altogether. Or thus: [[27:16|He that retaineth her|Qui retinet eam]], that is, strives to draw her back from her restlessness, [[27:16|is as he that would hold the wind|quasi qui ventum teneat]]: that is, attempts something impossible, like one who tries to stop the wind from blowing; and empties [[27:16|the oil of his right hand|oleum dextræ suæ]]: that is, would hold oil held in his right hand by squeezing it, which the more it is squeezed, the more it slips away, so that his hand is emptied: so the more an angry or quarrelsome woman is restrained, the more she is inflamed and stirred by her passions. And by the contentious woman may be signified the teaching and loquacity of heretics, which has no shame and admits of no correction.

paras.t: Ferrum ferro acuitur: quia per malleum ferreum clavi formantur et acuuntur; et homo exacuit faciem amici sui: id est, unus homo suo apparatu, discursu ac persuasione, vultum atque ingenium alterius sibi dilecti, facit diligenter adspicere, profundiusque pensare ea quæ proponuntur.
paras.en: [[27:17|Iron sharpeneth iron|Ferrum ferro acuitur]]: for nails are shaped and sharpened by an iron hammer; [[27:17|so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend|et homo exacuit faciem amici sui]]: that is, one man by his preparation, his reasoning and persuasion makes the face and wit of another whom he loves look carefully at what is put before him and weigh it more deeply.

paras.t: Qui servat ficum, id est, a prætereuntibus arborem fici custodit, comedet fructus ejus: quia non auferuntur, sed remanent sibi. Sic spiritualiter, qui sacram Scripturam in suo conservat corde, fructibus (id est considerationibus et consolationibus) ejus reficietur, juxta illud primi Machabæorum: Nos nullo horum indigemus, solatio habentes sanctos libros qui in manibus nostris sunt. Et qui custos est domini sui, id est, dominum suum terrenum in bello a periculo eruit, et fidelis custos est capitis ejus, glorificabitur ab eodem, imo et a Deo, si ex caritate id agat, fitque famosus in populo: sic qui Deum custodit in cordibus in quibus per gratiam commoratur, id est, adversarios salutis humanæ non permittit ad peccata pertrahere corda hujusmodi, per quæ Deum amittant.
paras.en: [[27:18|He that keepeth the fig tree|Qui servat ficum]], that is, guards the fig tree from passers-by, [[27:18|shall eat the fruit thereof|comedet fructus ejus]]: for they are not carried off, but remain for him. So spiritually, he who keeps holy Scripture in his heart will be refreshed with its fruits (that is, its reflections and consolations), according to that saying of the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 12:9|We, though we needed none of these things having for our comfort the holy books that are in our hands|Nos nullo horum indigemus, solatio habentes sanctos libros qui in manibus nostris sunt]]. [[27:18|and he that is the keeper of his master|Et qui custos est domini sui]], that is, rescues his earthly master from danger in war, and is the faithful keeper of his head, [[27:18|shall be glorified|glorificabitur]] by him, and indeed by God too, if he does it out of charity, and becomes famous among the people: so too he who keeps God in the hearts in which He dwells by grace, that is, does not allow the enemies of man's salvation to draw such hearts into sins by which they would lose God.

paras.t: Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium ipsas aquas, quemadmodum et in speculo: sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus: id est, prudentes, ex dispositione vultuum, morum, verborum ac operum, probabiliter noscunt interiorem cordis dispositionem, quantum ad aliqua saltem, quamvis cogitationes affectionesque cordis, in speciali et certitudinaliter cognoscere nequeant sine revelatione. Unde et Plato de cognoscendis cogitationibus secretisque cordis edidit librum. De isto dictum est supra, super illud, Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem: et super illud, In facie prudentis lucet sapientia.
paras.en: [[27:19|As the faces of them that look therein, shine in the water|Quomodo in aquis resplendent vultus prospicientium]], that is, of those looking into the waters themselves, as also in a mirror: [[27:19|so the hearts of men are laid open to the wise|sic corda hominum manifesta sunt prudentibus]]: that is, the wise, from the bearing of men's faces, manners, words and works, know with probability the inner disposition of the heart, at least in some respects, although they cannot know the thoughts and affections of the heart in particular and with certainty without revelation. Hence Plato too published a book on knowing the thoughts and secrets of the heart. This was spoken of above, on the words [[Prov 15:13|A glad heart maketh a cheerful countenance|Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem]], and on the words [[Prov 17:24|Wisdom shineth in the face of the wise|In facie prudentis lucet sapientia]].

paras.t: Infernus et perditio non replentur: id est, dæmonum infernalium appetitus, quo cupiunt ad damnationem perducere homines, non satiatur usque ad sæculi finem; nec perditio, id est damnatio infernalis, accipit finem. Similiter et oculi hominum insatiabiles: quod de cupidis et avaris accipitur, qui instar hydropicorum, quo plus de temporalibus hauriunt, eo plura talia sitiunt. Communiter quoque videtur esurienti, quod plus de cibo indigeat, quam est. Propter quod vulgare est verbum: Citius satiatur venter, quam oculus.
paras.en: [[27:20|Hell and destruction are never filled|Infernus et perditio non replentur]]: that is, the appetite of the demons of hell, by which they long to bring men to damnation, is not satisfied until the end of the world; nor does destruction, that is, the damnation of hell, come to an end. [[27:20|so the eyes of men are never satisfied|Similiter et oculi hominum insatiabiles]]: which is understood of the covetous and avaricious, who, like men with dropsy, the more of temporal things they drink in, the more they thirst for. It commonly seems, too, to a hungry man that he needs more food than he does. Hence the common saying: The belly is filled sooner than the eye.

paras.t: Quomodo probatur in conflatorio argentum, et in fornace aurum, an verum argentum sit verumque aurum: ut dictum est plenius super illud, Sicut igne probatur argentum, et aurum camino; sic probatur homo ore laudantis: quoniam si ex laudibus hominum nequaquam inaniter gloriatur neque extollitur, sed magis humiliat semetipsum, atque ad meliora accenditur, et occulta Dei expavescit judicia, ne forte coram Deo reprehensibilis inveniatur; imo et contristatur audiens sibi adscribi, quod adscribendum est omnium largitori bonorum, nec valens æquanimiter ferre suam laudem, quum ipse de se longe aliter sentiat, et omni vituperatione dignum se reputet: tunc signum est quod vere sit virtuosus, et vere humilis, timoratus, sapiensque exsistat. Hinc ait Gregorius: Quum justus in facie laudatur, in corde affligitur. Et præsertim vitandum censetur, ne homines imperfecti, ad vanitatem proclives, laudentur. Imo, ut Climacus fassus est, qui tales laudat, venenum eis propinat. Ideo rursus ait Gregorius: Laus sua justos cruciat, iniquos exaltat: sed justos dum cruciat, purgat; iniquos dum lætificat, reprobos monstrat.
paras.en: [[27:21|As silver is tried in the fining-pot, and gold in the furnace|Quomodo probatur in conflatorio argentum, et in fornace aurum]], whether it be true silver and true gold, as was said more fully on the words [[Prov 17:3|As silver is tried by fire, and gold in the furnace|Sicut igne probatur argentum, et aurum camino]]; [[27:21|so a man is tried by the mouth of him that praiseth|sic probatur homo ore laudantis]]: for if he is in no way vainly puffed up or exalted by the praises of men, but rather humbles himself, is kindled to better things, and dreads the hidden judgements of God, lest perhaps he be found blameworthy before God; and indeed if he is saddened to hear ascribed to himself what is to be ascribed to the giver of all good things, and cannot bear his own praise with equanimity, since he thinks very differently of himself and reckons himself worthy of all blame: then it is a sign that he is truly virtuous, and truly humble, God-fearing and wise. Hence Gregory says: When the just man is praised to his face, he is afflicted in his heart. And it is held that care should especially be taken that imperfect men, prone to vanity, be not praised. Indeed, as Climacus declares, he who praises such men gives them poison to drink. Therefore Gregory says again: Their own praise torments the just and exalts the wicked; but in tormenting the just it purifies them, and in gladdening the wicked it shows them to be reprobate.

paras.t: Cor iniqui exquirit mala: quia in pravitatibus delectatur; cor autem rectum exquirit scientiam de necessariis ad salutem, et scientiam quæ est donum. Versus iste non est in Hebræo.
paras.en: [[27:21|The heart of the wicked seeketh after evils|Cor iniqui exquirit mala]]: for it delights in wickedness; [[27:21|but the righteous heart seeketh after knowledge|cor autem rectum exquirit scientiam]] of the things necessary for salvation, and the knowledge which is a gift [that is, the gift of the Holy Ghost called knowledge]. This verse is not in the Hebrew.

paras.t: Si contuderis, id est contriveris, stultum, id est habituatum et assuefactum in vitiis, in pila, id est in ligno concavo ad terendum frumenta facto, quasi ptisanas, id est hordea decorticata, feriente desuper pilo, id est instrumento quo in pila vel in mortariolo aliquid teritur aut comminuitur, non auferetur ab eo stultitia, id est pravitas et puerilitas ejus: hoc est, nulla correptione aut correctione poteris eum emendare, præsertim sine adspiratione atque auxilio gratiæ Dei. Idcirco non est desperandum, sed ad cœlestis omnipotentisque medici animarum cum orationum instantia confugiendum.
paras.en: [[27:22|Though thou shouldst bray|Si contuderis]], that is, crush, [[27:22|a fool|stultum]], that is, one grown habituated and accustomed to vices, [[27:22|in the mortar|in pila]], that is, in a hollowed piece of wood made for pounding grain, as it were [[27:22|sodden barley|quasi ptisanas]], that is, barley with the husks stripped off, [[27:22|as when a pestle striketh upon|feriente desuper pilo]] [*pila* is the mortar, *pilum* the pestle], that is, the instrument with which something is pounded or crushed in a mortar or a small bowl, [[27:22|his folly would not be taken from him|non auferetur ab eo stultitia]]: that is, his wickedness and childishness: that is, by no rebuke or correction wilt thou be able to amend him, especially without the inspiration and help of the grace of God. Therefore we must not despair, but take refuge with earnest prayer in the heavenly and almighty physician of souls.

paras.t: Diligenter agnosce vultum pecoris tui, id est, dispositionem, vitam et mores personæ tibi commissæ ac subditæ, stude cognoscere, ut juxta indigentiam ejus, ei succurras, consulas, et pastoralis officii actus impendas; et juxta hunc sensum tuosque greges, id est congregationes et oves Dei tibi creditas, considera, qualiter juxta suæ exigentiam vocationis Domino obsequantur, et quidquid in eis culpabile videris, sine personarum acceptione, discrete, instanter, ferventer increpa et exstirpa.
paras.en: [[27:23|Be diligent to know the countenance of thy cattle|Diligenter agnosce vultum pecoris tui]]: that is, study to know the disposition, life and manners of the person entrusted to thee and subject to thee, so that according to his need thou mayest help him, counsel him and bestow on him the acts of the pastoral office; and in this sense [[27:23|thy own flocks|tuosque greges]], that is, the congregations and sheep of God entrusted to thee, [[27:23|consider|considera]], how they serve the Lord as their calling requires, and whatever thou seest blameworthy in them, without respect of persons, discreetly, urgently and fervently rebuke and root out.

paras.t: Non enim habebis jugiter potestatem exercendi hos actus in subditis, quia vel per mortem tuam, seu subditorum tuorum, aut alio modo finietur præsidentia tua, et tunc recuperare non poteris neglecta atque omissa. Sed corona tibi tribuetur in generationem et generationem, id est, æterna beatitudo tibi præstabitur, si rite præfueris. Hoc est quod beatissimus Petrus in prima sua hortatur epistola: Seniores, obsecro, pascite qui in vobis est gregem, providentes non coacte, sed spontanee secundum Deum, non turpis lucri gratia, neque ut dominantes in cleris, sed forma gregis facti, et ex animo, ut quum apparuerit Princeps pastorum, percipiatis immarcescibilem gloriæ coronam. Denique ad præsidendum idonee, oportet uti præcipua discretione: et sicut medicus unicuique ægro adhibet medicinam juxta ægritudinis qualitatem, sic qui præest, singulis subditorum et omnibus debet prospicere, providereque documenta, ac remedia apta contra peccata opponere. Ideo Gregorius Nazianzenus fatetur: Revera mihi esse videtur ars artium et disciplina disciplinarum, regere hominem, qui inter omnia animalia maxime moribus varius, et voluntate diversus est. Defectus vero subditorum, ex defectu et negligentia prælatorum maxime derivatur. Propter quod dixit Chrysostomus: Quemadmodum videns arborem foliis pallentibus marcidam, intelligis quia aliquam culpam, id est corruptionem, habet circa radicem; ita quum videris populum indisciplinatum, sine dubio cognosce quia sacerdotium ejus non est sanum.
paras.en: [[27:24|For thou shalt not always have power|Non enim habebis jugiter potestatem]] to exercise these acts over thy subjects, for thy charge will be ended, either by thy death or that of thy subjects, or in some other way, and then thou wilt not be able to recover what was neglected and left undone. [[27:24|but a crown shall be given to generation and generation|Sed corona tibi tribuetur in generationem et generationem]]: that is, eternal beatitude will be bestowed on thee, if thou hast ruled rightly. This is what most blessed Peter exhorts in his first epistle: [[1 Pet 5:1|The ancients|Seniores]], [[1 Pet 5:1|I beseech|obsecro]], [[1 Pet 5:2|Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking care of it, not by constraint but willingly, according to God: not for filthy lucre's sake|pascite qui in vobis est gregem, providentes non coacte, sed spontanee secundum Deum, non turpis lucri gratia]], [[1 Pet 5:3|Neither as lording it over the clergy but being made a pattern of the flock from the heart|neque ut dominantes in cleris, sed forma gregis facti, et ex animo]], [[1 Pet 5:4|when the prince of pastors shall appear, you shall receive a never fading crown of glory|ut quum apparuerit Princeps pastorum, percipiatis immarcescibilem gloriæ coronam]]. Lastly, to rule fittingly one must use the greatest discretion: and as a physician applies to each sick man a medicine suited to the kind of sickness, so he who rules ought to look to each of his subjects and to all, and to provide teachings and set apt remedies against sins. Therefore Gregory Nazianzen declares: Truly it seems to me the art of arts and the discipline of disciplines to govern man, who of all animals is the most varied in his ways and the most diverse in his will. Now the failings of subjects come chiefly from the failings and negligence of prelates. Hence Chrysostom said: Just as, seeing a tree withered with pale leaves, thou understandest that it has some fault, that is, some rot, about the root; so when thou seest a people undisciplined, know without doubt that its priesthood is not sound.

paras.t: Aperta sunt prata, et apparuerunt herbæ virentes, id est, tempore æstivali ista a Domino conceduntur pro sustentatione pecorum; et collecta sunt fœna de montibus: quibus etiam tempore hiemali jumenta quædam pascantur. Agni sunt ad vestimentum tuum, id est, agni et oves tibi concessi sunt ut ex lana eorum facias tibi vestes; et hœdi, ad agri pretium, id est, hœdi quoque donati sunt tibi ut de eorum pretio emas et colas agros. Ista est expositio superficialis, et ut putant aliqui, litteralis.
paras.en: [[27:25|The meadows are open, and the green herbs have appeared|Aperta sunt prata, et apparuerunt herbæ virentes]]: that is, in summertime these are granted by the Lord for the sustenance of the cattle; [[27:25|and the hay is gathered out of the mountains|et collecta sunt fœna de montibus]]: with which some beasts are also fed in wintertime. [[27:26|Lambs are for thy clothing|Agni sunt ad vestimentum tuum]]: that is, lambs and sheep have been granted thee so that thou mayest make thyself clothes from their wool; [[27:26|and kids for the price of the field|et hœdi, ad agri pretium]]: that is, kids too have been given thee so that with their price thou mayest buy and till fields. This is the surface exposition, and, as some think, the literal one.

paras.t: Spiritualiter vero, Aperta sunt tempore evangelicæ legis prata, id est alimenta ac pascua sacramentorum cœlestium, olim clausa et tecta figuris legalium mysteriorum; et apparent nunc herbæ virentes, id est evangelicæ institutiones ac Christi consilia, doctrinæ, et diversa gratiarum charismata, quibus nutriuntur credentium animæ; et collecta sunt fœna de montibus, id est, de exemplis et documentis Patriarcharum ac Prophetarum accepta sunt spiritualia pabula, quibus aluntur fideles. Agni sunt ad vestimentum tuum, id est, de ovibus tibi commissis potes vestitum accipere; et hœdi, ad agri pretium, id est, a peccatoribus pœnitentibus sumere potes necessarium victum. Denique agni sunt ad vestimentum, dum pastor virtutibus subditorum ædificatur, seque spiritualiter vestit vestimento salutis, et induit indumento justitiæ, inflammatus eorum profectu ac meritis; et hœdi sunt ad pretium agri, dum per opera pietatis quæ circa pœnitentes exercent, cumulum felicitatis merentur qui præsunt, in patria regni cœlestis.
paras.en: But spiritually, in the time of the law of the Gospel [[27:25|The meadows are open|Aperta sunt prata]], that is, the food and pastures of the heavenly sacraments, once shut up and covered by the figures of the mysteries of the law; [[27:25|and the green herbs have appeared|et apparent nunc herbæ virentes]] now, that is, the institutions of the Gospel and the counsels of Christ, His teachings, and the various charisms of graces, by which the souls of believers are fed; [[27:25|and the hay is gathered out of the mountains|et collecta sunt fœna de montibus]]: that is, from the examples and teachings of the Patriarchs and Prophets spiritual fodder has been taken, by which the faithful are nourished. [[27:26|Lambs are for thy clothing|Agni sunt ad vestimentum tuum]]: that is, from the sheep entrusted to thee thou mayest receive clothing; [[27:26|and kids for the price of the field|et hœdi, ad agri pretium]]: that is, from penitent sinners thou mayest take the food thou needest. Lastly, lambs are for clothing when the shepherd is edified by the virtues of his subjects, and, kindled by their progress and merits, clothes himself spiritually with the garment of salvation and puts on the robe of justice [cf. Isaias 61:10]; and kids are for the price of the field when those who rule, by the works of mercy they exercise toward penitents, merit a heap of happiness in the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

paras.t: Sufficiat tibi lac caprarum in cibos tuos, et in necessaria alimenta domus, id est familiæ et sobolis tuæ, et ad victum ancillis tuis: id est, mediocri refectione contentus esto, nec delicata, sed necessaria quæras. De hoc in Ecclesiastico multa scripta sunt. Unde et Chrysostomus loquitur: Simplicior victus, et mensa mediocris, plurimum habent jucunditatis ac bonæ voluptatis. Econtrario divitum mensæ exsecrabiles sunt et horridæ, atque contaminationibus membrorum plenæ. Observanda est ergo sancta sobrietas: quæ mentem et corpus perornat, omniumque virtutum est ornamentum. De qua asserit Augustinus: Sobrietatis perseverantia est inæstimabilis animi fortitudo: quam universæ virtutes et omnes laudum tituli concupiscunt, quoniam sine ea ornari ac complacere non valent.
paras.en: [[27:27|Let the milk of the goats be enough for thy food|Sufficiat tibi lac caprarum in cibos tuos]], [[27:27|and for the necessities of thy house|et in necessaria alimenta domus]], that is, of thy household and thy children, [[27:27|and for maintenance for thy handmaids|et ad victum ancillis tuis]]: that is, be content with modest fare, and seek not dainties but necessities. Much is written of this in Ecclesiasticus[[Ecclus 29:28||]][[Ecclus 39:31||]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xxix, 28–30, and xxxix, 31]. Hence Chrysostom too says: Simpler food and a modest table hold the greatest pleasantness and good delight. On the contrary, the tables of the rich are detestable and horrid, and full of the defilements of the members. Holy sobriety, then, is to be kept: which adorns mind and body, and is the ornament of all the virtues. Of it Augustine declares: Perseverance in sobriety is an inestimable strength of soul, which all the virtues and all titles of praise desire, since without it they cannot be adorned or please.

28.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI VICESIMI OCTAVI : FUGIT IMPIUS NEMINE PERSEQUENTE.
28.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-eighth chapter: The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth.

paras.t: Fugit impius nemine persequente. Videmus quosdam iniquos esse valde audaces, et justis aliquibus audaciores : quomodo ergo fugit impius nemine persequente ? Sed dato quod in exteriori et humano bello sit audax et fortis, tamen in spirituali prælio contra aciem vitiorum frequenter fugit, succumbit, ac vincitur, antequam tentetur a persecutore aut dæmone. Mali etiam Christiani tempore persecutionum sæpe fugerunt solo timore, antequam a tyrannis insequebantur. Verumtamen Salomon loquitur juxta Mosaicæ legis tenorem, in qua transgressoribus legis inter cetera mala prædicebantur effeminatæ formidines et inordinatæ angustiæ ac tremores, ita ut sola suspicione et imaginatione verterentur in fugam. Unde legitur in Deuteronomio : Dabit Dominus tibi cor pavidum, et oculos deficientes, et animam mœrore consumptam, et erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te. Per unam viam egrediaris contra hostes tuos, et per septem fugias. Hinc scriptum est : Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii ; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur : quia quod ipse aliis intulit, sibi imminere veretur.
paras.en: [[28:1|The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth|Fugit impius nemine persequente]]. We see that some wicked men are very bold, and bolder than some just men: how then is it said that [[28:1|The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth|fugit impius nemine persequente]]? But granted that in outward and human warfare he is bold and strong, yet in the spiritual battle against the array of the vices he often flees, gives way and is overcome, before he is tempted by a persecutor or by the devil. Bad Christians too, in times of persecution, often fled from fear alone, before they were pursued by the tyrants. However, Solomon speaks according to the tenor of the Mosaic law, in which, among other evils, womanish fears and inordinate anguish and tremblings were foretold to the transgressors of the law, so that at a mere suspicion or fancy they would be turned to flight. Hence it is read in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 28:65|the Lord will give thee a fearful heart, and languishing eyes, and a soul consumed with pensiveness|Dabit Dominus tibi cor pavidum, et oculos deficientes, et animam mœrore consumptam]]. [[Deut 28:66|And thy life shall be as it were hanging before thee|et erit vita tua quasi pendens ante te]]. [[Deut 28:25|one way mayst thou go out against them, and flee seven ways|Per unam viam egrediaris contra hostes tuos, et per septem fugias]]. Hence it is written: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears: and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii ; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur]] [Denis has *in auribus impii*, "in the ears of the wicked man"]: because what he himself has brought upon others he fears is hanging over himself.

paras.t: Justus autem quasi leo confidens in Domino, absque terrore erit, id est, inordinatum, carnalem, sæcularem timorem abjiciet, et Deum pure timebit, nec aliud nisi in Deo et propter Deum. Imo pro Deo et justitia mori erit paratus, sicut jubet Salvator : Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt, etc. Verumtamen ista jam sæpe præhabita sunt, idcirco pertranseo.
paras.en: [[28:1|but the just, bold as a lion|Justus autem quasi leo confidens]] in the Lord, [[28:1|shall be without dread|absque terrore erit]]: that is, he will cast off inordinate, carnal, worldly fear, and will fear God purely, and nothing else except in God and for God's sake. Nay, he will be ready to die for God and for justice, as the Saviour commands: [[Matt 10:28|fear ye not them that kill the body|Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt]], etc. But these things have often been treated already, and so I pass over them.

paras.t: Propter peccata terræ, id est habitantium in terra, multi principes ejus. Nam propter peccata hominum, permittit Deus justo judicio regna vastari ac dividi, et habitatores inter se dissentire : sicut et regnum duodecim tribuum, propter scelera Salomonis, fuit divisum, et in adventu Christi Judæa sub multis erat tetrarchis, prout tertio Regum libro, et in Luca describitur. Regimen autem monarchicum, secundum Philosophum in Politicis, optimum est. Qui rursus duodecimo Primæ philosophiæ disseruit : Pluralitas principum mala. Et propter hominis sapientiam, et horum scientiam quæ dicuntur, vita ducis longior erit : id est, vita præsidentium, ceteris paribus, prolongabitur, si vel ipsi sapientiam in divinis et prudentiam in agendis habuerint, aut sapientium atque prudentium consiliis obtemperaverint.
paras.en: [[28:2|For the sins of the land|Propter peccata terræ]], that is, of those who dwell in the land, [[28:2|many are the princes thereof|multi principes ejus]]. For on account of men's sins God by a just judgment permits kingdoms to be laid waste and divided, and their inhabitants to be at variance among themselves: as the kingdom of the twelve tribes was divided on account of the crimes of Solomon, and at the coming of Christ Judæa was under many tetrarchs, as is described in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 11:31||]][[3 Kings 11:33||]][[3 Kings 12:16||]][[3 Kings 12:19||]] and in Luke[[Luke 3:1||]]. Now monarchical rule, according to the Philosopher in the *Politics*, is the best. And he also declared in the twelfth book of the *First Philosophy* [that is, the *Metaphysics*, where Aristotle quotes Homer]: A plurality of rulers is bad. [[28:2|and for the wisdom of a man, and the knowledge of those things that are said, the life of the prince shall be prolonged|Et propter hominis sapientiam, et horum scientiam quæ dicuntur, vita ducis longior erit]]: that is, the life of rulers, other things being equal, will be prolonged if either they themselves have wisdom in divine things and prudence in what is to be done, or obey the counsels of the wise and prudent.

paras.t: Vir pauper calumnians pauperes, id est in temporalibus aut virtutibus inops, improperans et insultans sibi similibus, quibus merito condoleret, similis est imbri vehementi, in quo paratur fames, id est pluviæ segetes corrumpenti : ex qua corruptione caristia sequitur, quam fames multorum concomitatur. Quemadmodum enim hujusmodi imber paupertatem inducit, sic calumnia pauperis talis, tam ipsum quam alium facit spiritualiter pauperiorem : ipsum quidem directe, quia calumniando sic graviter peccat ; et alium indirecte, cui occasionem dat impatientiæ.
paras.en: [[28:3|A poor man that oppresseth the poor|Vir pauper calumnians pauperes]] [*calumnians*, "that oppresseth", properly "that slanders", which Denis takes as reproaching], that is, one needy in temporal things or in virtues, who reproaches and insults those like himself, with whom he ought rightly to feel compassion, [[28:3|is like a violent shower, which bringeth a famine|similis est imbri vehementi, in quo paratur fames]], that is, like a rain that spoils the crops: from which spoiling there follows dearth, and with it the hunger of many. For as such a shower brings on poverty, so the slander of such a poor man makes both himself and the other spiritually poorer: himself directly, because in slandering so he sins gravely; and the other indirectly, since he gives him occasion of impatience.

paras.t: Qui derelinquunt legem, laudant impium : quia similis simili sibi applaudit. Qui custodiunt legem, succenduntur zelo justitiæ, et ex divino ac fraterno amore, contra eum : quemadmodum princeps Apostolorum contra Simonem magum, Phinees contra Zambri, Mathathias contra Judæum idololatram, imo et Christus contra vendentes et ementes in templo.
paras.en: [[28:4|They that forsake the law, praise the wicked man|Qui derelinquunt legem, laudant impium]]: for like applauds like. [[28:4|they that keep it|Qui custodiunt legem]] [[28:4|are incensed|succenduntur]] with zeal for justice, and out of love of God and of their brethren, [[28:4|against him|contra eum]]: as the prince of the Apostles was against Simon Magus[[Acts 8:20||]], Phinees against Zambri[[Num 25:7||]][[Num 25:8||]][[Num 25:14||]], Mathathias against the idolatrous Jew[[1 Mach 2:23||]][[1 Mach 2:24||]], nay, and Christ against those who sold and bought in the temple[[John 2:15||]][[John 2:16||]].

paras.t: Viri mali non cogitant judicium, id est, discretionis judicium non advertunt, neque divini rigorem judicii pensant, nec dijudicant semetipsos, nec proximis justitiam facere meditantur; qui autem requirunt Dominum, id est, Deo placere conantur, et ejus honorificentiam optant, animadvertunt omnia ad salutem spectantia, et provident sua novissima, ac quid unicuique teneantur.
paras.en: [[28:5|Evil men think not on judgment|Viri mali non cogitant judicium]], that is, they pay no heed to the judgment of discretion, nor weigh the rigour of the divine judgment, nor judge themselves, nor think of doing justice to their neighbours; [[28:5|but they that seek after the Lord|qui autem requirunt Dominum]], that is, who strive to please God and desire His honour, [[28:5|take notice of all things|animadvertunt omnia]] that bear on salvation, and look ahead to their last things, and to what they owe to each one.

paras.t: Melior est pauper in simplicitate sua columbina ambulans, quam dives in pravis itineribus.
paras.en: [[28:6|Better is the poor man walking in his simplicity|Melior est pauper in simplicitate sua]], his dovelike simplicity, [[28:6|than the rich in crooked ways|quam dives in pravis itineribus]].

paras.t: Qui custodit legem, filius sapiens est : utpote Deo obediens, quod est summa sapientia ; et sapientiæ dono ornatur, quo summo bono uniri et placere conatur. Qui autem comessatores, id est gulosos et helluones, pascit, confundit, id est, perturbat et inhonorat, patrem suum, qui de filii sui perversitate tristatur.
paras.en: [[28:7|He that keepeth the law, is a wise son|Qui custodit legem, filius sapiens est]]: as one who obeys God, which is the highest wisdom; and he is adorned with the gift of wisdom, by which he strives to be united to the highest good and to please it. [[28:7|but he that feedeth gluttons|Qui autem comessatores]], that is, the greedy and the gormandizers, [[28:7|shameth|confundit]], that is, troubles and dishonours, [[28:7|his father|patrem suum]], who is grieved at his son's perversity.

paras.t: Qui coacervat, id est congregat, divitias usuris et fœnore liberali. Per usuram hoc loco quidam intelligunt, capere aliquid ultra sortem ex pacto; per fœnus liberale, quando hoc fit absque pacto. Alii per usuram intelligunt horum utrumque; per fœnus vero liberale, quando usura (id est usurarie acquisitum) datur ad usuram. Potest autem fœnus liberale vocari, id quod pro mutuato ultra sortem exigitur, non quasi usura, sed tanquam in recognitionem et vicissitudinem impensi beneficii, prout super Matthæum tangit Hieronymus: et tamen hoc ipsum usurarium est, ac lege prohibitum, Domino per Ezechielem jubente: Usuram et superabundantiam non accipietis. Unde et Christus: Date (inquit) mutuum, nihil inde sperantes. Ideo dicit Ambrosius: Et vestis, usura est; et esca, usura est; et quidquid sorti accedit, usura est: quod velis nomen ei imponas, usura est. Qui ergo his modis colligit opes, in pauperes congregat eas, id est contra egenos, quia in damnum indigentium: vergit enim in damnum eorum. Idcirco usura est contra caritatem atque justitiam, et valde enorme peccatum. Imo, ut etiam Aristoteles naturali ratione inductus fatetur: Ipsa est maxime contra naturam.
paras.en: [[28:8|He that heapeth together|Qui coacervat]], that is, gathers, [[28:8|riches by usury and loan|divitias usuris et fœnore]] *liberali*, by usury and "liberal interest" [Denis joins *liberali* to *fœnore*; in the Vulgate it goes with what follows, *liberali in pauperes*, "for him that will be bountiful to the poor"; *fœnus*, "loan" in the Douay-Rheims, is properly the interest on a loan]. By usury in this place some understand taking something beyond the principal by agreement; by liberal interest, when this is done without agreement. Others understand by usury both of these; but by liberal interest, when usury (that is, what has been got by usury) is itself lent out at usury. Or that may be called liberal interest which is required for a loan beyond the principal, not as usury, but as in acknowledgement and return for a kindness done, as Jerome touches on in his commentary on Matthew: and yet this very thing is usurious, and forbidden by the law, since the Lord commands through Ezechiel: Ye shall not take [[Ezech 18:17|usury and increase|Usuram et superabundantiam]][[Ezech 22:12||]] [Denis's wording, *non accipietis*, "ye shall not take"; the margin gives Ezech. xviii, 17 and xxii, 12, where the words *usuram et superabundantiam* stand]. Hence Christ too: [[Luke 6:35|lend|Date]], He says, [[Luke 6:35|hoping for nothing thereby|mutuum, nihil inde sperantes]]. Therefore Ambrose says: Clothing is usury, and food is usury, and whatever is added to the principal is usury: whatever name you give it, it is usury. He then who gathers wealth in these ways [[28:8|gathereth them|congregat eas]] [[28:8|to the poor|in pauperes]] [*in pauperes*, which can mean "against the poor" or "for the poor": Denis takes it first one way, then the other], that is, against the needy, since to the loss of those in want: for it turns to their loss. Therefore usury is against charity and justice, and a very grave sin. Nay, as even Aristotle, led by natural reason, admits: It is most of all against nature.

paras.t: Vel: In pauperes congregat eas, id est, pauperibus seu indigentibus, a quibus eas acquisivit, eas restituere obligatur. Denique, sicut ait Chrysostomus, similis est pecunia usurarii, morsui aspidis, quia per ipsam usurarius se ipsum occidit: et sicut percussus ab aspide, quasi delectatus cadit in somnum, ac per suavitatem soporis moritur, quia tunc venenum per omnia membra latenter decurrit; sic qui sub usura accipit, ad tempus quasi beneficium sentit, sed usura per omnes ejus facultates decurrit, et totum convertit in debitum.
paras.en: Or: [[28:8|gathereth them|congregat eas]] [[28:8|to the poor|In pauperes]], that is, he is bound to restore them to the poor or needy from whom he acquired them. Lastly, as Chrysostom says, a usurer's money is like the bite of an asp, for by it the usurer kills himself: and as one bitten by an asp falls asleep as if delighted, and dies through the sweetness of the slumber, because meanwhile the poison runs secretly through all his limbs; so he who borrows at usury feels it for a time as a kindness, but the usury runs through all his means and turns the whole into debt.

paras.t: Qui declinat aures suas ne audiat legem: id est, auditum suum avertit ne discat, sciat, vel audiat præcepta Dei sive Ecclesiæ, quatenus peccet liberius et sine remorsu; vel aures cordis avertit ne audiat, id est, audiendo impleat, legem, id est præcepta, ita quod ex proposito peccat, nec pœnitet; oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis, id est contemptibilis coram Deo, quum non veniat ex affectu, nec præparet se ad gratiam, sed operibus suis destruat propriam precem. Ideo Jacobus ait apostolus: Petitis, et non accipitis, eo quod male petatis. Etiam alibi asseritur: Scimus quia peccatores Deus non audit (eos videlicet qui in peccandi manent proposito); sed si quis Dei cultor est, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc exaudit.
paras.en: [[28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law|Qui declinat aures suas ne audiat legem]]: that is, turns away his hearing so as not to learn, know or hear the precepts of God or of the Church, so that he may sin more freely and without remorse; or turns away the ears of his heart so as not to hear the law, that is, the precepts, *to hear* meaning to fulfil by hearing, so that he sins of set purpose and does not repent; [[28:9|his prayer shall be an abomination|oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]], that is, contemptible before God, since it does not come from the heart, nor does he prepare himself for grace, but by his works he destroys his own prayer. Therefore the apostle James says: [[Jas 4:3|You ask and receive not: because you ask amiss|Petitis, et non accipitis, eo quod male petatis]]. And elsewhere it is declared: [[John 9:31|we know that God doth not hear sinners|Scimus quia peccatores Deus non audit]] (those, that is, who remain in the purpose of sinning); but [[John 9:31|if a man be a server of God and doth his, will, him he heareth|si quis Dei cultor est, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc exaudit]].

paras.t: Qui decipit justos in via mala, id est falsa doctrina, pravo exemplo, occasioneve scandali, interitu suo corruet, id est, proprio vitio quo id agit, peribit, quia iniquitas sua redundat in ipsum, et damnationem eum adjiciet; et simplices possidebunt bona ejus: id est, si ante aliquid meritorie egit, non sibi, sed electis cedet in gloriam. Nullum etenim bonum manet irremuneratum.
paras.en: [[28:10|He that deceiveth the just in a wicked way|Qui decipit justos in via mala]], that is, by false teaching, bad example, or occasion of scandal, [[28:10|shall fall in his own destruction|interitu suo corruet]] [the margin notes the other reading *in interitu*, as in the Vulgate], that is, he will perish by the very vice by which he does it, for his iniquity rebounds upon himself, and will cast him into damnation; [[28:10|and the upright shall possess his goods|et simplices possidebunt bona ejus]]: that is, if he did anything meritorious before, it will go to the glory not of himself but of the elect. For no good remains unrewarded.

paras.t: Sapiens sibi videtur vir dives: divitiæ enim superbiam nutriunt; et eo ipso quo temporalia acquisivit astute, aut conservat avare, sapiens sibi videtur, quia in temporalibus et caducis ultimum sibi constituit finem: ideo sapientiale arbitratur, media sua bene disponere ad temporalium copiam. Pauper autem prudens scrutabitur eum, id est, insipientiam ejus considerabit, videns eum ita præferre transitoria atque carnalia cœlestibus ac divinis, spiritualibus et æternis.
paras.en: [[28:11|The rich man seemeth to himself wise|Sapiens sibi videtur vir dives]]: for riches feed pride; and by the very fact that he has gained temporal things shrewdly, or keeps them greedily, he seems wise to himself, because he has set his last end in temporal and perishable things: and so he thinks it the part of wisdom to order his means well towards an abundance of temporal goods. [[28:11|but the poor man that is prudent shall search him out|Pauper autem prudens scrutabitur eum]], that is, will consider his folly, seeing him thus prefer passing and carnal things to heavenly and divine, spiritual and eternal ones.

paras.t: In exaltatione justorum multa gloria est : id est, valde jucundum et gloriosum est, quod justi ac sapientes ad officia et præsidentiam sublimantur, quia ex hoc bonum commune et salus multorum, honorque Dei procurantur, augentur et conservantur. Propter quod quinto de Civitate Dei loquitur Augustinus : Illi qui vera pietate præditi bene vivunt, si habent scientiam regendi populos, nil est felicius rebus humanis, quam si, Deo miserante, habeant potestatem. Et Bernardus : Si rebus raritas pretium facit, nil in Ecclesia pretiosius, nil optabilius bono utilique pastore. Nempe rara est avis ista in terra. Proinde si quis talis interdum reperiatur, et occasio detur, confestim injiciendæ sunt manus, et totis viribus satagendum, ne qua vi, ne qua arte malitiæ, fructuosa promotio valeat impediri. Hinc Dominus pro grandi beneficio tales promittit præsidentes se concessurum : Dabo, inquiens, vobis pastores secundum cor meum, et pascent vos scientia et doctrina. Rursus, quando quotidie in spiritualibus donis sortiuntur profectum, salubriter exaltantur : et de tali eorum exaltatione magna est gloria, præsertim dum ad dona gloriæ, altitudinemque cœlorum feliciter provehuntur. Porro aliqui [textus] habent : In exsultatione justorum multa gloria est. Exsultant enim in Deo et in rebus divinis, in quibus habent copiosam gloriandi materiam.
paras.en: In the exaltation [Denis reads *exaltatione*, "exaltation", where the Vulgate has *exsultatione*, "joy"; he gives that reading below] [[28:12|of the just there is great glory|justorum multa gloria est]]: that is, it is a very joyful and glorious thing that the just and wise are raised to offices and to authority, because by this the common good and the salvation of many, and the honour of God, are procured, increased and preserved. For this reason Augustine says in the fifth book of *The City of God*: If those who, endowed with true piety, live well have the knowledge of ruling peoples, nothing is happier for human affairs than that, by the mercy of God, they should have power. And Bernard: If rarity gives things their price, nothing in the Church is more precious, nothing more to be desired, than a good and useful pastor. Truly this is a rare bird on the earth. And so if such a one is sometimes found, and the occasion is given, hands must at once be laid on him, and every effort made, lest by any force or any art of malice his fruitful promotion be hindered. Hence the Lord promises, as a great benefit, that He will grant such rulers: [[Jer 3:15|I will give|Dabo]], He says, [[Jer 3:15|you pastors according to my own heart, and they shall feed you with knowledge and doctrine|vobis pastores secundum cor meum, et pascent vos scientia et doctrina]]. Again, when day by day they gain progress in spiritual gifts, they are exalted to their salvation: and of such exaltation of theirs there is great glory, above all when they are happily carried up to the gifts of glory and the height of the heavens. Some texts, however, have: [[28:12|In the joy of the just there is great glory|In exsultatione justorum multa gloria est]]. For they rejoice in God and in divine things, in which they have abundant matter for glorying.

paras.t: Regnantibus impiis, ruina hominum : id est, subditi ad diversa labuntur peccata, et interdum ad corporalem interitum, ex negligentia, scandalosaque vita, et abusu regiminis impiorum. Nam, ut Seneca protestatur, quemadmodum subditos nil magis ædificat, quam probitas, sapientia et exemplaritas eorum qui præsunt; sic nil amplius scandalizat, quam perversitas eorumdem. Ideo scriptum est : Quia stulte egerunt pastores, et Dominum non quæsierunt, propterea omnis grex eorum dissipatus est. Ideo ait Gregorius : Dum pastor per abrupta graditur, grex per devia imitatur; et vehementer culpa diffunditur, dum is qui peccat, pro suæ dignitatis officio honoratur.
paras.en: [[28:12|when the wicked reign, men are ruined|Regnantibus impiis, ruina hominum]]: that is, subjects slide into various sins, and sometimes into bodily destruction, through the negligence, the scandalous life and the abuse of rule of the wicked. For, as Seneca declares, just as nothing edifies subjects more than the uprightness, wisdom and example of those set over them, so nothing scandalizes them more than their perversity. Therefore it is written: [[Jer 10:21|Because the pastors have done foolishly, and have not sought the Lord|Quia stulte egerunt pastores, et Dominum non quæsierunt]], therefore [[Jer 10:21|all their flock is scattered|omnis grex eorum dissipatus est]]. Therefore Gregory says: When the shepherd walks over steep places, the flock follows him along byways; and guilt spreads mightily when he who sins is honoured for the office of his dignity.

paras.t: Qui abscondit scelera sua, ea negando aut colorando, vel in sacramento Confessionis ea non aperiendo plenarie, non dirigetur ad veram salutem, nec curabitur, nec crescet in Domino. Initium enim bonorum, confessio est malorum. Qui autem confessus fuerit, et reliquerit ea, non recidivando, vel ad minus plenum propositum relinquendi ea habendo, misericordiam consequetur, id est, veniam et gratiam obtinebit. Ideo sanctus Job dixit : Vias meas in conspectu Dei arguam, et ipse erit salvator meus ; itemque, Si abscondi ut homo scelera mea. Et Psalmista : Dixi, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino ; et tu remisisti impietatem peccati mei. Quocontra de impœnitente transgressore in libro Job legitur : Quum dulce fuerit malum in ore ejus, abscondet illud sub lingua sua. Denique tam grave peccatum est, iniquitatem propriam non fateri loco et tempore opportuno, potissime coram præsidente et judice, ut reus mortis peccet mortaliter, negando judici crimen suum, pro quo, si illud panderet, occideretur, quum tamen metus, præsertim formido mortis, soleat culpam minuere : et istud Thomas in secunda secundæ bene declarat.
paras.en: [[28:13|He that hideth his sins|Qui abscondit scelera sua]], by denying or colouring them, or by not opening them fully in the sacrament of Confession, [[28:13|shall not prosper|non dirigetur]] [*non dirigetur*, literally "shall not be directed"] to true salvation, nor be healed, nor grow in the Lord. For the beginning of good things is the confession of evil ones. [[28:13|but he that shall confess, and forsake them|Qui autem confessus fuerit, et reliquerit ea]], by not falling back, or at least by having a full purpose of forsaking them, [[28:13|shall obtain mercy|misericordiam consequetur]], that is, will obtain pardon and grace. Therefore holy Job said: [[Job 13:15|I will reprove my ways in his sight|Vias meas in conspectu Dei arguam]], [[Job 13:16|and he shall be my saviour|et ipse erit salvator meus]]; and again, [[Job 31:33|If as a man I have hid my sin|Si abscondi ut homo scelera mea]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 31:5|I said I will confess against my self my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven the wickedness of my sin|Dixi, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino ; et tu remisisti impietatem peccati mei]]. On the other hand, of the impenitent transgressor it is read in the book of Job: [[Job 20:12|when evil shall be sweet in his mouth, he will hide it under his tongue|Quum dulce fuerit malum in ore ejus, abscondet illud sub lingua sua]]. Lastly, it is so grave a sin not to confess one's own iniquity at the fitting place and time, above all before a superior and judge, that one guilty of death sins mortally by denying to the judge his crime, for which he would be put to death if he disclosed it, although fear, and especially the dread of death, usually lessens guilt: and Thomas explains this well in the Second Part of the Second Part.

paras.t: Beatus homo in merito et spe, qui semper est pavidus filiali timore. Quum enim in actibus humanis ex deliberatione procedentibus, dicatur non esse indifferens, sed omnis hujusmodi actus sit moraliter bonus aut malus, atque communiter meritorius aut demeritorius, debemus esse jugiter timorati, ne Deum in aliquo offendamus. Ideo sanctus Job fassus est : Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. Et in Isaia jubetur : Dominum exercituum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester. Qui vero mentis est duræ, ita quod nec comminatione pœnarum, nec pollicitatione præmiorum, nec ipso summi boni amore, a sua iniquitate ac pertinacia flectitur, nec modo prætacto Deum veretur, corruet in malum, id est in cumulum vitiorum, et in profunditatem infernalium tormentorum. Ideo in Ecclesiastico scriptum est : Cor durum male habebit in novissimo. Tali lapideum cor habenti, Dominus per Isaiam loquitur: Scio quia durus es tu, et nervus ferreus cervix tua, et frons tua ærea.
paras.en: [[28:14|Blessed is the man|Beatus homo]], in merit and in hope, [[28:14|that is always fearful|qui semper est pavidus]] with filial fear. For since among human acts proceeding from deliberation none is said to be indifferent [that is, morally neither good nor bad], but every such act is morally good or bad, and commonly meritorious or demeritorious, we ought to be continually God-fearing, lest we offend God in anything. Therefore holy Job confessed: [[Job 31:23|For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]] [the margin gives Job xxx, 23; the words are Job 31:23]. And in Isaias it is commanded: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread|Dominum exercituum sanctificate; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester]]. [[28:14|but he that is hardened in mind|Qui vero mentis est duræ]], so that neither by the threat of punishments, nor by the promise of rewards, nor by the very love of the highest good is he turned from his iniquity and obstinacy, nor fears God in the way just described, [[28:14|shall fall into evil|corruet in malum]], that is, into a heap of vices, and into the depth of the torments of hell. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:27|A hard heart shall fear evil at the last|Cor durum male habebit in novissimo]] [Latin "shall fare ill at the last"]. To one who has such a heart of stone the Lord speaks through Isaias: [[Is 48:4|I knew that thou art stubborn, and thy neck is as an iron sinew, and thy forehead as brass|Scio quia durus es tu, et nervus ferreus cervix tua, et frons tua ærea]].

paras.t: Leo rugiens, et ursus esuriens, princeps impius super populum pauperem : quia instar rugientis leonis, subditos inopes comminatione perterret, et tanquam ursus famelicus, bona eorum diripit ac consumit. De talibus Dominus in Michæa loquitur : Qui comederunt carnem populi mei, et pellem desuper excoriaverunt ; et alibi, Cum austeritate imperabatis eis et cum potentia. Hinc denuo Dominus est locutus : Sufficiat vobis, principes ; iniquitatem et rapinam intermittite, et judicium et justitiam facite ; separate eorum vestra a populo meo. Istud ergo vitandum est, quia tyrannicum est, quum et Seneca dicat : Relinque crudelitatem, et matrem ejus iram ; itemque, Crudelitas inficit assiduitate auctoritatem.
paras.en: [[28:15|As a roaring lion, and a hungry bear, so is a wicked prince over the poor people|Leo rugiens, et ursus esuriens, princeps impius super populum pauperem]]: for like a roaring lion he terrifies his needy subjects with threats, and like a famished bear he plunders and devours their goods. Of such men the Lord speaks in Micheas: [[Mich 3:3|Who have eaten the flesh of my people, and have flayed their skin off them|Qui comederunt carnem populi mei, et pellem desuper excoriaverunt]]; and elsewhere, [[Ezech 34:4|you ruled over them with rigour, and with a high hand|Cum austeritate imperabatis eis et cum potentia]]. Hence the Lord spoke again: [[Ezech 45:9|Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: cease from iniquity and robberies, and execute judgment and justice, separate your confines from my people|Sufficiat vobis, principes ; iniquitatem et rapinam intermittite, et judicium et justitiam facite ; separate eorum vestra a populo meo]]. This then is to be avoided, for it is tyrannical, since Seneca too says: Leave off cruelty, and her mother, anger; and again, Cruelty, by being constant, taints authority.

paras.t: Dux, id est princeps quicumque, seu judex, indigens prudentia, id est carens discretione et circumspectione in agendis, multos opprimet per calumniam : quoniam voluntate utitur pro lege justitiæ, et rigorem justitiæ nescit dulcedini pietatis contemperare, sicque opere ipso dicit illud Sapientiæ : Sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ. Qui autem odit avaritiam, longi fient dies ejus, id est, ad diem æternitatis pertinget, juxta quod Dominus spopondit in Psalmo : Longitudine dierum implebo eum. Justis quoque in veteri lege diuturnitas vitæ præsentis promittebatur.
paras.en: [[28:16|A prince|Dux]], that is, any ruler, or a judge, [[28:16|void of prudence|indigens prudentia]], that is, lacking discretion and circumspection in what is to be done, [[28:16|shall oppress many by calumny|multos opprimet per calumniam]]: for he uses his will in place of the law of justice, and does not know how to temper the rigour of justice with the sweetness of mercy, and so by his very deeds he says that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 2:11|But let our strength be the law of justice|Sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ]]. [[28:16|but he that hateth covetousness, shall prolong his days|Qui autem odit avaritiam, longi fient dies ejus]], that is, he will reach the day of eternity, according as the Lord promised in the Psalm: [[Ps 90:16|I will fill him with length of days|Longitudine dierum implebo eum]]. To the just in the old law, too, length of the present life was promised[[Ex 20:12||]][[Deut 11:21||]].

paras.t: Hominem qui calumniatur animæ sanguinem, id est, mortem seu vitia animæ deridet, habens ea pro nihilo, et parvi pendens proximi sui salutem, si usque ad lacum fugerit, nemo sustinet : id est, quantumcumque quærat evadere, juste expetitur ultio criminis sui.
paras.en: [[28:17|A man that doth violence to the blood of a person|Hominem qui calumniatur animæ sanguinem]] [Latin "who slanders the blood of the soul"], that is, who mocks at the death or the vices of the soul, holding them as nothing, and making little of his neighbour's salvation, [[28:17|if he flee even to the pit, no man will stay him|si usque ad lacum fugerit, nemo sustinet]]: that is, however much he seeks to escape, vengeance for his crime is justly exacted.

paras.t: Qui ambulat simpliciter, salvus erit, si in columbina simplicitate finaliter perseveret; qui perversis ingreditur viis, id est, actus vitiosos viis Dei contrarios agit, concidet semel, id est plenarie, quia finaliter damnabitur, nec resurget ; vel, Semel, id est tandem aliquando.
paras.en: [[28:18|He that walketh uprightly, shall be saved|Qui ambulat simpliciter, salvus erit]] [*simpliciter*, "in simplicity"], if he perseveres to the end in dovelike simplicity; [[28:18|he that is perverse in his ways|qui perversis ingreditur viis]], that is, who does vicious deeds contrary to the ways of God, [[28:18|shall fall at once|concidet semel]], that is, fully [*semel*, "once", that is, once for all], for he will be finally damned, and will not rise again; or, *Once*, that is, at length, some day.

paras.t: Qui operatur terram suam, satiabitur panibus. Hoc corporaliter sic solet contingere. Similiter qui agrum cordis sui expurgat a vitiis, seminans illum verbo doctrinæ cœlestis, spiritualiter reficietur : similiter qui corpus suum castigat, et in servitutem spiritus redigit, et membra sua exhibet arma justitiæ Deo. Istud tamen præhabitum est, sicut et id quod subditur. Qui sectatur otium, replebitur egestate spirituali, et sæpe etiam corporali.
paras.en: [[28:19|He that tilleth his ground, shall be filled with bread|Qui operatur terram suam, satiabitur panibus]]. This usually happens so in the bodily sense. Likewise he who clears the field of his heart of vices, sowing it with the word of heavenly doctrine, will be spiritually fed: and likewise he who chastises his body and brings it into subjection to the spirit[[1 Cor 9:27||]], and presents his members as instruments of justice to God[[Rom 6:13||]]. This, however, has been said before, as has what follows[[Prov 12:11||]]. [[28:19|but he that followeth idleness, shall be filled with poverty|Qui sectatur otium, replebitur egestate]], spiritual poverty, and often bodily poverty too.

paras.t: Vir fidelis multum laudabitur : quoniam justus et integer est, nec propter bona utilia aut delectabilia recedit a bono honesto, nec tempore adversitatis relinquit amicum. Qui autem festinat ditari in temporalibus, non erit innocens : quoniam immoderata sollicitudine et viis illicitis ad obtinendum divitias tendit. Imo, juxta Apostolum, Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem, laqueumque diaboli.
paras.en: [[28:20|A faithful man shall be much praised|Vir fidelis multum laudabitur]]: for he is just and upright, and does not depart from the honest good for the sake of useful or pleasant goods [the three kinds of good in the moral philosophy of the schools: the morally good, the useful and the pleasant], nor forsake a friend in time of adversity. [[28:20|but he that maketh haste to be rich|Qui autem festinat ditari]] in temporal things, [[28:20|shall not be innocent|non erit innocens]]: for he strives with immoderate anxiety and by unlawful ways to obtain riches. Nay, according to the Apostle, [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil|Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem, laqueumque diaboli]].

paras.t: Qui cognoscit in judicio faciem, id est, personam accipit, juxta illud Psalmi, Facies peccatoris sumitis ; non facit bene : imo graviter peccat, sicut præhabitum est. Iste et pro buccella panis, id est pro parvis et vilibus rebus, deserit veritatem justitiæ ac sermonis. De talibus per Ezechielem Dominus ait : Deceperunt populum meum propter pugillum hordei et fragmen panis. Quocontra Seneca quoque docet : Testimonium perhibe non amicitiæ, sed veritati.
paras.en: [[28:21|He that hath respect to a person in judgment|Qui cognoscit in judicio faciem]] [literally "who knows the face in judgment"], that is, who accepts persons, according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 81:2|accept the persons of the wicked|Facies peccatoris sumitis]], [[28:21|doth not well|non facit bene]]: nay, he sins gravely, as was said before[[Prov 18:5||]]. [[28:21|such a man even for a morsel of bread|Iste et pro buccella panis]], that is, for small and worthless things, [[28:21|forsaketh the truth|deserit veritatem]] of justice and of speech. Of such men the Lord says through Ezechiel: They deceived my people [[Ezech 13:19|for a handful of barley, and a piece of bread|propter pugillum hordei et fragmen panis]] [Denis has *Deceperunt populum meum*, "they deceived my people", where the Vulgate reads "they violated me among my people"]. Against this Seneca too teaches: Bear witness not to friendship, but to truth.

paras.t: Vir qui festinat ditari, et aliis invidet, eo quod ditiores sint ipso, ignorat quod egestas superveniet ei, id est defectus gratiæ in præsenti, et gloriæ in futuro, pœnaque sensus in inferis : hoc etenim non perpendit.
paras.en: [[28:22|A man that maketh haste to be rich, and envieth others|Vir qui festinat ditari, et aliis invidet]], because they are richer than he, [[28:22|is ignorant that poverty shall come upon him|ignorat quod egestas superveniet ei]], that is, the lack of grace in the present and of glory in the future, and the pain of sense [the positive torment of hell, as distinct from the pain of loss, the loss of God] in hell: for this he does not weigh.

paras.t: Qui corripit hominem non penitus malitiosum, quamvis adhuc sit passionabilis, gratiam postea inveniet apud eum : quia etsi ad tempus ægre accipiat correptionem, rediens tamen ad mentem, advertet quod ex caritate et zelo justitiæ, pro sua salute corripuerit eum ; magis quam ille qui per linguæ blandimenta decipit : qui licet ad tempus complaceat, postea tamen dolus ejus percipitur. Ideo loquitur Augustinus : Qui phreneticum ligat, et lethargicum excitat, ambobus molestus est : quamdiu sunt ægri, indignantur; sed ambo sanati, gratulantur et regratiantur.
paras.en: [[28:23|He that rebuketh a man|Qui corripit hominem]] who is not wholly malicious, though still subject to passion, [[28:23|shall afterward find favour with him|gratiam postea inveniet apud eum]]: for though for a time he takes the rebuke ill, yet when he comes to himself he will see that the other rebuked him out of charity and zeal for justice, for his salvation; [[28:23|more than he that by a flattering tongue deceiveth him|magis quam ille qui per linguæ blandimenta decipit]]: who, though he pleases for a time, yet afterwards his guile is found out. Therefore Augustine says: He who binds the frenzied man and rouses the lethargic is a trouble to both: as long as they are sick they are indignant; but once both are healed, they rejoice and give thanks.
