paras.t: Qui subtrahit aliquid magnum et notabile, a patre suo et a matre, furando, et dicit, Hoc non est peccatum : quia bona parentum putat pertinere ad se; participes homicidæ est, id est homicidæ quodammodo similis in peccato : quia et parentibus suis inobediens est, et non sua invadit, quum adhuc sit sub potestate, curæ atque regimine suorum parentum, ad quos spectat dispensatio rerum. Verum in hac re multi filii et filiæ graviter errant et peccant : quorum errorem, infidelitatem, et furtum dire redarguit Augustinus. Potest quoque exponi hoc modo : Qui subtrahit aliquid, id est, parentibus suis indigentibus denegat honorem, obsequium, subventionem in victu, participes homicidæ censetur.
paras.en: [[28:24|He that stealeth any thing|Qui subtrahit aliquid]] great and notable [[28:24|from his father, or from his mother|a patre suo et a matre]], by theft, [[28:24|and saith, This is no sin|et dicit, Hoc non est peccatum]], because he thinks his parents' goods belong to him, [[28:24|is the partner of a murderer|participes homicidæ est]]: that is, he is in some way like a murderer in sin: for he is both disobedient to his parents and seizes what is not his own, since he is still under the power, care and rule of his parents, to whom the disposal of the property belongs. In this matter, however, many sons and daughters err and sin gravely: and Augustine sternly rebukes their error, faithlessness and theft. It can also be expounded in this way: [[28:24|He that stealeth any thing|Qui subtrahit aliquid]], that is, denies his needy parents honour, service and help with their living, is reckoned [[28:24|the partner of a murderer|participes homicidæ]].

paras.t: Qui se jactat et dilatat, magnificando se ipsum inaniter, suos terminos extendendo, jurgia concitat : quoniam jactantiæ ac superbiæ et avaritiæ ejus alii indignantur ac renituntur; qui vero sperat in Domino, sanabitur a peccatis, et interdum etiam a corporalibus morbis.
paras.en: [[28:25|He that boasteth and puffeth up himself|Qui se jactat et dilatat]] [*dilatat*, "spreads himself"], by magnifying himself vainly, by extending his own bounds, [[28:25|stirreth up quarrels|jurgia concitat]]: for others are indignant at his boasting, pride and avarice, and resist them; [[28:25|but he that trusteth in the Lord, shall be healed|qui vero sperat in Domino, sanabitur]] of his sins, and sometimes also of bodily diseases.

paras.t: Qui confidit in corde suo, id est in propriis viribus aut scientiis, stultus est : quia ignorat se ipsum, quemadmodum in Apocalypsi dicitur tali : Quia dicis, Quod dives sum; et nescis quia tu es miser et miserabilis, pauper, cæcus et nudus. Qui autem graditur sapienter, vitando viarum pericula, et exemplariter se habendo, juxta illud Apostoli, In sapientia ambulate ad eos qui foris sunt: ipse laudabitur.
paras.en: [[28:26|He that trusteth in his own heart|Qui confidit in corde suo]], that is, in his own strength or knowledge, [[28:26|is a fool|stultus est]]: for he does not know himself, as is said to such a one in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:17|Because thou sayest: I am rich|Quia dicis, Quod dives sum]]; [[Apoc 3:17|and knowest not that thou art wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked|et nescis quia tu es miser et miserabilis, pauper, cæcus et nudus]]. [[28:26|but he that walketh wisely|Qui autem graditur sapienter]], by avoiding the dangers of the ways, and by bearing himself as an example to others, according to that of the Apostle, [[Col 4:5|Walk with wisdom towards them that are without|In sapientia ambulate ad eos qui foris sunt]]: he shall be praised [Denis reads *laudabitur*, "shall be praised", where the Vulgate has *salvabitur*, "shall be saved"].

paras.t: Qui dat pauperi liberaliter propter Deum, non indigebit : quia et in præsenti Dominus ei providebit, et bonis gratiæ ac gloriæ eum ditabit. Qui despicit deprecantem, sustinebit penuriam divinorum charismatum, sicut apostolus Jacobus loquitur : Judicium sine misericordia fiet ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam. Hinc ait Scriptura : Qui obturat aures suas ad clamorem pauperum, et ipse clamabit, et non exaudietur. Ideo Seneca dicit : Nihil neges, quod petiturus es: et rursus, Homo qui in homine ærumnoso misericors est, meminit sui. Imo et Dominus in Evangelio fatur : Omni petenti te tribue.
paras.en: [[28:27|He that giveth to the poor|Qui dat pauperi]] generously for God's sake [[28:27|shall not want|non indigebit]]: for the Lord will both provide for him in the present and enrich him with the goods of grace and of glory. [[28:27|he that despiseth his entreaty, shall suffer indigence|Qui despicit deprecantem, sustinebit penuriam]] of the divine gifts, as the apostle James says: [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy|Judicium sine misericordia fiet ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam]]. Hence the Scripture says: [[Prov 21:13|He that stoppeth his ear against the cry of the poor, shall also cry himself, and shall not be heard|Qui obturat aures suas ad clamorem pauperum, et ipse clamabit, et non exaudietur]]. Therefore Seneca says: Refuse nothing that you will yourself ask for; and again, A man who is merciful to a man in distress is mindful of himself. Nay, the Lord too says in the Gospel: [[Luke 6:30|Give to every one that asketh thee|Omni petenti te tribue]].

paras.t: Quum surrexerint impii, id est, prævaluerint in regnando tyrannice, persequendoque justos, abscondentur homines, id est, rationabiles homines se abscondent, sicut ait Salvator : Quum persecuti vos fuerint in una civitate, fugite in aliam. Quum illi perierint, multiplicabuntur justi numero et merito: quia sub virtuosis præsidentibus homines reformantur, convertuntur, proficiunt.
paras.en: [[28:28|When the wicked rise up|Quum surrexerint impii]], that is, prevail in ruling tyrannically and in persecuting the just, [[28:28|men shall hide themselves|abscondentur homines]], that is, men who use their reason will hide themselves, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:23|when they shall persecute you in this city, flee into another|Quum persecuti vos fuerint in una civitate, fugite in aliam]]. [[28:28|when they perish, the just shall be multiplied|Quum illi perierint, multiplicabuntur justi]] in number and in merit: for under virtuous rulers men are reformed, converted, and make progress.

29.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI VICESIMI NONI : VIRO QUI CORRIPIENTEM DURA CERVICE CONTEMNIT, ETC.
29.title_en: Exposition of the twenty-ninth chapter: The man that with a stiff neck despiseth him that reproveth him, etc.

paras.t: VIRO, imo cuilibet homini, tam viro quam mulieri, tam adolescenti quam seniori, qui corripientem caritative, discrete, juste ac pie, dura cervice cordis impatienter se habet, moritur in anima, peccando mortaliter, et tales incorrigibiles solent subito mori sive interfici; et eum sanitas animæ non sequetur: quia manet in vitiis et vulneribus animæ suæ.
paras.en: [[29:1|The man|VIRO]], or rather any human being whatever, man as well as woman, young as well as old, who bears himself impatiently, [[29:1|with a stiff neck|dura cervice]] of the heart, towards [[29:1|him that reproveth him|corripientem]] charitably, discreetly, justly and devoutly, dies in his soul by sinning mortally; and such incorrigible men are wont to die suddenly or to be slain; [[29:1|and health|et eum sanitas]] of soul [[29:1|shall not follow him|non sequetur]], because he remains in the vices and wounds of his soul.

paras.t: In multiplicatione justorum civium, aut regentium communitatem, lætabitur vulgus: quia tales sunt utiles valde rei publicæ. Quidam tamen vulgares sunt ita perversi, quod contra justos rectores faciliter indignantur ac murmurant, quoniam increpari, coerceri, punirique renuunt; sed de rationabili vulgo loquitur Salomon. Quum impii sumpserint principatum, gemet populus, timens exactionari, gravari ac opprimi, et bonum commune periclitari, turbationes, dissensiones ac lites oriri.
paras.en: [[29:2|When just men increase|In multiplicatione justorum]] (just citizens, that is, or just men ruling the community), [[29:2|the people shall rejoice|lætabitur vulgus]], because such men are very useful to the commonwealth. Some of the common people, however, are so perverse that they are easily indignant and murmur against just rulers, since they refuse to be rebuked, restrained and punished; but Solomon is speaking of the reasonable common people. But [[29:2|when the wicked shall bear rule, the people shall mourn|Quum impii sumpserint principatum, gemet populus]], fearing to be burdened with exactions, weighed down and oppressed, and fearing that the common good will be endangered and that disturbances, dissensions and quarrels will arise.

paras.t: Vir qui amat sapientiam, lætificat patrem suum. Hoc jam sæpe expositum est. Qui autem nutrit scortum, perdet substantiam: imo et animam suam, sicut in Evangelio fertur de prodigo filio.
paras.en: [[29:3|A man that loveth wisdom, rejoiceth his father|Vir qui amat sapientiam, lætificat patrem suum]]. This has often been explained already[[Prov 10:1||]][[Prov 15:20||]][[Prov 23:24||]]. But [[29:3|he that maintaineth harlots, shall squander away his substance|Qui autem nutrit scortum, perdet substantiam]]: nay, his soul as well, as is told in the Gospel of the prodigal son[[Luke 15:13||]][[Luke 15:18||]][[Luke 15:21||]].

paras.t: Rex justus erigit terram, id est, rem publicam promovet, statum patriæ meliorat, subditos incitat ad virtutes. Sic unusquisque virtuosus prælatus ac prædicator, gregem sibi commissum ad reformationem et profectum inducit pro posse. Vir avarus, puta tyrannus quærens propria commoda, et sui ipsius honorem, non bonum commune, nec subditorum salutem, destruet eam, spoliando et opprimendo subjectos, et discordias inter eos disseminando, ne forsan unanimiter sibi resistant.
paras.en: [[29:4|A just king setteth up the land|Rex justus erigit terram]], that is, advances the commonwealth, betters the state of the country, and stirs up his subjects to the virtues. So too every virtuous prelate and preacher leads the flock entrusted to him, as far as he can, to reform and to progress. But [[29:4|a covetous man|Vir avarus]], a tyrant, say, who seeks his own advantage and his own honour, not the common good nor the welfare of his subjects, [[29:4|shall destroy it|destruet eam]], by despoiling and oppressing his subjects and sowing discord among them, lest perhaps they should resist him with one mind.

paras.t: Homo qui blandis fictisque sermonibus loquitur amico suo, approbando peccata illius, et simulando amicitiam secum, rete expandit pedibus ejus, id est, deceptionum laqueos ei extendit, et profectum ejus in virtutibus impedit, quemadmodum Dominus protestatur per Prophetam: Popule meus, qui beatum te dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, et viam gressuum tuorum dissipant.
paras.en: [[29:5|A man that speaketh to his friend|Homo qui blandis fictisque sermonibus loquitur amico suo]], approving his sins and feigning friendship with him, [[29:5|spreadeth a net for his feet|rete expandit pedibus ejus]], that is, stretches out the snares of deceit for him and hinders his progress in the virtues, as the Lord declares through the Prophet: [[Is 3:12|O my people, they that call thee blessed, the same deceive thee, and destroy the way of thy steps|Popule meus, qui beatum te dicunt, ipsi te decipiunt, et viam gressuum tuorum dissipant]].

paras.t: Peccantem virum iniquum involvet laqueus, id est, deceptio quam alteri parat, irruet super ipsum; et dato quod alteri corporaliter noceat, se ipsum tamen spiritualiter perimit, et incomparabiliter gravius lædit, juxta illud in Psalmo: Veniat illi laqueus quem ignorat, et captio quam abscondit, apprehendat eum, et in laqueum cadat in ipsum. Et Jeremias dicit: Ecce turbo dominicæ indignationis egredietur, et tempestas erumpens super caput impiorum veniet.
paras.en: [[29:6|A snare shall entangle the wicked man when he sinneth|Peccantem virum iniquum involvet laqueus]], that is, the deceit he prepares for another shall rush upon himself; and granted that he harms the other in body, yet he slays himself in spirit, and wounds himself incomparably more gravely, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 34:8|Let the snare which he knoweth not come upon him: and let the net which he hath hidden catch him: and into that very snare let them fall|Veniat illi laqueus quem ignorat, et captio quam abscondit, apprehendat eum, et in laqueum cadat in ipsum]]. And Jeremias says: [[Jer 23:19|Behold the whirlwind of the Lord's indignation shall come forth, and a tempest shall break out and come upon the head of the wicked|Ecce turbo dominicæ indignationis egredietur, et tempestas erumpens super caput impiorum veniet]].

paras.t: Et justus laudabit Dominum, atque gaudebit in Deo, testimonium ei perhibente conscientia sua, quod coram Deo habuerit se sincere. Unde ait Apostolus: Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ. Gaudebit quoque potissime in futuro, quum felix evaserit, et cantabit: Laqueus contritus est, et nos liberati sumus.
paras.en: And [[29:6|the just shall praise|Et justus laudabit]] the Lord [[29:6|and rejoice|atque gaudebit]] in God, his conscience bearing him witness that he has borne himself sincerely before God. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 1:12|our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience|Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ]]. He shall rejoice also, and above all, in the life to come, when he has come through in happiness, and he shall sing: [[Ps 123:7|The snare is broken, and we are delivered|Laqueus contritus est, et nos liberati sumus]].

paras.t: Novit justus causam pauperum, id est, approbat atque justificat eam, quantum rationabiliter valet, non formidans in hoc vultum divitum aut potentium. Ideo sanctus Job fassus est: Quumque sederem quasi rex circumstante exercitu, eram tamen mœrentium consolator. Et de Christo prædictum est: Judicabit in justitia pauperes; atque in Psalmo, Judicabit pauperes populi, et salvos faciet filios pauperum.
paras.en: [[29:7|The just taketh notice of the cause of the poor|Novit justus causam pauperum]], that is, approves it and upholds it as just, as far as he reasonably can, not fearing in this the face of the rich or the powerful. Therefore holy Job confessed: [[Job 29:25|when I sat as a king, with his army standing about him, yet I was a comforter of them that mourned|Quumque sederem quasi rex circumstante exercitu, eram tamen mœrentium consolator]]. And of Christ it was foretold: [[Is 11:4|he shall judge the poor with justice|Judicabit in justitia pauperes]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 71:4|He shall judge the poor of the people, and he shall save the children of the poor|Judicabit pauperes populi, et salvos faciet filios pauperum]].

paras.t: Impius ignorat, id est, non habet, scientiam, quæ est donum, nec veram prudentiam: non, inquam, habet scientiam practicam et formatam, boni approbativam et efficacem, juxta illud Amos: Nescierunt facere rectum, thesaurizantes impietatem. De talibus demum loquitur Paulus: Confitentur se nosse Deum, factis autem negant, quum sint abominati et reprobi.
paras.en: [[29:7|the wicked is void|Impius ignorat]] (that is, has not) [[29:7|of knowledge|scientiam]], the knowledge which is a gift [that is, the gift of knowledge, one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost], nor true prudence: he has not, I say, a practical and formed knowledge [formed, that is, given its form and life by charity], one that approves the good and is effective, according to that of Amos: [[Amos 3:10|they have not known to do the right thing|Nescierunt facere rectum]], [[Amos 3:10|storing up iniquity|thesaurizantes impietatem]]. Of such men, finally, Paul speaks: [[Tit 1:16|They profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him|Confitentur se nosse Deum, factis autem negant]], [[Tit 1:16|being abominable|quum sint abominati]] and [[Tit 1:16|reprobate|reprobi]].

paras.t: Homines pestilentes, id est peste spirituali repleti, qui verbis et factis suis scandalizant, et male informant concives, dissensionesque nutriunt, et bono adversantur communi: quemadmodum secundo Machabæorum narratur de Simone quodam, quod moliebatur iniquum aliquod in civitate; dissipant civitatem, id est, bonum commune destruunt, habitatores perturbant, et interdum sunt causa quod oppida corporaliter destruuntur, prout tempore Jeremiæ civitati Jerusalem factum est a Chaldæis. Sapientes vero avertunt furorem, cives invicem reconciliando, et pro urbibus Deum rogando, ne juste puniantur, nec destruantur. Sic Moyses et Aaron sæpe averterunt iram Dei a populo. Et in Numeris loquitur Dominus: Phinees avertit iram meam a filiis Israel.
paras.en: [[29:8|Corrupt men|Homines pestilentes]] [*pestilentes*, literally "pestilent", hence Denis's gloss], that is, men filled with a spiritual plague, who by their words and deeds give scandal to their fellow citizens and inform them ill, nourish dissensions and oppose the common good, as is told in the second book of Machabees of a certain Simon, that he was striving to bring about some unjust thing in the city[[2 Mach 3:4||]]: such men [[29:8|bring a city to ruin|dissipant civitatem]], that is, destroy the common good and trouble the inhabitants, and are sometimes the cause of towns being destroyed in body, as was done to the city of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans in the time of Jeremias[[Jer 39:1||]][[Jer 39:2||]][[Jer 39:8||]]. But [[29:8|wise men turn away wrath|Sapientes vero avertunt furorem]], by reconciling the citizens to one another and by praying God for the cities, that they be not justly punished nor destroyed. So Moses and Aaron often turned away the wrath of God from the people[[Ex 32:11||]][[Num 14:13||]][[Num 16:22||]][[Num 16:47||]][[Num 21:7||]]. And in Numbers the Lord says: [[Num 25:11|Phinees|Phinees]] [[Num 25:11|hath turned away my wrath from the children of Israel|avertit iram meam a filiis Israel]].

paras.t: Vir sapiens si cum stulto, id est irrationabili et injusto, contenderit, redarguendo illius errores ac vitia, sive irascatur zelo justitiæ contra hujusmodi stultum, sive rideat, id est, peccata ejus juste derideat; [id est] sive rigorose loquatur, sive suaviter exhortetur; sive futura supplicia ei minetur, sive cœlestis beatitudinis gaudia ei (si se emendaverit) danda testetur: non inveniet requiem, id est, non proficiet, nec consolationem de illius correctione accipiet.
paras.en: [[29:9|If a wise man|Vir sapiens si]] [[29:9|contend|contenderit]] [[29:9|with a fool|cum stulto]], that is, with an unreasonable and unjust man, by refuting his errors and vices, [[29:9|whether he be angry|sive irascatur]] with the zeal of justice against such a fool, [[29:9|or laugh|sive rideat]], that is, justly deride his sins; that is, whether he speak severely or exhort gently, whether he threaten him with the punishments to come or assure him that the joys of heavenly bliss will be given him (if he amends): [[29:9|he shall find no rest|non inveniet requiem]], that is, he shall make no headway, nor have any consolation from that man's correction.

paras.t: Viri sanguinum, id est vitiis dediti, seu effusores sanguinis humani, prout Semei ait ad David: Egredere, vir sanguinum: oderunt simplicem. Dissimilitudo enim est causa aversionis et odii. Justi autem quærunt animam ejus, id est salutem animæ ejus, et cupiunt vitam ejus ab impiorum persecutione eruere.
paras.en: [[29:10|Bloodthirsty men|Viri sanguinum]] [literally "men of blood"], that is, men given to vices, or shedders of human blood, as Semei said to David: [[2 Kings 16:7|come out, thou man of blood|Egredere, vir sanguinum]]; these [[29:10|hate the upright|oderunt simplicem]] [*simplicem*, "the simple man"]. For unlikeness is the cause of aversion and hatred. But [[29:10|just men seek his soul|Justi autem quærunt animam ejus]], that is, the salvation of his soul, and desire to rescue his life from the persecution of the wicked.

paras.t: Totum spiritum suum profert stultus, id est, cor suum per loquacitatem seu iram et impatientiam importune et indiscrete effundit, nesciens se frenare, aut celanda celare. Unde antiqua translatio continet: Totam iram suam profert impius; sapiens autem dispensat per partes: quoniam stultus, ira inquietante, ad ultionem accenditur; sapiens autem ordinate procedit, et iram maturitate consilii paulatim extenuat ac repellit. Hinc subditur: Sapiens differt, et reservat in posterum: id est, statim non effundit totum spiritum suum, vel cordis conceptum, seu animi motionem: sed loco et tempore opportuno dicit dicenda, et agit agenda, sicque reservat in posterum. Quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico legitur: Sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabunt tempus.
paras.en: [[29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus]] [*spiritum*, literally "spirit"], that is, pours out his heart unseasonably and without discretion through talkativeness, or through anger and impatience, not knowing how to rein himself in or to hide what should be hidden. Hence the old translation [that is, the Old Latin version used before Jerome's] has: The wicked man uttereth all his anger; but the wise man dispenseth it by parts: because the fool, as anger disquiets him, is kindled to revenge; but the wise man proceeds in order, and by the ripeness of counsel little by little weakens his anger and drives it back. Hence it is added: [[29:11|a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards|Sapiens differt, et reservat in posterum]]: that is, he does not at once pour out all his spirit, or the conception of his heart, or the stirring of his mind, but at a fitting place and time says what is to be said and does what is to be done, and so keeps it till afterwards. As we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:7|A wise man will hold his peace till he see opportunity: but a babbler, and a fool, will regard no time|Sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabunt tempus]].

paras.t: Princeps qui libenter audit verba mendacii, præsertim perniciosi, omnes ministros habet impios, id est mendaces, et sibi consimiles: nam quærunt ei placere per talia, et tales acceptat. Veros autem et justos abhorret: idcirco non manent cum eo. Unde in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus.
paras.en: [[29:12|A prince that gladly heareth lying words|Princeps qui libenter audit verba mendacii]], especially pernicious ones, [[29:12|hath all his servants wicked|omnes ministros habet impios]], that is, liars, and like himself: for they seek to please him by such things, and he accepts such men. But the truthful and the just he abhors; therefore they do not stay with him. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:2|As the judge of the people is himself, so also are his ministers|Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus]].

paras.t: Pauper et creditor obviaverunt sibi, id est, concorditer occurrerunt, ita quod creditor pauperi pie subvenit, et accommodavit quod petiit; utriusque illuminator est Dominus: qui instigavit divitem ad subveniendum liberaliter, et pauperem ad petendum humiliter. Creditor quoque est, qui spiritualia misericordiæ opera exhibet indigenti, docendo, consulendo, ac consolando: quem Dominus ad talia peragenda illuminat, et pauperem, id est indigentem auxiliis illis, instruit unctione interna, ad intelligendum salubriter.
paras.en: [[29:13|The poor man and the creditor have met one another|Pauper et creditor obviaverunt sibi]], that is, have met in concord, so that the creditor has kindly come to the poor man's help and lent him what he asked; [[29:13|the Lord is the enlightener of them both|utriusque illuminator est Dominus]], who moved the rich man to help generously and the poor man to ask humbly. He too is a creditor who shows the spiritual works of mercy to one in need, by teaching, counselling and consoling: him the Lord enlightens to carry out such things; and the poor man, that is, the one who needs those helps, he instructs by an inward unction, so that he understands to his salvation.

paras.t: Rex qui judicat in veritate pauperes, eos ab injustis molestiis eruendo, thronus ejus in æternum firmabitur: id est, Deo jugiter complacebit, et post præsidentiam temporalem consequetur regnum æternum; seu posteros habebit successores per omne tempus, nisi peccatis suis mereantur deficere. Hoc in Christo maxime est impletum, secundum illud in Psalmo: Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi.
paras.en: [[29:14|The king that judgeth the poor in truth|Rex qui judicat in veritate pauperes]], rescuing them from unjust vexations, [[29:14|his throne shall be established for ever|thronus ejus in æternum firmabitur]]: that is, he shall please God continually, and after his rule in time shall obtain an eternal kingdom; or he shall have descendants succeeding him through all time, unless by their sins they deserve to fail. This was fulfilled above all in Christ, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 44:7|Thy throne, O God, is forever and ever|Sedes tua, Deus, in sæculum sæculi]].

paras.t: Virga atque correctio tribuit sapientiam: quia reprimit et emendat correctum a peccatis, et facit eum bonis intentum, sicque ad sapientiæ infusionem ac studium disponit eumdem, quemadmodum Isaias loquitur Deo: In tribulatione murmuris, doctrina tua eis. Inde loquitur Paulus: Quid vultis? in virga veniam ad vos, an in spiritu mansuetudinis? Et in Jeremia habetur: Castigasti me, Domine, et eruditus sum quasi juveniculus indomitus. Oportet enim imprudentes atque indomitos, correctione verborum, et si illa non sufficit, disciplinatione verberum revocare ab insipientia, et ad meliora inducere. Puer autem qui permittitur voluntati suæ, id est exsequi propriam inclinationem et appetitionem ad mala proclivem, confundit matrem suam, quæ eum non increpavit, correxit ac refrenavit.
paras.en: [[29:15|The rod and reproof give wisdom|Virga atque correctio tribuit sapientiam]], because it checks the one corrected and amends him from his sins, and makes him intent on good things, and so disposes him for the infusion and the study of wisdom; as Isaias says to God: [[Is 26:16|in the tribulation of murmuring thy instruction was with them|In tribulatione murmuris, doctrina tua eis]]. Hence Paul says: [[1 Cor 4:21|What will you? Shall I come to you with a rod?|Quid vultis? in virga veniam ad vos]] or [[1 Cor 4:21|in the spirit of meekness|in spiritu mansuetudinis]]? And in Jeremias we have: [[Jer 31:18|thou hast chastised me|Castigasti me]], O Lord, [[Jer 31:18|and I was instructed, as a young bullock unaccustomed to the yoke|et eruditus sum quasi juveniculus indomitus]] [*indomitus*, "untamed", the word Denis takes up next]. For the imprudent and the untamed must be called back from folly and led on to better things by the correction of words and, if that is not enough, by the discipline of blows [*verborum … verberum*, "of words … of blows", a play on words]. But [[29:15|the child that is left to his own will|Puer autem qui permittitur voluntati suæ]], that is, to follow his own inclination and appetite, prone to evil, [[29:15|bringeth his mother to shame|confundit matrem suam]], since she did not rebuke, correct and restrain him.

paras.t: In multiplicatione impiorum multiplicabuntur scelera: quoniam unus trahit et incitat alium ad peccandum, et scandalizant, perturbant et impugnant se invicem. Unde primo Machabæorum asseritur: Multiplicata sunt mala super terram. Et ruinas eorum justi videbunt. Sapientes namque et justi perpendunt qualiter de peccato in peccatum labantur, æternaliterque damnentur, vel se mutuo destruant et occidant; in futuro autem judicio clarius cernent ruinam eorum in tartarum. Unde in Psalmo: Verumtamen oculis tuis considerabis, et retributionem peccatoris videbis.
paras.en: [[29:16|When the wicked are multiplied, crimes shall be multiplied|In multiplicatione impiorum multiplicabuntur scelera]], because one draws and stirs up another to sin, and they scandalize, trouble and attack one another. Hence it is said in the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 1:10|evils were multiplied in the earth|Multiplicata sunt mala super terram]]. And [[29:16|the just shall see their downfall|Et ruinas eorum justi videbunt]]. For the wise and the just weigh how such men slip from sin into sin and are damned eternally, or destroy and slay one another; and in the judgment to come they shall see their downfall into hell more clearly. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 90:8|But thou shalt consider with thy eyes: and shalt see the reward of the wicked|Verumtamen oculis tuis considerabis, et retributionem peccatoris videbis]].

paras.t: Erudi filium tuum in probitate morum et scientia necessariorum, et refrigerabit te ab æstu tristitiæ, et dabit delicias spirituales animæ tuæ: quemadmodum dictum est, Filius sapiens lætificat patrem; et rursus, Gloria patris, filius sapiens.
paras.en: [[29:17|Instruct thy son|Erudi filium tuum]] in uprightness of morals and in the knowledge of things necessary, [[29:17|and he shall refresh thee|et refrigerabit te]] from the heat of sadness, [[29:17|and shall give delight|et dabit delicias]], spiritual delight, [[29:17|to thy soul|animæ tuæ]]: as it has been said, [[Prov 10:1|A wise son maketh the father glad|Filius sapiens lætificat patrem]]; and again: The glory of the father is a wise son [these words are not found as such in the Vulgate].

paras.t: Quum Propheta defecerit, id est, quum viri sapientes et virtuosi rectores, futura impiorum supplicia, justorumque præmia denuntiantes, ac Scripturarum testimonia exponentes ac prædicantes, cessaverint, dissipabitur populus per vitiorum abrupta, ac vitiis spiritualiter destruetur, non habens ductorem, correptorem, pastorem idoneum. Specialiter autem in veteri Testamento solebat populus Israel per Prophetas dirigi ac doceri. Unde in Esdra narratur: Dixit eis sacerdos, ut non comederent de sanctificatis, donec surgeret Propheta. Et primo Machabæorum: Facta est tribulatio magna in Israel, qualis non fuit ex eo tempore, ex quo non est visus Propheta in Israel.
paras.en: [[29:18|When prophecy shall fail|Quum Propheta defecerit]] [Denis reads *Propheta*, "the prophet", where the Vulgate has *prophetia*, "prophecy"], that is, when wise men and virtuous rulers, who proclaim the punishments to come of the wicked and the rewards of the just, and expound and preach the testimonies of the Scriptures, have ceased, [[29:18|the people shall be scattered abroad|dissipabitur populus]] over the precipices of the vices, and shall be destroyed spiritually by vices, having no fit leader, corrector or shepherd. Especially in the Old Testament the people of Israel was wont to be directed and taught by Prophets. Hence it is told in Esdras: The priest told them that they should not eat of the hallowed things until a Prophet should arise[[1 Esd 2:63||]] [Denis quotes loosely; the Vulgate reads: Athersatha said to them, that they should not eat of the holy of holies, till there arose a priest learned and perfect]. And in the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 9:27|there was a great tribulation in Israel, such as was not since the day, that there was no prophet seen in Israel|Facta est tribulatio magna in Israel, qualis non fuit ex eo tempore, ex quo non est visus Propheta in Israel]].

paras.t: Qui vero custodit legem, id est universa legis præcepta ad suum statum spectantia, beatus est in spe, et inchoatione ac merito, juxta illud: Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini. Sed, ut asserit Christus, Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit. Jacobus quoque: Quicumque, inquit, totam legem impleverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus.
paras.en: But [[29:18|he that keepeth the law|Qui vero custodit legem]], that is, all the precepts of the law that concern his state, [[29:18|is blessed|beatus est]] in hope, and in its beginning, and in merit, according to that: [[Ps 118:1|Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord|Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini]]. But, as Christ declares, [[Matt 24:13|he that shall persevere to the end, he shall be saved|Qui perseveraverit usque in finem, hic salvus erit]]. James too: [[Jas 2:10|whosoever|Quicumque]], he says, [[Jas 2:10|shall keep the whole law, but offend in one point, is become guilty of all|totam legem impleverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus]].

paras.t: Servus verbis erudiri non potest. De quali servo dicatur hoc, pandunt verba sequentia. Quia quod dicis, intelligit, et respondere contemnit. Hoc igitur dicitur de servo contumaci et improbo, qui solo servili servit timore: idcirco indiget interdum verberibus erudiri, si sit servus empticius; vel expelli, si sit conducticius. Hinc scriptum est: Cibaria, et virga, et onus asino; panis, et disciplina, et opus servo.
paras.en: [[29:19|A slave will not be corrected by words|Servus verbis erudiri non potest]]. Of what kind of slave this is said, the following words make plain: [[29:19|because he understandeth what thou sayest, and will not answer|Quia quod dicis, intelligit, et respondere contemnit]]. This is said, then, of a stubborn and wicked slave, who serves with servile fear alone [servile fear: fear of punishment only, as against the filial fear of offending]; therefore he sometimes needs to be taught by blows, if he is a bought slave, or to be sent away, if he is a hired one. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 33:25|Fodder, and a wand, and a burden are for an ass: bread, and correction, and work for a slave.|Cibaria, et virga, et onus asino: panis, et disciplina, et opus servo.]]

paras.t: Vidisti hominem velocem ad loquendum, id est loquacem et garrulum, qui etiam inter seniores et sapientiores præceps et pronus est ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda, id est timenda est, quam illius correctio sit speranda. Talis enim difficulter corrigitur: qui si reprehendatur, sua mox loquacitate se excusat, resistit, opponit, et quasi dialecticus quidam efficitur, interrogando de loco et tempore, ac discutiendo negotium. Capitur autem hic Sperare improprie pro Timere, vel Exspectare, sicut in libro Judith: Speraverant eam non redituram. Circa hoc ait Glossa: Grave vitium est stultitia, sed non minus verbositas. Nam sæpe contingit, ut idiota quis citius verba correctionis accipiat, quam is, qui ea quæ novit, aut nosse se putat, libentius jactat, quam aliorum monita audiat.
paras.en: [[29:20|Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak|Vidisti hominem velocem ad loquendum]], that is, talkative and garrulous, who even among his elders and those wiser than he is headlong and quick to speak? [[29:20|folly is rather to be looked for|Stultitia magis speranda]] [*speranda*, literally "to be hoped for"], that is, is to be feared, [[29:20|than his amendment|quam illius correctio]] is to be hoped for. For such a man is hard to correct: if he is reproved, he at once excuses himself with his talkativeness, resists, objects, and turns into a sort of dialectician, asking questions about the place and the time and debating the matter. Here *to hope* is taken improperly for *to fear*, or *to expect*, as in the book of Judith: They had hoped [that is, expected] that she would not return[[Jdt 13:15||]] [so Denis; the Vulgate has *sperabant eam jam non esse venturam*, "they now had no hopes that she would come"]. On this the Gloss says: Folly is a grave vice, but talkativeness is no less so. For it often happens that some unlettered man accepts words of correction sooner than one who would rather boast of what he knows, or thinks he knows, than listen to the admonitions of others.

paras.t: Qui delicate a pueritia nutrit servum suum, id est ministrum, seu proprium corpus, postea sentiet eum contumacem, id est rebellem, et ad operandum quæ bona sunt, inobedientem, quia assuetus est dulcibus, ex quibus concupiscentia et animositas generantur. Propter quod in Proverbiis suis asserit Seneca: Nihil magis facit iracundum, quam educatio mollis et blanda. Porro alia translatio habet: Qui deliciatur a pueritia sua, servus erit; novissime autem contristabitur. Talis enim fit concupiscentiarum vitiorumque servus: unde vel sero dolebit.
paras.en: [[29:21|He that nourisheth his servant delicately from his childhood|Qui delicate a pueritia nutrit servum suum]], that is, his minister, or his own body, [[29:21|afterwards shall find him stubborn|postea sentiet eum contumacem]], that is, rebellious, and disobedient in doing what is good, because he is used to sweet things, from which concupiscence and hot temper are born. For this reason Seneca says in his Proverbs: Nothing makes a man more prone to anger than a soft and coaxing upbringing. Moreover, another translation has: He that liveth delicately from his childhood shall be a servant, and at the last he shall be sorrowful. For such a man becomes the slave of concupiscences and vices, and so he will grieve, if only late.

paras.t: Vir iracundus provocat rixas: proclivis est namque ad verba et facta injuriosa et impetuosa. Unde loquitur Glossa: Janua omnium vitiorum est iracundia: qua clausa, virtutibus intrinsecus requies datur; et qua aperta, ad omne facinus cor armatur. Et qui ad indignandum facilis est (quod superbis est proprium, eo quod alios parvi pendant, præsertim dum eis quid displicens faciunt, et se ipsos magnificant: similiter sapientibus in oculis suis; propter quod in Ecclesiaste habetur: In multa sapientia, multa est indignatio), erit ad peccata proclivior: quia ex indignatione multa ac magna oriuntur peccata. Interdum tamen indignatio sumitur pro motu aspernationis contra iniquitatem. Reprimamus ergo impiam indignationem, considerantes propriam defectuositatem, quum dicat Apostolus: Omnis amaritudo, et ira, et indignatio, et clamor tollatur a vobis.
paras.en: [[29:22|A passionate man provoketh quarrels|Vir iracundus provocat rixas]], for he is prone to injurious and violent words and deeds. Hence the Gloss says: Anger is the door of all vices: when it is shut, rest is given to the virtues within; when it is open, the heart is armed for every crime. And [[29:22|he that is easily stirred up to wrath|Et qui ad indignandum facilis est]] (which is proper to the proud, because they think little of others, especially when these do something displeasing to them, and they magnify themselves; and likewise to those who are wise in their own eyes; for which reason we have in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:18|in much wisdom there is much indignation|In multa sapientia, multa est indignatio]]) [[29:22|shall be more prone to sin|erit ad peccata proclivior]] [the text prints *ad peccata*, "to sins"; the margin gives *ad peccandum*, as in the Vulgate], because many and great sins arise from indignation. Sometimes, however, indignation is taken for a movement of disdain against iniquity. Let us therefore repress wicked indignation, considering our own defectiveness, since the Apostle says: [[Eph 4:31|Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamour|Omnis amaritudo, et ira, et indignatio, et clamor]] [[Eph 4:31|be put away from you|tollatur a vobis]].

paras.t: Superbum sequitur humilitas: id est, qui se extollit, humiliabitur; et humilem spiritu, id est vere et cordialiter humilem, suscipiet gloria, id est, in præsentia exaltabitur per gratiarum charismata copiosa, et in futuro per gloriæ dona; talis quoque frequenter ad honorem et prælationem assumitur, quoniam honor sequitur fugientem.
paras.en: [[29:23|Humiliation followeth the proud|Superbum sequitur humilitas]]: that is, he that exalts himself shall be humbled; and [[29:23|the humble of spirit|et humilem spiritu]], that is, the man truly and heartily humble, [[29:23|glory shall uphold|suscipiet gloria]], that is, he shall be exalted in the present by abundant gifts of graces, and in the future by the gifts of glory; such a man, too, is often taken up to honour and to prelacy, since honour follows him who flees it.

paras.t: Qui cum fure participat, consentiendo, instigando, consulendo, hospitando, non increpando, non impediendo, aut partem rei furatæ accipiendo, odit animam suam: quia peccando vult animæ suæ quod adversatur suæ saluti. Ideo fert Psalmista: Qui autem diligit iniquitatem, odit animam suam. Adjurantem, id est eum qui cum adjuratione inquirit a quo furtum commissum sit, audit participans ille, et non indicat a quo patratum sit furtum, quum sciat hoc: quod est uno modo participare cum fure. Unde in Psalmo: Si videbas furem, currebas cum eo.
paras.en: [[29:24|He that is partaker with a thief|Qui cum fure participat]], by consenting, urging, counselling, harbouring, not rebuking, not hindering, or taking part of the stolen goods, [[29:24|hateth his own soul|odit animam suam]], because by sinning he wills for his soul what is against its salvation. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 10:6|he that loveth iniquity, hateth his own soul|Qui autem diligit iniquitatem, odit animam suam]]. That partaker [[29:24|heareth|audit]] [[29:24|one putting him to his oath|Adjurantem]], that is, one who with an oath inquires by whom the theft was committed, [[29:24|and discovereth not|et non indicat]] by whom the theft was done, though he knows it: which is one way of being partaker with a thief. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 49:18|If thou didst see a thief thou didst run with him|Si videbas furem, currebas cum eo]].

paras.t: Qui timet hominem, cito corruet. Timere hominem timore carnali, mundano et immoderato, est vitiosum, sicut et amare carnaliter, quia per utrumque pax cordis, et libertas ejus in Domino, impeditur. Ideo præcepit Christus: Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt. Et per Isaiam jubetur: Nolite timere opprobria hominum, et blasphemias eorum ne metuatis. Quis es tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescet? Qui ergo sic metuit hominem, cito corruet in peccata, quia ex timore hujusmodi, ne hominem offendat, aut adversum aliquid patiatur, recedet a via justitiæ; et qui vitat peccata timore humano, tunc peccabit quando non timebit ab homine, a quo vereatur videri aut deprehendi. Porro timere hominem, in quantum est Dei vicarius, vel pater, sive superior, vel ob aliam rationabilem causam, timore filiali, laudabile est. Propter quod ait Apostolus: Servi, obedite in omni timore dominis.
paras.en: [[29:25|He that feareth man shall quickly fall|Qui timet hominem, cito corruet]]. To fear man with a carnal, worldly and immoderate fear is vicious, as is also to love carnally, because by both the peace of the heart and its freedom in the Lord are hindered. Therefore Christ commanded: [[Matt 10:28|fear ye not them that kill the body|Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt]]. And through Isaias it is commanded: [[Is 51:7|fear ye not the reproach of men, and be not afraid of their blasphemies|Nolite timere opprobria hominum, et blasphemias eorum ne metuatis]]. [[Is 51:12|who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a mortal man, and of the son of man, who shall wither away like grass?|Quis es tu, ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis, qui quasi fœnum arescet?]] He therefore who fears man in this way shall quickly fall into sins, because from fear of this kind, lest he offend a man or suffer something adverse, he will turn aside from the way of justice; and he who avoids sins out of human fear will sin when he has no man to fear by whom he might dread to be seen or caught. But to fear a man inasmuch as he is God's vicar, or a father, or a superior, or for some other reasonable cause, with a filial fear, is praiseworthy. For this reason the Apostle says: [[Eph 6:5|Servants, be obedient|Servi, obedite]] in all fear to your masters [the margin gives Eph. vi, 5; the words "in all fear" are as in 1 Pet 2:18].

paras.t: Qui sperat in Domino, sublevabitur, id est, per gratiæ opem erigetur in Deum, et stabilietur in ipso, ut non timeat hominem, sed Deum dumtaxat, alia vero non nisi in Deo. Ideo ait Psalmista: In Domino sperans, non infirmabor.
paras.en: But [[29:25|he that trusteth in the Lord, shall be set on high|Qui sperat in Domino, sublevabitur]], that is, by the help of grace he shall be raised up to God and established in him, so that he fears not man but God alone, and other things only in God. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 25:1|I have put my trust in the Lord, and shall not be weakened|In Domino sperans, non infirmabor]].

paras.t: Multi requirunt faciem principis, id est, potentioribus atque judicibus cupiunt complacere: quod si fiat sincera intentione, non est vituperabile; si autem intuitu proprii commodi et honoris, et ut audentius possint peccare, ac justa evadant supplicia quando excesserint, malum est. Sicque a multis fit: quod tamen vitare deberent, ne incidant in divini rigorem judicii. Unde subjungitur: et judicium a Domino egreditur singulorum: id est, Deus universos ac singulos vero et infallibili judicabit judicio. Ideo potius est optandum in præsenti vita judicari, purgari et castigari, quam divino judicio reservari: quia horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis, qui non judicabit bis in id ipsum.
paras.en: [[29:26|Many seek the face of the prince|Multi requirunt faciem principis]], that is, desire to please those more powerful and judges: which, if it is done with a sincere intention, is not blameworthy; but if it is done with an eye to their own advantage and honour, and so that they may sin more boldly and escape just punishment when they have transgressed, it is evil. And so it is done by many; which, however, they ought to avoid, lest they fall into the rigour of the divine judgment. Hence it is added: [[29:26|but the judgment of every one cometh forth from the Lord|et judicium a Domino egreditur singulorum]]: that is, God will judge all and each with a true and infallible judgment. Therefore it is rather to be wished to be judged, purged and chastised in the present life than to be kept for the divine judgment: because [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis]], who will not judge twice the same thing[[Job 33:14||]] [the margin gives Job xxxiii, 14, "God speaketh once, and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time"; Denis's words are the saying commonly drawn from Nah 1:9 in the Greek version].

paras.t: Abominantur justi virum impium, id est quemcumque iniquum, secundum quod talem, quia sic luto vilior est, et omni bruto deterior. Propter quod ait Psalmista: Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus. Hinc primo Machabæorum dicitur: A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quia gloria ejus stercus et vermis est; hodie extollitur, et cras non invenietur. Unus quoque amicorum Job, in persona sua et sociorum suorum, ait ad Job: Quare computati sumus ut stercora, et sorduimus coram te?
paras.en: [[29:27|The just abhor a wicked man|Abominantur justi virum impium]], that is, any wicked man whatever, inasmuch as he is such, because as such he is viler than mud and worse than any brute beast. For this reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus]]. Hence it is said in the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 2:62|fear not the words of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worms|A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quia gloria ejus stercus et vermis est]]; [[1 Mach 2:63|Today he is lifted up, and tomorrow he shall not be found|hodie extollitur, et cras non invenietur]]. One of the friends of Job, too, speaking for himself and his companions, says to Job: [[Job 18:3|Why are we reputed as beasts, and counted vile|Quare computati sumus ut stercora, et sorduimus]] before thee? [the text prints *stercora*, "dung"; the margin corrects it to *jumenta*, "beasts", as in the Vulgate]

paras.t: Et abominantur impii eos qui in recta via sunt, id est [in] observatione justitiæ, et arcta via salutis: quos tanquam sibi dissimiles, contrariosque affectui suo, abhorrent ac persequuntur.
paras.en: And [[29:27|the wicked loathe them that are in the right way|Et abominantur impii eos qui in recta via sunt]], that is, in the observance of justice and in the narrow way of salvation: these they abhor and persecute as unlike themselves and contrary to their own affections.

paras.t: Verbum custodiens filius, id est, qui verba Dei custodit memoria et effectu, fide et opere, extra perditionem erit: quia consequetur salutem, sicut ait Salvator: Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt. Verumtamen istud non est in Hebræo, neque de textu, sed sequitur ex prædictis.
paras.en: [[29:27|The son that keepeth the word|Verbum custodiens filius]], that is, he who keeps the words of God in memory and in effect, in faith and in work, [[29:27|shall be free from destruction|extra perditionem erit]], because he shall obtain salvation, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 11:28|blessed are they who hear the word of God and keep it|Beati qui audiunt verbum Dei, et custodiunt]]. This, however, is not in the Hebrew, nor part of the text, but it follows from what has been said.

30.title: EXPOSITIO CAPITULI TRICESIMI : VISIO QUAM LOCUTUS EST VIR, CUM QUO EST DEUS.
30.title_en: Exposition of the thirtieth chapter: The vision which the man spoke, with whom God is.

paras.t: SICUT fertur in Glossa, hucusque, scilicet a vicesimo quinto capitulo usque ad finem præcedentis capituli, introductæ sunt parabolæ Salomonis, quas transtulerunt viri Ezechiæ regis Juda. Hic rursus parabolæ Salomonis ponuntur :
paras.en: AS is said in the Gloss, up to this point, that is, from the twenty-fifth chapter to the end of the preceding one, there have been set down the parables of Solomon [[Prov 25:1|which the men of Ezechias, king of Juda, copied out|quas transtulerunt viri Ezechiæ regis Juda]]. Here again parables of Solomon are set down,

paras.t: quibus præmittitur titulus seu præfatio ista brevis : Verba Congregantis filii Vomentis, id est, verba sequentia sunt verba Salomonis : qui dicitur Congregans, quoniam ex divina infusione et propria exercitatione, collegit et adunavit in se sapientiam copiosam; qui etiam appellatur filius Vomens, quia hanc ipsam sapientiam aliis communicando evomuit, id est, abundanter diffudit et eructavit. Visio quam locutus est vir, cum quo est Deus : id est, id quod subditur, est visio, revelatio, seu consideratio Salomonis, cum quo fuit Deus in principio regni sui, et postea diu per gratiam et sapientiam magnam. Itaque Salomon loquitur hic de se ipso, quasi de alio, quemadmodum S. Joannes in evangelio suo : Hic est, inquiens, discipulus quem diligebat Jesus, et qui testimonium perhibet de his; et scimus quia verum est testimonium ejus. Et qui Deo secum morante, id est cor ipsius gratiose inhabitante, confortatus virtutibus, ait :
paras.en: and before them is put this title or short preface: [[30:1|The words of Gatherer the son of Vomiter|Verba Congregantis filii Vomentis]]; that is, the words that follow are the words of Solomon, who is called Gatherer because, by divine infusion and by his own exercise, he gathered and united in himself abundant wisdom[[3 Kings 4:29||]]; and who is also called son of Vomiter, because by imparting this same wisdom to others he vomited it forth, that is, poured it out and uttered it [eructavit, literally "belched forth"] abundantly. [[30:1|The vision which the man spoke, with whom God is|Visio quam locutus est vir, cum quo est Deus]]: that is, what follows is the vision, revelation or consideration of Solomon, with whom God was at the beginning of his reign, and for a long time afterwards, through grace and great wisdom. So Solomon speaks here of himself as if of another, as St John does in his Gospel: [[John 21:24|This is|Hic est]], he says, [[John 21:20|that disciple whom Jesus loved|discipulus quem diligebat Jesus]], and [[John 21:24|who giveth testimony of these things|qui testimonium perhibet de his]]; [[John 21:24|and we know that his testimony is true|et scimus quia verum est testimonium ejus]]. [[30:1|And who|Et qui]] [[30:1|by God, abiding with him|Deo secum morante]], that is, dwelling by grace in his heart, [[30:1|being strengthened|confortatus]] in virtues, [[30:1|said|ait]]:

paras.t: Stultissimus sum virorum. Istud uno modo exponitur sic : Stultissimus sum virorum, id est inter homines valde stultus respectu æternæ, infinitæ et increatæ sapientiæ Dei, quam quanto profundius contemplatus sum, tanto insipientiorem me reputavi. Unde alibi scriptum est : Stultus factus est omnis homo a scientia sua. Sic comparatione divinæ justitiæ, omnis nostra justitia quasi pannus menstruatæ (quo nihil immundius est) appellatur. Hinc scribit Apostolus : Soli sapienti Deo honor et gloria. Legitur quoque apud Job : Cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus. Et sapientia hominum non est mecum, id est prudentia sæculi hujus : de qua in Evangelio asserit Christus : Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores filiis lucis in generatione sua sunt; atque Apostolus, Si quis videtur esse sapiens in hoc sæculo, stultus fiat, ut sit sapiens, id est, sapientiam illam sæcularem relinquat. De qua alibi ait Apostolus : Prudentia carnis, mors est; et rursus ibidem : Sapientia carnis inimica est Deo; legi enim Dei non est subjecta. Hæc sapientia seu prudentia fallax et falsa, est quædam versutia, qua homo colligit, providet, et conservat sibi ea quæ pertinent ad divitias, delicias, et honores sæculi hujus ac carnis. Hanc ergo non habuit Salomon, quamdiu in caritate Dei et sapientia salutari (quæ est donum Spiritus Sancti) permansit.
paras.en: [[30:2|I am the most foolish of men|Stultissimus sum virorum]]. This is expounded in one way thus: [[30:2|I am the most foolish of men|Stultissimus sum virorum]], that is, very foolish among men in respect of the eternal, infinite and uncreated wisdom of God: the more deeply I have contemplated it, the more foolish I have reckoned myself. Hence it is written elsewhere: [[Jer 10:14|Every man is become a fool for knowledge|Stultus factus est omnis homo a scientia sua]]. So too, in comparison with the divine justice, all our justice is called [[Is 64:6|as the rag of a menstruous woman|quasi pannus menstruatæ]] (than which nothing is more unclean). Hence the Apostle writes: [[Rom 16:27|To God, the only wise|Soli sapienti Deo]] [[Rom 16:27|be honour and glory|honor et gloria]]. We read also in Job: [[Job 15:15|the heavens are not pure in his sight|Cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus]]. [[30:2|And the wisdom of men is not with me|Et sapientia hominum non est mecum]], that is, the prudence of this world, of which Christ declares in the Gospel: [[Luke 16:8|the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light|Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores filiis lucis in generatione sua sunt]]; and the Apostle: [[1 Cor 3:18|If any man among you seem to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise|Si quis videtur esse sapiens in hoc sæculo, stultus fiat, ut sit sapiens]], that is, let him leave that worldly wisdom. Of it the Apostle says elsewhere: [[Rom 8:6|the wisdom of the flesh is death|Prudentia carnis, mors est]]; and again in the same place: [[Rom 8:7|the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God. For it is not subject to the law of God|Sapientia carnis inimica est Deo; legi enim Dei non est subjecta]]. This false and deceitful wisdom or prudence is a kind of cunning, by which a man gathers, provides and keeps for himself the things that belong to the riches, pleasures and honours of this world and of the flesh. This, then, Solomon did not have, as long as he remained in the charity of God and in saving wisdom (which is a gift of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]).

paras.t: Non didici sapientiam, id est, per humanum studium sapientiam meam non accepi, sed per infusionem a Deo : ut patet tertio Regum ; et novi scientiam sanctorum, id est, veram et salubrem scientiam, sacræ Scripturæ notitiam, propheticam revelationem, et scientiam quæ est donum, a Deo accepi, ac novi. De qua in libro Sapientiæ fertur : Dedit illi scientiam sanctorum ; et alibi, Scientiam Dei volo plus quam holocausta.
paras.en: [[30:3|I have not learned wisdom|Non didici sapientiam]], that is, I did not receive my wisdom through human study, but by infusion from God, as is plain in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 3:12||]]; and I have known [[30:3|the science of saints|scientiam sanctorum]] [Denis's text reads et novi, "and I have known", without the "not" of the Douay-Rheims and the Clementine Vulgate; his second exposition below supplies it], that is, I have received from God, and known, true and wholesome knowledge, the knowledge of Holy Scripture, prophetic revelation, and the knowledge that is a gift[[Is 11:2||]]. Of this it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 10:10|gave him the knowledge of the holy things|Dedit illi scientiam sanctorum]] [scientia sanctorum, the same words as "the science of saints" here]; and elsewhere: [[Osee 6:6|the knowledge of God|Scientiam Dei]] I desire [[Osee 6:6|more than holocausts|plus quam holocausta]].

paras.t: Secundo exponitur sic : Stultissimus sum virorum. Salomon enim peccavit gravissime, et inde (ut dicunt Judæi, ac multi Catholici, Hieronymus quoque et Ambrosius) postea valde pœnituit. Propter quod reversus ad cor pœnitens, dixit : Stultissimus sum virorum, id est, qui sapientissimus eram ex dono Dei, propriis vitiis insipientissimus sum effectus. Et sapientia hominum, qui scilicet rationabiliter conversantur, et digni sunt homines nuncupari, rationem sequendo, non est mecum, id est, mecum non fuit quamdiu tam turpiter ac libidinose vixi, idololatriamque exercui. Deinde culpam suam exaggerando, ut moris est pœnitentium, eamdem sententiam sub aliis repetit verbis. Non didici sapientiam, id est, sapientiam consummatam, qua quis in obsequio Dei manet usque in finem, non didici, nec accepi, et eam quam desuper sumpsi, non didici opere adimplere perseveranter; et novi, id est, non novi, repetendo videlicet negativum hoc signum, Non, in principio hujus versus seu clausulæ positum. Itaque, Non novi scientiam sanctorum, id est, scientiam per quam Sancti Deo stabiliter adhæserunt ac servierunt, et vitia quibus succubui, devitarunt, non habui perseveranter et per approbationem. Prima expositionum istarum apertior, et textui consonantior esse videtur.
paras.en: It is expounded in a second way thus: [[30:2|I am the most foolish of men|Stultissimus sum virorum]]. For Solomon sinned most grievously[[3 Kings 11:1||]], and afterwards (as the Jews say, and many Catholics, Jerome too and Ambrose) repented greatly of it. Therefore, returning penitent to his heart, he said: [[30:2|I am the most foolish of men|Stultissimus sum virorum]], that is, I who by the gift of God was the wisest, have been made the most foolish by my own vices. [[30:2|And the wisdom of men|Et sapientia hominum]], that is, of those who live according to reason, and by following reason are worthy to be called men, [[30:2|is not with me|non est mecum]], that is, was not with me as long as I lived so shamefully and lustfully and practised idolatry. Then, heightening his fault, as penitents are wont to do, he repeats the same thought in other words. [[30:3|I have not learned wisdom|Non didici sapientiam]], that is, I have not learned nor received the perfect wisdom by which one remains in the service of God to the end, and the wisdom I received from above I did not learn to fulfil in deed with perseverance; and I have known, that is, I have not known, repeating, that is, the sign of negation, Not, set at the beginning of this verse or clause. So: I [[30:3|have not known the science of saints|Non novi scientiam sanctorum]], that is, I did not have, with perseverance and with approval, the knowledge by which the Saints steadfastly clung to God and served him, and shunned the vices to which I gave way. The first of these expositions seems plainer, and more in accord with the text.

paras.t: Quis ascendit in cælum, atque descendit? Quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis? Quis colligavit aquas quasi in vestimento? Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ ? Quod nomen est ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti? Totum hunc passum quidam (aliquos forsan sequens Hebræos) exponit de Moyse, ut sit sensus : Quis ascendit in cælum, atque descendit, sicut Moyses fecit? qui ascendit super montem Sinai in cælum aerium ad Dominum, et inde descendit ad populum, ut habetur in Exodo. Quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis, sicut fecit Moyses? qui cineres ardentes de camino accepit. Quis colligavit aquas quasi in vestimento, sicut fecit Moyses in mari Rubro? quia meritis ejus aquæ fuerunt divisæ. Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ, sicut Moyses? qui in erectione tabernaculi suis meritis immisit terrorem omnibus gentibus, in omnibus finibus terræ promissionis et circa habitantibus, sicut in Deuteronomio dicitur: Hodie incipiam mittere terrorem atque formidinem tuam in populos. Quod nomen est ejus? quasi diceret : Si dicatur quod alius fuit, qui ante Moysen talia fecit, dicatur quis fuit ille, et quod fuit nomen ejus; et si dicatur, Mortuus est, et nomen ejus oblivioni est traditum, dicatur quod sit nomen filii ejus, id est, quæ generatio remansit ab eo, ex qua possit aliqua de eo haberi notitia.
paras.en: [[30:4|Who hath ascended up into heaven, and descended? who hath held the wind in his hands? who hath bound up the waters together as in a garment? who hath raised up all the borders of the earth? what is his name, and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?|Quis ascendit in cælum, atque descendit? quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis? quis colligavit aquas quasi in vestimento? quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ? quod nomen est ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti?]] This whole passage someone (following, perhaps, certain Hebrews) expounds of Moses, so that the sense is: [[30:4|Who hath ascended up into heaven, and descended|Quis ascendit in cælum, atque descendit]], as Moses did? who went up on Mount Sinai into the heaven of the air to the Lord[[Ex 19:3||]][[Ex 19:20||]], and came down thence to the people[[Ex 19:14||]][[Ex 19:25||]], as we have it in Exodus. [[30:4|who hath held the wind in his hands|Quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis]], as Moses did? who took burning ashes from the furnace[[Ex 9:10||]]. [[30:4|who hath bound up the waters together as in a garment|Quis colligavit aquas quasi in vestimento]], as Moses did in the Red Sea? for by his merits the waters were divided[[Ex 14:21||]]. [[30:4|who hath raised up all the borders of the earth|Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ]], as Moses did [suscitavit, "raised up", also means "stirred up, roused"]? who at the setting up of the tabernacle by his merits struck terror into all the nations, in all the borders of the land of promise and those dwelling round about, as is said in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 2:25|This day will I begin to send the dread and fear of thee upon the nations|Hodie incipiam mittere terrorem atque formidinem tuam in populos]]. [[30:4|What is his name|Quod nomen est ejus]]? as if to say: If it be said that it was another who did such things before Moses, let it be said who he was, and what his name was; and if it be said: He is dead, and his name has been given over to oblivion, let it be said what is the name of his son, that is, what offspring remained of him, from which some knowledge of him might be had.

paras.t: Sed (sicut prætactus, expositionem hanc introducens, fatetur) expositio jam prætacta secundum quosdam Hebræos, videtur falsa atque extorta. Unde prætactus, scilicet Nicolaus de Lyra, circa hoc inter cetera ait : Hæc expositio Hebræorum videtur in multis deficere. Et primo, quantum ad ejus fundamentum, scilicet quod Salomon in fine pœnituerit vere, et ideo pœnitens protulerit verba hæc, Stultissimus sum virorum, etc. Quia si vere pœnituisset, quum esset rex potentissimus, templa idolorum quæ construxerat, destruxisset : quæ tamen steterunt usque ad tempus Ezechiæ, ut legitur in quarto Regum libro. Sed quid de Salomonis pœnitentia videatur tenendum, super tertium Regum librum induxi. Ubi etiam est ostensum, quod argumentum hoc non concludat. Nam et Manassen regem constat de sua idololatria valde pœnituisse : qui tamen quum post suam pœnitentiam multis viveret annis, in magna prosperitate atque potentia, ut Josephus refert, non tamen destruxit altaria quædam sacrilega, quæ ad sacrificandum idolis fecerat, quum scriptum sit : Altaria quæ fecerat Manasses in duobus atriis templi Domini, destruxit rex, puta Josias. Deinde Lyra per singula, prætactam satis reprobat expositionem, præsertim quod subintelligit, Non, ubi dictum est, Et novi scientiam sanctorum; et quod per spiritum intelligit cineres, quos Moyses accepit de camino, quoniam in Scripturis alibi non invenitur spiritus accipi pro cineribus; et quod dicit Moysen suscitasse omnes terminos terræ in tabernaculi erectione : quod penitus falsum est.
paras.en: But (as the aforesaid author himself admits in introducing this exposition) the exposition just mentioned, following certain Hebrews, seems false and forced. So the aforesaid, that is, Nicholas of Lyra, says among other things on this point: This exposition of the Hebrews seems to fail in many respects. And first, as to its foundation, namely that Solomon at the end truly repented, and so, repenting, uttered these words: [[30:2|I am the most foolish of men|Stultissimus sum virorum]], etc. For if he had truly repented, since he was a most powerful king, he would have destroyed the temples of the idols that he had built; and yet they stood until the time of Ezechias, as we read in the fourth book of Kings[[4 Kings 18:4||]] [the margin gives 4 Kings 18:4, where Ezechias destroys the high places; those that Solomon built are defiled by Josias at 4 Kings 23:13]. But what seems to be held about Solomon's repentance I have set out on the third book of Kings; where it is also shown that this argument does not conclude. For it is certain that King Manasses too repented greatly of his idolatry; and yet, though after his repentance he lived many years in great prosperity and power, as Josephus relates, he did not destroy certain sacrilegious altars which he had made for sacrificing to idols, since it is written: [[4 Kings 23:12|the altars which Manasses had made in the two courts of the temple of the Lord, the king broke down|Altaria quæ fecerat Manasses in duobus atriis templi Domini, destruxit rex]], that is, Josias. Then Lyra rejects the aforesaid exposition point by point, well enough: especially that it understands a Not where it is said: And I have known [[30:3|the science of saints|scientiam sanctorum]]; and that by spirit [spiritus, which the Douay-Rheims renders "wind" in v. 4] it understands the ashes which Moses took from the furnace, whereas nowhere else in the Scriptures is spirit found to be taken for ashes; and that it says that Moses [[30:4|raised up all the borders of the earth|suscitasse omnes terminos terræ]] in the setting up of the tabernacle, which is wholly false.

paras.t: Ponit ergo Lyra aliam horum expositionem, dicendo, quod Salomon in juventute sua Spiritum Sanctum habens, prævidit in Spiritu, tempore Christi, homines simplices et illitteratos illuminandos a Deo de pertinentibus ad salutem : quemadmodum in Nicæno concilio, quum quidam præclarus philosophus doctores multos confutasset catholicos, tandem quidam sanctus et simplex episcopus dixit philosopho quædam verba fidei christianæ : ex quibus philosophus ita fuit compunctus et victus, quod nequivit resistere; sed fatebatur se virtutem Dei in verbis illis sensisse : sicque ad fidem conversus fuit. Itaque in persona cujuslibet talium simplicium desuper illuminatorum, Salomon ait : Visio quam locutus est, id est, quam loquetur : quia in prophetalibus locutionibus frequenter ponitur præteritum pro futuro, ad insinuandum certitudinem prophetiæ. Itaque, Visio quam locutus est vir, cum quo est Deus, id est quicumque talis illitteratus, desuper doctus et illustratus : Stultissimus sum virorum, id est illitteratus, idiota et simplex : sicut in Actibus dicitur de beatissimis apostolis Petro et Joanne, quod idiotæ et sine litteris erant; et sapientia hominum non est mecum, id est scientia politica : secundum quod ait Philosophus, quod eremita non est bonus aut malus politice, quia non curat civilia. Non didici sapientiam, id est philosophicam scientiam, et novi scientiam sanctorum, quæ disponit ad æternam salutem.
paras.en: So Lyra gives another exposition of these words, saying that Solomon in his youth, having the Holy Ghost, foresaw in the Spirit that in the time of Christ simple and unlettered men would be enlightened by God in the things that belong to salvation: as at the Council of Nicaea, when a certain distinguished philosopher had confuted many Catholic doctors, at last a holy and simple bishop spoke to the philosopher certain words of the Christian faith, by which the philosopher was so pierced and overcome that he could not resist, but confessed that he had felt the power of God in those words; and so he was converted to the faith. So in the person of any such simple men enlightened from above, Solomon says: [[30:1|The vision which the man spoke|Visio quam locutus est]], that is, which he will speak; for in prophetic speech the past is often put for the future, to suggest the certainty of the prophecy. So: [[30:1|The vision which the man spoke, with whom God is|Visio quam locutus est vir, cum quo est Deus]], that is, any such unlettered man, taught and enlightened from above: [[30:2|I am the most foolish of men|Stultissimus sum virorum]], that is, unlettered, unlearned and simple; as is said in the Acts of the most blessed apostles Peter and John, that they were unlearned and without letters[[Acts 4:13||]]; [[30:2|and the wisdom of men is not with me|et sapientia hominum non est mecum]], that is, political knowledge; according to what the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle] says, that the hermit is neither good nor bad politically, because he takes no care of civil affairs. [[30:3|I have not learned wisdom|Non didici sapientiam]], that is, philosophical knowledge, and I have known [[30:3|the science of saints|scientiam sanctorum]], which disposes to eternal salvation.

paras.t: Quamvis autem expositio ista catholicæ consonet veritati, propter quod non est immoderantius impugnanda, videtur tamen deficere, quia beatissimis Apostolis infusa fuit non solum scientia Scripturarum, sed et prudentia gubernativa politiæ fidelium. Siquidem gloriosissimi apostoli Petrus et Paulus, in suis scripserunt epistolis, qualiter fideles habere se debeant circa suos superiores, tam sæculares quam ecclesiasticos, et circa plebem atque familiam; et quomodo conjugati mutuo debeant conversari, ac circa actus matrimonii dirigi. Erant etenim constituti principes super omnem terram : ideo scientia instituendi regendique populos, necessaria eis fuit.
paras.en: But although this exposition agrees with Catholic truth, and so is not to be attacked too immoderately, it seems nevertheless to fall short; for there was infused into the most blessed Apostles not only the knowledge of the Scriptures but also the prudence to govern the commonwealth of the faithful. For the most glorious apostles Peter and Paul wrote in their epistles how the faithful ought to conduct themselves towards their superiors, secular as well as ecclesiastical[[1 Pet 2:13||]][[Rom 13:1||]][[Heb 13:7||]][[Heb 13:17||]], and towards the common people and the household[[Eph 6:1||]]; and how married people ought to live with one another, and be directed in the acts of marriage[[1 Pet 3:1||]][[1 Cor 7:1||]][[1 Cor 7:10||]][[1 Cor 7:39||]][[Eph 5:22||]]. For they had been made [[Ps 44:17|princes over all the earth|principes super omnem terram]]: therefore the knowledge of ordering and ruling peoples was necessary to them.

paras.t: Est igitur sensus : Quis ascendit in cœlum, atque descendit? id est, quis universorum providentiam habet, et ad omnia intuenda se vertit? quasi dicat : Nullus utique nisi Deus. De quo in Job asseritur : Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est? Qui in Genesi ait : Descendam, et videbo. De quo rursus ibidem legitur : Ascendit Deus ab Abraham. Et Amos ait : Qui ædificat in cœlo ascensionem suam, et fasciculum suum super terram fundavit. Ideo incircumscriptibilis et incommutabilis Deus dicitur in cœlum ascendere atque descendere, non locum mutando, sed providendo et operando, sicut fertur in Psalmo : Exaltare super cœlos, Deus, et super omnem terram gloria tua. Verumtamen Unigenitus Patris incarnatus ascendit in cœlum vero et corporali ascensu, descensurus inde ad terram, ut judicet omne genus humanum. Paulus quoque raptus in paradisum Dei et in tertium cœlum, ac inde reversus ad evangelizandum, nonne aliquo, imo et sublimi modo ascendit in cœlum, et descendit?
paras.en: The sense, then, is: [[30:4|Who hath ascended up into heaven, and descended?|Quis ascendit in cœlum, atque descendit?]] that is, who has providence over all things, and turns himself to behold all things? as if to say: None surely but God. Of whom it is declared in Job: [[Job 34:13|What other hath he appointed over the earth? or whom hath he set over the world which he made?|Quem constituit alium super terram? aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est?]] Who says in Genesis: [[Gen 18:21|I will go down and see|Descendam, et videbo]]. Of whom again we read there: [[Gen 17:22|God went up from Abraham|Ascendit Deus ab Abraham]]. And Amos says: [[Amos 9:6|He that buildeth his ascension in heaven, and hath founded his bundle upon the earth|Qui ædificat in cœlo ascensionem suam, et fasciculum suum super terram fundavit]]. So God, who is uncircumscribable and unchangeable, is said to ascend into heaven and descend, not by changing place but by providing and working; as is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 56:12|Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: and thy glory above all the earth.|Exaltare super cœlos, Deus, et super omnem terram gloria tua]] Nevertheless the Only-begotten of the Father, made flesh, ascended into heaven by a true and bodily ascent[[Acts 1:9||]], and will come down thence to the earth to judge the whole human race[[Acts 1:11||]]. Paul too, caught up into the paradise of God and into the third heaven[[2 Cor 12:4||]][[2 Cor 12:2||]], and returning thence to preach the gospel, did he not in some way, and indeed a sublime way, ascend into heaven and descend?

paras.t: Quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis? id est, Deus omnipotens in potestate sua conservavit, et conservat omnem angelicum spiritum et humanum, seu animas hominum, imo et spiritum jumentorum : quoniam sine incessabili manutenentia Creatoris, nulla creatura posset ad momentum subsistere. Continet quoque ventos in manu sua, quos de thesauris suis producit, atque ad libitum suum emittit et retrahit, auget ac minuit. Quod et exponi potest de Christo, de quo legitur : Surgens Jesus, comminatus est vento, et dixit mari, Tace, et obmutesce; et facta est tranquillitas magna. Denique scriptum est : Vidi quatuor angelos stantes super quatuor angulos terræ, tenentes quatuor ventos, ne flarent. Quis colligavit, id est, infra terminos sibi præfixos arctavit ac tenet, aquas maris Oceani quasi in vestimento? juxta illud Psalmi, Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris. Ad Job quoque Deus locutus est : Quis conclusit ostiis mare? Et per Prophetam dicit : Posui arenam terminum mari. De hoc dictum est plenius supra, super illud : Certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos.
paras.en: [[30:4|who hath held the wind in his hands?|Quis continuit spiritum in manibus suis]] [spiritus means both "wind" and "spirit": Denis takes it first of spirits, then of the winds] That is, almighty God in his power has preserved, and preserves, every spirit, angelic and human, or the souls of men, and indeed the spirit of beasts too; for without the unceasing upholding of the Creator no creature could subsist for a moment. He also holds the winds in his hand, which he brings forth out of his stores[[Ps 134:7||]], and sends out and draws back, increases and lessens, at his pleasure. This can also be expounded of Christ, of whom we read: [[Mark 4:39|rising up, he rebuked the wind, and said to the sea: Peace, be still|Surgens Jesus, comminatus est vento, et dixit mari, Tace, et obmutesce]]; [[Mark 4:39|and there was made a great calm|et facta est tranquillitas magna]]. Lastly it is written: [[Apoc 7:1|I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that they should not blow|Vidi quatuor angelos stantes super quatuor angulos terræ, tenentes quatuor ventos, ne flarent]]. [[30:4|Who hath bound up|Quis colligavit]], that is, has confined within the bounds set for them, and holds, [[30:4|the waters|aquas]] of the Ocean sea [[30:4|together as in a garment|quasi in vestimento]] according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 32:7|Gathering together the waters of the sea, as in a vessel|Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris]]. To Job also God spoke: [[Job 38:8|Who shut up the sea with doors|Quis conclusit ostiis mare]]? And by the Prophet he says: [[Jer 5:22|I have set the sand a bound for the sea|Posui arenam terminum mari]]. Of this more has been said above, on the text: [[Prov 8:27|with a certain law, and compass, he enclosed the depths|Certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos]].

paras.t: Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ? id est, quis in esse produxit orbem terrarum, et terminos terræ habitabilis ab aquis esse discoopertos præcepit ac fecit, atque per climata, regna provinciasque distinxit? Utique omnium conditor Deus. De quo loquitur Paulus : Deus qui fecit mundum, et omnia quæ in eo sunt, hic cœli et terræ quum sit Dominus, fecit ex uno omne genus hominum inhabitare super universam faciem terræ, definiens statuta tempora, et terminos habitationis eorum. De quo fertur : Dixit Deus : Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Hinc in Timæo disseruit Plato, quod opifex Deus in exordio jussit terram, tanquam matrem et altricem cunctorum animalium, pro parte esse ab aquis nudatam, ut habitationi ac necessitatibus hominum et ceterorum animantium deserviret.
paras.en: [[30:4|who hath raised up all the borders of the earth?|Quis suscitavit omnes terminos terræ]] that is, who brought the world into being, and commanded and caused the borders of the habitable earth to be uncovered by the waters, and divided it into climes, kingdoms and provinces? Surely God, the maker of all things. Of whom Paul speaks: [[Acts 17:24|God, who made the world and all things therein, he being Lord of heaven and earth|Deus qui fecit mundum, et omnia quæ in eo sunt, hic cœli et terræ quum sit Dominus]], [[Acts 17:26|hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, determining appointed times and the limits of their habitation|fecit ex uno omne genus hominum inhabitare super universam faciem terræ, definiens statuta tempora, et terminos habitationis eorum]]. Of whom it is said: [[Gen 1:9|God also said; Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Dixit Deus : Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. Hence Plato taught in the Timæus that God the craftsman in the beginning commanded the earth, as the mother and nurse of all living things, to be laid bare of the waters in part, so that it might serve the dwelling and the needs of men and of the other animals.

paras.t: Quod nomen est ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti? Ecce hic Salomon de Patre æterno, et unigenito ejus Filio apertissime loquitur, insinuans et protestans, tam Deum creatorem, quam Filium ejus innominabilem et incomprehensibilem esse. Unde concluditur : Filius Dei, Deo Patri esse æqualis et consubstantialis, ac increatus.
