Omnis etenim pura creatura, nominabilis comprehensibilisque consistit; nec Scriptura divina alicui, nisi vero Deo, innominabilitatem et incomprehensibilitatem adscribit. Ideo prætacta excæcatissimorum Hebræorum extorta omnino ac fatua expositio, de Moyse ejusque filio prædicta exponens, ideo ab eis conficta est, ne hac evidenti auctoritate cogerentur unicum Dei Filium et ejus deitatem fateri; quum tamen etiam supra de æterna generatione ac deitate Filii Dei, Salomon manifeste loquutus sit, sicut ibi probatum est. Denique, quamvis Deus Pater et Filius ejus, multa habeant nomina, nihilo minus innominabiles esse dicuntur, quoniam nullo nomine perfecte possunt cognosci aut comprehendi. Idcirco, teste Apostolo, Deus lucem habitat inaccessibilem : et hoc ipsum cognoverunt philosophi. Unde sexta propositione libri de Causis, habetur: Causa prima est superior omni narratione, quoniam ipsa est supra omnem causam, et non narratur, nisi per causas secundas. Item vicesima secunda propositione ejusdem libri inducitur : Causa prima est super omne nomen quo nominatur. De hoc in Elementatione theologica Procli Platonici multa subtiliter conscribuntur.
paras.en: [[30:4|what is his name, and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?|Quod nomen est ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti]] Here Solomon speaks most openly of the eternal Father and of his only-begotten Son, suggesting and declaring that both God the Creator and his Son are unnameable and incomprehensible. Hence it is concluded that the Son of God is equal and consubstantial with God the Father, and uncreated. For every mere creature can be named and comprehended; nor does divine Scripture ascribe unnameableness and incomprehensibility to anyone but the true God. Therefore the aforesaid utterly forced and foolish exposition of the most blinded Hebrews, which expounds these words of Moses and his son, was invented by them so that they should not be compelled by this evident authority to confess the only Son of God and his Godhead; although Solomon has also spoken plainly above of the eternal generation and Godhead of the Son of God[[Prov 8:22||]] [the margin gives only Prov. viii; the passage is 8:22–31], as was proved there. Finally, though God the Father and his Son have many names, they are nonetheless said to be unnameable, because by no name can they be perfectly known or comprehended. Therefore, as the Apostle witnesses, God [[1 Tim 6:16|inhabiteth light inaccessible|lucem habitat inaccessibilem]]; and this very thing the philosophers knew. Hence in the sixth proposition of the book On Causes we have: The first cause is above all telling, since it is above every cause, and is not told except through second causes. Likewise in the twenty-second proposition of the same book it is stated: The first cause is above every name by which it is named. On this many subtle things are written in the Elements of Theology of Proclus the Platonist.

paras.t: Omnis sermo Dei ignitus, id est purus ab omni errore et iniquitate, tanquam ab increata Veritate emanans, ac revelatus a Spiritu Sancto, ac ejus directione conscriptus. Circa hoc asserit Glossa : Proprietatem Græci nominis, quod est πεπυρωμένος, pro quo habetur, Ignitus, unum Latinum nomen non exprimit. Nam aliquando ignitum, aliquando examinatum transfertur. πεπυρωμένος ergo significat, quod igne conflatum est atque purgatum. Sicut enim metalla conflata igne, sordem in se alienam non retinent; ita eloquium Domini, nil falsitatis habet admixtum. Unde in Psalmo : Eloquia Domini, eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum, probatum terræ, purgatum septuplum. Insuper, Omnis sermo Dei ignitus, id est caritatem redolens et accendens, ac ignea verba continens, atque ab illo qui essentialiter caritas est et ignis, procedens. Ideo ait Psalmista: Ignitum eloquium tuum vehementer. Et per Prophetam Dominus dicit: Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis? Quod Jeremias expertus: Factus est, inquit, sermo Domini in corde meo, quasi ignis exæstuans. Hinc Moyses fassus est: In dextera ejus ignea lex.
paras.en: [[30:5|Every word of God is fire tried|Omnis sermo Dei ignitus]], that is, pure from all error and iniquity, as flowing from the uncreated Truth, and revealed by the Holy Ghost, and written under his direction. On this the Gloss declares: No single Latin word expresses the proper sense of the Greek word πεπυρωμένος, for which we have ignitus [that is, "fiery"; the Douay-Rheims has "fire tried"]. For it is translated sometimes fiery, sometimes tried. πεπυρωμένος, then, means what has been melted and purged in the fire. For as metals melted in the fire keep no foreign dross in them, so the word of the Lord has no falsehood mixed in it. Hence in the Psalm: [[Ps 11:7|The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire, purged from the earth, refined seven times.|Eloquia Domini, eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum, probatum terræ, purgatum septuplum]] Moreover, [[30:5|Every word of God is fire tried|Omnis sermo Dei ignitus]], that is, breathing of charity and kindling it, and containing fiery words, and proceeding from him who is essentially charity and fire[[1 John 4:8||]][[Deut 4:24||]]. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:140|Thy word is exceedingly refined|Ignitum eloquium tuum vehementer]] [ignitum, the same word as in this verse, literally "fiery"]. And by the Prophet the Lord says: [[Jer 23:29|Are not my words as a fire|Numquid non verba mea sunt quasi ignis?]]? Which Jeremias experienced: [[Jer 20:9|there came|Factus est]], he says, the word of the Lord [[Jer 20:9|in my heart as a burning fire|in corde meo, quasi ignis exæstuans]]. Hence Moses confessed: [[Deut 33:2|In his right hand a fiery law|In dextera ejus ignea lex]].

paras.t: Clypeus est, id est armatura ac protectio contra vitiorum ac dæmonum impugnationem, contra afflictionem tristitiæ, contra motum concupiscentiæ, omnibus sperantibus in se tanquam in auxilio quodam. In solo autem Deo sperandum est, tanquam in principali et finali objecto. Sed in quibusdam creaturis speratur, tanquam in adminiculis secundariisque objectis. Itaque sermonem Dei nostris mentibus imprimamus, ut eo contra omnia saluti adversantia protegamur. Nempe, ut ait Apostolus, Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum, et erudiendum in justitia, ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum instructus. Hinc denuo loquitur: Quæcumque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam et consolationem Scripturarum, spem habeamus. Ideo dicit Gregorius: Scriptura sacra oculis mentis, tanquam speculum quoddam opponitur, ut in ea interna nostra facies conspiciatur. Ibi enim fœda, ibi pulchra nostra videmus. Ibi cognoscimus quantum proficimus, quantumve a profectu distamus. Verum, ut idem asserit, ad sacræ Scripturæ cognitionem, potius opus est intima compunctione, quam profunda lectione; suspiriis, quam argumentis; crebris gemitibus, quam copiosis argumentationibus; lacrimis, quam sententiis; oratione, quam lectione; contemplatione cœlestium, quam occupatione terrestrium. Ecce quanta utilitas divini sermonis. Nam et sordes excoquit vitiorum, scientia illustrat, caritate inflammat.
paras.en: [[30:5|he is a buckler|Clypeus est]], that is, armour and protection against the assault of vices and of demons, against the affliction of sadness, against the motion of concupiscence, to all [[30:5|them that hope in him|sperantibus in se]] as in a help. Now hope is to be placed in God alone, as in its principal and final object; but in certain creatures hope is placed as in aids and secondary objects. Let us, then, imprint the word of God on our minds, that by it we may be protected against all that is opposed to salvation. For, as the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 3:16|All scripture, inspired of God, is profitable to teach, to reprove, to correct, to instruct in justice:|Omnis Scriptura divinitus inspirata, utilis est ad docendum, ad arguendum, ad corripiendum, et erudiendum in justitia]] [[2 Tim 3:17|That the man of God may be perfect, furnished to every good work.|ut perfectus sit homo Dei, ad omne opus bonum instructus]] Hence he says again: [[Rom 15:4|For what things soever were written were written for our learning: that, through patience and the comfort of the scriptures, we might have hope.|Quæcumque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam et consolationem Scripturarum, spem habeamus]] Therefore Gregory says: Sacred Scripture is set before the eyes of the mind like a mirror, so that our inward face may be seen in it. For there we see what is foul in us and what is fair; there we learn how far we are advancing, and how far we are from advancing. But, as the same says, for the knowledge of Sacred Scripture there is more need of inward compunction than of deep reading; of sighs than of arguments; of frequent groans than of copious reasonings; of tears than of sentences; of prayer than of reading; of the contemplation of heavenly things than of busying oneself with earthly. See how great is the usefulness of the divine word: for it burns out the dross of vices, enlightens with knowledge, and inflames with charity.

paras.t: Ne addas quidquam verbis illius, id est, textui sacræ Scripturæ nihil apponas, quasi ad integritatem Scripturæ et textum pertineat; tamen exponendo addi quid potest, quod concordet omnino Scripturis. Hinc scriptum est: Non adjicietis ad verbum quod ego loquor, neque auferetis ex eo. Unde et ait Joannes apostolus: Contestor ego: Si quis apposuerit ad hæc, apponet Deus super illum plagas scriptas in libro isto; et si quis diminuerit de verbis prophetiæ libri hujus, auferet Deus partem ejus de libro vitæ. Et arguaris, id est, juste reprehendaris de tali additione, inveniarisque mendax, id est vanus et inobediens Deo, si feceris hoc. Et certe qui aliquid Scripturæ contrarium addit, mentitur. Scriptura enim increatæ veritati innititur, et ab ea tanquam ejus radius derivatur, testimoniumque sortitur. Idcirco nil falsius, quam quod Scripturis repugnat. Propter quod scribit Apostolus: Licet nos, aut angelus de cœlo evangelizet vobis, præterquam quod evangelizavimus, anathema sit.
paras.en: [[30:6|Add not any thing to his words|Ne addas quidquam verbis illius]], that is, add nothing to the text of Holy Scripture as though it belonged to the integrity and the text of Scripture; yet in expounding something may be added that wholly agrees with the Scriptures. Hence it is written: [[Deut 4:2|You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, neither shall you take away from it|Non adjicietis ad verbum quod ego loquor, neque auferetis ex eo]]. And so John the apostle says: [[Apoc 22:18|I testify|Contestor ego]]: [[Apoc 22:18|If any man shall add to these things, God shall add unto him the plagues written in this book|Si quis apposuerit ad hæc, apponet Deus super illum plagas scriptas in libro isto]]; [[Apoc 22:19|And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life|et si quis diminuerit de verbis prophetiæ libri hujus, auferet Deus partem ejus de libro vitæ]]. [[30:6|lest thou be reproved|Et arguaris]], that is, be justly blamed for such an addition, [[30:6|and found a liar|inveniarisque mendax]], that is, vain and disobedient to God, if thou do this. And surely he who adds anything contrary to Scripture lies. For Scripture rests on the uncreated truth, and is derived from it as its ray, and receives its witness from it. Therefore nothing is more false than what is contrary to the Scriptures. For this reason the Apostle writes: [[Gal 1:8|though we, or an angel from heaven, preach a gospel to you besides that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema|Licet nos, aut angelus de cœlo evangelizet vobis, præterquam quod evangelizavimus, anathema sit]].

paras.t: Sequitur oratio Salomonis: quæ potius videtur fieri in persona imperfectorum, et secundum statum veteris Testamenti, quam in persona perfectorum, et juxta evangelicæ statum legis. Duo rogavi te, Domine Deus; ne deneges mihi ea, antequam moriar. Vanitatem et verba mendacii longe fac a me: id est, da mihi gratiam abjiciendi et contemnendi omnem vanitatem (id est gloriam vanam, complacentiam mei ipsius in me, finalem inhæsionem circa creata caduca, appetitum laudis humanæ, propriique honoris) et omne mendacium, præsertim perniciosum. Mendicitatem, id est tantam inopiam terrenorum, ut mendicare indigeam, et divitias, id est abundantiam temporalium, ultra exigentiam et condecentiam status mei, ne dederis mihi, nec mihi provenire permittas. Porro istud de mendicitate, videtur secundum statum Mosaicæ legis peti, quoniam scriptum est : Omnino indigens et mendicus non erit inter vos. Tribue tantum victui meo necessaria pro sustentatione mei ipsius, et eorum qui mihi conjuncti sunt, ita quod eorum provisio spectat ad me. Sic et Apostolus ait : Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Itaque in his verbis primo petit auferri a se, ea quæ sunt simpliciter mala, utpote vitia, quæ sunt vanitas atque mendacium: et petit tolli a se ea quæ communiter sunt occasio vitiorum, quamvis non sint mala in se, scilicet mendicitatem et opulentiam.
paras.en: There follows Solomon's prayer, which seems to be made rather in the person of the imperfect, and according to the state of the Old Testament, than in the person of the perfect, and according to the state of the law of the Gospel. [[30:7|Two things I have asked of thee|Duo rogavi te]], O Lord God; [[30:7|deny them not to me|ne deneges mihi]] [[30:7|before I die|antequam moriar]]. [[30:8|Remove far from me vanity, and lying words|Vanitatem et verba mendacii longe fac a me]]: that is, give me the grace to cast off and despise all vanity (that is, vainglory, complacency in myself, final cleaving to perishable creatures, the desire of human praise and of my own honour), and every lie, especially the pernicious lie [that is, one that does harm to another, the gravest kind]. [[30:8|Beggary|Mendicitatem]], that is, such want of earthly things that I must needs beg, [[30:8|nor riches|et divitias]], that is, an abundance of temporal things beyond what my state requires and befits it, [[30:8|give me neither|ne dederis mihi]]: nor let them come to me. Now this about beggary seems to be asked according to the state of the law of Moses, since it is written: [[Deut 15:4|there shall be no poor nor beggar among you|Omnino indigens et mendicus non erit inter vos]]. [[30:8|give me only the necessaries of life|Tribue tantum victui meo necessaria]], for the support of myself and of those joined to me, in so far as providing for them falls to me. So too the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 6:8|having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. So in these words he asks first that the things which are simply evil be taken from him, namely vices, which are vanity and lying; and he asks that the things which are commonly an occasion of vices, though not evil in themselves, be taken from him, namely beggary and wealth.

paras.t: Ideo subdit causam, cur duo hæc postulet sibi non dari. Et primo, cur divitias horreat. Ne forte saturatus : saturatio enim divitias solet concomitari, et gulæ species est ; illiciar, id est attrahar, ad negandum omnipotentiam ac providentiam Dei : quia carnalitas ita obtenebrat intellectum, ut quandoque alliciat eum ad prætactam similemve blasphemiam, sicut Pharaonem, qui ait : Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, et dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam. Hinc subditur : et dicam : Quis est Dominus ? tanquam dicatur : Aut non est Deus, aut si est, non tamen habet notitiam inferiorum, nec providentiam actuum humanorum : juxta illud in Psalmo : Dixerunt, Quomodo scit Deus, et si est scientia in Excelso? Atque in Ezechiele : Dixerunt, Reliquit Dominus terram, et Dominus nos non videt. Quamvis autem pauci ad tantam devolvantur insaniam, ut ista formaliter aut expresse dicant aut sentiant, plurimi tamen tam impudenter, irrefrenate, intemperateque peccant, ut ipso facto hæc dicant, et taliter conversantur ac si ita sentirent. De quibus ad Titum ait Apostolus : Dicunt se nosse Deum, factis autem negant.
paras.en: Then he gives the reason why he asks that these two things be not given him; and first, why he dreads riches. [[30:9|Lest perhaps being filled|Ne forte saturatus]] (for fullness is wont to go with riches, and is a species of gluttony), [[30:9|I should be tempted|illiciar]], that is, drawn, [[30:9|to deny|ad negandum]] the omnipotence and providence of God: for carnality so darkens the understanding that it sometimes entices it to this or a like blasphemy, as it did Pharao, who said: [[Ex 5:2|Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice, and let Israel go?|Quis est Dominus, ut audiam vocem ejus, et dimittam Israel?]] [[Ex 5:2|I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go|Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam]]. Hence there follows: [[30:9|and say: Who is the Lord|et dicam : Quis est Dominus]]? as if it were said: Either there is no God, or if there is, he has no knowledge of things below, nor providence over human acts; according to that in the Psalm: They said: [[Ps 72:11|How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?|Quomodo scit Deus, et si est scientia in Excelso?]] And in Ezechiel: They said: [[Ezech 8:12|the Lord hath forsaken the earth|Reliquit Dominus terram]], and [[Ezech 8:12|The Lord seeth us not|Dominus nos non videt]] [Denis gives the two clauses in the order of Ezech 9:9]. And though few fall into such madness as to say or think these things formally or expressly, yet very many sin so shamelessly, so unrestrainedly and intemperately, that by the very deed they say them, and live as if they thought so. Of whom the Apostle says to Titus: [[Tit 1:16|They profess that they know God: but in their works they deny him|Dicunt se nosse Deum, factis autem negant]].

paras.t: Deinde subjungitur, cur mendicitatem abhorreat. Aut egestate compulsus, id est, ne ex inopia incitet et inducar ad hoc, ut furer, et perjurem nomen Dei mei. Multi equidem occasione indigentiæ suæ, ad furta, rapinam, mendacia, fraudes, violentiamque labuntur. Unde superius dictum est : Furatur ut esurientem repleat animam. Verum tantæ esse fragilitatis, ut ex mendicitate et opulentia ruat quis ad prætacta facinora, et hac ratione mendicitatem divitiasque horrere, formidare ac refutare, ne ex eis ad tantam deveniatur ruinam, videtur esse imperfectorum, nescientium bene uti eufortuniis ac diffortuniis, prosperis et adversis, opulentia ac indigentia. Quocontra loquitur Paulus : Scio abundare, scio et penuriam pati ; ubique et in omnibus institutus sum, et satiari, id est ad sufficientiam vesci, et esurire. Christus quoque non solum paupertatem, sed et mendicitatem exemplo et verbo docuit, atque consuluit et elegit : qui in Psalmo testatur, Ego autem mendicus sum et pauper ; itemque, Persecutus est hominem inopem et mendicum, ipse videlicet traditor Christi. Nec dubium, quin psalmi in quibus hæc continentur, ad litteram de Christo conscripti sunt. Hinc perfecti imitatores evangelicæ paupertatis, nec in communi, neque in particulari, aliquid habent terrenæ possessionis aut hereditatis. Hinc Seneca in libro de Quatuor virtutibus ait : Magnus ille est, qui sic fictilibus utitur, quemadmodum argento; nec minor ille est, qui sic auro utitur, quemadmodum testa. Infirmi animi est, non posse pati divitias. Et rursus : Quotidie aliquid auxilii contra paupertatem acquire. Honesta res est læta paupertas. Illa vero jam non est paupertas, si læta est. Non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est. Non est in rebus vitium, sed in animo. Quemadmodum nihil differt, utrum ægrum in ligneo lecto, an in aureo colloces; quocumque illum transtuleris, morbum suum deferet secum : sic nihil refert, utrum æger animus in divitiis, an in paupertate ponatur ; malum suum sequitur eum. Hæc Seneca. Hinc etiam olim in lege naturæ, deinde in lege scripta, copiosius autem in lege evangelica fuerunt quidam ditissimi, et tamen perfecti. Verumtamen Christus sapientissime paupertatem consulit, quia perpauci sunt qui non abutuntur divitiis, et multa vitia eis solent esse annexa.
paras.en: Then is added why he abhors beggary. [[30:9|or being compelled by poverty|Aut egestate compulsus]], that is, lest from want I be stirred and led to this, that [[30:9|I should steal, and forswear the name of my God|furer, et perjurem nomen Dei mei]]. Many indeed, by occasion of their need, slip into thefts, robbery, lies, frauds and violence. Hence it was said above: [[Prov 6:30|he stealeth to fill his hungry soul|Furatur ut esurientem repleat animam]]. But to be so frail that one falls into the aforesaid crimes from beggary or from wealth, and for this reason to dread, fear and refuse beggary and riches, lest one come to so great a ruin through them, seems to belong to the imperfect, who do not know how to use well good fortune and ill, prosperity and adversity, wealth and want. Against this Paul says: [[Phil 4:12|I know how to abound|Scio abundare]], I know also [[Phil 4:12|to suffer need|penuriam pati]]; [[Phil 4:12|every where and in all things I am instructed|ubique et in omnibus institutus sum]], [[Phil 4:12|both to be full|et satiari]], that is, to eat enough, [[Phil 4:12|and to be hungry|et esurire]]. Christ too taught not only poverty but also beggary, by example and by word, and counselled and chose it: who testifies in the Psalm: [[Ps 39:18|But I am a beggar and poor|Ego autem mendicus sum et pauper]]; and again: he [[Ps 108:17|persecuted the poor man and the beggar|Persecutus est hominem inopem et mendicum]], namely the betrayer of Christ. Nor is there any doubt that the psalms in which these words stand were written of Christ according to the letter. Hence the perfect imitators of evangelical poverty have nothing of earthly possession or inheritance, either in common or of their own. Hence Seneca says in the book On the Four Virtues [a work ascribed to Seneca in the Middle Ages; it is by Martin of Braga]: He is great who uses earthenware as if it were silver; nor is he less who uses gold as if it were clay. It is the mark of a weak mind not to be able to bear riches. And again: Each day gain some help against poverty. A cheerful poverty is an honourable thing; but it is no longer poverty, if it is cheerful. Not he who has little, but he who desires more, is poor. The vice is not in things but in the mind. Just as it makes no difference whether you lay a sick man in a wooden bed or in a golden one, for wherever you move him he will carry his sickness with him, so it matters nothing whether a sick mind be set in riches or in poverty: its evil follows it. Thus far Seneca. Hence too there were of old, in the law of nature, then in the written law, and more abundantly in the law of the Gospel, some who were very rich and yet perfect. Nevertheless Christ most wisely counsels poverty[[Matt 19:21||]], because very few do not abuse riches, and many vices are wont to go with them.

paras.t: Ne accuses servum ad dominum suum. De quali accusatione intelligendum sit hoc, constat ex eo quod subditur : ne forte maledicat tibi, et corruas, id est, ne servus sic accusatus, imprecetur tibi adversa, et exaudiatur a Domino, ita quod pressus adversis labaris. Itaque de accusatione ex invidia, aut crudelitate, seu alia prava radice prodeunte, intelligitur istud. Compatiendum est etenim servis, præsertim empticiis, et qui dominos habent duros : ideo seorsum sunt admonendi. Quod si non acquieverint, vel aliquid contra bonum commune attentare præsumpserint, essent utique accusandi.
paras.en: [[30:10|Accuse not a servant to his master|Ne accuses servum ad dominum suum]]. Of what kind of accusation this is to be understood is clear from what is added: [[30:10|lest he curse thee, and thou fall|ne forte maledicat tibi, et corruas]], that is, lest the servant thus accused call down misfortunes upon thee and be heard by the Lord, so that, borne down by adversities, thou fall. So this is to be understood of an accusation springing from envy, or cruelty, or some other evil root. For we ought to have compassion on servants, especially those bought with money, and those who have harsh masters: so they are to be admonished privately. But if they do not comply, or presume to attempt something against the common good, then they certainly ought to be accused.

paras.t: Generatio, id est, quædam hominum collectio est, quæ patri suo carnali, seu spirituali, aut etiam Deo omnipotenti, maledicit : sicut Marcionitæ et Manichæi, dicentes Deum legis ac Prophetarum, esse totaliter malum atque crudelem; et quæ matri suæ non benedicit, id est generatio non benedicens Ecclesiæ, aut matri carnali, aut spirituali.
paras.en: There is a [[30:11|generation|Generatio]], that is, a certain gathering of men, [[30:11|that curseth their father|quæ patri suo]], whether their father in the flesh or their spiritual father, or even almighty God, as do the Marcionites and the Manichees, who say that the God of the Law and of the Prophets is wholly evil and cruel; [[30:11|and doth not bless their mother|et quæ matri suæ non benedicit]], that is, a generation that does not bless the Church, or its mother in the flesh, or its spiritual mother.

paras.t: Generatio quædam est, quæ sibi munda esse videtur, id est immunis a vitiis, ut pauperes de Lugduno, et Novatiani hæretici, dicentes se pœnitentia non egere, et liberi spiritus, asserentes se peccare non posse; et tamen non est lota a sordibus suis.
paras.en: [[30:12|A generation that are pure in their own eyes|Generatio quædam est, quæ sibi munda esse videtur]], that is, free from vices, like the Poor Men of Lyons [that is, the Waldensians], and the Novatian heretics, who say that they have no need of penance, and the Free Spirits, who assert that they cannot sin; [[30:12|and yet are not washed from their filthiness|et tamen non est lota a sordibus suis]].

paras.t: Generatio quædam est, cujus excelsi sunt oculi, et palpebræ ejus in altum surrectæ : id est, quidam sunt ita superbi et animosi, quod eadem contumacia apparet in dispositione, apparatu, erectione corporalium oculorum eorum. Unde Isaias dicit : Oculi sublimis hominis humiliati sunt. Et in Job dicitur : Quid te elevat cor tuum, et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos? Tales fuerunt superbissimi Ariani.
paras.en: [[30:13|A generation, whose eyes are lofty, and their eyelids lifted up on high|Generatio quædam est, cujus excelsi sunt oculi, et palpebræ ejus in altum surrectæ]]: that is, some are so proud and high-spirited that the same arrogance shows in the set, the bearing and the lifting up of their bodily eyes. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 2:11|The lofty eyes of man are humbled|Oculi sublimis hominis humiliati sunt]]. And in Job it is said: [[Job 15:12|Why doth thy heart elevate thee, and why dost thou stare with thy eyes, as if they were thinking great things?|Quid te elevat cor tuum, et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos?]] Such were the Arians, proudest of men.

paras.t: Generatio quædam est, quæ pro dentibus gladios habet, id est, cujus dentes et lingua gladiis assimilantur, juxta illud in Psalmo : Filii hominum, dentes eorum arma et sagittæ, et lingua eorum gladius acutus. Tales sunt qui venenatis ac perfidis documentis inficiunt alios, et detractores ac seminatores discordiæ, et qui bona devorant aliorum, præsertim impotentium. Unde subjungitur : et commandit molaribus suis, id est, majoribus dentibus suis manducat, ut comedat inopes de terra, id est, pauperum bona consumat, vel eos occidat, et pauperes ex hominibus, id est, de medio hominum tollat, expellat, interficiatve egenos, vel spiritualiter pauperes et egenos, puta pusillos, simplices, imperfectos, scandalizet, decipiat, ac intus in anima perimat. Unde loquitur Dominus per Prophetam : Vos depasti estis vineam meam, et rapina pauperis in domo vestra. Quare atteritis populum meum, et facies pauperum commolitis? Et Malachias propheta ait : Vos autem recessistis de via, et scandalizastis plurimos in lege.
paras.en: [[30:14|A generation that for teeth hath swords|Generatio quædam est, quæ pro dentibus gladios habet]], that is, whose teeth and tongue are like swords, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 56:5|The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword|Filii hominum, dentes eorum arma et sagittæ, et lingua eorum gladius acutus]] [the margin gives Ps. lxvi, 5; the words are Ps 56:5]. Such are those who infect others with poisonous and faithless teachings, and detractors and sowers of discord, and those who devour the goods of others, especially of the powerless. Hence it is added: [[30:14|and grindeth with their jaw teeth|et commandit molaribus suis]], that is, chews with its larger teeth, [[30:14|to devour the needy from off the earth|ut comedat inopes de terra]], that is, to consume the goods of the poor, or to kill them, [[30:14|and the poor from among men|et pauperes ex hominibus]], that is, to take away, drive out or kill the needy from the midst of men; or else to scandalize, deceive and slay inwardly in the soul the spiritually poor and needy, that is, the little ones, the simple, the imperfect. Hence the Lord speaks through the Prophet: [[Is 3:14|you have devoured the vineyard, and the spoil of the poor is in your house|Vos depasti estis vineam meam, et rapina pauperis in domo vestra]] [Denis has "my vineyard"]. [[Is 3:15|Why do you consume my people, and grind the faces of the poor?|Quare atteritis populum meum, et facies pauperum commolitis?]] [the margin gives v. 13; the words are Is 3:15]. And Malachias the prophet says: [[Mal 2:8|But you have departed out of the way, and have caused many to stumble at the law|Vos autem recessistis de via, et scandalizastis plurimos in lege]].

paras.t: Sanguisugæ duæ sunt filiæ, dicentes : Affer, affer. Sanguisuga dicitur quasi sanguinem sugens : cujus dicuntur esse filiæ duæ, quoniam duo sunt vitia, bestiam hanc specialiter imitantia, utpote avaritia atque luxuria. Nam sicut sanguisuga velut insatiabiliter sanguinem sitit ac ebibit, sic vitia ista semper ad ampliora anhelant. Ideo unumquodque eorum perhibetur dicere, Affer, affer : quia inclinat suum subjectum ad dicendum, Adhuc, adhuc mihi plura objecta, vel eadem sæpius repetita. Hinc ait Hieronymus : Libido transacta pœnitudinem semper relinquit; nec unquam satiatur, imo exstincta reinflammatur, usu crescit; nec rationi obedit, quoniam impetu ducitur. De avaritia vero asserit Augustinus : Avarus inferno est similis. Infernus enim quantoscumque deglutiat, nunquam dicit, Satis est : sic et si omnes thesauri confluxerint in avarum, non ei sufficiet. Quæ est ista cupidorum aviditas, quum et bestiæ habeant modum? Tunc enim rapiunt, quando esuriunt; parcunt autem prædæ, quum senserint satietatem. Insatiabilis est avaritia iniquorum : quæ rapit, nec satiatur; nec Deum timet, nec hominem reveretur; nec patri paret, nec matrem cognoscit; nec fratri obtemperat, nec amico fidem conservat. Viduam opprimit, pupillum invadit, liberos in servitium revocat; testimonium falsum profert, mortuorum res occupat. At vero juxta Glossam, sanguisuga est diabolus, qui siti peccandi et peccata suadendi perpetuo ardet. Duæ filiæ ejus, quæ ipsius imitantur ardorem, sunt luxuria et philargyria.
paras.en: [[30:15|The horseleech hath two daughters that say: Bring, bring|Sanguisugæ duæ sunt filiæ, dicentes : Affer, affer]]. The horseleech is so called as being a blood-sucker [Latin *sanguisuga*, from *sanguis*, blood, and *sugere*, to suck]: it is said to have two daughters because there are two vices which especially imitate this beast, namely avarice and lust. For as the horseleech thirsts for blood and drinks it up as if it could never be sated, so these vices always pant after more. Therefore each of them is said to say: [[30:15|Bring, bring|Affer, affer]], because it inclines its subject to say: More, more objects for me, or the same ones over and over again. Hence Jerome says: Lust, once spent, always leaves regret behind; it is never sated, but when quenched is kindled again, and grows with use; nor does it obey reason, since it is driven by impulse. And of avarice Augustine says: The avaricious man is like hell. For hell, however many it swallows, never says, It is enough: so too, if all treasures flowed together into the avaricious man, they would not suffice him. What is this greed of the covetous, when even beasts have a measure? For they seize when they are hungry, but spare their prey once they feel themselves sated. Insatiable is the avarice of the wicked: it seizes and is not sated; it neither fears God nor reveres man; it does not obey a father, nor acknowledge a mother, nor heed a brother, nor keep faith with a friend. It oppresses the widow, assails the orphan, calls the free back into slavery, bears false witness, seizes the goods of the dead. But according to the Gloss, the horseleech is the devil, who burns perpetually with the thirst of sinning and of urging others to sin. His two daughters, which imitate his burning, are lust and philargyria [Greek for the love of money, that is, avarice].

paras.t: Tria in specie sunt insatiabilia, et quartum nunquam dicit, Sufficit. Infernus, id est locus infernalis, ob suam capacitatem, vel diabolus, ob suam invidiam, et os vulvæ, id est incontinens libidinosaque mulier, et terra, præcipue arenosa, quæ non satiatur aqua : quia celeriter eam absorbet. Ignis vero nunquam dicit ipso facto, Sufficit : quia ex combustibilium appositione augetur, non minoratur. Ignis quoque infernalis nunquam dicit, Sufficit, quia ab impiorum cruciatibus nunquam cessat.
paras.en: There are [[30:15|three things|Tria]] in particular [[30:15|that never are satisfied|sunt insatiabilia]], [[30:15|and the fourth never saith: It is enough|et quartum nunquam dicit, Sufficit]]. [[30:16|Hell|Infernus]], that is, the infernal place, on account of its capacity, or the devil, on account of his envy, [[30:16|and the mouth of the womb|et os vulvæ]], that is, an incontinent and lustful woman, [[30:16|and the earth|et terra]], especially sandy earth, [[30:16|which is not satisfied with water|quæ non satiatur aqua]], because it swiftly soaks it up; [[30:16|and the fire never saith|Ignis vero nunquam dicit]] by its very nature [[30:16|It is enough|Sufficit]], because it is increased, not lessened, by the adding of fuel. The fire of hell too never says, It is enough, because it never ceases from the torments of the wicked.

paras.t: Oculum qui subsannat patrem carnalem, aut spiritualem, aut summi Patris deridet judicia, et qui despicit partum matris suæ, id est fratrem suum, aut laboriosam et ærumnosam matris parturitionem, aut deformitates quæ in facie feminæ accelerantur ex partu frequenti; suffodiant eum corvi de torrentibus, id est, a dæmonibus eruatur, vel sepultura privetur, et comedant eum filii aquilæ, id est, ab angelis Satanæ absorbeatur, seu a bestiis devoretur.
paras.en: [[30:17|The eye that mocketh at his father|Oculum qui subsannat patrem]], his father in the flesh or his spiritual father, or that derides the judgments of the most high Father, [[30:17|and that despiseth the labour of his mother in bearing him|et qui despicit partum matris suæ]], that is, his brother [Latin *partum matris*, "his mother's offspring"], or his mother's toilsome and painful labour in childbirth, or the disfigurements that frequent childbearing hastens on in a woman's face; [[30:17|let the ravens of the brooks pick it out|suffodiant eum corvi de torrentibus]], that is, may it be plucked out by demons, or be deprived of burial, [[30:17|and the young eagles eat it|et comedant eum filii aquilæ]] [Latin *filii aquilæ*, "the sons of the eagle"], that is, may it be swallowed up by the angels of Satan, or devoured by beasts.

paras.t: Quidam tamen per corvos intelligunt prædicatores sagaces et oculatos : qui de Scripturarum fluentis procedunt ad extrahendum oculum talem a sua perversitate, sicque purgatum comedunt filii aquilæ, id est contemplativi, qui instar aquilarum oculum mentis infigunt Soli justitiæ, et intuendo, amando, cœliformiterque vivendo, volant in altum. Hi comedunt, id est, mystico corpori suo innectunt, et sibi incorporant, oculum talem, id est hominem sic videntem. Itaque, per filios seu imitatores aquilæ, ratione rapacitatis designantur spiritus mali; ratione autem acuminis ac alti volatus, contemplativi.
paras.en: Some, however, understand by the ravens shrewd and clear-sighted preachers, who come forth from the streams of the Scriptures to draw such an eye out of its perversity; and when it is thus cleansed, the sons of the eagle eat it, that is, the contemplatives, who like eagles fix the eye of the mind on the Sun of justice, and by gazing, by loving and by living a heavenly life, fly on high. These eat, that is, join to their mystical body and incorporate into themselves, such an eye, that is, the man who sees thus. So by the sons or imitators of the eagle are signified, by reason of its rapacity, the evil spirits; but by reason of its keen sight and lofty flight, the contemplatives.

paras.t: Tria sunt difficilia mihi, et quartum penitus ignoro. Quæ autem sint tria illa, mox subditur. Viam aquilæ in cœlo aerio : in quo aquila hinc inde viam variat sui volatus, ita ut difficulter valeat deprehendi; viam colubri super petram : supra quam serpens sic dictus celeriter ac multipliciter circumagit et circumvolvit se; viam navis in medio mari : ubi hinc inde jactatur vi ventorum ac fluctuum; et viam viri in adolescentia sua. Hoc est quartum prorsus ignotum. In adolescentia namque sanguine fervente, cogitationes, desideria, verba et opera adolescentium investigabiliter ineffabiliterque mutantur.
paras.en: [[30:18|Three things are hard to me, and the fourth I am utterly ignorant of.|Tria sunt difficilia mihi, et quartum penitus ignoro]] What those three are is added at once. The way of an eagle in the air [Denis reads *in cœlo aerio*, "in the airy heaven"], in which the eagle varies the path of its flight this way and that, so that it can hardly be traced; the way of a serpent upon a rock, on which the serpent of that name [*coluber*] swiftly turns and coils itself about in many ways; the way of a ship in the midst of the sea, where it is tossed this way and that by the force of the winds and waves; and the way of a man in his youth. This is the fourth, which is wholly unknown. For in youth, when the blood is hot, the thoughts, desires, words and deeds of the young change past tracing and past telling [the print has *investigabiliter*, evidently for *ininvestigabiliter*, "unsearchably"].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per viam aquilæ in cœlo, designatur profectus et actio contemplativorum in militante Ecclesia : quorum conversatio est in cœlis; quorum actus et processus juxta variam inspirationem ac influentiam Spiritus Sancti, indicibiliter immutantur. Per viam colubri super petram, accipitur occupatio callidorum circa terrena, quorum curæ ac studia inexplicabiliter variantur; per viam navis in medio mari, conversatio, tentatio, et peregrinatio Ecclesiæ in hoc sæculo nequam, in quo tanquam in procellosissimo Oceano fluctibus tentationum, ventis persecutionum, directionibus prælatorum atque spirituum supernorum, processu virtutum, inenarrabiliter alteratur. Per viam viri in adolescentia sua, instabilitas designatur cordis humani, quod suis desideriis assidue juvenescit, sive in bono, sive in malo; cujus varietas soli Creatori est patula.
paras.en: Spiritually, by the way of the eagle in heaven is signified the progress and activity of contemplatives in the Church militant, whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]], and whose acts and advance change unspeakably according to the varied inspiration and influence of the Holy Ghost. By the way of the serpent upon the rock is understood the busyness of the crafty about earthly things, whose cares and pursuits vary inexplicably; by the way of the ship in the midst of the sea, the life, temptation and pilgrimage of the Church in this wicked world, in which, as in a most stormy ocean, she is changed beyond telling by the waves of temptations, the winds of persecutions, the guidance of prelates and of the spirits above, and the progress of the virtues. By the way of a man in his youth is signified the instability of the human heart, which is ever growing young again in its desires, whether in good or in evil; whose changeableness lies open to the Creator alone.

paras.t: Præterea, quidam per viam aquilæ in cœlo, intelligunt Christi ascensionem; per viam colubri super petram, Christi resurrectionem de sepulcro lapideo. Significatur equidem Christus per serpentem, juxta illud : Sicut Moyses exaltavit serpentem in deserto, ita exaltari oportet Filium hominis. Per viam navis in medio mari, intelligunt conversationem Christi in sæculo isto, in quo persecutionibus et tormentis est pressus; per viam viri in adolescentia sua, Christi incarnationem. Et dicunt in Hebræo haberi, In adolescentula : per quam intelligunt Virginem gloriosam, in qua Christi via fuit incarnatio sua, quæ est incomprehensibilis prorsus; et in ea fuit Christus vir perfectus, non corporis quantitate, aut tempore, sed omni sapientiæ atque scientiæ ac virtutum perfectione. Unde Jeremias prædixit : Novum faciet Dominus super terram : Mulier circumdabit virum. Verum expositio ista videtur allegorica magis quam litteralis. Nec enim ad litteram consonat ei quod subditur.
paras.en: Moreover, some understand by the way of the eagle in heaven the ascension of Christ; by the way of the serpent upon the rock, Christ's resurrection from the tomb of stone. For Christ is indeed signified by the serpent, according to that text: [[John 3:14|as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up|Sicut Moyses exaltavit serpentem in deserto, ita exaltari oportet Filium hominis]]. By the way of the ship in the midst of the sea they understand Christ's life in this world, in which he was pressed by persecutions and torments; by the way of a man in his youth, the incarnation of Christ. And they say that the Hebrew has *In a young girl*, by whom they understand the glorious Virgin, in whom Christ's way was his incarnation, which is altogether incomprehensible; and in her Christ was a perfect man, not in size of body or in age, but in every perfection of wisdom, knowledge and the virtues. Hence Jeremias foretold: [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: A WOMAN SHALL COMPASS A MAN|Novum faciet Dominus super terram : Mulier circumdabit virum]] [Denis's wording: "The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall compass a man"]. But this exposition seems allegorical rather than literal. For in the letter it does not agree with what is added.

paras.t: Talis est via mulieris adulteræ. Per quam sive perfida Synagoga, sive quæcumque conjugalis fidei violatrix intelligatur, non est putandum quod Salomon viam ejus incarnationi Verbi æterni comparavit. Et quamvis Salomoni fuit naturalium rerum infusa scientia, quantum ad cognitionem naturæ specificæ et accidentium propriorum, non tamen quantum ad universa accidentia communia. Ideo quartum jam præfatum nescivit, quantum ad accidentia talia, sicut expositum est. Forsitan etiam in Hebræo habetur dictio talis, quæ tam adolescentiam quam adolescentulam signet. Itaque via adulterarum similis est viæ adolescentium, quoniam in desideriis, phantasiis, cogitationibus, verbis et factis suis prorsus instabiles sunt.
paras.en: [[30:20|Such also is the way of an adulterous woman|Talis est via mulieris adulteræ]]. Whether by her is understood the faithless Synagogue or any violator of conjugal faith, it is not to be thought that Solomon compared her way to the incarnation of the eternal Word. And although Solomon had an infused knowledge of natural things as regards the knowledge of their specific nature and proper accidents, yet he had it not as regards all their common accidents [that is, the properties that flow from a thing's species, as against the passing states it shares with many other things]. Therefore he did not know the fourth thing already mentioned, as regards such accidents, as has been explained. Perhaps too there is a word in the Hebrew that signifies both youth and a young girl. So the way of adulteresses is like the way of the young, since they are wholly unstable in their desires, fancies, thoughts, words and deeds.

paras.t: Quæ comedit : adultera enim pro posse libenter intenta est comessationi; et tergens os suum, dicit : Non sum operata malum : quia frontose excusat se, et ita obscurata est mente, ut adulteria sua vix reputet esse peccata. Hinc dicit Jeremias in vitiis habituato : Frons mulieris meretricis facta est tibi, noluisti erubescere; et rursus, Ecce ego judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi.
paras.en: [[30:20|who eateth|Quæ comedit]]: for the adulteress, as far as she can, gladly gives herself to feasting; [[30:20|and wipeth her mouth, and saith: I have done no evil|et tergens os suum, dicit : Non sum operata malum]]: because she brazenly excuses herself, and is so darkened in mind that she scarcely reckons her adulteries to be sins. Hence Jeremias says to one hardened in vices: [[Jer 3:3|thou hadst a harlot's forehead, thou wouldst not blush|Frons mulieris meretricis facta est tibi, noluisti erubescere]]; and again: [[Jer 2:35|Behold, I will contend with thee in judgment, because thou hast said: I have not sinned|Ecce ego judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per mulierem adulteram intelligitur quæcumque anima vitiosa, quæ relicto Sponso cœlesti, per consensum illicitum commiscetur diabolo, et rebus caducis inhæret finaliter. Ideo asserit Augustinus, quod omnis anima christiana, est Dei sponsa, vel dæmonum adultera. De hoc adulterio dicitur : Omnes adulterantes quasi clibanus succensus a coquente.
paras.en: Spiritually, by the adulterous woman is understood any vicious soul which, forsaking the heavenly Bridegroom, mingles with the devil by unlawful consent, and clings to perishable things as its final end. So Augustine asserts that every Christian soul is either the bride of God or the adulteress of demons. Of this adultery it is said: [[Osee 7:4|They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker|Omnes adulterantes quasi clibanus succensus a coquente]].

paras.t: Per tria in genere movetur terra, id est, habitantes in terra inquietantur ac perturbantur; et quartum est quod non potest sustinere : id est, tam irrationabile atque absurdum est, ut nequeat tolerari. Deinde tria illa exprimuntur.
paras.en: [[30:21|By three things|Per tria]] in general [[30:21|the earth is disturbed|movetur terra]], that is, those who dwell on the earth are disquieted and troubled; [[30:21|and the fourth it cannot bear|et quartum est quod non potest sustinere]]: that is, it is so unreasonable and absurd that it cannot be tolerated. Then those three are set out.

paras.t: Per servum, quum regnaverit. Servi enim ad regnandum et præsidendum promoti, communiter insolescunt, extolluntur ac sæviunt, suspiciosique sunt, de facili suspicantes se a subditis sperni. Ideo per dura et aspera volunt illis terrorem sui incutere. Secundum est : per stultum, quum saturatus fuerit cibo, id est per hominem passionatum, quum fuerit gulose refectus et inebriatus : tunc enim specialiter pronus est ad lites, contentiones, injurias.
paras.en: [[30:22|By a slave when he reigneth|Per servum, quum regnaverit]]. For slaves promoted to reign and to preside commonly grow insolent, are puffed up and rage; and they are suspicious, readily suspecting that they are despised by their subjects. Therefore they want to strike terror of themselves into them by harsh and rough measures. The second is: [[30:22|by a fool when be is filled with meat|per stultum, quum saturatus fuerit cibo]], that is, by a man ruled by passion, when he has been gluttonously fed and made drunk: for then especially he is prone to quarrels, contentions and injuries.

paras.t: Tertium est : per odiosam mulierem, quum in matrimonium fuerit assumpta. Mulier enim odiosa, id est odio plena sive odibilis, vel ad invidiam prona, quum fuerit maritata, mox incipit contra maritum passionibus iræ, impatientiæ, odii agitari. Sicque fit marito gravissima, imo et cunctis domesticis, et inter eam et virum mirabile odium generatur. Unde mutua eorum conversatio est tanto molestior, quanto conjunctior ac inseparabilior. Sequitur quartum, quod sustinere non valet : et per ancillam, quum fuerit heres dominæ suæ, id est ad honorem et opulentiam dominæ suæ promota, seu dilecta a viro, suam propriam uxorem repudiante aut deprimente : hoc quippe est intolerabile malum. Unde et Agar ancilla Saræ, videns se concepisse, dominam suam contempsit : quod illa non ferens, expulit eam, ut legitur.
paras.en: The third is: [[30:23|By an odious woman when she is married|per odiosam mulierem, quum in matrimonium fuerit assumpta]]. For an odious woman, that is, one full of hatred, or hateful, or prone to envy, once she is married, soon begins to be stirred against her husband by passions of anger, impatience and hatred. And so she becomes most grievous to her husband, and indeed to the whole household, and an astonishing hatred grows up between her and her husband. Hence their life together is the more irksome the closer and the more inseparable it is. There follows the fourth, which it cannot bear: [[30:23|and by a bondwoman when she is heir to her mistress|et per ancillam, quum fuerit heres dominæ suæ]], that is, raised to the honour and wealth of her mistress, or loved by the husband, who puts away or puts down his own wife: for this is an intolerable evil. So too Agar, the handmaid of Sara[[Gen 16:1||]], seeing that she had conceived, despised her mistress[[Gen 16:4||]]; and Sara, not bearing it, drove her out, as we read[[Gen 16:6||]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per servum regnantem, intelligitur homo servituti passionum ac vitiorum subjectus, qui ad prælationem promotus, subditos sæpe graviterque conturbat; per stultum satiatum, homo in naturalibus eruditus, et prudens in oculis suis, qui inflatus scientia, nulli obedit, et contra proximos frequenter rixatur; per odiosam mulierem, collectio hæreticorum, schismaticorum, Judæorum ad fidem conversa, quæ sæpe invenitur vacillare in catholica veritate; per ancillam dominæ suæ heredem, anima spiritualibus charismatibus ad tempus repleta, consolationibusque divinis refecta, ac postmodum lapsa, quæ vix recuperatur, juxta illud ad Hebræos : Impossibile est, eos qui semel sunt illuminati, gustaverunt etiam donum cœleste, et participes facti sunt Spiritus Sancti, et prolapsi sunt, rursus renovari ad pœnitentiam.
paras.en: Spiritually, by the slave reigning is understood a man subject to the slavery of passions and vices who, promoted to a prelacy, often and grievously troubles his subjects; by the fool that is filled, a man learned in natural things and prudent in his own eyes, who, puffed up with knowledge, obeys no one and often quarrels with his neighbours; by the odious woman, a gathering of heretics, schismatics and Jews converted to the faith, which is often found to waver in the catholic truth; by the bondwoman who is heir to her mistress, a soul filled for a time with spiritual gifts and refreshed with divine consolations, and afterwards fallen, which is scarcely recovered, according to that to the Hebrews: [[Heb 6:4|it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have tasted also the heavenly gift and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost|Impossibile est, eos qui semel sunt illuminati, gustaverunt etiam donum cœleste, et participes facti sunt Spiritus Sancti]], [[Heb 6:6|And are fallen away: to be renewed again to penance|et prolapsi sunt, rursus renovari ad pœnitentiam]].

paras.t: Quatuor sunt minima terræ, id est animalia valde parva; et ipsa sunt sapientiora sapientibus : id est, industriam habent naturalem ingenitam, per quam plus de sapientia seu prudentia participant, quam animalia quædam majora, quæ tamen callida reputantur.
paras.en: [[30:24|There are four very little things of the earth|Quatuor sunt minima terræ]], that is, very small animals, [[30:24|and they are wiser than the wise|et ipsa sunt sapientiora sapientibus]]: that is, they have a natural, inborn skill, by which they share more of wisdom or prudence than certain larger animals which are nevertheless reckoned cunning.

paras.t: Horum quatuor minimorum primum, est formicæ, populus infirmus, id est formica quæ infirmo populo assimilatur, quia in abdito commoratur, ne consumatur, qui populus, id est quæ formica seu congeries formicarum (populus enim pro quacumque congregatione accipi solet), præparat in messe cibum sibi : ut dictum est plenius super illud : Formica, quum non habeat ducem aut præceptorem, parat æstate cibum sibi, et congregat in messe quod comedat.
paras.en: The first of these four least things is [[30:25|The ants, a feeble people|formicæ, populus infirmus]], that is, the ant, which is likened to a feeble people because it dwells in hiding, lest it be destroyed; [[30:25|which|qui]] people, that is, which ant or swarm of ants (for *people* is commonly used of any gathering), [[30:25|provide themselves food in the harvest|præparat in messe cibum sibi]]: as was said more fully on the text: The ant, [[Prov 6:7|although she hath no guide, nor master|quum non habeat ducem aut præceptorem]], [[Prov 6:8|Provideth her meat for herself in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest|parat æstate cibum sibi, et congregat in messe quod comedat]].

paras.t: Secundum, est lepusculus, plebs invalida, id est similis plebi formidolosæ ac debili, qui collocat in petra cubile suum, id est, habitaculum sibi eligit infra terram in cavernis petrarum, aut profundis solidisque latibulis, ne ab hominibus venatione canum apprehendatur. Denique (sicut fertur in Glossa) pro lepusculo alia translatio habet, Chœrogryllus : qui est animal non minus hericio, simile urso, cujus in Palæstina magna est copia in cavernis petrarum et foveis. Unde in Psalmo ubi dicitur, Petra refugium hericiaciis, alii habent, Leporibus, alii, Chœrogryllis; hic quoque aliqui pro lepusculo, hericium habent. Hieronymus enim verbum istud Hebræum, Saphan, in Jeremia interpretatur chœrogryllum : et hericium, transfert in leporem.
paras.en: The second is [[30:26|The rabbit, a weak people|lepusculus, plebs invalida]], that is, like a fearful and feeble people, [[30:26|which maketh its bed in the rock|qui collocat in petra cubile suum]], that is, it chooses itself a dwelling below the ground in the caverns of rocks, or in deep and solid hiding places, lest it be caught by men hunting with dogs. Further (as is said in the Gloss), for *lepusculus* [little hare] another translation has *Chœrogryllus*, which is an animal no smaller than a hedgehog, like a bear, of which there is a great number in Palestine in the caverns of rocks and in pits. Hence in the Psalm where it is said [[Ps 103:18|the rock for the irchins|Petra refugium hericiaciis]], some have *for the hares*, others *for the chœrogrylli*; here too some have *hedgehog* for *lepusculus*. For Jerome, in Jeremias, renders this Hebrew word *Saphan* as *chœrogryllus*, and turns *hedgehog* into *hare*.

paras.t: Sequitur tertium. Regem locusta non habet, id est, congeries seu multitudo locustarum, non habet suæ speciei rectorem ac directorem : tamen ars increata, deinde intelligentia, universalisque quoque natura, rectrix et directrix est rerum, et animalium, ac mixtorum; et egreditur universa per turmas, id est per partes et acies ordinate dispositas : quod est opus prudentiæ. Sapientis enim est ordinare.
paras.en: The third follows: [[30:27|The locust hath no king|Regem locusta non habet]], that is, the swarm or multitude of locusts has no ruler and director of its own species; yet the uncreated Art, and next the Intelligence [that is, the angelic mover of the heavens, in the philosophy of the schools], and universal nature too, rules and directs things, animals and mixed bodies; [[30:27|yet they all go out by their bands|et egreditur universa per turmas]], that is, in companies and battle lines set in order: which is a work of prudence. For it belongs to the wise man to set in order.

paras.t: Stellio manibus nititur, id est, obsequio pedum (quibus pro manibus utitur) procedit ac graditur; et moratur in ædibus, id est domibus, regis : præsertim in regionibus calidis; in aliis autem magis moratur in silvis. Et ita patet agilitas stellionis : qui est reptile conforme lacertæ, pictum in cute lucentibus guttis seu maculis, instar stellæ.
paras.en: [[30:28|The stellio supporteth itself on hands|Stellio manibus nititur]], that is, it goes forward and walks by the service of its feet (which it uses as hands); [[30:28|and dwelleth in kings' houses|et moratur in ædibus]], in the houses, that is, the dwellings, of the king, especially in hot countries; in others it dwells rather in the woods. And so the nimbleness of the stellio is plain: it is a creeping thing like a lizard, its skin painted with shining drops or spots, like a star [*stellio*, from *stella*, star].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per formicam significatur plebs humilis, de suis viribus non præsumens, ac Domino dicens : Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus. Quæ sollicita est ad cavendum periculum, ac provida ad necessaria obtinendum. Imo in isto parat exsilio, unde beatificetur in cœlesti palatio. Per lepusculum, exprimitur pusillus et imperfectus, qui in Christi vulneribus se abscondit, ne tentationum jaculis vulneretur, et ne per impatientiam succumbat in adversis : juxta illud Isaiæ, Ingredere in petram, abscondere in fossa humo. Hinc Sponsus loquitur Sponsæ in Canticis : Amica mea in foraminibus petræ, in caverna maceriæ. Per locustam, exprimitur quæcumque plebs timorata, præsertim anachoretæ, et qui præsidentem non habentes in terris, nihilo minus timore Dei confixi, ac supernæ sapientiæ unctione directi, ordinate incedunt, et decenter serviunt Deo. Postremo, nomine stellionis alii destituti, signantur idiotæ et simplices, in activæ operibus vitæ detenti, non valentes contemplando perfectionis attingere montem, et tamen per corporalia misericordiæ opera et obedientiam, in regno Christi quiescunt, et de necessariis ad salutem agiliter provident sibi. Itaque harum exemplis bestiolarum docemur, ut instar formicæ, providi simus; instar lepusculi, in turre fortitudinis commoremur; et instar locustæ, contra aciem vitiorum ac dæmonum ordinate progrediamur.
paras.en: Spiritually, by the ant is signified the humble people, who do not presume on their own strength, but say to the Lord: [[Ps 117:14|The Lord is my strength and my praise|Fortitudo mea et laus mea Dominus]]; who are careful to beware of danger and provident in obtaining what is needful. Indeed, in this exile they prepare that whereby they may be made blessed in the heavenly palace. By the little hare is expressed the little and imperfect one, who hides himself in the wounds of Christ, lest he be wounded by the darts of temptations, and lest he give way through impatience in adversities: according to that of Isaias, [[Is 2:10|Enter thou into the rock, and hide thee in the pit|Ingredere in petram, abscondere in fossa humo]]. Hence the Bridegroom speaks to the Bride in the Canticles: My love, [[Cant 2:14|in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow places of the wall|in foraminibus petræ, in caverna maceriæ]] [Denis has *Amica mea*, "my love", where the Vulgate has *columba mea*, "my dove"]. By the locust is expressed any God-fearing people, especially anchorites, and those who, having no superior on earth, are nonetheless pierced with the fear of God and, directed by the anointing of the wisdom from above, go forward in order and serve God fittingly. Lastly, by the name of the stellio are signified others, destitute ones [the print has *alii destituti*; perhaps for *alis destituti*, "lacking wings"]: the unlettered and simple, held fast in the works of the active life, who cannot by contemplation reach the mountain of perfection, and yet by bodily works of mercy and by obedience rest in the kingdom of Christ, and nimbly provide themselves with what is needful for salvation. So by the examples of these little beasts we are taught to be provident like the ant; like the little hare, to dwell in the tower of strength; and like the locust, to advance in good order against the battle line of vices and demons.

paras.t: Tria sunt animalia, quæ bene gradiuntur : quia in suo genere fortia sunt, et valenter incedunt; et quartum est quod incedit feliciter, id est potentius ac victoriosius tribus prætactis.
paras.en: There are three living things which go well, because they are strong in their kind and go forward mightily; and the fourth that walketh happily, that is, more mightily and more victoriously than the three already mentioned.

paras.t: De quorum primo subjungitur : Leo fortissimus bestiarum : quarum rex appellatur. Verumtamen inveniuntur bestiæ quædam fortiores leonibus, sed paucæ, et raro. Ad nullius pavebit occursum : imo vult ut animalia occurrentia sibi deferant ei. Gallus succinctus lumbos, id est, instar succincti quasi animose progrediens : hoc est secundum. De tertio subditur, et aries : qui ductor est ovium, et cornibus suis incedit armatus. Quartum est rex, nec est qui resistat ei. Unde in Hebræo fertur haberi : Et rex contra quem non levabit. Hoc est quartum, incedens feliciter. Per quod accipi potest animal rationale ad beatitudinem ordinatum : cui in exordio dictum est, ut præsit bestiis terræ, piscibus maris, omnique volatili cœli; quod et potestate sæculari et auctoritate spirituali ornatur.
paras.en: Of the first of them it is added: [[30:30|A lion, the strongest of beasts|Leo fortissimus bestiarum]], of which he is called the king. Yet some beasts are found stronger than lions, but few, and seldom. [[30:30|who hath no fear of any thing he meeteth|Ad nullius pavebit occursum]]: rather, he wants the animals that meet him to give way to him. [[30:31|A cock girded about the loins|Gallus succinctus lumbos]], that is, going forward boldly, like one girded: this is the second. Of the third it is added: [[30:31|and a ram|et aries]], who is the leader of the sheep and goes armed with his horns. The fourth is [[30:31|a king, whom none can resist|rex, nec est qui resistat ei]]. Hence the Hebrew is said to have: And a king, against whom none shall rise. This is the fourth, which walks happily. By it can be understood the rational animal, ordained to beatitude, to whom it was said in the beginning that he should rule over the beasts of the earth, the fishes of the sea and every fowl of the air[[Gen 1:28||]]; and who is adorned both with secular power and with spiritual authority.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per leonem accipitur regalis seu imperialis potestas, vel quicumque dono atque virtute fortitudinis decoratur; per arietem, spiritualis prælatus, ovium Christi pastor et ductor; per gallum lumbos succinctum, prædicator castus, exemplaris, magnanimus, animas credentes verbo et exemplo fecundans; per quartum, papalis auctoritas, universo orbi prælata, cui nemo licite valet resistere.
paras.en: Spiritually, by the lion is understood royal or imperial power, or anyone adorned with the gift and the virtue of fortitude; by the ram, a spiritual prelate, the shepherd and leader of Christ's sheep; by the cock girded about the loins, a preacher who is chaste, exemplary and great-hearted, making believing souls fruitful by word and example; by the fourth, the papal authority, set over the whole world, which no one may lawfully resist.

paras.t: Et qui stultus apparuerit, postquam elevatus est in sublime : id est, quum insipiens fuerit ad officium seu præsidentiam elevatus, tanto plus tunc ostendit imperitiam suam, quanto liberius operatur, et plura agere habet, in quibus multipliciter deficit.
paras.en: And there is one [[30:32|that hath appeared a fool after he was lifted up on high|qui stultus apparuerit, postquam elevatus est in sublime]]: that is, when a foolish man has been raised to an office or a post of command, he then shows his want of skill the more, the more freely he acts and the more things he has to do, in which he fails in many ways.

paras.t: Quidam tamen exponunt istud de quarto, quod incedit feliciter : per quod intelligunt Antichristum : quem dicunt feliciter incessurum, quia cuncta ei succedent ad libitum. Et textum præcedentem sic legunt : Et aries, nec est rex qui resistat ei, id est, nullus persecutor aut tyrannus intentionem et fructum prælatorum et prædicatorum virtuosorum ac continentium, poterit impedire.
paras.en: Some, however, expound this of the fourth, which walks happily, by which they understand Antichrist, who, they say, will walk happily, because everything will succeed for him as he pleases. And they read the preceding text thus: [[30:31|and a ram|Et aries]], and there is no king who can resist him; that is, no persecutor or tyrant will be able to hinder the aim and the fruit of virtuous and continent prelates and preachers.

paras.t: Si enim intellexisset, id est, si propriam stultitiam bene pensasset stultus ad prælationem promotus, ori imposuisset manum, id est, nequaquam pro sua promotione instituisset, vel aliis quoque imposuisset silentium, ne loquerentur de sua provectione.
paras.en: [[30:32|for if he had understood|Si enim intellexisset]], that is, if the fool promoted to prelacy had weighed his own folly well, [[30:32|he would have laid his hand upon his mouth|ori imposuisset manum]], that is, he would by no means have pressed for his own promotion [the print has *instituisset*, perhaps for *institisset*], or else he would also have imposed silence on others, so that they should not speak of his advancement.

paras.t: Præterea, per quatuor jam præfata, quidam intelligunt quatuor magna regna seu monarchias, intelligendo per leonem, regnum Chaldæorum, cujus primus monarcha (videlicet Nabuchodonosor) in Scripturis vocatur leo, juxta illud : Surrexit leo de cubili suo. Per gallum succinctum, intelligunt regnum Persarum, cujus reges (videlicet Cyrus et Darius) demoliti sunt regnum Chaldaicum, interficiendo Balthasar regem, destruentesque Babylonem. Per arietem, intelligunt Alexandrum, primum monarcham Græcorum. Per quartum autem accipiunt imperium Romanorum, quod instar ferri, cetera cuncta vastavit.
paras.en: Moreover, by the four already mentioned some understand the four great kingdoms or monarchies: by the lion, the kingdom of the Chaldeans, whose first monarch (namely Nabuchodonosor) is called a lion in the Scriptures, according to that text: [[Jer 4:7|The lion is come up out of his den|Surrexit leo de cubili suo]]. By the girded cock they understand the kingdom of the Persians, whose kings (namely Cyrus and Darius) overthrew the Chaldean kingdom, killing king Baltasar and destroying Babylon. By the ram they understand Alexander, the first monarch of the Greeks. And by the fourth they take the empire of the Romans, which like iron laid waste all the rest.

paras.t: Qui autem fortiter premit ubera ad eliciendum, id est extrahendum, lac, elicit butyrum, id est materiam solidiorem pinguioremque lacte, non extrahendam, sed magis in corpore animalis dimittendam, tanquam suæ bonæ habitudini opportunam. Et qui vehementer emungit, id est, nimis violenter purgat et ejicit immunditiam nasi, elicit sanguinem in corpore dimittendum, et ei convenientem. Per hæc edocetur, quod non debemus nimium importune ab alio aliquid postulare, nec eum qui bonæ est voluntatis, immoderantius molestare, vel nimis acriter increpare, ne exasperetur et totum neget quod petebatur, sicque viscera pietatis extrahantur ab eo, quæ nomine exprimuntur butyri, et vitam animæ (quæ est gratia Dei) amittat. Hinc Seneca loquitur : Nihil petas quod negaturus es, nihil neges quod petiturus es; itemque, Furor fit, patientia sæpius læsa; et denuo, Bonus animus læsus, gravius multo irascitur.
paras.en: [[30:33|And he that strongly squeezeth the paps|Qui autem fortiter premit ubera]] [[30:33|to bring out|ad eliciendum]], that is, to draw out, [[30:33|milk|lac]], [[30:33|straineth out butter|elicit butyrum]], that is, a matter more solid and richer than milk, which is not to be drawn out, but rather to be left in the animal's body as suited to its good condition. [[30:33|and he that violently bloweth his nose|Et qui vehementer emungit]], that is, cleanses and expels the uncleanness of the nose too violently, [[30:33|bringeth out blood|elicit sanguinem]], which ought to be left in the body and is fitting for it. By these things we are taught that we ought not to ask anything of another too importunately, nor trouble immoderately one who is of good will, or rebuke him too sharply, lest he be exasperated and refuse the whole of what was asked, and so the bowels of tenderness, which are expressed by the name of butter, be drawn out of him, and he lose the life of the soul (which is the grace of God). Hence Seneca says: Ask nothing that you would refuse; refuse nothing that you would ask; and again: Patience too often wounded turns to fury; and once more: A good mind, when wounded, is angered far more grievously.

paras.t: Spiritualiter ubera premere, est utriusque Testamenti Scripturas profunde pensare : ex quarum pensatione dum lac quæritur, invenitur butyrum, quia dum in Scripturis sensum mediocriter ac simpliciter juxta litteram reficientem requirimus, subtilem ac mysticum intellectum, pinguissime nos alentem, sensusque anagogicos reperimus. Attamen talis perscrutatio est moderanda, ne sanguis sequatur : quia dum divina eloquia immoderate discutiuntur, in carnalem et erroneum sensum mens labitur.
paras.en: Spiritually, to squeeze the paps is to weigh deeply the Scriptures of both Testaments: from the weighing of which, while milk is sought, butter is found; because while we seek in the Scriptures a sense that refreshes moderately and simply according to the letter, we find a subtle and mystical understanding that feeds us most richly, and anagogical senses. Yet such searching must be kept in measure, lest blood follow: because when the divine words are discussed without measure, the mind slips into a carnal and erroneous sense.

paras.t: Et qui provocat rixas, id est, alios injuriose et insipienter alloquitur, ita quod ad rixandum contra se vel contra alios excitantur, producit discordias inter se et illum, vel inter plures : quoniam ex rixa oriuntur simultates, dissensiones, iræ, invidiæ.
paras.en: [[30:33|and he that provoketh wrath|Et qui provocat rixas]] [Denis reads *rixas*, "quarrels"; the margin gives the variant *iras*, "wrath", the Vulgate's reading], that is, he who speaks to others insultingly and foolishly, so that they are stirred up to quarrel against him or against others, [[30:33|bringeth forth strife|producit discordias]] between himself and the other, or among many: since from quarrelling arise enmities, dissensions, angers and envies.
